#5823. Lack of wildfire reform is having ‘dire and escalating impacts’: SCE

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

“While we remain confident that California policymakers will ultimately take action, delay into 2027 will have significant and costly consequences,” said Edison International CEO Pedro Pizarro.

Wildfire liability reform is key to the financial health of Southern California Edison, ideally in the form of a long-term solution that “includes a clear and durable liquidity source for funding claims resolution, and a true shareholder liability cap that is not connected to the Wildfire Fund,” said Pedro Pizarro, president and CEO of Southern California Edison’s parent company Edison International, on a Thursday earnings call.

Pizarro voiced many of the same concerns — such as credit rating stability and potential impacts to customers — expressed by his fellow California utility CEO, PG&E Corp.’s Patti Poppe, during PG&E’s earnings call last week.

“We estimate that the currently elevated credit spreads could cost customers an incremental $300 million over the life of the bonds we expect SCE will issue in 2027 alone,” Edison International’s Chief Financial Officer Aaron Moss said during the call.

In September, the California Legislature opted not to advance Gov. Gavin Newsom’s proposal to amend a wildfire reform bill to limit the liability of utilities. The news that lawmakers rejected Newsom’s proposal caused Edison International’s stock to drop by 23%. The session ended without a final vote on the legislation, but Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas said work on the issue would continue.

Pizarro said that while Edison International is focused on items like the shareholder liability cap, “we recognize that other pieces may be needed to develop a package that gains support from stakeholders and ultimately the Senate, the Assembly, and the governor in time to send a bill to the governor by the constitutional deadline of November 15.”

“If we do not succeed in 2026, we must continue the effort with the new governor and legislature in 2027,” he added. “While we remain confident that California policymakers will ultimately take action, given the dire and escalating impacts on customers and the economy, delay into 2027 will have significant and costly consequences.”

SCE and Edison International are named in around 2,000 lawsuits from 38,000 plaintiffs concerning damages from the 2025 Eaton Fire, according to Edison International’s third quarter U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing. Those plaintiffs include individual plaintiffs as well as lawsuits by subrogation and public entity plaintiffs.

“As of September 30, 2026, SCE had recorded $1.8 billion in losses” related to Eaton Fire settlements, said the filing. “SCE had also recorded expected recoveries from customer-funded self-insurance of $917 million, from the Wildfire Fund of $859 million, and through FERC electric rates of $70 million related to the settlements.”

Despite wildfire headwinds, Edison International had a “strong” year-to-date performance and has a strong outlook for the remainder of the year, said Moss.

On paper, the company’s third-quarter core earnings declined year-over-year from $901 million to $738 million, but 2025’s third-quarter core earnings “reflect a 55-cent true-up resulting from the receipt of SCE's general rate case final decision,” Moss said. “Looking through that item, the quarter reflected continued stability in our core operations.”

When examined year to date, Edison International’s core earnings for 2026 are $1.88 billion compared to 2025’s $1.8 billion.

According to the company’s presentation slides, “SCE forecasts investing $38–41 billion from 2026 to 2030 to support SCE’s wildfire mitigation strategy and clean energy transformation in California.”

Edison International’s 2026–2030 capital plan devotes 22% each to load growth/electrification and infrastructure replacement, 14% to maintenance and inspections, and 12% to wildfire management.

In response to an analyst question about the potential for Edison International to reduce its investment if durable wildfire reform is not realized, Moss said the company would “prioritize spending in safety, reliability, and compliance-related areas. And that just means, by definition, we'd have less for load growth and clean energy policy.”

#5822. Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the issue by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

HYDAC’s new “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

Field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

Field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later showed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another important advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” said Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”

More recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

For wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

As the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” said HYDAC’s Erickson.

For wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

As fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Now is the time to evaluate whether existing cooling systems are supporting — or limiting — long-term turbine reliability goals.

“HYDAC’s goal is to help wind owners and service providers solve practical operational challenges in ways that create long-term value across the entire asset lifecycle. Innovations like the Square Wave heat exchanger are designed to improve reliability, simplify maintenance, and support greater energy production over time.”

Don’t let cooling system limitations impact turbine performance.

Proactive cooling optimization can help operators reduce maintenance exposure, protect critical drivetrain components, and maximize energy production across the asset lifecycle. #5821. Toyota & Waymo Advance Autonomous Driving Collaboration for Safer Streets and Freedom of Movement for All

Toyota Motor Corporation (“Toyota”) and Waymo today announced the next phase of their autonomous driving collaboration, in pursuit of a world with safer streets and freedom of movement for all.

Building on the preliminary agreement announced in April 2025, Toyota and Waymo will begin initial operations to test and validate an autonomous Toyota bZ4X fleet in Japan in 2027, with deployment to the United Kingdom and other Waymo-serviced markets planned for the following years. This partnership marks a major milestone in the expansion of Japan’s first fully autonomous ride-hailing service using high-volume, domestically manufactured vehicles.

Toyota will build the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan. The entire process will take place under one roof, from assembling the base vehicle to integrating Waymo’s AV hardware.

By pairing Toyota’s global manufacturing and vehicle development expertise with Waymo’s fully autonomous technology, the companies will accelerate scaling safety-validated Level 4 autonomous vehicles globally — helping provide people with transit that reduces human-error accidents, and opening up freedom of movement for those who can’t easily get around.

Beyond safety, the custom-outfitted bZ4X is designed for comfort and greater accessibility. Generous rear legroom and features such as automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting will provide seamless entry and exit for riders.

Toyota and Waymo will continue to explore the future of autonomous driving technology for personally owned Toyota vehicles. Alongside Woven by Toyota, they will also explore additional initiatives that support their shared goal of fewer road safety incidents, including how insights from Waymo’s real-world operations, data-driven intelligence, and technology could holistically improve safety for other road users.

“Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo, and we’re proud to work together toward safer roads for all,” said Dmitri Dolgov, co-CEO of Waymo. “In areas where Waymo operates, we’ve demonstrated that we are up to 20x safer than human drivers when it comes to serious crash injuries, and our partnership with Toyota will help us bring the safety and convenience of autonomous driving to more people around the world, including key international markets like Japan. We chose Toyota because of our respect for the legendary safety, reliability, and quality of their vehicles, and we look forward to deepening our collaboration as we scale our fully autonomous Waymo Driver technology globally.”

“We are deeply grateful that Waymo, which helped pioneer fully autonomous driving technology, has chosen Toyota as its partner,” said Hiroki Nakajima, member of the board of directors and executive vice president of Toyota. “Safety technology makes the biggest difference when it reaches as many people as possible. This collaboration will help scale that technology and bring it to customers in Japan and beyond through Waymo’s ride-hailing service, and in parallel, Toyota will continue to explore how integrating vehicles with traffic infrastructure can make those roads safer still. No single company can achieve the goal of zero traffic accidents alone, but with partners like Waymo, we will get there one step at a time.”

#5820. Donated solar project powers community center in unincorporated New Mexico village  Solar Power World’s Projects of Impact

A building that started as a one-room schoolhouse has through the decades expanded to become a lifeline for a New Mexico community far from any city infrastructure, and a recent solar installation has brought new resilience to this place.

Children run outside of Ojo Sarco, New Mexico’s one-room schoolhouse in a photo from January 1943. The structure still stands today as the Ojo Sarco Community Center. Credit: John Collier, Jr./Library of Congress

The structure housing the Ojo Sarco Community Center (OSCC) was founded in the early 20th century. Ojo Sarco is an unincorporated community home to about 300 people that is located about 43 miles northeast from Santa Fe.

“We have no political voice, really,” said Carol Miller, a grant writer and board member for the Ojo Sarco Community Center. “We’re pretty neglected. We’ve lost resources in the past. We were the first wave of people to lose our post office many years ago. Everybody has to commute pretty much for everything.”

That commute is about 40 minutes round trip for basic amenities, she said.

The community center has tried to fill in those resource gaps with services like a twice-monthly food bank, summer meal programs for kids, safety classes and outings for its residents, such as a night at the opera. The OSCC also recently met all the qualifications to be a state library.

PPC Solar, also known as Paradise Power Company, from Taos, built a 7.5-kW solar project paired with 10.6-kWh of LFP energy storage at the OSCC. The contractor built the array at no-cost to the community center. Every year PPC donates a solar array to a regional nonprofit organization, and after three years of applying, the OSCC was awarded the project.

CEO Daniel Weinman’s father founded Paradise Power Company in the 1970s, and the company has installed solar in off-the-grid communities since the start. Its PV donation program is built out of that tradition.

“We’ve always wanted to find a way to give back to the community,” Weinman said. “The best thing that we found — and we’ve been doing it for over a decade now — is doing an annual nonprofit donation system … We’ve had farming organizations, land conservation organizations, and it goes on and on. Really, it’s about finding the right fit. We wanted to make a good impact for this community center, and we felt resiliency was the best way to do that.”

Solar Power World spoke to both PPC Solar and organizers with the OSCC about what effect this solar project has had in the village since it was built in fall 2025.

Larry Miller, project manager and OSCC board member: I think it’s a transformative project for our small community. We like to talk about the history of the community center, and now this is part of it. If someone doesn’t notice the solar panels on the roof, we point it out to them. It’s integrated into our lives here.

Carol Miller: It’s lowered our electric costs, which is really important for us, because we’re such a shoe-string operation. We’ve had some fun talks with the community because they all know we’ll have the charging capacity. We still have internet available, even with the power out. All the kids that come to our library programs, they’re solar oriented. The benefit of this company and its staff just has ripple effects throughout our greater community.

PPC Solar donated a solar plus storage project to the Ojo Sarco Community Center. This array will keep power running in this facility that has become a haven for Ojo Sarco residents. Credit: PPC Solar

Preston Bastardo, sales and design, PPC Solar: The building itself had some challenges with mounting the array on the roof, but that just took some exploration in the attic and making sure that we could land things where we needed to. The building has two large areas, and so fo installation of batteries had some restrictions, there was a good mechanical closet that we were able to use for batteries. Then as far as backup circuits, we did a partial facility backup where we had a critical loads panel next to their main panel. I think everything went pretty smoothly.

Weinman: Well, it really goes back to our roots. In 1972, there was no technology supporting solar at the time. My dad was a pioneer in the industry and he really developed his own controls and safety protections and found used panels and used batteries and was bringing power to places where there was no power. Our house, for example, we started with kerosene lanterns. We didn’t have electricity until we had a solar power system, and it was really life changing.

Being able to build on that legacy and look at our community in that light and be able to offer systems like this to communities that need it — I think that really adds to that legacy and really is profound in a lot of ways. It feels great to be able to do this and be in a position where we can help others realize and experience the benefits of solar power. We want to continue to participate in any way we can.

Carol Miller: We’re a very old community and proud of it. And having worked with local businesses and our electrical co-op, we know it’s really the exception and not the rule because we own our power. Any technology that is shared equally in a low-income community has ripple effects beyond what I think some of us imagined a number of years ago. It’s for everyone.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5819. Hitachi’s nuclear revenue rises as SMR delivery date approaches

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The bulk of the Japanese conglomerate’s Energy segment business is in electrical grid equipment. Sales are strong, but inflation and long delivery timelines bear watching, company executives said.

Power grid equipment continued to make up the vast majority of Hitachi, Ltd.’s Energy segment revenues in the most recent quarter, but its nuclear division saw a 48% year-over-year increase as the company prepares to deliver the first of four small modular reactors to Ontario Power Generation in 2030.

The 300-MW BWRX-300 small modular reactors are being developed in partnership with GE Vernova.

In the United States, the Tennessee Valley Authority has tapped the joint venture to build at least one BWRX-300 in its territory, with delivery set for 2032.

“With the start of the construction of the first [SMR] in Canada as a foothold, we will advance the deployment of the SMR business in North America, Poland and other parts of Europe,” Hitachi said in its 2025 annual report.

However, it also spoke generally about the potential risks the company faces as it takes on ambitious projects around the world, without mentioning its nuclear investment specifically.

“High-risk projects, such as long-term projects or projects involving new technologies … may result in significant changes to the assumptions underlying the estimates related to those contracts … or their termination,” the company said.

The Japanese conglomerate’s Energy segment is divided into Nuclear Energy and Power Grids, which manufactures and markets high-voltage components, power conversion products, energy storage systems and other electrical equipment for commercial, industrial and utility customers.

Its Power Grid division saw revenues of ¥893.7 billion, or about $5.7 billion, in the most recent quarter — a 27% increase over the same period last year, the company said this week. Nuclear Energy took in ¥65.3 billion, or about $415 million, over the same period.

In total, Hitachi’s Energy segment saw a 28% increase in revenue and a nearly 50% increase in orders, the company said. Significant drivers included large-scale power infrastructure projects and demand from data center customers, with “notable strength” in North America.

Tomomi Kato, Hitachi’s chief financial officer, told investors and stock analysts on Wednesday that the company has seen broad-based order growth thanks to the data center boom. Those orders will be reflected in company revenues beginning next year, he said.

The Energy segment reported second-quarter orders of ¥1,566.2 billion, or nearly $10 billion, with particular strength from transmission and data center customers.

Speaking in Japanese, Tomomi said the conglomerate has seen no signs of a pullback in AI-related investment.

“So far, we are not seeing any delays or any payment issues,” he said through a translator.

Some of the company’s other segments are also increasing their focus on the energy sector.

Anand Birje, CEO of Hitachi’s newly consolidated, California-based digital services business, said the conglomerate was using its proprietary technology platform to improve performance and productivity for its energy customers.

The company says HMAX Energy, its energy-oriented digital solution, can help its customers reduce revenue loss from equipment downtime by up to 60%.

“There’s massive transformation happening [in] everything from transmission to distribution to pricing to load management using data, cloud and AI, along with our ecosystem partners,” Birje said in English.

One of those partners is chipmaking giant NVIDIA. Last October, Hitachi said it would provide “grid-to-rack architecture” to the 800-volt data center architecture NVIDIA and its customers expect to become the industry standard for high-performance computing facilities.

With its order backlog swelling thanks to AI and general electrification demand, Tomomi said Hitachi was doing its best to meet delivery timelines — and manage cost pressures in an inflationary environment.

On long-lead contracts, “we use indexing” to ensure Hitachi can pass along cost increases during production and fulfillment, he said.

“Otherwise, we cannot accept a long-term contract …. I think we are doing a good job managing the process,” Tomomi said.

#5818. Rethinking the outage map for a multi-hazard world

For many, fall means sweater weather and all things pumpkin spice. For utilities, these months have other, less festive sides. Hurricane season, wildfire season and the start of the heating season all converge in the same 8-12-week window.

Hurricane season may be quieter this year, thanks to El Niño, but data shows climate change has intensified Atlantic hurricanes. Meanwhile, fall is peak wildfire season, particularly in California, when Santa Ana winds kick up. And the northern half of the country is switching furnaces back on after months of inactivity. Individually, these are known risks utilities plan for. Layered together, they're a bigger threat.

Because of this, utilities are starting to ask more of their outage maps, moving beyond "when will my power be back on?" to "what's happening around me?" Maps are becoming less of a status tracker and more of a situational awareness tool.

For decades, utility outage maps told customers when their power would be back on, along with repair status and outage cause. That’s still valuable, but outages aren’t the only thing causing sleepless nights. Hazards now stack and planned maintenance often lands in the same week and region as storms, wildfires and seasonal gas-related risk.

Historically, customers pieced this information together from disconnected sources like text alerts, county web pages, weather apps and wildfire trackers. Now, hazard layers bring it together in one place, drawing on GIS, OMS and weather feeds.

This shift isn’t just about the growing frequency and overlap of hazards. It also reflects rising customer expectations for self-service, with the map as their first stop before the call center.

During a crisis, utility customers want access to whichever channel responds fastest and most clearly. If the utility’s map can’t deliver, their next stop is usually the already strained call center.

Utilities say they want the same thing. Chartwell's 2024 benchmark survey found that 77% named reducing call center and crew impacts as a strategic objective and 93% named satisfying customers as a strategic objective. The stakes are real. Annual call center cost is $20-40 million for a typical two-million-customer utility fielding two to three million calls a year.

What does this look like in practice? During a major winter storm, Rappahannock Electric Cooperative added richer hazard context to its outage map, adding outage polygons to outline affected areas and damage photos to explain long restoration times. The result: 500,000+ views in two days and an average session time of approximately 12 minutes, well above the global benchmark of 2.5 minutes. This shows customers used the map as a primary source, not a quick check-in.

It wasn’t an outlier. During a major multi-state storm, outage maps across affected utilities drew 9.78 million views in three days. Mobile traffic climbed from 75% to 86%, as customers checked and rechecked maps from their phones. Every customer who self-serves on the map is one less person tying up phone lines.

Visibility upgrades only matter if everyone can benefit. Language, disability and access barriers mean some customers still get left behind in a crisis. Addressing these challenges means making map information clear and in actionable language across all channels.

Text, email and voice reach different populations in different ways. During Hurricane Idalia, opt-in data to alerts showed just that: text and email led at 45.3% and 40.3%, respectively, with voice trailing at 14.4%, underscoring the value of offering multiple channels, delivered in language customers can actually act on.

Channel reach is only half the equation; plain language is the other. Most utilities are still catching up. Very few have fully simplified their messaging or removed jargon. The message needs to be clear to work.

Uptime and map refresh rates still matter, but next-gen outage maps will be judged on more than restoration times. As storms, wildfires and gas risks pile up alongside planned maintenance, utilities need to keep every customer informed, not just report on uptime. That means investing in multiple communication channels. As the Idalia data shows, each channel reaches a different slice of the customer base and no single channel is enough alone.

Treating hazard visibility, communication equity and channel diversity as one problem, not three, is what builds trust.

#5817. Hyundai IONIQ 3 Named European Car of the Year 2027 Finalist

SEOUL/OFFENBACH — Hyundai Motor’s all-electric IONIQ 3 has been named one of seven finalists for the European Car of the Year 2027 award. Selected by an independent jury of automotive journalists from across Europe, the nomination places IONIQ 3 among the contenders for one of Europe’s most established automotive awards. The winner will be announced on 8 January 2027 at the Brussels Motor Show.

Designed in Europe and produced at Hyundai Motor Türkiye’s İzmit plant, IONIQ 3 has been developed specifically for European customers. The fully electric compact hatchback combines Hyundai’s distinctive ‘Art of Steel’ design language, a spacious interior and intuitive technology with a driving range of up to 497 km (WLTP) in the Long Range version. With a starting price below €30,000 across European markets, IONIQ 3 aims to make electric mobility accessible to a broader range of customers.

“Being named a finalist for European Car of the Year is important recognition for IONIQ 3 and for the work that has gone into its development. We set out to create an electric car designed around the needs of European customers, combining distinctive design with class-leading aerodynamics, strong driving range and exceptional interior space, together with advanced technology at an accessible price. The response from customers has been very encouraging, with orders already exceeding our initial expectations. This nomination reflects the strength of that overall package and our ambition to make electric mobility both desirable and practical for more people.” —Christopher McKinnon, Vice President, Head of Product and Product Director Office for Europe at Hyundai Motor Europe.

IONIQ 3 combines several class-leading features that address key requirements of European customers. Its aerodynamic design contributes to driving efficiency, while its spacious interior offers the practicality of a larger vehicle despite its compact exterior dimensions. Intuitive technology supports everyday usability, and accessible pricing makes electric mobility available to a broader range of customers.

The European Car of the Year award is an independent automotive competition established in 1964. Its international jury consists of 65 automotive journalists from across Europe, who evaluate eligible new vehicles based on criteria including design, innovation, performance, value for money and market positioning.

Seven finalists are selected from the initial list of candidates. Following further evaluation and voting, the overall winner of the 2027 award will be announced on 8 January 2027 at the Brussels Motor Show.

#5816. The industry races into Las Vegas for RE+

The largest tradeshow focused on the U.S. solar, storage and clean energy markets is back in Las Vegas for 2026. RE+ was the 24th largest tradeshow in the United States in 2025 by attendance, and this year’s showing (Nov. 16-19) is expected to be just as large.

The Formula 1 series will race the Las Vegas Grand Prix the weekend after RE+ concludes. Photos courtesy: F1 and the Las Vegas Grand Prix

The U.S. solar and storage industries have gotten so big that it appears only the Las Vegas Convention Center can accommodate a tradeshow bringing together nearly 40,000 clean energy professionals in one place. RE+ will be held at the Las Vegas Convention Center each November for the foreseeable future.

The convention center is tucked away from the main strip of casinos, but there is still plenty in the area to see and do. The site is also easily accessible, with a stop on the Las Vegas Monorail.

Conference education programming begins on Monday and sessions continue throughout the show at various stages on the exhibit hall floor. The exhibition opens on Tuesday.

Exhibitors will be spread across three halls in the convention center — the main entrance is at West Hall which extends via an over-street walkway to North Hall, and then Central Hall is accessed beyond a lobby area. There will also be a few outdoor booths to peruse located near food trucks. #5815. Utilities need to become project developers. Are they ready?

Load growth is no longer an abstract number in an electricity market report or forecast; it’s a reality. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), U.S. electricity load will increase nearly 2 percent in 2026 and 2.5 percent next year, driven by large loads like data centers and manufacturing as well as increased electrification of transportation and building heating and cooling. To put that number in perspective, annual load growth between 2005 and 2019 was about 0.1 percent, meaning the next two years will see nearly 50 times the growth that the industry experienced in the last 15 years.

Rapid load growth changes nearly everything for utilities, from how they plan and invest to how they engage and communicate with customers. Load growth is also compelling many utilities to do something they haven't done at this scale and pace before: develop their own generation. “Utilities are used to designing and building a gas plant once every five or 10 years, and then they would contract via PPAs (power purchase agreement) everything else,” said Alex Pope, Manager of Power Development Portfolios 1898 & Co. “But the systems utilities have in place to self-develop generation projects were never built to handle the volume necessary to meet the demand and timelines of today’s customer needs.”

As PPAs and BTAs (Build-Transfer Agreement) alone become insufficient to close the generation and load gap, many utilities that recognize the need to build more projects themselves face an important question: how do we start? One avenue is to focus inward and develop the internal expertise and resources needed to move projects from concept to commercialization—everything from land acquisition and permitting to financing, regulatory approvals, procurement strategies, and construction.

While this approach gives utilities complete control over the development of new generation, it also has meaningful challenges. One significant hurdle is the need to either augment the teams responsible for each phase of a successful new project or completely build from scratch. “You may have to quadruple your internal team of environmental specialists because you need to be pushing multiple projects forward,” Pope said. “The challenge is that everyone is trying to hire for these project-related roles and competition is stiff.”

Beyond adding personnel, what utilities also find is that the underlying internal processes and coordination needed to efficiently develop a large pipeline of generation projects simply don’t exist. Creating that necessary foundation involves hard choices about responsibilities and collaboration that inevitably take time that utilities don’t have if they are to meet this historic moment of load growth.

There’s another option, one that leverages existing utility expertise without requiring a vast expansion of staff. That option is to bring in a partner like 1898 & Co. to work alongside utility staff, increase their impact across projects, provide industry lessons and best practices from other utility peers, and act as the connective tissue between departments that need to collaborate for generation projects to move forward efficiently.

The rationale for the partnership is simple: utilities already have exceptionally capable people to handle environmental review, land rights, interconnection, regulatory approvals, and other aspects of project development. What utilities often lack, however, is a foundational infrastructure to ensure their internal teams work together rather than at cross-purposes across a large portfolio of projects in simultaneous development. This is necessary when utilities are trying to expand their self-development capacity from one or two projects per decade to a large and growing portfolio. “Their groups are industry best at what they do,” said Pope, who works directly with major utilities across the country to bolster the utility’s self-development capabilities. “But what they did was suited for one thermal project every five years. It was never set up to handle the throughput of what they’re being asked to do right now.”

1898 & Co.’s partnership approach is intentionally flexible, designed to supplement a utility’s existing self-development capacity and expand it to align with its goals and strategies. For example, Pope says some utilities start with development transfers, in which a third-party developer brings a shovel-ready project, and the utility completes due diligence before moving forward. This offers a lower-risk way to better understand the demands of self-development before attempting a larger portfolio of self-originated projects.

Other utilities have embraced full self-development, choosing to outsource only the capital-intensive step of land acquisition while keeping the rest of project management in-house. Utilities like Xcel Energy and DTE Energy, with support from 1898 & Co, leverage a blend development-transfer, self-development, PPA, and BTA structures to avoid putting all their eggs in one basket. No matter what model a utility chooses, Pope says 1898 & Co. provides a “single source of truth” across a portfolio of projects. This is possible because 1898 & Co. screens potential sites, manages due diligence, helps steer overall strategy, tracks deliverables, and coordinates across environmental, permitting, interconnection, and land rights teams. That combination of coordination and analysis ensures that a utility’s internal specialists, consulting partners, and selected EPC firms can all work together as one cohesive self-development team.

The financial rationale for pursuing a partnership that enhances a utility’s self-development is also compelling. 1898 & Co.’s services not only help investor-owned utilities keep up with the demands of their customers but also create strong shareholder value in the process.

Ultimately, though, what matters is whether a partnership approach allows utilities to function as high-volume generation project developers. In a recent all-source request for proposals (ASRFP), 1898 & Co. supported over 60 gigawatts of generation projects for its utility clients. Of those, 22 gigawatts were then bid in competitive RFPs. The result: 10 gigawatts won.

#5814. Can Silicon Valley Build A Safe Class 8 Truck? Early EV Semi Fires Expose The Experience Gap

If you drove through the East Bay area of California on Tuesday night, you probably got caught in a nightmare. A Tesla Semi traveling down Interstate 880 in Hayward caught fire during the evening commute. There was no crash, no multi-vehicle pileup, and no obvious collision. The driver noticed something was wrong, pulled over near Highway 92, and got out unharmed.

Then the lithium-ion pack did what high-energy battery chemistry does when it gets pushed past its thermal limits… By the time crews finished foaming down the wreckage, all that remained of the tractor was its rear axles and a pile of ash.

The California Highway Patrol shut down both directions of the freeway out of concern over toxic chemical smoke. Northbound lanes eventually opened back up, but southbound lanes stayed closed for nearly ten hours while fire crews managed the blaze and let the pack burn itself out. When the sun came up, all that remained of the tractor was its rear axles and a pile of ash.

This is the second time in just over two years that a single Tesla Semi has shut down a major California highway for half a day. Back in August 2024, a Tesla-operated Semi drifted off Interstate 80 near Emigrant Gap, hit a tree, and caught fire. It took 50,000 gallons of water, air drops from Cal Fire, and a 15-hour closure to clear the road.

Whenever this happens, the anti-EV crowd immediately pounces and claims electric trucks are rolling time bombs. That’s a lie, as we’ve repeatedly explained here, but the knee-jerk reaction from tech enthusiasts, which claims this is just normal trucking business, is equally disconnected from reality.

Something deeper is going on here, and it highlights an important cultural divide between Silicon Valley and the century-old world of heavy-duty commercial trucking. Instead of trashing people and pointing fingers, let’s look at a deeper lesson the industry can learn from this.

First, let’s look at the numbers before anyone starts cherry-picking data.

According to the National Fire Protection Association, US fire departments respond to roughly 15,000 large truck fires every single year. That is about 40 diesel rigs catching fire every day across the country. Blown turbochargers spray oil on hot exhaust manifolds, wheel-end bearings seize at 70 mph, and dragging drum brakes ignite recap tires. Diesel trucks burn all the time, so fire is not a phenomenon unique to electric trucks.

The difference is how they burn. When a diesel tractor catches fire, the local volunteer fire department can usually knock it down with an engine tank and some foam in 45 minutes. A heavy tow truck drags the scorched chassis off the road, sweepers clear the debris, and traffic starts moving again before the morning rush hour is ruined.

When an 800-plus kilowatt-hour commercial battery pack enters thermal runaway, the playbook goes out the window. The cells generate their own oxygen as they break down, turning the battery into a self-sustaining furnace. First responders cannot just drown it and walk away. Their only choice is to pump tens of thousands of gallons of water on it for hours or stand back in defensive mode to keep it from spreading while half a county gets gridlocked. At best, all they can do is hopefully cool it down enough to get it off the road before it might catch fire again.

Then there is the sample size problem. There are roughly 4 million Class 8 commercial diesel trucks on American roads. By contrast, the active Tesla Semi fleet is estimated somewhere between 150 and a few hundred early-production and pilot tractors.

Mathematically speaking, you cannot calculate a clean failure rate on an N of two. A single flat tire that catches fire and spreads to a battery pack can swing the statistical safety record of a 100-truck pilot fleet by 50%. But you also cannot ignore it when two trucks in a tiny pilot fleet cause catastrophic, 10-to-15-hour interstate shutdowns.

So, instead of being lazy and relying on just the numbers, we need to look for more context.

This is not uniquely a Tesla problem. It is an electric startup problem.

Remember Nikola? In the summer of 2023, several of their Tre battery-electric trucks caught fire, including one at their Phoenix headquarters and another in customer testing. Nikola initially hinted at foul play, but third-party investigators quickly found the real culprit: a coolant leak inside the battery packs supplied by Romeo Power had caused an internal electrical short. Nikola had to issue a voluntary recall on all 209 trucks they had built, halting sales and dragging every pack back to the shop to fix the design.

Startups approach trucking like consumer electronics. They design from a clean sheet, prioritize maximum aerodynamic efficiency, integrate components into custom monolithic structures, and move fast.

But, when you take the “move fast and break things” approach, the stakes are a lot higher in the trucking world.

Class 8 trucking is a brutal environment that eats clever ideas for breakfast. A big rig does not live the gentle life of a passenger car in sunny California. It flexes under 80,000 pounds of gross weight, takes violent torsional twisting over uneven loading docks, endures constant low-frequency road battering, and rattles across millions of frost heaves.

If there is a slightly loose coolant quick-connect, an undersized wire harness, or a busbar that flexes half a millimeter under torsional load, commercial duty cycles are like Liam Neeson in Taken. If you’re a problem of any kind, the duty cycle will find you, and it will kill you.

This brings us to the traditional truck builders. Why aren’t we seeing Freightliner eCascadias or Volvo VNR Electrics burning down to the rims on I-80? They’re electric, too, right?

It’s not because traditional truckmakers possess magical, fireproof battery chemistry. They buy lithium-ion cells from the same tier-one suppliers as everyone else. In fact, if you dig into public regulatory filings, other manufacturers have run into the exact same terrifying failure modes that bit Nikola.

In 2023, Volvo and Mack filed safety recall reports with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) covering hundreds of electric trucks. What was the defect? Their battery supplier had two separate manufacturing errors: coolant lines that were not fully locked into place, creating the risk of conductive fluid leaking across cells, and over-torqued internal fasteners that could snap off and rattle around inside the pack as loose metallic debris. Both defects created direct short-circuit and fire risks.

Why didn’t you read about those trucks burning down on the highway? Because the so-called legacy manufacturers have spent a century building institutional safety systems.

They caught this problem when a small fire actually broke out in a battery pack in the factory. The fire stayed contained within the pack, but Volvo didn’t try to hide it or explain it away. Instead, they did what the old school companies do, even if it slowed them down. Within a week, there was a stop-ship order on the packs and trucks already on the road were called in for a swap.

Traditional truckmakers move at a glacial pace compared to Silicon Valley, and tech fans love to criticize them for it. But, that slow pace comes from decades of scar tissue earned in battle. When an old school builder sees an internal assembly error or gets a strange sensor reading in fleet monitoring, their reflex is not to push an over-the-air firmware patch and hope for the best. They trigger stop-ship orders, use their huge dealer networks to ground the fleet, file Part 573 defect notices with the feds, and tear the battery packs open in a service bay.

Their systems caught the defect in the shop before it had the chance to catch fire on the freeway.

There is also an important philosophical divide in how these trucks are packaged.

Tesla chose the moonshot approach. To hit a 500-mile range target while hauling full freight, they needed maximum energy density and minimal tare weight. That led them to build a massive, integrated, structural battery pack that sits low between the frame rails. It is an engineering marvel in packaging efficiency, but it is also a monolithic block of energy. If one section suffers an internal failure, the entire pack is at risk.

Traditional builders like Volvo and Freightliner (Daimler Truck) took a far more conservative, regional-haul route. Instead of packing nearly a megawatt-hour of energy into a single tightly integrated structural assembly under the cab, they use smaller, lower-capacity modular packs—with Volvo literally hanging separate battery enclosures off the outside of the frame rails where diesel saddle tanks normally sit.

Hanging heavy battery boxes on the side of the chassis is terrible for maximum range and adds unnecessary weight, and may leave them more vulnerable to collisions. But, from a safety and service standpoint, it is brilliant. The packs are physically isolated from each other. If one module suffers a mechanical puncture, a coolant leak, or a thermal event, the damage is far easier to contain, inspect, and unbolt.

Silicon Valley brought the heavy trucking industry kicking and screaming into the electric era. Without Tesla pushing the envelope on megawatt charging and long-range electric haulers, diesel truckmakers would still be dragging their feet with compliance pilot programs, if even that.

Building an electric truck that can pull 82,000 pounds is not just a software problem, and it’s not just a battery chemistry problem. It is a mechanical durability problem that has to survive millions of miles of rough roads, rough drivers, and unpredictable operating conditions.

Experienced truck builders know how to build a chassis that survives that abuse, but they were slow to embrace the battery. Silicon Valley knows how to build the battery, but they are still learning how punishing the road really is.

Until those two worlds finally learn from each other, fire crews are going to keep having very long nights on the interstate. Hopefully more cross-pollination and experience eventually lead to improvements for all sides of the industry.

Jennifer Sensiba is a long time efficient vehicle enthusiast, writer, and photographer. She grew up around a transmission shop, and has been experimenting with vehicle efficiency since she was 16 and drove a Pontiac Fiero.

#5813. Antwerp’s Electric Cranes Can Handle More Than Today’s Cargo

Katoen Natie has put two all-electric mobile harbour cranes into service at the Port of Antwerp, with four more joining them across three deep-sea multipurpose terminals. The completed fleet will include four 200-tonne cranes and two 150-tonne machines, with paired lifting capacity reaching 400 tonnes. Katoen Natie expects the six cranes to displace as much as 500,000 litres of diesel annually once they’re operating.

The October commissioning announcement is worth attention because these are heavy, mobile machines working in a commercial port. They aren’t small demonstrations, and the engineering addresses the conditions that historically made mobile harbour cranes difficult to electrify.

Fixed container cranes were straightforward candidates for electrification. They stay in one location, have repetitive operating patterns and can be connected to substantial electrical supplies. Mobile harbour cranes travel along the quay, move between assignments and handle cargo that can vary considerably from one vessel to the next. An onboard diesel generator provided that mobility without requiring the terminal to build electrical connections everywhere the crane might work.

Konecranes’ solution separates the energy needed for lifting from the energy needed for travel. External grid electricity supplies the heavy working loads, while rechargeable batteries allow the cranes to move between operating positions. This avoids carrying an enormous battery for work that can be powered directly from the grid. It also eliminates diesel exhaust at the equipment and reduces local noise.

The bigger advantage is that the investment isn’t tied to one type of cargo. A mobile harbour crane can handle steel, industrial equipment, large transformers, wind components, scrap, project cargo, conventional bulk and containers. Port operators can change their handling arrangements as customers and cargo flows change without replacing the basic lifting machinery.

That matters as the energy transition changes maritime trade. In an earlier CleanTechnica analysis, I examined how ports face rising capital requirements even as fossil-fuel cargoes begin their long-term decline. Coal, oil and gas have supported major investments in berths, terminals, channels and inland connections. Their declining role creates commercial risks for infrastructure designed around individual commodities.

Ports are looking for new business in containers, renewable-energy equipment, industrial products and alternative fuels. Some will succeed, but they cannot all capture the same growth in container traffic, and low-carbon molecules will not replace fossil-fuel cargo tonne for tonne. Equipment investments have to make sense under more than one plausible freight forecast.

Electric mobile cranes are well suited to that uncertainty. A machine capable of lifting a transformer today can handle scrap steel or construction machinery tomorrow. Its electrical supply can also be part of a wider investment supporting yard equipment, trucks, shore power and harbour craft.

That doesn’t make every new crane or grid connection worthwhile. A terminal still needs sufficient durable activity, suitable electrical infrastructure and a sound operating case. But investing in flexible electric equipment is less dependent on predicting which replacement cargo wins than building another dedicated fossil-fuel or specialized alternative-fuel facility.

Katoen Natie’s investment demonstrates how ports can reduce diesel consumption today while retaining more options for the freight they handle tomorrow.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing article connects Antwerp’s electric mobile harbour cranes with the larger challenge of investing in ports as fossil bulk declines, new industrial cargoes emerge and electrical infrastructure serves more of the waterfront.

#5812. How To Tell Your Car's Oil Pump Is Going Bad

A car's oil pump plays a critical role in keeping the engine running smoothly. The pump circulates pressurized engine oil through the vehicle's lubrication system, sustaining critical components such as the crankshaft, camshaft, bearings, and valve train. The oil reduces friction between moving parts, limits wear, and helps carry a significant amount of heat away from the components it lubricates. If the pump fails to maintain adequate oil pressure, the engine can suffer severe damage, potentially requiring an expensive repair or even replacement.

Oil pumps are designed to last for years, and many can operate for over 100,000 miles with proper maintenance. That said, wear and tear, contaminated oil, sludge accumulation, and prolonged maintenance can affect an oil pump's performance.

Recognizing the warning signs of a failing oil pump early can naturally help prevent a major issue. Low oil pressure, unusual noises, and increased engine temperatures are among the most important symptoms to look out for when it comes to oil pumps. While these signs do not automatically mean a pump is failing, they warrant a prompt investigation.

Possibly the clearest warning sign of an oil pump going bad is seeing an illuminated oil pressure light on your instrument cluster. This alert indicates that there may not be enough force pushing oil through your engine's components.

Unusual engine noises are another symptom of a failing oil pump. When the pump cannot deliver enough oil, components like valves and bearings may receive inadequate lubrication and start making contact with one another. This can produce ticking, whining, or knocking sounds, particularly during engine startup or idling. These sounds may grow louder the longer the issue is unresolved.  That said, these noises can have different causes, so a proper mechanic's diagnosis is essential.

A faulty pump is not the only possible cause of low oil pressure. Insufficient oil levels, a clogged oil filter, unsuitable oil viscosity, or worn-out engine bearings can produce similar symptoms to a failing oil pump. A faulty sensor may also trigger an oil pressure alert.

The first step in investigating a possible oil pump problem is to check the engine oil level. If the oil warning light comes on while driving, park on level ground and switch the engine off. Wait a few minutes and check the oil level using a dipstick (pictured above). Remove and wipe the dipstick before fully reinserting it into the metal guide tube. After removal, the oil line should sit between the dipstick's upper and lower markers, or reach the upper marker. If it's low, add the manufacturer-recommended oil and inspect for leaks or excessive oil consumption. If an oil pressure warning doesn't go away post top-up, do not continue driving.

A mechanic can check the oil pressure sensor and its wiring, inspect the filter and pickup strainer, and measure actual oil pressure with a mechanical gauge. If the problem persists, the mechanic may also need to inspect the pump's drive mechanism and the pressure-relief valve.

The best way to reduce the risk of oil pump failure is on-time preventive maintenance. Change the engine oil and filter at recommended intervals, use your manufacturer's suggested oil grade, and avoid running the engine with insufficient oil. Sludge buildup and contamination can also restrict oil flow, and prolonged operation under poor lubrication conditions can accelerate wear on the pump and other engine components, alongside increasing overheating risk.

If your oil pump is no longer fit for use, replacing it can be expensive because the job may require removing the oil pan or timing cover. The final cost depends on your car, parts prices, and labor, but you can end up paying $600 to over $2,000. Additional repairs may be necessary if oil starvation has already damaged some engine components.

#5811. CDC Says These Superbugs Kill 50,000 Americans Per Year

— Agency flags 19 pathogens, including four drug-resistant bugs for its "urgent threats" list

Candida auris, Acinetobacter, Enterobacterales, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae topped the CDC's revised list of drug-resistant pathogens that threaten public health and demand aggressive action.

The CDC's updated 2026 Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Report outlined the nation's most troubling infectious agents, including 19 pathogens whose threat levels range from "concerning" or "serious" to top-tier "urgent," plus half a dozen that made the agency's watch list of potential threats.

Taken together, the pathogens cause an estimated 9.7 million infections annually and 50,800 deaths, according to the agency.

"These numbers are alarming by any measure, but they are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience," cautioned Wendy Armstrong, MD, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, in a statement.

"Drug-resistant infections prolong hospital stays, drive up healthcare costs, and make it increasingly difficult -- and sometimes impossible -- for doctors to safely provide care like cancer chemotherapy, organ transplants, hip and knee replacements, and other medical care and surgeries," she added.

The pathogen report's newcomers and category movers include:

Armstrong called for the passage of the PASTEUR Act, which would create a federal program to develop antimicrobial drugs against the most threatening pathogens and infections. Both versions of the bill remain stalled in congressional committees.

Four drug-resistant pathogens earned spots on the CDC's top-tier "urgent threats" list:

C. auris, also known as Candidozyma auris, is an emerging, multidrug-resistant yeast that can cause severe, life-threatening infections, particularly in patients who already have serious medical conditions. The number of reported U.S. cases has jumped from 48 in 2016, when it was first reported, to 4,523 in 2023.

Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter can cause infections nearly anywhere in the body, and it's a particular menace for patients in hospitals and nursing homes, where it spreads through contaminated surfaces and equipment. Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter led to 9,497 U.S. hospitalizations in 2023, with most cases beginning outside the hospital (63%). The drug-resistant pathogen was responsible for an estimated 817 U.S. deaths that year.

Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales include strains of Escherichia coli and Klebsiella. Patients on ventilators or with catheters, as well as those on longer antibiotics courses, face a greater risk of these infections, which have limited treatment options. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales fueled 14,878 hospitalizations in 2023, and the pathogen led to an estimated 1,252 deaths.

Drug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae complicates treatment of the resulting sexually transmitted infection gonorrhea, increasing the risk of pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility, as well as acquiring and transmitting HIV. The FDA last year approved gepotidacin (Blujepa) and zoliflodacin (Nuzolvence) as the first new antibiotics for gonorrhea in decades. In 2023, drug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae caused an estimated 787,000 infections in the U.S. Overall, 55.4% of gonorrhea cases in 2023 were either resistant to any of six antibiotics or showed elevated minimum inhibitory concentrations.

#5810. 10 Of The Most Influential Concept Cars Ever Made

What is a concept car? The technical definition describes it as a single model built by an automaker to explore new engineering or design ideas. But with the current state of affairs, most concept cars seem more like PR stunts built to slip into people's algorithms. Take the color-shifting BMW I Vision Dee as an example. Is its E-Ink-covered body cool? Absolutely. Will we ever see this tech in a production car? Probably not.

Some automakers use concepts to preview an upcoming model. The cute and cheerful Citroën 2CV Concept will surely result in an inexpensive production EV. That's great, but there's nothing really revolutionary in these concepts. These concepts don't often become the new gold standard for the company behind them, and other automakers aren't incensed to rush and replicate the design or technology of them. Sometimes, though, a concept car introduces a brand-new idea that then gets widespread, making it truly influential.

Some concepts introduce a new design direction or invent a new vehicle category, while others showcase advanced tech that now we take for granted. In this piece, we'll have a closer look at many of those influential concepts. These cars all had major impacts on the industry, from the Buick Y-Job — the world's first concept car — to the GM Autonomy Concept, which introduced the skateboard chassis used in most modern EVs.

Before Harley Earl (one of the world's most famous designers) showcased the first concept car, automakers mainly worked with coachbuilders to produce one-off cars for wealthy customers. The Y-Job, however, was never listed for sale. Instead, GM notes that Earl used it to demonstrate how a "Car of the Future" might look like.

The result was nothing short of a masterpiece. It might not be immediately obvious from a modern-day standpoint, but the Y-Job looks way sleeker and more elegant than other cars of its era. Earl achieved this thanks to longer and wider proportions to accentuate the car's stance – a design approach that's arguably followed to this day, particularly in coupes and sedans. There were other styling techniques from the Y-Job that other automakers implemented later, like hidden headlights, flush door handles, and integrated taillights.

The standout feature, though, was the intricate retractable roof that stayed hidden under the rear metal deck for a sleek topless look. Once opened, it uncovered a tech-forward interior with a top-mounted radio and electric windows. Adding to the futuristic experience, the Buick Y-Job also features a three-speed automatic transmission, two years before GM took the technology mainstream with the Hydra-Matic. The real kicker is that the Y-Job was a fully-functioning car powered by a 5.2-liter inline-eight engine with 141 horsepower. In fact, Harley Earl drove the Y-Job daily, as he thought the best way to showcase its design and technology was on the street — not in showrooms.

While they could certainly pass as Batmobiles, the B.A.T. designation of Alfa Romeo's 1950 concepts actually means "Berlinetta Aerodinamica Tecnica." Penned by legendary designer and aeronautic engineer Franco Scaglione, the B.A.T. concepts were designed with one idea in mind: cheating the wind. Showcased in 1953 at the Turin Motor Show, the B.A.T. 5 was the first of the trio. Based on the Alfa Romeo 1900 SS sedan, the concept featured a striking body. It had a pointy front end, convex windshield, and streamlined sides with covered front and rear wheels to minimize turbulence, while a big vent behind the front wheels discharged air from under the hood.

Still, it's the three rear fins that catch the most attention. They weren't styling gimmicks; instead, Scaglione used them to smooth out the airflow and allow it to converge at a single trailing point behind the car. By doing this, he has virtually elongated the car's body without using a tapered rear end. As a result, the B.A.T. 5 had a drag coefficient of 0.23 Cd and a top speed of over 124 mph. The B.A.T. 7 brought the former figure down to whopping 0.19 thanks to even more extreme wings, while the B.A.T. 9 was a simpler, more production-ready design.

Many modern cars picked up this trick, and most of them are high-performance machines. Think the Ford GT's and Ferrari 599 GTB Fiorano's flying buttresses, or the BMW i8's floating buttresses over the rear taillights. Similarly, the Mercedes-AMG One uses a central dorsal fin to stabilize airflow, further echoing the design ideas introduced by the B.A.T. concepts.

The Lamborghini Countach is arguably the most poster-worthy car ever made. Marcello Gandini's wedge-shaped masterpiece has sharp lines and striking scissor doors, screaming drama and speed even when it stands still. The design was so influential that Lambo's supercars stuck to that formula ever since. There is one missing part of that story, though: the revolution actually started with the Alfa Romeo Carabo, one of your favorite failed concept cars.

Like the Countach, the Carabo was also penned by Marcelo Gandini at Bertone, who was tasked with creating new bodywork for the Alfa Romeo 33 Stradale. That's no small task, considering Scaglione's legend is widely considered as one of the most beautiful cars ever designed. However, Gandini didn't disappoint. Instead of the 33 Stradale's sensual curves, he went with a wedge-shaped, angular body, using low and wide proportions to give the car a better stance. Gandini also hid the headlights behind motorized flaps to make the front end as pointy as possible, and he implemented front and rear gills for a more futuristic look. Still, nothing made jaws drop quite like the scissor doors — pieces of automotive theater that are as visually striking today as they were back in 1968.

Like the Y-Job, the Alfa Romeo Carabo was more than just a styling exercise. Because it was based on the 33 Stradale, it ran the same 2.0-liter V8 that produced 230 horsepower at an astronomical 8,800 rpm, paired to a six-speed manual. It weighed only about 1,543 pounds, too. As a result, the Carabo sprinted to 62 mph in around 5.5 seconds and reached a top speed of over 155 mph.

While Italian automakers were busy designing attractive sports cars, Mercedes-Benz used its wedge-shaped C111 concept as a test bed for new technologies. The C111 wasn't as visually striking, but it influenced the auto industry with its internals. Despite its 280-horsepower potency, though, the three-rotor Wankel rotary engine isn't what caused so much influence. The 1963 NSU Wankel Spider beat it to the punch, and those engines aren't so widespread today.

What did stand the test of time is C111's multi-link rear axle. After extensively testing it in the mid-engine sports car, Mercedes brought the design to production for the first time with the 1982 190. Since then, many automakers implemented some type of a multi-link rear suspension in their models. Yes, these aren't carbon copies of the original design, but they all have the same goal of improving comfort and handling at the same time.

The C111 wasn't a one-off, though, with Mercedes building six units of the first iteration. Then, in 1970, it introduced a four-rotor version with 345 horsepower, followed by the 1976 C111-IID and C111-IIID models powered by the legendary OM 617 inline-five turbodiesel. With 230 horsepower on tap, the C111-IIID broke multiple speed records at the Nardo circuit, including an impressive average speed of nearly 200 mph over a 500-mile distance. Since then, turbodiesel engines have been used in many high-performance machines, like the 3.0-liter quad-turbo-diesel BMW M550d xDrive and the Audi Q7 6.0-liter V12 TDI.

Penned by Pail Bracq for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, the BMW E25 Turbo Concept followed the wedge-shaped craze Gandini made popular a few years ago. However, while it certainly looks attractive with Gullwing doors and pop-up headlights included, it's the safety tech that made this concept significant. The front end has a huge bumper that houses the BMW logo, kidney grilles, and daytime running lights. There's also a hefty gap between the bumper and the body. That's because of the hydraulic shock absorbers, which absorbed impacts and even returned the bumper back after smaller collisions. The E25 Turbo also stopped the driver from starting the engine if the seat belts weren't fastened — an early version of seat belt reminders in all modern cars. Heck, the concept's striking orange paint is phosphorescent, making it easier to see on the road.

Yet, it's the active safety systems that made the biggest splash. The E25 Turbo had a radar-based brake distance monitor that calculated and displayed the braking gap to the vehicle ahead, notifying the driver if they got too close. This concept car was also one of the earliest with anti-lock braking, and it even measured lateral G forces — a feature present in many modern performance cars. The E25 Turbo was practically a rolling laboratory, but that didn't stop it from also being a fully-operational mid-engine sports car. It packed a 2.0-liter turbocharged engine with 280 horsepower and a four-speed manual, which allowed the sports car to reach 62 mph from a standstill in 6.6 seconds.

People might be craving SUVs, but minivans are cool, too. They might not look that way visually, but they offer a more spacious and functional interior. And, because of their lower, flat floors, minivans are easier to get in and out of. It's all thanks to the "monovolume" architecture where the cabin and all mechanical components reside into one single, continuous volume. And while it was born much earlier, that architecture reached widespread popularity with the 1978 Italdesign Lancia Megagamma concept.

Now, sure, what you are looking it is a wedge shape. But that shouldn't be surprising, as the Megagamma was penned by Giorgetto Giugiaro. Still, it's the revolutionary interior space that proved more influential. Giugiaro opted for a taller roof and upright seating, which, along with the flat floor, opened up significantly more room for passengers and cargo. In fact, despite being more than 11 inches shorter than the Gamma (Lancia's flagship car), the Megagamma offered about 6.7 inches more interior space.

The real kicker was that the Megagamma used the same front-wheel-drive architecture as the Gamma — including its 2.5-liter engine — meaning it could be easily turned into a production car. However, Lancia left that to other automakers, and they soon turned it into a gold rush. In 1981, Nissan launched the Prairie, which looked like the Megagamma with three seating rows and rear sliding doors. Then, in 1983, Chrysler followed the Megagamma footprint and gave birth to North America's minivan segment with the Dodge Caravan and Plymouth Voyager. The same year, Renault pioneered Europe's MPV segment with the Espace, turning the "monovolume" concept into a global phenomenon.

From 1930s streamliners to Alfa Romeo's B.A.T. concepts, car designers toyed with the idea of reducing aerodynamic drag for decades. However, aerodynamics still didn't play a huge role during 1970s car development, particularly for regular passenger vehicles. That all changed in 1981 with the Ford Probe III. This sleek concept previewed the Sierra, but more importantly, it influenced a change to more aerodynamic designs after the 1970s.

With a drag coefficient of 0.22 Cd, the Probe III had 50% lower drag than the best production car in its time. The fluid, rounded body did the heavy lifting, but there were other meaningful improvements that helped Ford achieve that astonishing figure. It featured a twin-deck rear spoiler, semi-covered rear wheels, a raked windshield, and a smooth underbody which minimized lift alongside the active front section. The finer details were just as dialed in, with the concept featuring flush door handles, flush-mounted windows, rear skirts, integrated outer mirrors, and a smooth roof without the usual drainage channels.

The Probe III resulted in the Europe-bound 1983 Ford Sierra, which had a drag coefficient of 0.34 Cd. That wasn't as impressive as the concept, but it was still better than many passenger cars of its time. Ford used similar design principles in the 1983 Taurus "Aero Bird" (0.35 Cd), the 1984 Tempo (0.36 Cd), and the 1986 Taurus (0.32 Cd). Other automakers followed suit, too; in 1982, Audi introduced the third-gen 100, which had smoother body panels, flush windows, and a raked windshield, achieving a drag coefficient of 0.30 Cd.

Until the Toyota RAV-FOUR concept arrived at the 1989 Tokyo Motor Show, most SUVs utilized a "body-on-frame" chassis. Yes, automakers already sold small off-roaders, like the Suzuki Samurai and Isuzu Amigo, but each of them had a ladder frame that was similar to larger trucks and SUVs of the era. The RAV-FOUR concept, however, was a car-based SUV; it featured a unibody chassis. To say that this move was influential would be an understatement. Today, each of the top 10 best-selling SUVs in the U.S. — including the current-gen RAV4 — features unibody construction. That's not just the compact models, but also large SUVs like the Jeep Grand Cherokee and Toyota Grand Highlander.

Despite its influence, the RAV-FOUR concept itself wasn't as dull as a modern crossover. Instead, Toyota went with a tried-and-true (at the time) adventure-focused design, reminding the public that the RAV-FOUR could be a capable off-roader regardless of its car-like platform. The concept featured quite a lot of body cladding, a front skid plate, more aggressive tires, high ground clearance, and — of course – four-wheel drive. The design was retro cute, too, featuring circular headlights reminiscent of early Land Cruisers.

Four years later, Toyota introduced the production-bound concept at the 1993 Tokyo Motor Show, which followed many of the same principles. While the retro styling was gone, it still had all the body cladding you could desire, a high ground clearance, and a compact, two-door design. Crucially, it continued to be based on a unibody platform, with independent suspension on all its wheels and a front 2.0-liter gas engine.

The GM Impact certainly didn't invent the electric car. Battery-powered vehicles have been around since the 1830s, and at the beginning of the 20th century, 600 New York cabs were propelled by electricity. Heck, even Porsche's first car was an EV. However, the internal combustion engine quickly took over and cast EVs aside. From there, it took until 1990 for the GM Impact to arrive and truly reignite the conversation around electric cars. Driven by the recently-discovered global warming caused by fossil fuels and the need for cleaner, emission-free vehicles, the Impact immediately caught attention at the 1990 LA Auto Show.

The sleek, wind-cheating coupe with two seats looked highly futuristic — just as you'd expect from an EV. It had good specs for the time, too. Equipped with 32 Delco lead-acid batteries, the Impact could travel 120 miles on a charge, largely thanks to the aerodynamic body and low-drag tires. Meanwhile, two electric motors on the front two wheels provided enough strength for a 0-60 sprint of only 8 seconds. At the time, this was enough to beat the Mazda Miata and Nissan 300ZX.

GM followed the Impact with a production model, the EV-1. Launched for 1997, the EV-1 had a similar design and novel features like regenerative braking. It also had a much shorter range of up to 90 miles with the base battery. GM later upgraded the EV1 with a Panasonic lead-acid pack that stretched range to 100 miles, alongside an optional NiMH pack good for up to 140 miles. GM sold only 1,117 units, but the concept and production models paved the way for the modern EV.

The 2002 GM AUTOnomy is one of those wild concepts where the automaker throws multiple emergent technologies in a striking, hyper-futuristic body. Indeed, the AUTOnomy Concept was equipped with a hydrogen fuel-cell power train, which was still seen as a viable solution at the time. It was also fully drive-by-wire, meaning steering, braking, and throttle were executed by electric actuators rather than direct mechanical linkages to the driver. As a cherry on top, the AUTOnomy was also a fully-autonomous car, which is something so prevalent today that automated driving has different levels of definitions.

The concept's killer feature, however, was the skateboard chassis. Today, most EVs are based on this design, featuring a skateboard-like base that houses the battery and electronics while also providing structural rigidity. It's so prevalent because it's easily scalable across a wide range of vehicles and provides packaging benefits, such as maximizing interior room. Since the skateboard chassis sits at the lowest point of the vehicle, EVs also have a low center of gravity, which aids stability. On top of pioneering the physical design choices, the AUTOnomy Concept's skateboard chassis had all the features of its modern alternatives. It housed GM's existing HydroGen III fuel cell hardware, which fits electronics, cooling, and crush zones in a flat, 6-inch-tall structure.
