#5809. Elon Musk’s Attack Ads Are Backfiring As Midterms Near

US Federal Election Commission data revealed this week that Elon Musk has donated at least $445 million into Republican-aligned political action committees and groups since last year. Interestingly, it seems that Musk’s deep influence isn’t enough, and he is worried.

If Democrats win big on Tuesday in midterm elections, Musk insists US democracy will come to an “end.”

“This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word,” Musk wrote Friday on X. “All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029.”

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a long track record of engaging in political quid pro quo. His companies receive billions in federal contracts. The once climate-is-all advocate now weighs heavily on the side of oil/fossil fuels. His DOGE actions may have forced labor shortages in regulatory agencies that were scrutinizing his businesses.

But now Musk seems distraught that newfound Democratic Congressional power could make him a target of investigations after the midterms.

And his fears may have merit. Musk’s blatant attempts to influence election results are getting a lot of recent analysis and condemnation.

“I worry about what Musk’s impulsive bullying is doing and has done to others more vulnerable than I am,” former Secretary of Labor Robert Reich wrote earlier this month after Musk exclaimed, “Prison for Reich.” Such extreme comments are part of Musk lifelong pattern, Reich continued, in which “he’s threatened and racially denigrated and pushed around (people) his whole life.”

Reich added that he is worried for that voters whom Musk has been “deluging with TV ads for Republican candidates” as well as for “federal workers who have been hurt by his so-called Department of Government Efficiency, Americans who have been harmed by his wanton destruction of public services, and people around the globe who are worse off because of cuts to USAID pushed by Elon’s DOGE.”

Musk’s America PAC has contributed to 43 US House and Senate races, and that influx of cash has funded vast amounts of television commercials, digital ads, text messages, and mailers. It’s almost easy to forget that Musk became a persona non grata with Trump and the Republican Party last year.

America PAC stands for “secure borders, safe cities, free speech, sensible spending, fair justice system, and self-protection,” according to its website.

These objectives might sound fair and reasonable to many voters, yet a majority of America PAC money goes to attack ads. Musk typically cross-posts America PAC’s damaging content to his more than 200 million followers on X, the social media site he owns and whose social commentary he controls.

Ezra Klein, co-author of Abundance, recently interviewed Quinn Slobodian, professor of international history at Boston University. Slobodian interprets Musk’s midterm campaign finance moves as “his flexing of his own power to make or break candidates, as he wishes,” which, in turn, is a way “fine-tune that control over the media and messaging ecosystem and get out ahead of what he worries would be a regulatory wave that would accompany a Democratic majority.”

Why are such media messages — even those that are based on false premises — so compelling during the run-up to the 2026 US midterm elections? Voters frequently base their own political decisions on fake information and images rather than on reality. Social historian Heather Cox Richardson explains that many such techniques draw scenarios of a chaotic society and destroy individuals’ “ability to make sense of the world.” Some media consumers “turn to a strongman who promises to create order.” Others will get so exhausted they simply refuse to fight back. The path of least resistance is succumbing to the manipulation and “giving up control of their government to an authoritarian.”

In Texas alone, America PAC has provided more than $33 million toward the Ken Paxton Senate campaign. Additionally, Musk donated $168 million contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund, which routes money back to the Paxton campaign.

“Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars,” James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, said at a recent rally. “He wants his very own personal United States senator.” Talarico’s comments were supported by loud boos from the crowd.

At a rally at the University of Texas, Talarico said Musk was trying to “stop the movement that we are building in our state.” In contrast, he offered that his own campaign is “funded by 1.3 million individuals who have donated their hard-earned money.” Instead of corporate PAC money, Talarico has depended on small-dollar donations.

The day before that, Talarico’s campaign released a digital advertisement accusing Paxton of being a mere pawn to Musk. “Let’s remind Elon: Texas is not for sale.”

Interestingly, Democratic candidates in Texas and elsewhere across the US are holding their own — many electoral races are too close to call, even with Musk’s influence and campaign finance imbalances helping out Republicans.

Carolyn Fortuna, PhD, is a writer, researcher, and educator with a lifelong dedication to ecojustice. #5808. Why Cars And Long Scarves Don't Mix

Cars are dangerous. There's no shortage of studies reiterating that fact, from the frequent running down of pedestrians over the last century to the not-so-obvious deaths outside of traffic crashes. It's why many of today's cars are inundated with those darn safety features we'd sacrifice if given the option. And yet another danger lurks in an unexpected place: the closet. Caution the fashionistas in your life, because your car and a scarf could be a deadly combination.

Death by scarf via the automobile became a phenomenon nearly 100 years ago, when in 1927, famous American dancer Isadora Duncan met her tragic end from the combination of the two in France. The New York Times wrote that on the night of the accident, she wore an "immense iridescent silk scarf wrapped about her neck and streaming in long folds, part of which was swathed about her body with part trailing behind."

The story continues that after a walk along the promenade in Nice, she hopped into a rented car and neither she nor the driver had realized one of the ends of her massive scarf had fallen outside of the car. The stray piece caught in the rear wheel and wound around enough that it then pulled Duncan from out of the car where she was dragged behind it for several feet. The driver stopped the car, but it was too late. When aid arrived on scene, they stated she had been killed instantly from strangulation.

Duncan's death became so well-known that similar occurrences were deemed Isadora Duncan syndrome (also referred to as long-scarf syndrome). These are typically accidental strangulations with trauma injuries sustained to the larynx and trachea (the airway), and potentially the carotid arteries (delicate mainlines of blood to the brain). Damage to either of these throughways for vital resources could starve the brain of oxygen and lead to death, like it tragically did for Duncan.

Scarf-induced deaths do still happen in modern times, and they're more likely to happen when the mode of transportation is wide open to the elements — something like an auto-rickshaw or a convertible is a dangerous place to wear a long scarf. The prevalence of modern scarf incidents actually inspired an Indian study which specifically looked at scarf deaths from 2013 to 2015 within a Level 1 trauma center. Over the nearly two years the study was conducted, 76 injuries were recorded, and approximately three of those individuals died from related injuries.

Other recent instances outside of India include two women who were maimed by scarves worn for special occasions just this month. The first, a Dallas woman, opted to wear a long dress with a scarf to a wedding. Post-wedding, with friends, they got into a car to go to dinner. Her scarf became stuck in the door, and trailed off enough to get caught in the tire. It pulled on her neck hard enough to cause a nasty friction burn across the lower part of her neck and shoulder.

A video account of the Dallas event was stitched by another woman who also had a physically scarring scarf experience. She shared that she too had been "nearly killed by fashion" when she wore the scarf part of her newly purchased dress for a gala. Caught in the seatbelt and the door of a rideshare vehicle, the woman's scarf was eventually pulled by the tire, which led to an eventual trip to the emergency room.

Both women were somewhat lucky to have only suffered deep burns to their neck and not more serious injuries, or death like Duncan. The lesson here: If you're going to wear a scarf, be vigilant about where that scarf is when you get into a vehicle.

#5807. Relaunched Mitsubishi Pajero Is Already Stealing Land Cruiser Customers

It's been less than two months since the Mitsubishi Pajero officially re-entered the off-road-focused SUV scene, and it's already making waves. Long-beleaguered Mitsubishi says that a whopping 80% of the Pajero's customers in Japan are coming from competitors as it looks to move upmarket with a $39,000 base price — primed to challenge the mighty Toyota Land Cruiser. Of course, a great deal of that 80% number makes sense, considering Mitsubishi doesn't really make anything all that compelling right now, and hasn't for some time. Honestly, I'd assume the other 20% of non-conquest buyers are just folks coming from old Pajeros.

In any case, Mitsu' unveiled domestic pricing and specs for its new flagship this week, adding that it had already received 5,500 orders in Japan for the Japan-built body-on-frame SUV — 1,500 more than what was expected, according to Automotive News. It puts the seven-seater well on its way to hitting Mitsubishi's goal of 10,000 sales through March of 2027. Sales are officially slated to begin in Japan on December 17, with the Australian market getting theirs the following month. It's already on sale in Thailand, with 1,500 orders so far.

Mitsubishi clearly had its sights set on the Toyota Land Cruiser lineup when designing, engineering and pricing the new Pajero. In Japan, it's priced at the equivalent of $39,212, which places it slightly above the entry point of the Land Cruiser 250 ($36,596) and directly in line with the base-level utilitarian version of the twin-turbo Land Cruiser 300 ($39,890). Volume versions of the LC300 start at a far higher $55,406, according to Automotive News, and they go all the way up to $64,586 for the top-end GR Sport hybrid. Stateside, the only Land Cruiser we get is the smaller 250, and it starts at $59,775, including destination. If the Pajero/Montero were to come here, I wouldn't be shocked if it were to cost somewhere in that neighborhood.

In any case, Mitsubishi has to be feeling good about what the Pajero is already bringing to the table. That 80% conquest number is nothing to sneeze at, and the company says many former Pajero owners who left the brand when the company dropped the nameplate globally in 2020 are returning, Automotive News reports. Those buyers are also going for big options — ignoring the bargain-basement attitude Mitsubishi has cultivated in the past years. About 70% of Japanese orders are for vehicles equipped with premium packages, which has to be amazing news for a company looking to switch up its image in a major way.

Despite all of this, there's still no word on whether we're going to get our Montero stateside, but by all that's holy, I want it. Mitsubishi says it's evaluating other markets and plans other power trains beyond the current diesel, but I won't hold my breath.

#5806. Hackers Figured Out How Flock Camera Systems Actually Work By Pulling One Apart

If you've ever wondered exactly how easy it is to hack Flock cameras, the results are in, and it seems they're pretty darn vulnerable to hacking attempts. For the past couple years, several hacking groups have targeted Flock cameras and other Fourth Amendment-breaking automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) and proven their security vulnerabilities time and again. In some cases, Flock cameras have been found to be streaming live and archived video over the open internet, and in others, it took only about 30 seconds to gain access to a camera's stored footage after getting the box open.

Another recent hacking attempt has caught the public's attention, revealing the extent of the cameras' so-called encryption (spoiler: it's not good) and showing how much data ALPRs capture daily. The initial report of this hacking attempt — covered together by Wired and 404Media — details how the hackers acquired a Flock camera, cracked open its shell, and made a nearly perfect copy of the data inside.

The hacking collective behind this recent hacking attempt is known as stegan0gram, and the members represent just a small fraction of the people around the United States who keep vandalizing these ALPRs tracking our every move. Stegan0gram is taking things a step further, though. In an interview with 404Media, one of the hackers discussed "liberating" the hardware and reverse engineering it. The anonymous agent laid our their philosophy, asking "Why just destroy them when we can reverse engineer them and find the secrets of those spying on us?"

A good question, indeed, stegan0gram. With cities all over the country ditching the ALPR laughing stock that is Flock Safety in favor of companies like Axon, which collect similar data and give law enforcement agencies unfettered, warrantless access to it, such secrets are well worth uncovering.

When the hackers opened up their camera and looked inside, they found some data unencrypted, including a section of the camera's memory bank titled "media," inside which was stored an encryption key that opened up previously encrypted data. In effect, a company that sells your location, driving patterns, and life story to law enforcement, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, hid the key to their house under the welcome mat.

With the newly decrypted data, the hackers had access to records of over 50,000 vehicles, including over 1.5 million images. The camera's highlights also clearly showed that the technology knows how to detect individuals, license plates, and bicycles, in addition to motor vehicles. The collective also found that the camera had logged bumper stickers, license plate frames, and other graphics, likely misidentifying them as plates.

What doesn't seem to happen inside the camera is also notable. From when stegan0gram could determine, Flock cameras don't actually read license plates locally. Nor do they build a car's signature, using data like make, model, color, and identifying features. Instead, these operations are likely done on Flock's own servers after the data is transferred from the camera.

The reason we know so much — perhaps anything at all — about how ALPRs function, what data they gather, how incredibly widespread they are, and how troubling their security is, has nothing to do with transparency from the companies making millions spying on us. In reality, companies like Flock and Axon try to keep mum in public. Flock cameras even come with guidance for police agencies on how to own the narrative surrounding these creepy cameras so that they can get them installed in cities without getting push-back from the citizenry. Much of what we know about how ALPRs function is thanks to the tireless work of people who take issue with law enforcement being allowed unilateral access to what ought to be protected data.

This push-back isn't all coming from one area or group, either. DeFlock.org has been one of the most constant presences in ALPR education and awareness. This website maps Flock cameras across the country and started in 2024 as the passion project of a curious software engineer. It's irked Flock's mission so sorely that Flock CEO Garrett Langley publicly called the site and those who support it a terrorist organization. Recently, MapQuest jumped on the DeFlock bandwagon and started showing Flock cameras on its own maps.

Hackers like the stegan0gram collective, GainSec, and Benn Jordan have been instrumental in bringing the mysteries of ALPRs to light. The next time you see a Flock camera while driving down the road, take a second to appreciate the hard work of the people who taught you how to look for them, and if you have strong feelings about spy cams logging your car's every movement, consider writing to your city government, who could be persuaded to drop Flock and other ALPRs entirely.

#5805. Alabama's Frozen Embryo Ruling Didn't Change Disposal Choices, for the Most Part

— Results from neighboring state did, however, suggest some patient concerns

BALTIMORE -- Following the 2024 Alabama Supreme Court ruling that frozen embryos could be considered children in the state, most patients at a clinic in neighboring Georgia didn't make different disposition choices about their frozen embryos than before the ruling, with the exception of one group.

In the 2 years before and 2 years after the ruling, there were no significant changes in the percentage of patients that opted for minimal-harm frozen embryo disposition in some circumstances, including patient death, death of a spouse or partner, simultaneous death of patient and partner, or divorce, according to Leah Ginn, DO, of the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University, and colleagues.

However, among couples who mutually decided to discontinue in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatment, there was a shift towards embryo destruction after the ruling, with fewer choosing minimal-harm disposition methods (80.3% versus 67.9%, P=0.03), they reported at the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) annual meeting.

Ginn told MedPage Today that the shift in this group was interesting but unexpected. It may reflect that "patients were likely concerned about the legal and ethical implications of their embryos" sitting in storage, she said, and they may be electing to make more definitive decisions about what to do with those embryos in some circumstances.

"Policy decisions that are made at not only the federal level, but also the state level, are really likely to impact the decisions that patients are making about their reproductive care," Ginn said.

Rachel Weinerman, MD, an ob/gyn and reproductive endocrinologist at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland who wasn't involved in the study, told MedPage Today that the Alabama ruling "was very challenging for everybody in the field of IVF because it demonstrated the risks that we are taking."

"If the legal climate were to consider a fertilized egg the status of a person under the law, then there's really no way that IVF can be done," Weinerman said. Discarding embryos is inherent to the IVF process, hence why many clinics in Alabama paused their operations after the ruling.

For physicians, it's legally risky to do IVF in that climate, she said. Moreover, patients may be nervous that they won't have the autonomy to make decisions about their embryos.

"I think that we have to understand that the legal climate not only affects the physician's ability to perform IVF, but also affects patient choices and may limit their ability to grow their families because they're concerned about lack of autonomy over embryo disposition choices," Weinerman said.

Ginn said her team's Georgia clinic saw an influx in out-of-state patients around the time of the Alabama ruling and they were curious if patients' frozen embryo disposition choices were changing.

To assess the impact of the Alabama ruling, Ginn and team conducted a retrospective analysis from June 2022 to February 2026. They included patients at their clinic undergoing IVF for the first time who completed embryo disposition consent forms on what to do with embryos in various circumstances.

In all, 145 patients presented to the clinic during this time period, with 61 before the ruling and 84 after. Patients had similar sociodemographic and clinical characteristics. Nine patients who were single were excluded from the analysis.

The primary outcome was the selection of minimal-harm options before and after the February 2024 ruling. Minimal harm options included embryo donation, use by one partner, use or donation as part of a court decree, and transfer to a storage facility. On the flip side, discarding embryos or donating them to research were considered likely to result in harm to the embryo.

Ginn noted the modest sample size, which was not powered to detect very small differences, as a limitation. She also said this analysis was around the time of the Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health decision that upended the federal right to abortion, which likely shaped patients' understanding of the legal reproductive care landscape.

#5804. 5 New Cars With Deep, Deep Discounts

If you haven't been new car shopping in a while, you might be disappointed that automakers and dealers are getting stingier with incentives. Cox Automotive reports that the average incentive dropped to $3,359 per vehicle in September 2026, down from about $3,680, or 8.8%, a year earlier. But the fall can be a golden time for new car buyers as the new model year arrives and dealers need to push out old inventory.

Looking at guidance from TrueCar and our own research, we've compiled a best-to-worst list of discounts on new cars right now. Predictably, these are all 2026 models, as the 2027 editions are already in showrooms or on their way. And while some automakers are pushing eye-popping cash incentives right now, deals like these are mostly on pricier vehicles. For example, Audi is offering $20,000 off the e-tron GT, but that's still a six-figure EV after the discount.

That's why we focused on models with original MSRPs near or below $50,000, which is about the average price of a new car these days, and still decent cash incentives that make for even sharper deals. If you don't mind driving something from the outgoing model year or with varying degrees of electrification, you can get discounts of up to 30%. The list includes the Kia Niro EV, Nissan Rogue Plug-In Hybrid, Chevrolet Silverado 1500, Volkswagen ID.4, and Chrysler Pacifica.

A few housekeeping notes. This list isn't exhaustive, so you may find better deals on different models. Our TrueCar discount data is based on the wider Chicago area. Pricing in your area may be better or worse. All MSRPs mentioned include factory destination charges. Finally, our real-world pricing check included dealer listings on Autotrader from across the country for new models with fewer than 100 miles on the odometer.

With Kia offering stylish electric vehicles like the EV6 and EV9, it's easy to forget that the Niro crossover is available as an EV. Even more surprising, the automaker is offering a whopping $10,000 cash incentive before any dealer discounts. But there's a reason why: 2026 is the last model year of the Niro EV. The 2027 Kia EV3 will take its place, offering 321 miles of range for well under $40,000. In the meantime, the remaining 2026 Niro EVs are one heck of a deal.

TrueCar says the base Wind trim, with an MSRP of $41,195, has an average offer price of around $40,060 as of writing. That discount is chump change until you add in the $10,000 promotion. Combined, the savings can total up to $11,135, or 27% off the original window sticker price. Some dealers seem especially eager to offload Niro EVs. Numerous listings show dealers promising prices below $29,000 (before taxes and tags), pushing discounts above 30%.

Admittedly, the Niro EV may not be the most compelling all-electric on the market, with 253 miles of range in a world where 300 miles or more has become the de facto standard. There's also no all-wheel-drive option; this SUV is front-wheel-drive only. However, it's zippy, with a 0-to-60 mph time of 6.7 seconds, has DC fast-charging capability, is compatible with Tesla Superchargers, includes a suite of driver-assistance features, and has a dual-screen dashboard setup.

You may have heard people calling a decaf cappuccino with skim milk a "why bother." Well, that term could equally apply to the 2026 Nissan Rogue Plug-In Hybrid (PHEV): a one-year-only rebadged Mitsubishi Outlander designed to placate dealers until the arrival of the 2027 Rogue Hybrid. Nissan ordered only 3,000 Rogue PHEVs for the U.S., and Autotrader listings suggest about one-third are still unsold.

A discontinued model and ample inventory often equal generous manufacturer incentives. In this case, Nissan is offering $6,500 toward the purchase of a 2026 Rogue PHEV. Before this cash, TrueCar says the starter SL trim, with an MSRP of $49,140, has an average discount of about $1,977. Throw in the factory discount, and the price reduction could climb up to $8,477, or 17.3% in savings. But wait, there's more money still on the table. About 26% of the dealer listings for the SL trim on Autotrader are priced under $40,000, including dealer fees. A couple dozen currently listed are priced below $38,000, which increases the discount to over 22%.

If you're not bothered by the Rogue PHEV's near-unicorn status, this is a chance to buy a well-specced crossover. A 38-mile all-electric range falls well within the average daily commute of 27 miles, and a combined fuel economy rating of 26 mpg translates into 420 miles of total range; more than enough for a road trip. Like its Outlander counterpart, the Rogue PHEV seats seven; however, 19.1 inches of third-row legroom can be a tight squeeze. The SL trim's bells and whistles include heated front seats and 20-inch wheels.

Crossovers aren't the only vehicles with extra-sharp discounts. 2027 will bring an all-new Chevrolet Silverado 1500, so dealers are ostensibly eager to move the 2026 models. Marketplace listings show plenty of leftovers. Chevy has sped up the clearance process by offering cash incentives ranging from $2,500 to $6,500, depending on the trim. Surprisingly, the entry-level WT grade qualifies for the top bonus (along with the Custom Trail Boss, LT, and LTZ).

In WT trim, a Silverado 1500 crew cab with a short bed and rear-wheel drive (RWD) has an MSRP of $45,795. For our area, typical negotiations settle at $41,197 before the factory discount, according to TrueCar. That's a 10% savings off the top. However, in the murky world of car pricing, that discounted price likely already reflects some promotional cash from Chevy, but clearly not the full $6,500.

That said, dealer pricing appears to reflect the complete discount, and more. Across the dozens of listings (with dealer fees included), the average MSRP for a 2026 Silverado 1500 LT (crew cab, RWD) is $45,712, and the average asking price on Autotrader is $35,554. That amounts to 22.2% in savings. Buyers looking to step up a trim level will find the Custom grade comes with only $2,500 in factory cash. The amount increases to $5,250 for the RST, LT Trail Boss, High Country, and ZR2.

The Volkswagen ID.4 is another EV being consigned to the history books after 2026. It launched for the 2021 model year as the company's first purpose-built electric vehicle for the U.S., but its sales couldn't match the brand's high hopes for the car. Last year, VW sold about 22,000 ID.4s, a fraction of the Ford Mustang Mach-Es and Tesla Model Ys that hit the streets. The ID.4's poor showing continues into 2026; about 500 are listed for sale nationwide on Autotrader, with roughly 60% of those being the base Pro trim.

TrueCar says that edition's MSRP of $46,570 has an average offer price of $43,547, which equates to a 6.5% discount. That reduction may not motivate buyers, but adding a $6,000 bonus might. Percentage-wise, this extra cash makes the Pro trim particularly appealing. A sample of 90 Pro trim listings averaged an MSRP of $48,804 (including dealer fees) and an asking price of $39,908, an 18.2% discount. Numerous listings are currently priced under $36,000.

The Pro trim has rear-wheel drive; moving up to all-wheel drive requires a higher grade, but they are all eligible for the $6,000 cash discount. The base model has a 291-mile range and supports DC fast charging at 30 minutes for a 10% to 80% charge (under peak conditions). The equipment list includes heated front seats and driver-assistance features, including automatic parking.

A minivan may not be on everyone's shopping list, but nothing beats space when hauling people and things. In 2025, the Chrysler Pacifica earned bragging rights as the category's top seller. Nonetheless, Stellantis still needs to clear out the 2026 models as a refreshed 2027 Pacifica is already on dealer lots.

The average offer on the entry-level 2026 Select trim with FWD is $45,298 – a modest 2.6% discount off the $46,440 MSRP. However, adding $5,500 in factory cash significantly changes the calculation. Using TrueCar's transaction estimate as a base, the price drops to $39,798 when you factor in the incentive. That increases the savings to 14.3%. Looking at inventory, there are over 1,100 new 2026 Pacificas listed through Autotrader, with almost half of this group being the base Select grade with FWD. These more affordable Pacificas have an average MSRP of $48,870 and an average asking price of $41,012, reflecting a 16.1% discount.

Along with the Toyota Sienna, the Pacifica is the only gas-powered minivan on the market available with all-wheel drive. As the starter trim, the Select isn't overloaded with amenities, but Chrysler includes leatherette upholstery, heated front seats, and parking sensors. Seven-passenger seating is standard, with eight-passenger seating available as an option.

#5803. Dodge Entered The US Compact Truck Market Late With A Rebadged Mitsubishi Forte

Heading into the 1960s, Detroit's Big Three had begun to realize some folks preferred cars that were more agile and more efficient than the typically massive machines they were producing. Their response was to introduce a wave of home-grown compacts in 1960, led by GM's Chevrolet Corvair, the Chrysler Valiant, and the Ford Falcon.

On the truck side of the ledger, though, things played out differently. Datsun had been exporting compact trucks to the West Coast since the first half of the 1960s, with Toyota following soon after. The Big Three at the time offered car-based trucks like the Corvair forward-control models and the Falcon-based ute-style Ranchero, but they didn't look like the real deal the way the Japanese mini-trucks did. So when the mini-truck segment began taking off, the U.S. automakers went straight to the easiest option. Ford rebadged Mazda's B-series truck to sell as the Courier for 1972. The same year saw GM give that treatment to the Isuzu Faster, with the result being the Chevy LUV — a truck way ahead of its time.

As a result, the Courier and LUV, and their Japanese-branded rivals, were in the right place at the right time when the fuel crises of 1970s hit, starting in 1973. Chrysler's entry, though, was way behind. Based on the Mitsubishi Forte, the Dodge D-50 didn't debut until 1979, some seven years after the Courier and LUV. (To be clear, the D-50 would be renamed the Dodge Ram 50 in 1981, and Mitsubishi's Forte is unrelated to Kia's former compact sedan of the same name.)

Unlike today, compact pickups of the past were literally compact. So the 1979 Dodge D-50 pickup had a slightly smaller footprint than a 2026 Honda Civic sedan. The D-50 is 184.6 inches in length and 65 inches wide, while the Civic is 0.2 inches longer and 5.9 inches wider. As for a modern "compact" pickup, the Ford Maverick is 15.2 inches longer, 7.6 inches wider, and 8 inches taller.

The D-50's power train was likewise fairly small. The standard mill was a 2.0-liter overhead-cam inline-4 capable of 93 horsepower and 108 pound-feet of torque, and it was paired with a four-speed manual transmission. For the D-50 Sport, a 2.6-liter I4 with 105 horses and 139 lb-ft was standard with a five-speed automatic with overdrive. A three-speed automatic was optional with both versions.

More impressive was the D-50's maximum payload of 1,400 pounds. By 1981, when the D-50's payload rating reached 1,525 pounds, it could out-carry the '26 Maverick, which has a 1,500-pound payload.

The year 1981 further marked two other milestones for the Dodge. The first was a marketing change. Ram and Dodge aren't the same brand anymore, having split up in 2009, but they were still connected at the time. And in 1981, when Chrysler was readying its new truck lineup for the year, the decision was made to add the Ram name to the roster – transforming its compact into the Dodge Ram 50. The next year saw the Ram 50 welcome its first 4x4 configuration, complete with another new marketing move that positioned the truck as the Power Ram 50. The truck even offered a diesel power plant from 1983 to 1985.

The Dodge Ram 50 would go on to get a second generation in 1987, and that model would remain in production until 1994. Yet not only wasn't it the smallest Dodge pickup ever produced, it wasn't even the smallest Dodge pickup of its era. That honor goes to the Dodge Rampage.

Only in production from 1982 through 1984, the Rampage was a car-based coupé utility built from the foundation of the Dodge Omni 024. Now, the Rampage wasn't that much smaller than the Ram 50. Indeed, it was only an inch shorter in length and actually 1.8 inches wider. That said, the Rampage was significantly shorter — by 9 inches — in height, and down 380 pounds in the payload department versus the Ram 50.

Remember those 1960s forward-control pickups mentioned above? Dodge's entry, the A100, undercut the Ram 50's length by more than a foot. Of course, that was a baked-in benefit of the cab-forward body style. These vehicles were configured with the driver sitting over the front wheels. Think of the VW Type 2 Transporter pickup, for example — basically a commercial-duty VW microbus with an open bed. The layout makes the vehicles shorter because they don't have traditional front ends. The engines are mounted either in the rear, like the Transporter or Chevrolet Corvair trucks, or also tucked under the cabin, as in the A100 or the Ford E100.

Because of this layout, the A100 was only about 170 inches long. To put that into perspective, the Toyota GR86/Subaru BRZ twins are a tick under 168 inches in length and the BMW Z4 is nearing the end of its road at 170.7 inches long.

#5802. Record Demand Catches (Some) OEMs with Their Pants Down — Europe September 2026

BEVs remain in high demand in Europe, with pure electrics reaching a record 31% share last month thanks to a record 422,000 fully electric passenger cars being registered in Europe, which is not only a 63%(!) increase year over year (YoY), but is also the fastest growth rate in over three years!

Overall, plugin vehicles were up 49% YoY, dragged down by plugin hybrids, which grew only 23%, to 167,000 units, which was also a new record high for plugin hybrids in Europe, thus placing September’s total plugin volume at a best ever 590,000 units and its share at 43% (31% for BEVs only).

With BEVs pulling the market upwards, the year-to-date share for BEVs is now at 25% (36% for PHEVs and BEVs combined), which is already higher than the 2025 final result (20% BEV share, 29% adding PHEVs). This is an encouraging sign if we want to be close to 100% PEV share by the mid-2030s.

Looking at other powertrains, while petrol (18% share in September, down 21% YoY) and diesel (4%, down 28% YoY) continue their downward trend into irrelevance, the main news is the fact that we could have already passed the point of peak HEV — in September, plugless hybrids still grew, albeit less (+5% YoY) than the overall market (+10%, to 1.4 million units).

More important than that, if we compare the 34% share earned by HEVs in September 2026 with the share they had 12 months ago (36% then), we might be witnessing the beginning of plugless hybrids’ downward slope. So … if 2026 is the year of peak HEVs, how far are we from peak PHEVs?

Looking at the best sellers in several size categories, the EV push is starting to get visible. While we are far from the EV domination we see in China, things are indeed evolving in Europe.

Before, the only EVs that we saw on the overall podiums were Teslas. Now, besides those two usual suspects, the 3rd placed model in the midsize category, the Mercedes GLC, is also heavily electrified, with 59% of all its sales coming from either its new BEV model (representing 44% of its total sales) or the PHEV versions (15% of sales), leaving the ICE versions representing just 41% of total sales.

The A-segment has the Renault Twingo as the 2nd placed model. Like in China before, expect this category to be quickly electrified. Firstly, the ICE competition is shrinking. Secondly, not only do we have the Renault Twingo already on the podium, but the new Dacia Spring is set to become a success, so expect it to join the Renault sibling on the podium. As a third musketeer, the VW ID.Up is set to land sometime next year, which is another strong bet from the German brand — and nothing shorter than a podium position would do.

And even if all these competitors cannot remove the eternal Fiat Panda from the podium … then the 2028 Fiat Koala and Citroen 2CV surely will. And let’s not forget the Chinese competition, namely the future second-generation Leapmotor city car, said to be developed together with the Koala and 2CV. Not counting others, by 2028, we will have half a dozen serious candidates for podium positions in the city car category.

Looking at the other segments, the B-segment is still ICE-heavy, with none of the top 3 models having a plugin version, the C-segment is getting increasingly electrified (#1 VW Golf is 31% PHEV, #2 VW Tiguan is 32% PHEV, and #3 Jaecoo 7 is 47% PHEV).

In the full size category, electrification is also significant, with the #1 BMW 5 Series (including the BMW i5) having 74% of sales coming from either the BEV or the PHEV version; the #2 BMW X5 being 28% electrified (either with the BEV i5 or the PHEV version); and the #3 Range Rover Sport having 33% of its sales coming from the PHEV versions.

So, electrification in the D-segment is quite advanced, while the A, C, and E segments are showing good potential, with real progress being made. But the all-important B Segment is showing that it is in the laggard category.

(A note on the full size category and its importance on the European market: the best selling E-segment model was just #109 overall … which says a lot about the (in)significance of it in the larger scheme of things. True, margins are attractive, but it’s a faaar smaller market than its counterpart categories in the USA or China. The full size category represents 18% of the market in both China and the USA, while in Europe, it represents only 6%.)

Looking at September’s best selling EV models, the big news this month was Tesla winning 1st and 2nd place, and by a large margin — so much so that the #1 plus #2 win extended into the overall market! Yes, you have read that right — for only the second time ever, the other time being in December 2022, Tesla placed the Model Y in 1st and the Model 3 in 2nd on the overall market! Notice, also, BYD placing two models in the top 5. Here’s a more detailed analysis of the top 5 EVs in September:

#1 Tesla Model Y — Tesla’s midsize crossover is back in the driver’s seat, thanks to an amazing 41,987 registrations in September, a 52% increase YoY, and its best result in four and a half years! The Berlin-made crossover was the overall #1 in Germany, France, Iceland, Ireland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Norway, Switzerland, Denmark, Finland, and … maybe a few more I might be forgetting. This was its second best performance ever in Europe, only behind the 46,512-unit score of March 2023. With Model Y prices starting at €40,000, and even after six years on the market, the crossover offers an appealing package and, together with its Model 3 sibling and a few Chinese models, is reviving a lost category on the European automotive market — the midsize mainstream market. Remember a time when the Ford Mondeo, Opel Vectra, and others sold at least as much as the models of the premium Germans? Well, it seems that with their prices now starting above 50,000 euros, that has created a hole in the market, where between 40,000 to 50,000 euros you can get a lot of great midsize models (both Teslas, the Xpeng G6, the Mazda 6e/CX-6e, the Deepal S07, the BYD Seal/Seal U, the Leapmotor C10, the Zeekr 7 GT, etc.), for a fair bit less money than the German brands. Currently, you buy one of these with your wallet/head, not your heart. And that’s exactly where the market is headed. People don’t care as much about badge, they care about value. That is exactly the kind of buyer that is now searching for EVs. These people don’t want a badge, they simply want to lower their costs by switching from ICEVs to BEVs.

#2 Tesla Model 3 — Tesla’s sedan was 2nd in September thanks to 26,770 registrations, an awesome surge of 120% YoY that allowed it to be 2nd in the overall European market. Benefiting from the same tailwinds as the Model Y (mass surge in EV demand, competitive pricing, and rapid production ramp-up), the 10-year-old sedan is racing to meet soaring demand, as proven by the current 3- to 4-month waiting list. Its demand surged because price-conscious buyers are in the market and its prices, starting around €35,000, place it, a midsize sedan, in competition with models one segment below, compact hatchbacks. As of this moment, it seems Tesla’s sedan will recover its podium position in 2026, and maybe even provide a gold plus silver win for Tesla at the end of the year … which is no mean feat for a 10-year-old model wearing a body type (sedan) not popular in Europe.

#3 BYD Seal U (BEV+PHEV) — The Chinese SUV remained in the top 5 and hit a record 12,779 registrations last month, meaning that while the BYD’s star is recovering in China, thanks to its new-generation Ultra body, the old generation is still able to win medals in Europe all by itself (a bit like when veteran football/soccer players leave top leagues and semi-retire in less competitive ones…). September’s 3rd place finish was much thanks to generous discounts, but still, with the model’s development costs now well behind it, BYD can afford to go into hard discount territory with this one.

#4 Skoda Elroq — The Elroq continues surfing the BEV wave, with the 12,592 registrations representing a record result. Looking ahead, the Czech crossover will have to face fierce internal competition, as the new, smaller, and more affordable Skoda Epiq crossover is about to land. Being simultaneously cheaper and more modern than the Elroq, will the Epiq become Skoda’s new best seller at the cost of the Elroq?

#5 BYD Atto 2 (BEV+PHEV) — The Chinese make has another hit on its hands, with the small crossover scoring 11,111 registrations, mostly thanks to the new PHEV version. Why so popular in Europe? Besides not having real competition in the small PHEV category, the top range version has a 18 kWh battery, providing a usable range (90 km/56 mi). Additionally, it has increasingly important vehicle-to-load (V2L) capability. With the recent Dolphin G PHEV small hatchback using the same powertrain, expect the Shenzhen make to have another representative on the European table soon, especially considering that the new hatchback will be made in Hungary.

Outside the top 5, there were a number of record scores to mention, as would be expected in a record month.

Starting with Mercedes, we have both its representatives, the CLA EV (15th place with 7,206 registrations) and the new Mercedes GLC EV (16th place, 7,099 units) scoring record results.

Regardless of what might happen to the GLC, I am now curious to see whether the Mercedes GLC will be able to surpass to the BMW iX3’s volumes. I mean, the three-pointed-star model’s specs are a degree below the Bimmer’s, but on the other hand, it looks like Mercedes is ramping up production faster than BMW, as one can see from the waiting lists of both models (5 to 6 months for the Mercedes, around 9 months for the BMW). An example of that is that Mercedes is working its Bremen factory 24/6 to make the GLC, while BMW only now added a second shift to its Debrecen plant.

Good news also in the Kia stable: Its star player, the EV3, scored a record high, 7,385 registrations, ending the month in 11th. Even better than that, the new EV2 small crossover (it’s basically a hatchback on stilts, but anyway … marketing oblige) continues to ramp up, now reaching a record 6,458 registrations. With production still in ramp-up mode and a sizeable waiting list, the EV2 looks destined to become the automaker’s best seller in Europe.

Renault’s new baby also shined, with the Twingo rising to 10th thanks to a record 7,776 registrations. How high will the cutesy French EV go? Will 10,000 units in a month be possible?

Despite Volvo’s headaches due to battery issues that are hurting the production ramp-up of the Volvo EX60, its smaller sibling, the EX30, has given the brand something to smile about — the small crossover had its best result in two years thanks to 7,245 registrations.

Finally, a reference has to be given to the Chinese models. Besides the record performance of the #3 BYD Seal U, three other made-in-China models hit top 20 positions and record scores — the Jaecoo 7 PHEV was 13th, with 7,262 units; the Geely Starray plugin hybrid crossover was 17th, with 6,888 units; and the Leapmotor B10 was 19th, with 6,262 units. All three models are compact crossovers. And together with the BYD models, they add up to five Chinese representatives in the top 20. Something to think about….

Outside the top 20, there were records galore, so I won’t mention all of them. Instead, I will mention this:

Looking at the 2026 ranking, the big surprise was the four-position jump of the Tesla Model 3, into 2nd place.

It was to be expected that the Tesla sedan could climb onto the podium, thanks to September being a peak month for Tesla, but that it could surpass a 13,000-unit disadvantage over the (then) 2nd placed Skoda Elroq … now that was a surprise. And all of this is despite the Skoda Elroq posting a record month.

A podium position is now guaranteed for the veteran sedan, and we can even say that it is now the favorite for the 2026 runner-up spot, something few could have foreseen at the start of this year.

Just below the podium, another question is arising — will the Renault 5 be able to resist the advances of the BYD Seal U and Atto 2? As for the latter, the current distance allows Renault some peace of mind. When it comes to the former, … it will be difficult for the Renault 5 to stay ahead of the up and coming model, especially considering that the R5 has to share its factory line with several other models, like the R4, Nissan Micra, Renault Scenic, and Renault Megane, preventing it from ramping its production up further.

As for the remaining changes, the Skoda Enyaq was up one spot, to 8th, surpassing the soon-to-be-retiring VW ID.4. Will the new VW ID.Tiguan improve on the ID.4’s performance? The high point of the outgoing crossover was two 3rd place finishes, in 2022 and 2023. That’s a tall order for the new contender….

In the second half of the table, the Kia EV3 profited from its record score to jump two positions, into 14th, while the Audi Q6 e-tron and Volvo EX30 profited from their Volvo XC60 PHEV and Audi Q4 e-tron siblings’ horrible September performances to surpass them and reach the 17th and 18th positions, respectively.

Finally, a reference must be given to the deliveries of the #11 Mercedes CLA EV. It might not sound like much of a highlight, but the point here is that, historically, the CLA was a niche model for Mercedes, sandwiched between the poor man’s Mercedes A-Class and the more properly statutary Mercedes, the C-Class. As a consequence, the CLA’s overall sales in Europe were no more than 65,000 to 70,000 units per year, in a good year. With the BEV version of the CLA now above 52,000 units, and still three months to go, it won’t be hard for the CLA to beat the upper limit of the sales target this year.

Sure, neither the A-Class nor the C-Class (yet) have BEV versions to cast a shadow over the CLA, but it is a significant performance nevertheless, and with the CLA having a BEV station wagon version, that neither the A or C-classes will have, it sure looks like the CLA will continue to sell in significant numbers. Adding to its fortunes is the fact that it’s one of the most energy efficient EVs around, which allows it to post above-average range despite having average-sized batteries. Go, Mercedes CLA!

Having a quick look at the overall brand ranking, the highlights were the contrasting fortunes of Tesla (7th, up 71% YoY) and Ford (16th, down 18% YoY), as well as the usual rise and rise of the Chinese brands.

Two comments regarding the US automakers:

BYD, also known as the Chinese Toyota, ended the month in 11th, with 49,340 units, up 102% YoY. That’s ahead of mainstream staples like Dacia (12th), but, above all, MG (13th). Yep, despite having a few years of advance and also selling ICE models, SAIC’s MG is now behind BYD in Europe.

But the strength of the Chinese automotive industry is the fact that it doesn’t rely on one major OEM, but rather the diversity it offers to European buyers — China has 15 brands in Europe’s top 50! Of them, the highlights are surging Jaecoo (#22, +157%), Omoda (#27, +111%), Leapmotor (#28, +324%), and Chery (#29, 688%).

(One could say that the overall European market is growing — +10% YoY — thanks to the rise of Chinese OEMs….)

As for the plugin auto brand ranking, the leader, Volkswagen, remained in the lead, but again lost share (8.7%, down from 8.9% in August and down from 9.3% in May). Sure, it still holds a sizeable advantage over rising BYD (8.2%, up 0.2%), and its new EVs (VW ID.Polo, ID.Cross, ID.Tiguan, etc.) should help it recover some sales, but … the German brand cannot allow itself to slow down. If it does, the company will get BYD on its back real fast … in its home market. And if you can’t win at home.…

#3 BMW (6.9%, down 0.3%) is stable in the last place on the podium, but it ended the month just 100 units ahead of Tesla (6.9% share, up from 6% in August). Tesla did benefit from a higher than usual end of quarter high tide, though. This looks to be an entertaining race in the last months of the year, as BMW currently lacks models that can add significant volume that might counterweight the surging demand that Tesla is now experiencing. I mean, the iX3 alone is not enough, the new i3 sports sedan will need to ramp up fast and deliver significant volume in Q4 if BMW wants to have any chance of keeping the bronze medal in 2026.

In 5th we have Mercedes (5.8%). It is holding steady in the last position of the top 5 and even gained a little bit more distance over #6 Audi (5.3%) and #7 Skoda (5.2%).

Arranging things by automotive group, everybody lost share except BYD.

Leader Volkswagen Group lost a significant amount of share, going from 23.9% share in August to its current 23.3%. Sure, the title is more than secured, but, for 2027, the fresh metal coming soon needs to correspond with expectations if the German OEM wants to stay comfortable in the lead.

#2 BMW Group (8.4%, down 0.3%) lost a worrying amount of share, especially considering that the new 3rd placed model is a rising BYD (8.2%, up 0.2%), just 0.2% behind it. At this point, it seems all but inevitable that the Chinese OEM will end the year in the runner-up spot, as its lineup is so vast and the volume deliveries increasing at such speed that it seems BYD’s true target is not BMW’s #2 spot but … VW’s throne.

As for now-4th-placed Stellantis … the never ending slide continues (7.9%, down 0.2%). The multinational OEM’s drops seem to have no end in sight. Worst of all, in a record month when every top OEM had several models scoring record results, Stellantis had … none. The multinational conglomerate lacks a star player. It has plenty of models selling okay — some 2,000–3,000 units per month — but the company lacks a frontrunner. Will that be the next Peugeot 208? One thing is for certain: that new generation has a lot of weight on its shoulders. If it fails….

Outside the top 5, #6 Geely (6.9%, up from 6.8% in August) gained ground on #5 Hyundai–Kia (7.5%). And with 7th placed Tesla (5.9%) now showing up on the radar as well, there could be an interesting race for 6th place.

2026 has been a wild ride in the EV world.

At the beginning of the year, legacy OEMs were happy with the growth of EV share in Europe — 20% to 30% BEV growth rates were good enough to keep investments in EVs steady, investments that would be funded by their still significant ICE business.

2025 ended with only one Chinese model in the European top 20, and Tesla ended the year in 4th, behind VW, BMW, and Mercedes. For the status quo to be perfect, you only need to convince those pesky eurocrats to soften CO2 targets….

Only, on the 28th of February 2026, with US and Israeli attacks on Iran, oil prices surged and the world has changed, and with it, so has the EV world.

In many markets, fuel prices escalated and people saw their wallets grow a hole. So many people who could buy a new car went and bought a BEV, preferably one that was readily available and cheap. It was not an ego-related buy, but a necessity-related one. And that changes the game.

Added to the Chinese auto market slump that was already happening towards the end of 2025, it was perfect timing for local OEMs to launch into export markets — sending production there that was originally meant for demand at home which had gone missing.

Now focusing on Europe, the increased EV demand quickly bought whatever existing stock was available, and waiting lists quickly started to grow.

Only, many people didn’t wanted to wait several months for their new BEV, they wanted to start saving money immediately, so they turned to whoever allowed them to receive a new electric vehicle the next day.

That was the perfect timing for Chinese OEMs and Tesla, which had been seeing its sales slowly erode in the previous couple of years. Because Tesla had competitively priced BEVs and an easily scalable production structure, it managed to quickly profit from the demand surge.

So, a win for Tesla and the Chinese EV makers.

Here’s what most numbers available do not show — how their sales are now compared to a year ago. Are they surfing the EV demand wave? Here’s a sample of European results in September:

Surfing the wave — Kia (+110% YoY), Toyota (+94%), Renault (+73%).

Trying to keep up — Stellantis (+53% YoY).

With their pants down — Ford (+3% YoY), Volvo (+4%), Hyundai (0%), Volkswagen Group (+19% YoY), BMW (+12%), Mercedes (+15%).

Always interested in the auto industry, particularly in electric cars, Jose has pioneered on documenting the plug-in sales evolution through the EV Sales blog, allowing him to gain an expert view on where EVs are right now and where they are headed in the future. Extending that work and expertise, Jose was co-founder of EV-Volumes and currently works with the European Alternative Fuels Observatory on EV sales matters.

#5801. Here's What Congress Might Do on Healthcare After the Midterms

— Chances for Medicare 'doc fix' are good; not so for No Surprises Act or 340B changes

As everyone in the health policy world anxiously awaits the outcome of next week's midterms, some Congress-watchers are looking ahead to the next question: What will be on the healthcare menu when the House and Senate return after the election to finish out the year?

In part, what happens will be determined by who wins the midterms, even though the new members won't yet have taken office, according to Michael Baker, director of healthcare policy at the American Action Forum, a right-leaning Washington think tank.

"Post-election health policy productivity will depend not only on projected party control of the chambers, but also which sitting members are returning next year, and who may be expected to assume gavels in the new Congress," he wrote in an email to MedPage Today. "A prospective chairmanship or ranking membership slot may influence what policies a member or committee consider for passage in the remaining 2026 legislative days or [what they decide to] hold for action in the new year."

Any healthcare bills are likely to be attached to other "must-pass" legislation, Baker explained. "More specifically, the appropriations bills, the NDAA [National Defense Authorization Act], and the Farm Bill are all 'must-move' vehicles that could have healthcare policies attached to them."

In addition, there are some "high-profile" extenders that have already been authorized beyond this year, including Medicare telehealth authority and acute hospital care at home, he said. "The more standard extenders are all that are left. I expect these to be noncontroversial."

One area that might be considered is a "doc fix" to raise physician reimbursement rates under Medicare, Joe Antos, PhD, senior fellow emeritus at the right-leaning American Enterprise Institute in Washington, said in an email.

"Congress will be under pressure to override CMS's proposed 1%+ reduction in Medicare physician payment as well as a CMS plan to limit payment for same-day physician services," he said. "Since this is mostly just money, I can see some change included in the final budget bill."

One thing that could present more of a challenge is passing a fix to the No Surprises Act, the measure that barred patients from receiving surprise bills for getting out-of-network care at an in-network facility. Although everyone agrees that the law has achieved its main goal, the arbitration system included in the bill has been generating headaches for payers and providers.

"It's not clear what the fix is, but the current system is creating a lot of friction," Antos said.

Wendell Primus, PhD, visiting fellow at the left-leaning Brookings Schaeffer Initiative on Health Policy in Washington, and former health advisor to former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, agreed.

"No way surprise billing gets done – too big – they will do that next year," he said in an email. Instead, extenders will be the big thing, he said, adding that the "extenders package will include community health centers – at a cost of $4.4 billion."

Then there are the proposed changes to the 340B outpatient drug discount program used by hospitals; the Trump administration has proposed switching the program to a rebate program from the current configuration, in which hospitals get the discounts right away. Primus predicts a delay in any kind of fix to 340B "because [a delay] is what hospitals want."

However, he said, one surprise piece of legislation that might come into play deals with price transparency -- "maybe [with] a cost offset by doing more on drug pricing."

Baker, of the American Action Forum, pointed to the general lack of agreement on many of these issues.

"While No Surprises Act tweaks and 340B program reforms could be debated, I am not sure that there is enough consensus on the preferred solution to have them move in rapid fashion, even if attached to a must-pass vehicle," he said. "On the other hand, there are bipartisan transparency bills that have passed out of committee that could be reconciled and attached to a package, as well as [the] doc fix."

Overall, "I think the question is whether there is significant legislation that is ready to attach to a budget/reconciliation bill in December," said Antos. "Congress hasn't been at work for a long time, Democrats and Republicans have no incentive to negotiate with each other even if they did come into town, and the White House isn't pushing anything on health."

"For those reasons, I wouldn't expect new policies, and at most, there might be some fixes on existing policies that are causing problems," he said. "But small fixes, not fundamental changes."

#5800. Corvette Skidpad Grip Ranked Best To Worst Across Generations

The Chevrolet Corvette has been Detroit's answer to the European sports car for more than seventy years. Since 1953, it has gone through eight distinct generations. The idea behind the Corvette came from Harley Earl, former head of design at General Motors, who envisioned an affordable two-seat roadster that could stand beside the imports returning stateside with World War II veterans. The first Corvette shipped with a six-cylinder engine, and it was Zora Arkus-Duntov (later nicknamed the "Father of the Corvette") who pushed the car towards the V8 power it would become known for.

From there, the Corvette never stopped evolving. The front-engine layout that defined the nameplate for decades was finally abandoned when the eighth generation arrived with its engine behind the driver, a change that purists argued about — and the stopwatch quietly settled. What makes the Corvette so interesting is that it has always been judged by two audiences. One cares about straight-line muscle and badge pride. The other, which is usually more critical, cares about how a car handles when the road bends. And for a car built to take on Porsche, Jaguar, and Ferrari, that second audience matters just as much as the first — if not more.

That is where skidpad grip comes in. Measured in g-force, it shows how hard a car can corner before the tires let go of the road. This measurement largely sidesteps horsepower and driver skill (as you'll see throughout this article), instead mostly being affected by tires, suspension, and chassis balance. To keep the numbers easier to digest, this article leans on Car and Driver's skidpad, which is 300 feet across in its modern tests and 200 feet in older ones. Other testers will be relied on only where necessary.

In terms of available and credible test results online, the C7 is where the front-engine Corvette actually peaked. On Car and Driver's 300-foot skidpad, the 2015 Z06 with the Z07 package "scorched the skidpad with 1.19 g." At the time, no production car had logged a higher figure on that pad. The Z06 also managed to stop in 128 feet from 70 mph to 0, cross the quarter mile in just 11 seconds at 126 mph, and do a 0 to 60 mph run in just 2.9 seconds.

Behind that number sat a supercharged 6.2-liter V8 rated at 650 horsepower, as well as Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 ZP tires. Weight-wise, the car itself is rated at 3,558 pounds. Car and Driver also posted impressive numbers with the 2017 Corvette Grand Sport, which managed to hold 1.18 g even with 190 fewer horsepower than the Z06, showing how engine strength doesn't matter as much as other factors for grip. Braking from 70 mph took 129 feet, the quarter-mile took 12.2 seconds, and 60 mph arrived in 3.8 seconds. And the Grand Sport is only slightly lighter than the Z06, tipping the scales at 3,452 pounds.

Interestingly, the Z06's 1.19 g is also higher than anything the C8 posted in Car and Driver's tests. Even the 1,064-horsepower 2025 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 managed a curiously low 1.13 g. In other words, the C7 Z06's 1.19 g is a measurement that no other Corvette generation could match.

The mid-engine C8 had every reason to beat the C7 here. It is the newer car, it has the newer rubber, and it has more horsepower across the board. The Z06's 5.5-liter flat-plane-crank V8 makes 670 horsepower, and the Z07 package has the car riding on Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 R tires. But on Car and Driver's 300-foot skidpad, the Z07-equipped Z06 recorded 1.16 g. Chevrolet's own number for the car was 1.22 g, and Car and Driver noted that this result was "well below the company's estimate." The publication later explained that the Z07's tires had been inflated to the door-placard pressure rather than Chevrolet's lower track recommendation, potentially limiting its measured grip.

Regardless, even if we look at the rest of the lineup, the C8 failed to match the C7 in Car and Driver's tests. The non-Z07 version of the Z06 convertible hit 1.12 g, and the Stingray reached just 1.03 g. Later Car and Driver tests didn't move the number; as mentioned, the ZR1 reached 1.13 g, while the 1,250-horsepower ZR1X came in at 1.15 g. That leaves the C8 0.03 g behind the C7 Z06's result in Car and Driver's testing.

MotorTrend measured nearly the same thing in a different way. Through the 200-foot-diameter turns of its figure-eight course, the Z07 coupe held 1.16 g and the Z06 convertible achieved 1.10 g, against Car and Driver's 1.16 g and 1.12 g on a 300-foot pad. The figure-eight also shows how far apart the trims sit. The Z07 coupe lapped it in 21.9 seconds, while MotorTrend's $78,090 base Stingray needed 24.1 — the same as the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N that beat the Corvette in MotorTrend's comparison test.

Taking third place is the C6 Corvette, and the C6's best skidpad number belongs to its flagship ZR1. It actually beat the factory's own estimate here; GM put the supercharged ZR1 at 1.05 g, while Car and Driver's skidpad led to a result of 1.07 g on Michelin ­Pilot Sport PS2 tires. The same 638-horsepower beast stopped from 70 mph in 142 feet, which Car and Driver called "the shortest stopping distance we've ever recorded for a production car" at the time. (As mentioned previously in the article, the C7 Z06 would later stop from 70 mph in 128 feet.)

Car and Driver's write-up also lined the ZR1 up against pricier cars. The Lamborghini Murciélago LP640 managed 1.01 g, the Ferrari 599GTB Fiorano achieved 0.98 g, and the Aston Martin DBS went to 0.97 g. Those three were listed at $325,200, $318,045, and $266,350, while the ZR1 cost just $105,000. Another tester saw the same thing on track. At Roebling Road Raceway in Georgia, MotorWeek's test showed how good the C6 Corvette ZR1 was: the ZR1 lapped faster than any car the publication had tested there, including the Ferrari Enzo. As a result, MotorWeek called it the "ultimate production Corvette."

The rest of the C6 range sat lower in Car and Driver's tests, but they still held respectable numbers for the time. The 2006 Z06 held 0.98 g, and a Z51-equipped 2008 Corvette managed 0.95 g. The 2010 Grand Sport matched the Z06 at 0.98 g in Car and Driver's Buttonwillow comparison, though Chevrolet had claimed 1.0 g for the former. All in all, that leaves the C6 0.12 g behind the C7 Z06.

When the C5 Corvette came about in 1997, it got a new LS1 V8, a near-50/50 weight balance, and an ultra-stiff hydroformed steel frame. In terms of skidpad numbers, though, the best result belonged to the 2001 Z06. When Car and Driver tested this model, its 300-foot pad recorded 0.98 g, a figure the magazine called "one of the best we've ever seen for a production car" — a recurring theme thus far with every new generation of the Corvette (except the C8).

The 2001 C5 Z06 used a 385-horsepower LS6 V8 and had a curb weight of 3,126 pounds, with Goodyear Eagle F1 SC tires sized 265/40 in front and 295/35 in back. The rest of the C5 range wasn't too far behind, either. Every non-Z06 C5 that Car and Driver had tested by 2004 topped out at 0.90 g. Car and Driver's 1997 preview listed no skidpad figure among its own test results; the 0.92 g in its write-up was secondhand. Meanwhile, MotorTrend's test of the 2002 car (rated at 405 horsepower), recorded a "stellar" 0.99 g on its own skidpad with stability control off.

In Car and Driver's other tests, the 2005 Z51 also held 0.98 g. The 2006 Z06 matched that measurement despite carrying 120 more horsepower and weighing 21 pounds more than the 2001 C5 Z06 — which isn't surprising when considering how they both used the same Goodyear tires. That leaves the C5 0.09 g behind the C6 ZR1; in other words, a 2005 Z51 matched the 0.98 g that the C5 needed a Z06 to reach.

The earliest C4s took criticism for their engines. The Cross-Fire V8 it used was known for being underpowered, which is why enthusiasts nicknamed it "Cease-Fire." But this is another example of how grip is affected by more than just horsepower, as one of the C4's best skidpad numbers came on day one — with a caveat. In the Car and Driver's test of the Z51-equipped 1984 car, the 200-foot skidpad recorded 0.90 g, making for a favorable comparison against 0.82 g for its Porsche 928 rival. The Corvette made 205 horsepower and stopped from 70 mph in 173 feet, and its grip came courtesy of Goodyear Eagle VR50 tires.

Later tests moved to Car and Driver's 300-foot pad, where the numbers ran a tad bit lower. Despite gaining 40 horses, the 1988 Corvette held 0.87 g (with new Goodyear Eagle ZR40 tires), while the 330-horsepower 1996 Grand Sport reached 0.89 g (with Goodyear Eagle GS-C tires). To another magazine, though, the ZR-1 looked to be a bit more impressive. Road & Track measured 0.94 g for the 1990 ZR-1, and also noted the result is "bet­ter than any production-built automobile, bar none." On Car and Driver's 300-foot pad, though, none of the C4s mentioned here topped 0.89 g, which leaves the generation 0.09 g behind the C5 Z06.

The Corvette C3 was in production for 14 years, and during that time, it managed to set quite a few different skidpad numbers. The first C3 numbers here come from Car and Driver's June 1971 issue, when the publication tested four Corvettes: a 270-horsepower 350, a 330-horsepower LT1, a 365-horsepower LS5, and a 425-horsepower LS6. The LT1 topped the group at 0.80 g, and it was also the lightest of the four. That figure sits in the exact middle of the 0.75 to 0.85 g band that Zora Arkus-Duntov — who was present during the testing — gave for production Corvettes. (That LT1 350 also used the ZR1 package, and as we found when ranking every ZR1 by horsepower, the C3 version sits dead last in that comparison.)

A decade later, in March 1982, Car and Driver put a 1962 roadster and a new 1982 coupe on its 200-foot pad and referred to them as "Old Red" and "New Blue," respectively. The 360-horsepower Old Red held 0.77 g on Sears Road Handler GR78-15 tires. New Blue — with 200 horsepower, a 3,300-pound curb weight, and Goodyear Eagle GT P255/60R-15 tires – held 0.82 g. That's 0.02 g above the 1971 LT1 in separate tests despite the much lower horsepower numbers. Of course, the C4 showed up a year later and blew all versions of this generation out of the water, with its best numbers coming about 0.08 g short of its successor.

Today, we don't look at a Toyota Camry and immediately think of a sports car. But on a skidpad, a modern one can beat a 1960s Corvette — specifically a 2015 Toyota Camry V6 against a 1966 Corvette Sting Ray. Edmunds tested both on July 7, 2015, recording 0.75 g for the Camry XLE and 0.70 g for the Corvette, a car with a 300 horsepower (gross), a 3,159-pound curb weight, and 7.75-15 Firestone Deluxe Champion bias-ply tires.

The same table lists a 2015 Corvette Stingray without the Z51 package at 0.96 g. Car and Driver can't referee, as you won't find a skidpad figure in its April 1963 test of the Sting Ray, nor its May 1967 test of the 427. The 1963 panel does record a 14.4-second quarter mile at 103 mph, and the text says the independent suspension "completely transformed the Corvette in terms of traction and cornering power." Too bad it didn't include grip numbers to back up this claim.

At least MotorTrend put a number on one. MotorTrend's July 2019 tally has a 1967 427, tested in 1997, at 0.75 g – the lowest skidpad figure of any Corvette in the tally. The highest is 1.17 g from the 2015 Z06 with the Z07 package, which is the same model and package that took the crown at 1.19 g on Car and Driver's pad. The C2 does at least show up in the first two entries of our ten-car list of track-worthy Corvettes: the 1963 Grand Sport and the L88.

Welcome to 1953, a time when the Corvette actually rocked a six-cylinder engine. Built for the 1953 Corvette, the six pot in question was the 150-horsepower Blue Flame six backed by a two-speed Powerglide transmission. Although skidpad numbers are difficult to find for the 1950s era, MotorTrend at least has acceleration numbers. It timed the 1954 car to 60 mph in 11.5 seconds. The 1962 car — a four-speed with 360 horsepower — reached a figure of 5.9 seconds.

A 1962 roadster is also where the C1's skidpad number comes from, but it has a rather big asterisk attached to it. In Car and Driver's March 1982 comparison, the 200-foot skidpad recorded 0.77 g. That's the same test that gave the C3 its previously-mentioned 0.82 g. The asterisk is the tires, as the C1 used Sears Road Handler GR78-15s, not the 6.70-15 bias-plies it left the factory on. Therefore, it's reasonable to assume the C1's actual skidpad performance was worse than this.

The rest of the car's numbers put it at 3,150 pounds, 6.1 seconds to 60 mph and 238 feet to stop from 70 mph. Car and Driver called it "a nasty beast to drive anywhere near its limit," and a skidpad is nothing but the limit. It's really no surprise that the only C1 number we could find arrived twenty years after the car did. On paper, 0.77 g would edge out the C2's 0.70 g, but this measurement doesn't come from its original tires, so the C1 takes last place on this list by technicality.

#5799. AI Balloon in China Deflates by Half a Trillion Dollars

There’s been a lot of talk this year about a humongous AI bubble. We’ve written about that many times here on CleanTechnica, but focused on the US market. AI software companies have massive valuations/market caps based on hype and growth in AI use but without demonstrating anything close to profitability or a clear plan for profitability. AI hardware company growth is dependent on continued software growth, of course. Well, if it’s a bubble or a balloon, it’s still fully blown up in the US, but there’s reporting now that the AI balloon has been deflating (a lot) in China.

“A report from Reuters suggests that the AI bubble in China ‘has already burst.’ Or it might be more apt to say that it shriveled like a rapidly deflating balloon,” Futurism writes. “Over the past four months, Reuters notes, the country’s STAR50 index of AI and semiconductor companies collapsed by 40 percent, wiping out $480 billion in market value. That is not a typo.”

It seems the same thing has been happening in China with AI hype as we’ve seen in the US, and there have thus also been people over there warning of it being a big bubble. “The stock market later evolved into a speculative crazy bull,” Dong Baozhen, a fund manager in Beijing, told Reuters. “And now we see the bubble bursting.”

Of course, the robotics craze and the AI craze have been going hand in hand for the past year or two. This reporting seems to link the two.

“Shares of Unitree, China’s buzzy robotics company, have halved since the company went public in a much-hyped IPO in August,” Futurism adds. “The chipmaker CXMT, meanwhile, has lost more than a quarter of its value over the past month.”

Is this just the beginning of a much more massively deflation or popping of AI bubbles? We will see.

#5798. Steve McQueen's Ferrari 275 NART Spider Is Heading To Auction, So Start Saving Your Nickels

Many celebrities and cultural icons claim to love cars and their engineering, but they don't know the first thing about either. McQueen, though, was different.

Dubbed the "King of Cool," McQueen was a hugely talented presence on-screen and unquestionably suave off it. He also had a genuine appreciation for cars and motorcycles. McQueen competed in various levels of motorsport throughout his years and was once even a road tester for Sports Illustrated. As you can imagine, his personal garage was pretty insane, with five vehicles selling for over $1 million at major auction houses.

One of McQueen's cars, his old Ferrari 275 GTB/4*S NART Spider, is heading to auction at Gooding Christie's upcoming New York event, which takes place from November 20 to 21 at the Javits Center in Midtown Manhattan. The Spider is projected to sell for anywhere between $15 million and $20 million, which actually isn't so insane considering the most expensive car ever sold at $143 million.

Ferrari built 10 examples of the NART Spider, and this car, number six, is one of only two finished in 'Blu Sera' (Evening Blue). McQueen purchased it sometime in 1967 and made several modifications soon after, including a darker metallic blue paint finish and reupholstered seat patterns. He also added a smaller motorsport-esque rearview mirror and a quick-fill gas cap, among other things.

It was already a true one-of-one car, but following an accident along the Pacific Coast Highway, which badly damaged the front and rear, McQueen saw further opportunity to customize. He took the car to famed automotive restorer and master painter, Hershel Conway of Junior's House of Color, who flared the fenders a little further and added the 'flip tail' upward-facing rear spoiler.

Oh, and if you're wondering about performance at this point, this diminutive drop-top beauty has around 300 hp in stock form courtesy of a 3.3-liter V12. That's the Ferrari 'Colombo' V12, to be specific, which is considered by many as one of the best engines of all time. If you get the changes right on the five-speed manual shifter, you'll hit 60 mph in just 6.7 seconds and pass a quarter-mile in 14.7 seconds. Remember: this car is almost six decades old.

McQueen sold the Spider in 1971 to designer, inventor, machinist, and amateur racer J. David Kopf, who sold it to NYC's Ferrari specialist, Grand Prix SSR, in 1985. There, the team reverted the Spider to its original Blu Sera paint and completed any other vital work necessary before it found a new home with collector and tech businessman Anthony Wang. It has been with him ever since, and is believed to have only been showcased twice — once in 1996, and another time in 2003.

This car has reached mythical status, given its rarity, history, and condition. We fully expect it to reach the estimated auction price, and then some. McQueen's Porsche 917K from "Le Mans" was previously sold for ... a lot of money, as did the 1926 Excelsior Super X motorcycle he used to ride around his ranch. So, what's stopping this one from landing an eye-watering hammer price? After all, who doesn't want such a significant piece of automotive history floating around their home?
