#5797. Novel Sarcoidosis Drug Fails to Improve Steroid Dose Reduction

— Phase III trial's steroid-reduction protocol works just as well in placebo-treated patients

The novel immunomodulatory agent efzofitimod failed to reduce steroid use in pulmonary sarcoidosis, a phase III trial showed.

Monthly infusions of the fusion protein targeting the neuropilin 2 receptor had no impact on placebo-adjusted change in daily oral corticosteroid dose from baseline to 48 weeks whether at the 3-mg/kg dose (0.02 mg, 95% CI -1.49 to 1.52, P=0.98) or the 5-mg/kg dose (-0.73 mg, 95% CI -2.21 to 0.75, P=0.33), Daniel A. Culver, DO, of the Cleveland Clinic, and colleagues reported in the Lancet Respiratory Medicine.

While efzofitimod was designed as a steroid-sparing agent, the researchers found that corticosteroid tapering was possible in 40-52% of patients across treatment groups.

"[T]he data indicate that a large proportion of patients treated with corticosteroids and implementing a prescribed steroid withdrawal protocol can be managed with substantially lower doses of steroids for a period of up to 32 weeks," the researchers concluded, pointing to "mounting evidence" tying prolonged steroid use to excess morbidity and mortality.

Alternatives to corticosteroids have been hard to come by in the field, leaving them as the first-line treatment, although guidelines have relied "largely on common sense rather than high-quality evidence," noted an accompanying editorial by Marlies Wijsenbeek, MD, PhD, of the Center of Expertise for Interstitial Lung Diseases and Sarcoidosis at Erasmus Medical Centre in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

The researchers noted that "successful steroid reduction in the placebo group demonstrates that steroid reduction is unlikely to be a useful endpoint in future pulmonary sarcoidosis trials, although it could be a part of the trial design to unmask biological effectiveness of a proposed intervention."

Wijsenbeek agreed, pointing also to the recent PREDMETH and RESOLVE trials that both aimed at corticosteroid avoidance or minimization in pulmonary sarcoidosis.

"All three of these trials underscore that the door to corticosteroid reduction as (part of) a primary endpoint is closed," she wrote. "In EFZO-FIT, oral corticosteroid could be tapered irrespective of treatment group. In both EFZO-FIT and RESOLVE, the number of patients with disease relapse after oral corticosteroid tapering within 1 year was too low to be a good endpoint. Finally, PREDMETH strengthens the case for using less corticosteroids in the first place."

EFZO-FIT included 264 participants with pulmonary sarcoidosis who were randomly assigned to efzofitimod 3 mg/kg, efzofitimod 5 mg/kg, or placebo. All three groups had protocolized 16-week oral corticosteroid tapering with the target of discontinuation.

Average corticosteroid duration was 4.6 years at baseline, with 53% on a dose of 10 to under 20 mg a day (mean 10.7 mg/day) and only 38% on steroid-sparing therapies. By the primary endpoint assessment at week 48, the average dose had dropped to 2.9 mg per day across the whole trial cohort. Both efzofitimod groups had 52% of patients become steroid-free by that point, as did 40% on placebo, without a significant difference between groups.

"These data illustrate that even when guidelines advise corticosteroid tapering and steroid-sparing therapies, reality is different," Wijsenbeek said. "Besides investing in novel therapies, we should optimize and standardize how we use the existing ones first. Protocolized corticosteroid tapering seems a realistic and cheap win for many patients. This study teaches us that using simple tools as a patient global assessment numerical scale combined with investigator assessment (stable, improved, or worsened) could be easily implemented to taper corticosteroids."

Drug developer aTyr Pharma announced another planned phase III trial for efzofitimod focused on the subset of chronic, symptomatic pulmonary sarcoidosis with restrictive lung disease based on a post hoc unpublished analysis from EFZO-FIT. In patients with forced vital capacity (FVC) percent predicted ≤80% with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio, 5 mg/kg of efzofitimod yielded a "clinically meaningful" benefit in FVC and improvements in multiple patient-reported outcomes, including the King's Sarcoidosis Questionnaire (KSQ)-Lung score, compared to placebo. The primary endpoint will be FVC rather than steroid sparing.

Wijsenbeek expressed skepticism that even this endpoint would be met, as the consensus FVC response threshold of at least 10% predicted change has not been achieved in any recent sarcoidosis trial.

"Both phase II and III efzofitimod studies showed a positive effect on patient-reported outcomes. It seems a missed opportunity that these were not positioned higher in the endpoint hierarchy," she wrote.

In EFZO-FIT, efzofitimod improved health-related quality of life measures, including scores on the KSQ-Lung, KSQ general health status, and Fatigue Assessment Scale.

The drug appeared well-tolerated, according to the researchers. Serious treatment-emergent adverse event rates were similar between groups. More treatment-emergent events occurred with efzofitimod in terms of headache, sinusitis, wheezing, and increased aspartate aminotransferase. Two deaths in the efzofitimod 3-mg/kg group (one respiratory failure and one incarceration of a pre-existing inguinal hernia) were deemed not causally related to the treatment.

#5796. Boeing Once Developed A Vehicle For The Navy Called, Adorably, 'Phantom Badger'

Sometimes, people will give serious things unserious names. A velvet ant, for example, may sound like a tiny critter that's covered in the sort of material you'd find in an old Land Rover's interior, but it actually has one of the most painful stings in the animal kingdom. Then there's the panhandle hooker: though it sounds like a questionably frisky profession, it actually refers to a dangerous storm that develops in the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma.

Or how about the Phantom Badger? We'd have thought it was a mischievous weasel that has a mask-like face, but no. It's actually the name of a military vehicle that was built by Boeing, in partnership with MSI Defense Solutions, starting in 2013. The Phantom Badger was designed to assist U.S. Marine and Air Force squads with a variety of tasks, including, but not limited to, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance missions, and search and rescue.

This versatility is owed to its modular rear section, which allows the Phantom Badger to be quickly repurposed for different roles. It was also built to be easily transported in a Bell-Boeing V-22 Osprey, which is a popular aircraft used by the military.

The Phantom Badger's unclear fate makes exploring its specs even more interesting. While the Navy certified that the Phantom Badger could be transported inside a V-22, the vehicle was not selected for the U.S. Special Operations Command contract it was designed for. Records appear to show no evidence of the Phantom Badger being mass-produced for widespread military service.

As you might be led to believe, the Phantom Badger isn't powered by earthworms and vegetation. Instead, it uses a 3.0-liter multi-fuel V6 turbocharged engine producing up to 240 horsepower and 420 pound-feet of torque. Though we don't really know its 0-60 mph time, we can confirm it hit a maximum of 80 mph on paved surfaces. Its fuel tank is also big enough to provide around 450 miles of range, returning an estimated fuel economy of 21 miles per gallon.

In truth, those are respectable figures. Obviously, it's not quite as fast as a Ford GT Mk IV, the fastest American car to lap the Nürburgring, nor as comfortable as the Rolls-Royce Spectre Series II. But can either of those skip through waters up to three feet deep? We think not. Thanks to the Phantom Badger's height-adjustable suspension and 35-inch tires, not even a mountain of badgers wearing actual phantom masks could stop it.

It is both shorter than a Tesla Model S (180 inches versus 197 inches) and narrower (60 inches versus 86 inches). Now, we're not saying this thing will handle like an Integra R-swapped, left-hand drive Series 1 Lotus Elise, but its turning radius is solid at 24 feet. Staying true to its military makings, it weighs in at a beastly 7,850 pounds and boasts a 3,356-pound maximum payload.

The Phantom Badger has room for five soldiers: two at the front, two at the rear, and one in the middle. Plus, since it's an open-top vehicle, passengers aren't lacking headroom. Let's not forget that the Phantom Badger can hold a 12.7mm machine gun or a 40mm grenade launcher on its weapon mount. The rear hull sits between a pair of swivel stations too, so there are extra places for machine guns up to 7.62mm. Could the infamous honey badger have met its match with the Phantom Badger?

#5795. Mitsubishi Outlander Diamond Trail Edition Is A Great Example Of How To Name This Sort Of Thing

Toyota has Woodland, Honda has TrailSport, Subaru has Wilderness, and now Mitsubishi is getting into the off-road crossover game with what I feel like is the best suffix of them all: the 2028 Mitsubishi Outlander Diamond Trail Edition.

This will take the compact crossover's dirt prowess beyond that of the existing Trail Edition with a tweaked off-road mode for the all-wheel-drive system, a new "Rock" driving mode, and 18-inch off-road wheels with Nexen Roadian ATX all-terrain tires. That new Rock mode automatically turns on Hill Descent Control, uses brakes to minimize wheel-slip, and, Mitsubishi says, does so faster than it would in other drive modes.

A lot of the appeal of an off-road variant is in the aesthetics, and the Diamond Trail Outlander gets a blacked-out grille, darkened headlights, and redesigned bumpers front and rear, meant to improve approach and departure angles. The approach angle is now 20.5 degrees versus 18.3 with the standard Outlander, while the departure angle goes from 22.2 to 23.1 degrees.

Inside, a new water-repellent gray material can be found on the seats, held together by khaki stitching. The digital instrument cluster features a new page that shows off-road-relevant info like front-wheel steering angle, individual wheel-slip, and what the traction control is doing, while the multi-view camera system that lets you see where you should and shouldn't step can now remain on at speeds of up to 18.6 mph versus 6.2 mph in the regular Outlander.

Worth noting is the fact that Mitsubishi is debuting this car at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas next month, marking the first time Mitsubishi is making an appearance there since 2012 — to illustrate how long ago that was in Mitsu terms, the Evo X was still being made and would go on being sold for another four years. A stock Outlander Diamond Trail Edition will be on display alongside two other examples with increasingly extreme aftermarket off-road parts, and we can already hear that booth attendant unironically uttering the words, "It's amazing what a set of wheels and tires can do for these cars."

That name, though, may just be our favorite part of the whole package. Not only does it conjure up images of difficult ski hills, but diamonds actually mean something in the context of this particular brand. In Japanese, "mitsubishi" literally translates to three diamonds, as in the three diamonds that make up its logo. When it entered into a joint venture with Chrysler in 1985, that company was called Diamond-Star Motors (DSM). Mitsubishi once sold a car called the Diamante, and its in-house soccer team is called the Urawa Red Diamonds.

In other words, "Diamond Trail" is very much a Mitsubishi thing, and unlike, say, Nissan's Rock Creek, it isn't just two random outdoorsy words slapped together by some marketing people who thought they'd sound fine together. Diamond Trail also just sounds fun. Just self-serious enough, admittedly a little goofy, and very much imbuing the energy of a brand that — we say this with love — has little to lose.

In any case, Mitsubishi seemingly isn't done making Diamond Trail cars because it says this Outlander "will head a new generation of off-road-capable vehicles." As of right now, Mitsubishi only offers three other models in the U.S. that aren't the Outlander: the smaller Eclipse Cross crossover, the even smaller Outlander Sport crossover, and the Eclipse Sportback EV that's basically a rebadged Nissan Leaf. Hey, Mitsubishi, you know what'd be real cool? A Diamond Trail Edition of that cool new Pajero.

#5793. Cranberry Bogs Were Unprofitable, Then Solar Saved The Day

One of the things many people still don’t realize is how much solar power and wind power help farmers to be more profitable or to become profitable. Agriculture has never been the easiest industry, but it has been getting especially challenging to make ends meet in some parts of the world and with some types of farming. Extra income from solar farms and wind farms can make all the difference.

I don’t think I’ve ever learned anything about cranberry farming, but, apparently, they are grown in bogs in the northern parts of the US — Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and New Jersey are the three largest producers in the country, in that order, while Oregon and Washington also contribute to the market. We now have news of a couple of cranberry bogs in Massachusetts that were out of service because of financial collapse but have now been saved by solar.

“Distributed Energy Infrastructure (DEI), a leading EPC provider for utility-scale solar and storage projects, announces the harvest of two groundbreaking cranberry agrivoltaics projects: the Black Cat Agrivoltaics Project in Plymouth, Massachusetts, and the Ring Road Agrivoltaics Project in Kingston, Massachusetts. Together, these projects have produced the first-ever agrivoltaic cranberry harvests — a milestone for expanding agrivoltaic applications into challenging wetland environments,” DEI shares.

“The projects are owned by developer Greenbacker Renewables were installed by Distributed. Cranberry farmer Iain Ward, who manages the bogs, was closely involved throughout design and construction to ensure that the sensitive wetland environment remained intact.”

“Building solar projects over active perennial wetland crops was an exciting challenge, and we’re thrilled to see the success of these harvests,” says Prateek Tare, Executive Vice President and Co-founder of DEI. “Iain’s collaboration and input at every stage was essential for us to ensure a reliable, cost-effective build while safeguarding the productivity of these heritage bogs.”

The Black Cat and Ring Road cranberry bogs had been out of service for years because they were no longer financially viable. However, the solar projects brought them back to life! “The solar projects now provide the landowner with additional income through land leasing, making the bogs’ cultivation economically viable again. Iain Warde is paid for agricultural management, in addition to his income from selling the cranberry crops.”

To close, here are some details of the project:

“Both projects were finalists for the North American Agrivoltaics Awards, and both Ward and DEI are founding members of the Solar & Farming Association (SAFA). SAFA is a coalition of organizations representing the interests of the agrivoltaics industry, including developers, agricultural producers, livestock producers, and affiliated organizations.”

Agrivoltaics wins again. Farming and solar power is one of the best combos we’ve seen since someone decided to spread peanut butter and jelly together inside some slices of bread.

#5792. Can One Tire Really Do It All? 8 All-Weather Tires Compete To Find Out

Generally speaking, no one can have it all, and no one thing can do it all. That's just not how life works. And for the longest time, that was true of tires. You basically had to pick summer performance, winter performance, or disappointing so-called "all-seasons." Like with engines, though, tire technology advances, and the latest crop of all-weather tires claims to pretty much be able to do it all. But can a single tire really handle every single situation well? Our friends at Tyre Reviews compared eight of them to find out.

The newest tire in the comparison is the Continental SecureContact AW, and when it comes to premium tires, a lot of times the newest one is the best. But is that the case here? Well, Tyre Reviews put it up against Michelin's legendary CrossClimate2, the Goodyear Assurance WeatherReady 2, Bridgestone's WeatherPeak, the Pirelli Cinturato WeatherActive, the Hankook Weatherflex GT, the Falken Aklimate, and the Atturo AZ810. And while this is supposedly a Continental-focused comparison, those of you who keep a sharp eye on Jalopnik's tire coverage will recognize that this is also an important comparison test for the much-improved Bridgestone WeatherPeak.

Tyre Reviews is a YouTube channel that tests tires, then scores them in a variety of categories, weights each category based on how important it is for the comparison in question, and provides some of the best unbiased tire information on the internet. The U.S. doesn't always get every single tire Tyre Reviews tests, but we definitely get the Continental, as well as the Bridgestone. So how did they do?

In the snow handling test, well, I have some bad news for Continental and Bridgestone fans. The Michelin won. That said, the Continental came in second, and the Bridgestone placed fourth. But there's more to winter performance than snow handling, and the Continental edged out the Michelin in snow traction. There's also more to all-weather tires than winter performance, and Tyre Reviews' tests include handling, braking, and performance tests in wet conditions, as well as dry, and they measure factors like noise and rolling resistance, too.

Unfortunately for the Bridgestone, it just didn't have what it took to win this particular comparison. Or beat any of the other tires in the test. Oh, well. As for the Continental, it actually tied with the Michelin ... in first place. Each tire arrived at its first-place score differently, though, so if you want to see which all-weather tire is best for you, you're going to have to watch the video.

#5791. Westward Ho! First Trip Cross Country with Our New 2026 Tesla Model Y & Full Self Driving V14

We were headed west again for the 6th time, driving the ~1500 miles from our lake house in Northern Wisconsin to our winter home near the grandchildren in Northern Utah. We had totaled our 2019 Tesla Model 3 in an accident in May; therefore, this was our first road trip in our new 2026 Model Y running Full Self Driving V14. As usual, we were carrying two big ebikes on the back. We plan to pause in Utah at our home for a few days and then on to Portland, Oregon, and the Pacific Ocean.

The experience was quite different this time because of the new car and the significant upgrade to Tesla’s driving automation: Full Self Driving Supervised V14.3.12.

As we approached our first Supercharger in Wausau, Wisconsin, it looked like the navigation was taking us the wrong way. However, once we got to our normal exit, it was closed. We had to drive a few miles beyond it, do a U-turn, and come back. It cost us roughly an extra 5 miles. I’m going to have to learn to trust the navigation. The Nav knows about road closures like this and even traffic jams. Unfortunately, it doesn’t explain ahead of time why it is suggesting an alternate route.

Our first stop was at the Wausau, Wisconsin Supercharger next to the Hilton Gardens Inn on highway NN. In 7 years, we’ve never seen more than a few cars charging there. For the first time, the charging station was full (see photo below). It was Sunday after a big fall-colors week in Northern Wisconsin and many tourists were headed home. On our screen, it gave a charger wait time of five minutes. As we drove the last 100 miles to Wausau, our computer screen alternated between showing an unspecified wait time and as many as two stalls open.

When we arrived, it listed two stalls as open, but, in fact, for nearly the first time across the last seven years that we’ve been Supercharging, all eight stalls were full. However, here’s the good part: within less than five minutes, one of the cars pulled out and we were able to back into the empty stall. Then, the bad part: it was the slowest charge we’ve ever experienced. It was an older V2 hardware Supercharger where you need to share charging with the adjacent car. That meant that we were charging at only a 50-kilowatt speed for the whole charge. The total charge took about 40 minutes. However, after the bathroom break and walking our small rescue dog, Zuni, we only needed to kill about 15 minutes before setting off again.

The next stop was Menomonee, Wisconsin, halfway to Minneapolis and the charger was showing three empty stalls. Since, as I mentioned, we were traveling on a Sunday, a beautiful day, with full fall colors in the Northwoods, we found another Supercharger that appeared to be full (see below), but there was one stall empty and we pulled in. When we came east in mid-May, there were seldom more than one or two cars in any of the 12 Superchargers en route.

The Menomonee Supercharger has a newer Hardware 4 charger, so we were charging faster, at almost 100 kW during our whole charge. As we pulled out, there were about three cars waiting, but the line moved quickly. No one had to wait more than a few minutes. Then we were on our way to Minneapolis.

About 20 miles east of Minneapolis, crossing the Saint Croix River on the border between Wisconsin and Minnesota, half the lanes of the bridge were shut down. The navigation took us on a town of Henderson detour going on highways U and UU, then back onto the I-90 route across the bridge. It probably saved time avoiding the worst of the traffic backup because of the closure on the bridge. Then we were on an east–west route right through the center of Saint Paul–Minneapolis. Full Self Driving V14 with Tesla navigation found its way through the big city freeways perfectly.

As we left the Minneapolis Supercharger, we couldn’t get Full Self Driving to work! It said “FSD Temporarily Unavailable.” However, temporarily lasted for a very long time. We went through a long troubleshooting process with Ara (the Grok bot) and with Tesla Customer Service on the phone. Not only did FSD fail to work, but it was reporting a speed limit of 15 mph when the actual speed limit was 65 mph. First, we stopped, put the car in park, and did the two-scroll button reboot. No luck. Then we were instructed to use the menu to reboot the car. No luck. Then we tried to recalibrate the cameras as suggested, but it was nighttime and the calibration wouldn’t finish. Not only was FSD not working, but smart cruise control also failed to operate. However, after partial re-calibration of the cameras, it did restore smart cruise control.

On day two of our cross-country trip, we left Worthington in the southwest corner of Minnesota on I-90, passing through a huge wind turbine field (see below) with hundreds of turbines on the north side of the road just as we got into South Dakota.

A short time later, we saw a wind turbine tower factory with hundreds of turbine tower sections laid down as you see in the photo.

As we began our drive through South Dakota we had smart cruise control, but no FSD.

The first Supercharger stop in South Dakota was at Murdo. I went into the pharmacy in the adjacent supermarket and bought some medical tape and taped over the back camera. I did this because we found that, with our older car, strangely, taping over the back camera was the only way to get full FSD to work with bikes on the back.

We restarted the camera celebration, which had failed the night before in the dark. This time we observed the little gray steering wheel icon in the upper-left-hand corner of the screen. A blue circle starts at the bottom around the icon, and it progresses all the way around to indicate that the calibration is in progress. However, when it was almost complete, it started over at the halfway point. It oscillated back and forth a few times for almost an hour before it finally completed the calibration and we got FSD back! We had lost FSD for the better part of two days of our 1500-mile trip. Since we pay $99/month for FSD, will Tesla give us a refund?????

Our stop in the middle of South Dakota was at the Supercharger in Wall, home of the famous Wall Drugstore. See my wife and our Tesla with the bikes at the Supercharger in the photo below.

We charged in Wall, South Dakota, and drove another 80 miles to the wildlife loop at Custer State Park. There, “we ran with the bulls” — I mean, we ran with the bison (buffalo). We were driving right in the middle of a big bison herd, as you see in the photos below.

My wife spotted hundreds of pronghorns on our trip west, and the visit to Custer State Park would not be complete without seeing one, as well as feeding and petting the donkeys.

We made it by 8:00 pm to the tiny town of Lusk, Wyoming, where a four-stall Supercharger is across the street from the Pioneer Best Western where we spent the night. The next morning, we were in eastern Wyoming, where we were following double railroad tracks used to ship coal from the huge, high-quality, low-sulfur coal deposits in northeast Wyoming to power plants farther east.

“Coal Area — The Powder River Basin spans over 1,000 square miles, making it one of the largest coal-producing regions in the US,” Google shares. “Depth of Coal Beds — Coal beds in the region can be as thick as 250 feet, with only 120 feet of soil overburden.”

The photos below show one of the unit coal trains bringing coal from the Powder River Basin as we passed. Clean power is on the rise, but coal is still an important part of electrical generation in the United States.

Powder Basin coal is also going to the Dave Johnson power plant in eastern Wyoming that we passed. It is an 817 MW plant that was scheduled to shut down next year (2027). However, the Trump administration has “rescued” it and it won’t shut down or be converted to gas for at least a couple more years.

On the third day of our trip, FSD was working and we stopped to charge at Evansville near Casper, Wyoming. Then we passed Devils Gap, Independence Rock, and the pioneer handcart company memorial on our way to Rawlins. At Rock Springs, I left my wife at the TJ Max while I charged at the Tesla Supercharger 100 yards away. The final charger was in Evanston, Wyoming, and then we crossed the Utah border and passed Park City, Heber, and drove down Provo Canyon to our winter home in Lindon just north of Provo (30 miles south of Salt Lake City). It took three 500-mile days to make the trip.

Summary: Our new 2026 Tesla Model Y seemed to charge a little slower than our old Tesla Model 3 Long Range. However, it appeared to have longer battery range. This meant that we could often travel as fast as 80 mph, whereas previously we never exceeded 75 mph and occasionally had to slow down as low as 60 mph to make the next charger — in our old Model 3 with the bikes on the back. FSD was a pleasure, keeping the car precisely in the middle of the lane, passing cars, and returning to the right-hand lane just as I would do myself … except when FSD failed to work for a big part of two days during the trip. I’m 86, and it was a strain keeping the car centered in the lane and keeping a foot on the accelerator when FSD wasn’t working.

#5790. 7 Luxury Vehicles From Throughout History That Used 4-Cylinder Engines

Luxury cars can differ massively from one another, but most of us make similar assumptions when describing the term "luxury car." We picture leather seats, 20-plus-inch chrome wheels, full-size silhouettes, and big displacement engines with a lot of cylinders. However, every once in a while, automakers mix things up a little and throw in an ingredient you might not expect. Four-cylinder engines are one such ingredient, and they found themselves in luxury cars from an assortment of automakers, spanning across what is almost the entire history of the automobile so far.

We're talking Fiats from the turn of the 20th century, British executive sedans produced by Rover in the late '60s and early '70s, hybridized BMW 5 Series sedans, Range Rover SUVs, and more. What's interesting here is that, for the most part, all of these cars were and are considered successes, with rare exceptions (Facel Vega Facellia, we're looking at you), which suggests luxury car buyers aren't actually all that hung up on the engine under the hood. Without further ado, here are our seven four-cylinder luxury cars, in chronological order.

Today, Fiat busies itself with budget-oriented and retro-themed compacts mainly, such as the seemingly evergreen 500, plus its new and immensely cute Panda Grande. Wind the clock back just over 120 years to 1905, though, and Fiat was a very different automaker. It was at this point that it debuted its 60 HP model to rival equivalent models from Mercedes. This thunderously powerful car was powered by a 647-cubic-inch inline-4 with dual-chain drive and a four-speed manual transmission. A 60-horsepower inline-4 might not sound like much at all by today's standards, but in vintage car circles, this Fiat is sometimes considered to be the original supercar.

The Fiat 60 HP had a split personality, designed to be capable both as a road-going vehicle and indeed as a racer, with removable wings and advanced cooling systems. It was also mightily expensive, commanding a $13,500 price tag in 1905, while the sole surviving example also wears a $4,000 coachbuilt touring body.

The craftsmen responsible for the body used only the finest materials available, including aluminum panels, silver solder to cover and hide fastening points, and brass mouldings to disguise the seams of the wooden framework. As for the interior, it was about as luxurious as one could expect for a car of this era, with leather seats and mohair floor mats. Remember, just owning a car in the early 20th century was a mind-boggling luxury, let alone one of this caliber.

There is much that could be said about the Facel Vega Facellia that is wholly negative, but for a car so imposing and bold in design, that seems unfair, so we shall begin with its stronger points. Facel Vega knew how to do style and opulence quite well, and although the Facellia was its entry-level model, this experience is still luxurious. It was poised as an excellent alternative to Mercedes' SL series, or indeed an equally charming Alfa Romeo of the same era. Inside, the expected amenities are all there in the form of leather seats and numerous gauges set into a hand-painted woodgrain-effect dashboard. On the outside, there is plenty of brightwork to enjoy, and the Facellia shares much in common stylistically with its bigger brother, the HK500.

However, what it sadly doesn't share with the HK500 is its hulking great Chrysler V8. Instead, the Facellia sported a notoriously unreliable French unit – a 115-hp 1.6-liter inline-4. It suffered from overheating issues, fragile internals, and troublesome chromed cylinder liners, which resulted in the majority of cars experiencing engine failure within the first six months of ownership. Facel Vega had no choice but to replace these engines free of charge, but those second engines didn't prove much better either. A final resolution came in the form of a genuinely bulletproof Volvo lump, but by this point, the firm's reputation was in the gutter, and the Facellia would ultimately prove a hurdle too high for the automaker.

This is a far more conventional offering than the other two covered so far. It replaced the aging P4 model in 1963, and production continued until 1977, so it was clearly a popular choice. With it, Rover successfully filled a notable gap in the UK's car market, where simple commuter cars generally sat at or below 1.5 liters in displacement, while large luxury models sported 3.0 liters or more. With its 2.0-liter inline-4, the P6 could jump between the two segments, offering a premium executive model that cost less than the larger luxury products.

Numerous engine options were offered throughout the model's life, including a twin-carb variant of the 2000, a 3.5-liter V8, and a 2.2-liter version of the 2000, which never made it onto U.S. shores as it arrived after Rover had withdrawn from the U.S. market in '71.

It might not have taken off well in the U.S., but with 322,302 examples sold throughout its life, the P6 was certainly anything but a failure in other markets. One key to its success was sublime handling, which was on par with sports cars of the era and at its best in the four-pot models, alongside a well-equipped cabin. Inside, plush leather seats provide impressive comfort, the steering wheel is adjustable, and faux-wood trim completes the look.

The 5 Series might not be the most opulent sedan BMW makes -– that accolade goes to the 7 Series, which also sported an inline-4 in certain global markets — but it's absolutely still a luxury car from a premium brand. Historically, the 5 Series usually sported a mix of six- and eight-cylinder engines, although a smattering of four-pots have also made their way under its hood. In fact, the first 5 Series (E12) debuted with an inline-4 way back in 1972, offering 115 and 130 hp. The U.S. never received the four-cylinder E12, though, and it would take several generations before a so-powered 5 Series found its way onto American shores.

For the 2012 model year, the F10 5 Series' naturally aspirated 3.0-liter inline-6 was replaced with a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4, which delivered 240 hp – identical to that of the inline-6 it replaced. However, real-world performance highlights that the smaller lump is the better performer thanks to additional turbocharged torque, earning it both a 0 to 60 mph and quarter-mile time roughly half a second quicker than the six-cylinder-powered variant.

Since then, four-cylinder engines have been a staple member of the 5 Series lineup, with such engines appearing in subsequent G30 and G60 generations, albeit alongside the usual smattering of larger mills. Those latter two generations use the B48 engine, a fuel-sipping four-cylinder that yields solid mpg, and options like these are only becoming more common in modern luxury cars.

The Velar arrived for the 2018 model year as a compact luxury crossover with a sleeker silhouette than the firm's usual offerings. Right from the get-go, it was offered with a fairly gutless 247-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4, and that option stayed, following on from a mild makeover for the 2024 model year Velar. It was also offered with a 180-hp turbodiesel inline-4, although that choice had fizzled out by 2020.

Regardless of the somewhat lackluster base engine options, the Velar is still every bit a luxury vehicle. Ever since a 2021 update, the model has boasted clever tech, such as active noise-cancellation technology and an enhanced air filtration system, plus all the typical goodies one might expect to find within a premium SUV. Even on the base models, heated and perforated leather seats are standard, as is a panoramic sunroof, while higher trim levels introduce larger 21-inch wheels, a Meridian sound system, plus cooled seats.

While opting for a 247-hp Range Rover might seem a little uninspiring, not every buyer is going to be chasing a higher-output engine in such a vehicle. Some will be happy to take the very nearly $10,000 discount in choosing a P250 instead of a six-cylinder P400, perhaps if it's to be predominantly used in cities or on school and grocery runs rather than highway commutes.

The four-cylinder C63 wasn't exactly a monumental excess, proving that downsizing can go too far, and upsetting purists and AMG enthusiasts by swapping out the thunderous V8s on which Mercedes' tuning arm built its reputation. As such, Mercedes-AMG is now killing the four-cylinder C63 in favor of an inline-6 C53, but on paper, the old four-cylinder car still got so much right.

Taking care of motivation is a boosted 2.0-liter inline-4, which works alongside an electric motor to produce a combined 671 hp — enough grunt to see it take the claim as the quickest production C-Class ever built. According to Car and Driver's testing, it can reach 60 mph in 2.9 seconds, 100 mph in 7.1 seconds, and cover the quarter-mile in just 11.2 seconds on its way to a 174-mph top speed. It does all this while still not ignoring the usual smattering of luxurious extras and options the tri-pointed-star brand is famed for.

Heated and optionally ventilated nappa leather seats accompany carbon-fiber trim, while a 15-speaker Burmester sound system is the standard affair. Buyers enjoy a panoramic sunroof as standard, along with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connectivity options. There's very little the C63 doesn't boast, in honesty, but that's surely what any buyer of a near-$90,000 C-Class should expect.

Lexus is the luxury arm of Toyota, and its models all boast plenty of premium features while also packing famous Toyota reliability — a trait often misplaced by its German competitors. The two brands share much with one another, including platforms and powertrains, and the 2027 NX 350h is no exception. The crossover shares its platform with the Toyota RAV4, and is offered in both front- and all-wheel drive. The former sports a naturally aspirated 2.5-liter inline-4 in addition to a pair of electric motors, while the latter boasts a trio of motors. In both instances, the combined output is a healthy 244 horsepower, and that oomph is channeled toward the wheels via a CVT.

It's no performance car, nor is it trying to be one, but with 0 to 60 mph times below seven seconds and a top speed of 124 mph, it's certainly peppy enough for most applications. Those with a hankering for more could always opt for the plug-in hybrid variant, which too boasts an inline-4 and a number of electric motors, but with a combined output of 324 hp. Details such as perforated leather seating, open-pore wood trim, 20-inch alloy wheels, and ambient lighting ensure the NX delivers a premium experience and help to differentiate it from its humbler Toyota roots. The NX Hybrid says the quiet luxury part out loud, but in our testing, it proved to be a genuinely enjoyable and comfortable luxury companion — inline-4 included.

#5789. Patrick Stewart's Death Highlights Lewy Body Dementia

— The actor faced "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia

Patrick Stewart, the classically trained stage actor known for his roles in the "Star Trek" franchise and "X-Men" films, died at age 86, his family announced Thursday.

His death followed what his spokesperson called "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia.

Stewart's diagnoses had not been previously disclosed, the Associated Press reported.

Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia in the U.S., affecting more than 7 million Americans. Lewy body dementia is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia in the country, affecting more than 1 million people.

"Lewy body dementia is more common than many people realize; however, it is often overlooked or mistaken for Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease," Michael Okun, MD, of the University of Florida Fixel Institute in Gainesville, told MedPage Today earlier this year.

"Awareness matters because recognizing the diagnosis early can change care, safety, and quality of life for families," he added.

Lewy bodies are abnormal clumps of alpha-synuclein, which is also associated with Parkinson's disease. Lewy body dementia is an umbrella term that includes two disorders: dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia. No single test can diagnose Lewy body dementia in living people.

Symptoms of Lewy body dementia can include memory and problem-solving deficits, hallucinations and delusions, slow or rigid movement, balance problems, sleep disorders including restless leg syndrome and dream enactment, anxiety and depression, and autonomic dysfunction. Loss of smell is often an early sign.

Because these symptoms overlap with those of other neurodegenerative disorders, Lewy body dementia can be difficult to diagnose. The process can be frustrating for patients and families, a challenge Susan Schneider Williams described in a Neurology essay about her husband, actor and comedian Robin Williams, who developed Lewy body disease and died by suicide.

"One of my early research studies involved interviewing former caregivers of individuals with dementia with Lewy bodies and asking them about the last 3 months of life," Melissa Armstrong, MD, MSc, also of the University of Florida, told MedPage Today. "I was surprised when -- even though the questions were about the end of life -- over a third of interview participants started by talking about how misdiagnosis, delays in diagnosis, or conflicting diagnoses remained important parts of their experiences."

Several factors might explain this, Armstrong noted. "Some key clues, like dream enactment, might be missed," she said. "Some clues, like hallucinations, might be misattributed to other issues like a psychiatric diagnosis -- for example, schizophrenia. Dementia with Lewy bodies requires clinicians to put a bunch of different pieces together. That can make the diagnosis more challenging."

Complicating the problem is the fact that abnormal alpha-synuclein and Alzheimer's pathology can co-exist, which may affect outcomes. About 30% to 60% of Alzheimer's autopsy cases show concurrent alpha-synuclein pathology in brain tissue.

"When families hear 'Lewy body dementia' for the first time, many say something like 'we knew something was different.' The combination of memory, movement, sleep, and behavioral symptoms can be confusing," Okun said.

"Lewy body dementia is not rare in older adults," he added. "We need better recognition, better tools, and more conversations about symptoms like hallucinations, dream enactment, and fluctuating thinking."

Reporting from the Associated Press contributed to this story.

#5788. These 4 Gas Discounts Can Fill The Void Kroger Left In Your Heart

Saving money on gas and groceries is an everyday struggle, but if you're lucky enough to get both at the same location, hurrah! One less place on that list, though, is Kroger, whose store-branded credit card lost its automatic discounts at the pump. This stemmed from Kroger and U.S. Bank parting ways.

To quote an old proverb: "When elephants fight, it is the grass that suffers." In this case, the stomped-on grass is credit card holders. As for the elephants, U.S. Bank, the now-former issuer of its Kroger Rewards World Elite Mastercard, switched to a cash-back Visa, and Kroger is now bedfellows with First Bank & Trust, yet confusingly did not file a post-divorce name change for its rewards credit card.

Cardholders of the U.S. Bank version previously received 2% cash back when shopping at Kroger, 1% elsewhere, and 5% on their first $3,000 spent through mobile wallet purchases. The biggest prize, however, was the automatic 5-cent-per-gallon discount at Kroger gas stations. First-year cardholders, and those who spent $6,000 a year on the card, got 25 cents off instead when redeeming fuel points. But poof, that's gone now. No more real-time card discounts. Granted, the 5 cents off was a credit card-only bonus, and although Kroger's store program also changed, fuel discounts at Kroger aren't completely off the table. You just have to be a bit more clever to earn them.

Because U.S. Bank-Kroger Mastercard holders need to apply for the new First Bank & Trust-Kroger ones, they risk carrying two credit cards. But there are other ways to save money on gas so you don't need either one.

The Costco Anywhere Visa by Citi will snag you 5% cash back at Costco-branded gas stations, and a respectable 4% back at other eligible fuel centers and EV chargers. But once you spend $7,000 in combined fill-ups in a year, the returns diminish to only 1%. The Sam's Club Mastercard is more flexible with 5% cash back on fuel and EV charging purchases, regardless of brand. But its threshold maxes out at a lower $6,000 per year. Then, like Costco, the discount is 1%.

Walmart has a OnePay CashRewards card that pays Walmart+ members 5% back at Walmart. Walmart+ membership itself gets you 10 cents off a gallon at participating store gas stations and partner brands like CITGO and Exxon, plus the wholesaler's member gas price at Sam's Club. Non-Walmart+ cardholders don't receive an at-the-pump discount but still get 3% cash back at Walmart, including its gas stations. Go elsewhere and the discount is 1.5%. Target fans get fuel savings, too. Despite Target not having gas stations or fuel partners, the Target Circle Mastercard still offers 2% cash back on all gas purchases.

Regional supercenter chain Meijer also has branded gas stations as well as a store credit card and co-branded Mastercard. Cardholders of either don't receive a flat rate cash-back percentage. Instead, you get $10 back every $750 spent, which is a middling 1%, but do snag a 10-cent-per-gallon Meijer-only gas discount. Some of Albertsons Companies' regional chains, like Albertsons and Safeway, have branded gas stations alongside their grocery stores. But all Albertsons Cos. stores offer a co-branded American Express card with an everyday 3% gas cash back, no matter where you fuel up.

Want to cut ties with Kroger accounts altogether but not lose out on cheaper fuel prices there? Simply use another cash-back credit card, one that you probably already have in your wallet.

Banks, from nationwide behemoths to regional chains, offer cash-back credit cards, and with no annual fee to boot. Bank of America has a few, including one with a sign-up bonus of 6% cash back in the first year, up to $2,500 per quarter. This applies to one category of your choice, such as gas and EV charging. Wells Fargo's deal is 2% back but with no categories to monitor.

And U.S. Bank's Smartly Visa, which replaced the grocer's branded card, offers a 2% return on all purchases, but the cash-back percentage rises with the balance you keep in deposit accounts, up to 4% on qualified balances of $100,000 or more. With that, you can probably tap to pay for a new Toyota 4Runner, but your credit score and interest rate will be a separate matter.

Even non-cash back credit cards offer gas savings, too. Banks and retailers are polyamorous. They both want to be involved in your spending, including how and where you buy. So, check your credit and debit cards for any incentives or bonus offers. They usually need to be formally activated, but chances are you'll find handsome rewards for fueling up at specific brands and locations, including Kroger.

Don't want more credit cards or to sign up for yet another customer loyalty program? There's an app for that! GasBuddy is a car-related app you can't live without. It offers plenty of money-saving tools online like gas price heat maps, but its app is where the sweet savings are. Its integrated GasBack marketplace lets you buy everything from apparel to parking, and qualified purchases earn either a lump sum credit or up to 10% back. When your balance reaches $5, you can cash out or exchange your earnings for gift cards. Wanna save more, like up to 33 cents off a gallon? You'll have to sign up for the Pay with GasBuddy+ card.

However, never mind its Mastercard logo; the Pay with GasBuddy+ card is not a credit card. Instead, it's connected to your bank account with payments made via ACH. The card includes a 3- or 5-cent-per-gallon discount, depending on the station, and adds up to 25 cents off through bonuses. Plus, every $25 spent on non-fuel purchases in convenience stores will net an additional 3-cent discount. When stacked, the per-gallon savings tops out at 33 cents.

Other popular shopping apps that offer money back for fuel stops are Checkout 51, Fetch Rewards, and Upside. Checkout 51 requires users to upload receipts, which earn cash back that can be cashed out via third-party payment methods like PayPal. Fetch also uses a receipt-based system but redemptions are only via gift cards.

Less complicated is Upside. No receipts needed. Just select a discount offer in the app, make a purchase, and the cash back is deposited into your account. Your earnings don't expire as long as your account stays active.

Of course, the gas brands themselves offer fuel discounts, too. Sure, we'd like Big Oil to just set affordable prices no matter what, but sometimes gas costs have more to do with what the feds are doing than the fuel companies.

Anyway, while cash back offers are nice, you still have to wait for the reward. More satisfying is paying a lower price from the get-go. And pretty much every gas brand has a loyalty program, from bigwigs like Chevron Texaco, Shell, and ExxonMobil to road trip familiars Love's Travel Stop and Pilot Flying J.

Chevron members earn 5 points per gallon toward future discounts, while Exxon rewards by fuel type. Premium earns 6 cents a gallon in points while all other gas octanes and diesel net only 3 cents. Shell has a tiered system as well but it's based on fill-ups, with Platinum members receiving 10 cents off per gallon.

Popular convenience stores that also happen to have gas stations, such as 7-Eleven, Circle K, and Casey's, offer savings as well. Along with a free Slurpee every July 11, 7-Eleven gives members a minimum 5-cent-per-gallon discount. There are special promotions, too. Circle K has similar bonus days that cut the per-gallon price by up to 40 cents. Keep in mind that despite the freebies and fuel, these famous chains don't always sell additive-rich Top Tier-rated fuel, which is said to be cleaner gas for your engine.

If you'd rather stay loyal to Kroger, here's some good news: shortly before parting ways with U.S. Bank, Kroger updated its Fuel Points perks. The loyalty program is now simply called Points, reflecting the plan's flexibility to reward customers with more than just cheaper fuel. With a Kroger Points account, every $1 spent earns one point, but qualifying purchases and special bonus events can double or quadruple that earnings rate. Additionally, Kroger Boost or Boost Essential members can earn twice the points on most purchases all the time.

A minimum of 100 points is required for redemption, but values differ between store buys and gas purchases. For fuel, 100 points converts to 10 cents off per gallon, with a maximum discount of $1 per gallon. For food, that same 100 points will save you $1 at checkout in-store or online, up to $10 per day.

Kroger Points can be redeemed at any of the grocer's 1,232 stores located in 16 states, and then some. Parent company, The Kroger Co., operates more than 2,700 stores nationwide, including regional grocery chains like Ralphs, Smith's, Harris Teeter, and Pick 'n Save, to name a few. Among its brands, The Kroger Co. manages more than 1,700 gas stations. Fuel partners, such as Shell, will also accept redemption of Kroger Points. Yet, not all Shell locations participate in Kroger's program, and partnering fuel brands do vary by region. Check the app or website's store locator feature first, which can be filtered to show fuel-only locations.

All things considered, what Kroger taketh away, you can easily get back. Stick with Points, bring your own savings hack to Kroger gas stations, or simply fuel up somewhere else.

#5787. New York officials share OUD treatment progress, plans for new pilot to treat stimulant use disorder

New York officials share OUD treatment progress, plans for new pilot to treat stimulant use disorder" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Two years after federal regulations permanently adopted greater flexibility for medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD), New York experts convened to discuss the benefits and challenges of take-home medications.

The annual COMPA Symposium, which was also livestreamed, was hosted by the Coalition of Medication-Assisted Treatment Providers and Advocates, a nonprofit membership organization in New York. State officials also discussed how to prevent interruptions to OUD services amid coming Medicaid eligibility and work requirement changes as part of H.R. 1.

Chinazo Cunningham, M.D., a commissioner of New York’s Office of Addiction Services and Supports (OASAS), presented on the successes the state has had thus far in expanding OUD treatment access.

“People of color in the state of New York are dying [at] the highest levels,” Cunningham began, adding that the good news is that Black New Yorkers had the largest reduction in overdose deaths from 2023 to 2025. Part of that is thanks to flexible dosing, first introduced during COVID-19 and made permanent by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) in 2024.

This flexibility has both pros and cons, highlighted by a separate clinical panel. Allowing patients to take vital MOUD home acknowledges various social determinants that present barriers to arriving in-person on a regular basis for treatment, speakers agreed. At the same time, some cases call for extra caution, like if a patient is unstable and may be using while in treatment.

“The safety of methadone—it is a medication that we have to be very careful with,” Brett Palmer, P.A.-C, an outpatient physician assistant, said during the clinical panel. There is real risk of diversion, which patients sometimes even own up to, he said. Thus, take-home allowance “is a frequent discussion” and requires strong judgment on the part of counselors.

Myra Mathis, M.D., medical director at Strong Recovery, a certified community behavioral health clinic and opioid treatment program (OTP) in Rochester, praised the new rule while acknowledging its drawbacks. “I think it’s a positive change that medication access is no longer tied to therapy requirements,” Mathis said. But taking home MOUD also means some patients will fall behind on therapy.

To help address this, Strong Recovery added a new role of engagement specialist, whose job is to track and identify disengaged patients who have not attended individual or group therapy in three months. They can then opt into a “dispensing-only” track. That program takes into account special considerations, like access to Narcan for unstable patients and other harm reduction supplies. Patients in the track also need safety planning and screening for suicidality. The specialist meets with them at least once quarterly, which helps the program meet its billing requirements.

The state has been making progress on MOUD access and uptake across a variety of settings.

There are currently 140 outpatient methadone programs in New York. “I’m so proud of that,” Cunningham said. As the drug market continues to rapidly evolve, with fentanyl and other powerful opioids, “the role of methadone has never been more important.

Also across the state, 41 prisons and 58 jails offer all forms of MOUD. These institutions are notoriously difficult to get treatment into. Fewer than half of jails offer MOUD nationwide.

“When you’ve seen one jail, you’ve seen one jail,” Cunningham said, explaining that every county and sheriff has a different mindset. But thanks to state and community partners, MOUD access is now widespread. “There is no other state that even comes close to this,” Cunningham said.

From 2022 to 2025, the number of people receiving MOUD in New York prisons increased 7x, and those starting MOUD for the first time increased 360x. The increase was largely driven by buprenorphine access, though even the number of people on methadone doubled. In jails, from 2022 to 2024, there has also been progress. The number of people enrolled in MOUD tripled, with buprenorphine making up the bulk of MOUD use in 2024 (83%).

“Individuals who are incarcerated have among the highest rates of overdose deaths,” Cunningham said, at over 100x the risk compared to the general population. Black and Hispanic New Yorkers, who have among the highest overdose deaths in the state, are also incarcerated at much higher rates. MOUD provision in jail settings has been shown to decrease overdose risk upon release.

A big focus of Cunningham’s presentation was stimulant use disorder, which slightly more Americans have than opioid use disorder. The condition has no FDA-approved medications. “It can be frustrating for providers and programs to provide treatment,” Cunningham said. New York’s approach is to pilot a treatment modality known as contingency management, which provides incentives to reinforce positive behavior change.

“Contingency management has been studied for decades around drug use, and it’s definitely known to be effective,” Cunningham said. The reason it’s not widely used is “implementing it in the real world is very difficult.” Cunningham led a seven-year-long NIH-funded study on the modality, and even with a large annual budget, she struggled to pull it off.

The pilot in the state will begin with eight outpatient non-OTPs, set to launch next month and run for 18 months. For 12 weeks, patients with primary stimulant use disorder will come to the clinic twice a week, several days apart, and get toxicology urine testing on the spot. If it is stimulant-negative, they will get a gift card of about $15. After 12 weeks, they will come in once weekly for another 12 weeks. The financial incentive will build over time, up to $750, as allowed by SAMHSA. If they miss an appointment or relapse, the incentive restarts at $0.

“Decades of data show this is the most effective treatment for stimulant use disorder,” Cunningham reiterated. If the pilots work well, “then the goal is to really expand this statewide.”

Some regulatory changes have helped make this treatment more feasible. SAMSHSA used to cap the financial incentives at $75, not nearly enough to drive behavior change, Cunningham said. The state can also use an 1115 waiver to get reimbursed for contingency management care, though its current waiver expires in March 2027. Its renewal request is under review.

Up to a million New Yorkers on Medicaid will be subject to new work requirements under H.R. 1 changes.

Trisha Schell-Guy, director of the Division of Program Development and Management in the Office of Health Insurance Programs, presented on the ways the state is preparing to minimize coverage loss.

There are three ways to meet the new requirements in New York. A household could have an income of at least $580 a month. A member could complete 80 hours of an approved activity in a month. Or it could be a combination of the two. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, new applicants must show compliance with the new requirements for the month before they apply. Existing members face renewal dates in March.

Certain groups are exempt from the work requirements, Schell-Guy noted, due to age or a certain condition. Groups like American Indian/Alaska Native people and foster care youth are also exempt. Additionally, there are short-term hardship exemptions, which last for six months and require an application. At the county level, these include high-unemployment areas and declared emergency or disaster areas. At the individual level, these include institutional or high-acuity care and extended travel for healthcare. The state is working to secure a short-term exemption for the Bronx as a high unemployment area, Schell-Guy noted.

For work requirements, New York is using an attestation approach for the first year—meaning members answer a short questionnaire—in recognition that it takes time to gather the necessary documentation. For 2028 and beyond, attestation will not be permitted.

“We have to use data,” Schell-Guy said, which will require collaboration between countless agencies. “There’s tons of data sources that we are trying to access here.”

Also under direction from CMS, New York has a plan for provider enrollment and re-validation. This is part of a new CMS push requiring every state to form a plan to re-validate Medicaid providers, especially those in “high-risk” areas. The state is taking a risk-tiered approach in phases. Providers considered high-risk include durable medical equipment providers, those that haven’t re-validated since the start of COVID-19, applied behavioral analysis therapy providers and home- or community-based services providers. The state’s re-validation process was on paper until 2025, proving unreliable, Schell-Guy said. Now, it is all digital.

To get the word out about coming changes, the state is staffing up its customer service center with a direct line for H.R. 1 questions; is sending member notices via a number of communication channels; has social media campaigns and TV ads; and is doing in-person events. It has also upped its number of assistors who can answer questions and help fill out applications.

“Now we expect there to be a lot of utilization of these assistors,” Schell-Guy said.

#5786. Car Design Has Gone Downhill Since The Plymouth Prowler

There must be something in the water, because there hasn't been a new car design in nearly 30 years that can even remotely be considered cool or fun. Most barely even scratch the surface of interesting these days. The most recent example I can think of when it comes to production cars that actually do something different at play with the visual form was the Plymouth Prowler of 1997. There wasn't anything like this on the road when it debuted in the late 1990s, and there still isn't today. The Prowler was a completely different way of looking at cars. Blending an element of retrofuturism and old-school hot-rod aesthetics, the Prowler was as much a baby boomer's fantasy as it was the car millennials drove in their adolescent dreams.

Then-Chrysler Corporation lead designer Tom Gale was responsible for so many great designs of the era, including a trio of the most unusual concept cars of all time: Chrysler's Thunderbolt, Atlantic, and Phaeton. I don't know if Gale just saw the world differently than other designers, or was just capable of more than they were — his work on the sublime Lamborghini Diablo indicates this may be true — but in either case the Prowler was immediately a stunning piece of automotive history.

Earlier in the 1990s, the Chrysler Corporation had launched the Dodge Viper, a study in function over form. That car was built exclusively to deliver hot nasty speed to its passengers. The Prowler was perhaps its foil, bringing the most style possible to the fight, but without any substance to back it up. For the purposes of this conversation, the substance doesn't matter. Prowler has style icon status and nothing has matched it, let alone beaten it, since. There are definitely cooler cars, but cooler looking? Fat chance.

I'm going to fess up right here and say that the Prowler was the first car I was obsessed with. When it hit dealerships in 1997, exclusively in purple metallic, I was 10 years old, and extremely impressionable. I fell head over heels in love with it. I had dozens of scale models, T-shirts, dealer posters, magazine article clippings, and advertisements for the strange car scattered around my room for its entire production run. You've all met those kids who are fixated on a single subject — well, for me it was the Prowler. I wished it was faster, I wished it drove better, and I wished it wasn't powered by a minivan-like V6. Most of all, I wished I owned one. I'm an adult now and I still think this was among the wildest swings a car designer could have made. Nobody's this brave anymore.

I can admit that there's more to making a good car than making it look cool, but why aren't designers trying? The Prowler couldn't exist today for myriad reasons, but its spirit can soldier on to bring a bit more levity and flair to car design. Apparently everything has to be egg-shaped, with thin slitty LED headlights, thick A-pillars, and sharp, angular minimalism. And you can forget about a convertible at all, really, because allegedly nobody buys them.

Even car interior design has become little more than a minimalist dashboard with a large touchscreen in the middle. I wouldn't say the Prowler's interior looks nice by any stretch of the imagination, but at least it has a little fun with the genre. The color-matched binnacle and center-high-mounted gauges are absolutely ace. You can't beat a column-mounted tach, I mean, come on.

The Prowler was an attempt to do something completely different. Plymouth was on the ropes at the time anyway, so, to use a mixed sports metaphor, why not swing for the fences? What good is it to keep producing boring rebadged models until you fade away?

Maybe this was the beginning of the end for car design, as it brought about a wave of retro-inspired ripoff designs that brought nothing new to the table and suddenly became de rigueur. Or maybe it was so good a first shot that it never should have been tried again.

We've since seen 30 years of Mustang/Mini/Challenger/ID.Buzz-style returns to the same well for diminishing result. Plymouth isn't absolved of this, as it quickly pushed out the PT Cruiser in an effort to stave off death. The brand died anyway and its replica-retro-for-the-everyman car was stolen for Chrysler. Result? Nothing feels stylistically special anymore. When even Ferrari is farming its own history for retro-modern designs, it's time to hang up and try again. The trend has been taken too far, and we need to look for the next thing. Please. I'm begging you.

I'm no design history scholar, but it seems that aesthetics tend toward bland aggression when there's a pessimistic societal weight. In the face of technofascism, uneasy economics, and a troubling climate outlook, it's difficult to be optimistic about anything, and design is seemingly suffering as a result. Practice radical optimism: In the face of everything, be joyful for a future better than the present. Even if it never comes, the infective nature of optimism can always make someone's day better. If there are any designers reading this, stop trying to emulate the Prowler's retro-coded look to the past. Please aim for its future-inspired optimism.

“Pape’s argument is basically a version of the phenomenon often called ‘gambling for resurrection.’ When a company is on the edge of failure, it makes sense for the owner to make highly speculative, even crazy investments that are highly likely to fail but might, just might, make enough money to pull the company back from the brink. Richardson wrote, “After ten years of Trump insisting that reports of his cooperation with Russia were a hoax, here we are, watching one profoundly unpopular man tear apart the global system under which we have lived for eighty years in order to climb into bed with Vladimir Putin.”

Writing in The Atlantic, national security scholar Tom Nichols said, “The American commander in chief has abandoned the Western order, the most successful — and powerful — security arrangement in human history.” Richardson observed:

“This decision appears to have had nothing to do with the national interest of the United States…. Instead, Trump appears to have thrown out the world order because of his own personal interests, his admiration for Putin, his resentment of Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky, and quite possibly other factors that so far have remained obscured from the American public.

“Outrage over Trump’s actions has come from across the political spectrum,” she wrote. “Nichols notes that former federal prosecutor turned conservative commenter Andrew McCarthy wrote that Trump is giving Putin ‘aid and comfort.’ Those words echo Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution, which defines treason against the United States, as ‘levying War against them, or in adhering to their Enemies, giving them Aid and Comfort.’

Krugman warned that a cornered Trump may resort to what he calls “policy looting” by “using his remaining power to take actions that are both deeply unpatriotic and deeply unpopular, but fit his own preferences and prejudices. With nothing left to lose, he will be free to be his worst self — a malignant narcissist who instinctively supports authoritarians and is preoccupied with revenge against anything and anyone that threatens his fragile grandiosity.” In other words, a raging lunatic with access to the nuclear codes.

“Anyone who believes Trump will become more cautious, more moderate in the aftermath of midterm defeat just doesn’t understand the new political reality. The truth is that political bankruptcy will free Trump to pursue his true desires. And those desires are horrifying,” he wrote.

Left to his own devices, Trump is an existential threat to the United States that came into being in 1776. Don’t overlook the fact that the US Supreme Court has enabled and emboldened him, based on a legal theory known as “the unitary executive,” a creation of conservative groups like the Federalist Society that has no basis in the Constitution.

Richardson concludes her essay with this observation:

“The Framers of the Constitution thought they had designed a system that would prevent the rise of a tyrant. They believed U.S. representatives would be so fearful of a leader’s abuse of power that they would impeach any president who overstepped his authority, and that U.S. senators would be so jealous of their own power they would convict, and tyranny would not be able to take root.

“The Framers especially did not anticipate that senators, to whom they deliberately gave longer terms than they gave the president, would put party over country and stand aside as a president and his appointees captured the prerogatives of the Senate.

“But even given the evidence of the past ten years, it is truly astonishing to see Republicans, who for more than forty years have championed President Ronald Reagan for his stance against the Soviet Union, stand aside as Trump trashes the post–World War II system of global security in order to ally the United States with a Russian dictator.”

In the end, the people who fashioned the Constitution simply failed to anticipate the overwhelmingly corrosive influence of power, nor did they provide a way to rein in a madman. RIP, America. The world may never see the likes of you again.

#5783. A look at Optum Rx's new program for managing menopause

A look at Optum Rx's new program for managing menopause" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Optum Rx is launching a new program that aims to integrate specialized care for women navigating menopause into the pharmacy benefit.

The program is a virtual-first offering that connects eligible women with clinicians that have been certified with the Menopause Society. Through the program, they can access both hormonal and nonhormonal therapies, symptom tracking, education and one-on-one patient coaching.

Tracy Spencer, senior vice president for product and strategy at Optum Rx, told Fierce Healthcare that 50 million women are currently experiencing symptoms related to either perimenopause, menopause and post-menopause. And 40% of those women say those symptoms impact their work performance.

"This is an area that remains one of the most underserved in healthcare, which is why we're here today, because closing that gap for women's health is really important," Spencer said.

Optum initially piloted the program beginning at the end of 2025, and Spencer said that pilot ended in September. She said that participants in the pilot reported that, on average, they eliminated five symptoms related to menopause. Most (80%) of the women in the pilot saw an improvement in their symptoms, she said.

And beyond the symptoms directly linked to menopause, having a program in place that supports women during this phase of life can also mitigate the risk of developing future conditions like osteoporosis, diabetes, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease, said Spencer.

When a member enrolls in the program, they'll be given a personalized health assessment by the clinical team to determine what their treatment plan should look like. The Optum Rx clinicians work with the member's existing clinical team, including primary care doctors or gynecologists.

Members can also access a digital interface that allows them to track symptoms, access educational materials and connect with the support coaches, Spencer said.

"It's really meant as a complement to the woman's current care team," she said.

Menopause can also be a lengthy stage of life for many women, with some experiencing symptoms for a decade or more. Spencer said the median length for hot flashes and night sweats, for example, is seven years.

So the program is built to support women in the long term over their menopause health journey, Spencer said.

"The ability to have those ongoing resources that are accessible for women when they want to receive them, how they want to receive them, is incredibly important," she said. "We always feel it's important to meet the patient where they're at."

#5782. Why Checking CarMax Makes Sense (Even If You End Up Buying Elsewhere)

You don't need me to tell you this, but I'm still going to say it: Cars are more expensive now than ever before. If you're a member of the 1%, then you probably couldn't care less about this, but for the remaining 99% of the people living in the United States, it makes the already costly prospect of car buying an even spendier endeavor. Unfortunately, even the old trick of buying used cars to save money is less effective than it once was, since used car prices are higher than ever, too, and used cars don't always come with the peace of mind that a new, warrantied car does. That's where CarMax comes in, as its business model relies on selling used cars that SAE-certified technicians have inspected over 125 components on, and if that's not enough, you can pay for an extended warranty.

The downside of CarMax is that its used cars tend to be more expensive than used cars from other dealerships or private sellers, and there's no haggling room in its prices (which is either a pro or a con, depending on your persuasion). Even if you're not ready to pay CarMax prices for a used car, though, it still pays to check the retailer's inventory, since not only don't you have to negotiate, they're picky about what they sell.

If finding the cheapest car around is your top priority, then CarMax isn't going to be the best place to start your search. If, however, you're sick of getting the runaround from other dealerships or you're burnt out from the dreaded act of haggling with private sellers, then the benefits of buying from CarMax may outweigh the drawbacks.

Every last vehicle in CarMax's national inventory has never experienced flood or frame damage, never has a salvage history, and never has odometer discrepancies. Every CarMax purchase includes a 10-day money-back guarantee, as well as at least a 30-day limited warranty, which may be longer depending on where you live. And they're all offered with CarMax's MaxCare warranty, which, for an extra cost, can extend up to five years after the purchase date on most cars.

I bought my 2017 Mini Cooper S four-door from CarMax in 2020, and I ended up buying the five-year extended warranty because I did not want to be on the hook for European car repair prices. Yes, the initial purchase price was higher than I would've paid at a normal dealership, or from a private party, but I really wanted the peace of mind provided by a warranty, and I have no regrets.

I ended up using the warranty several times over the course of my five-year contract, and I never had any trouble getting repairs covered, from replacing an engine mount to replacing a water pump to replacing a wobbly sunroof switch and a few other, smaller issues. It all depends on your priorities, but it never hurts to look at all options in front of you.

#5781. Batteries Beat Norway’s Hydrogen Bulk Carriers on Cost in Two Modeled Routes

Norwegian shipping company GMI Group is moving ahead with four hydrogen-electric bulk carriers for coastal freight. In October 2026, PowerCell confirmed a follow-up order that brings the program to 24 marine fuel-cell units with 5.4 MW of combined installed capacity. The first two ships, rated at 4,000 deadweight tonnes, are planned for 2027, while two additional 3,000-tonne vessels are expected in 2029.

The project has real shipbuilding commitments and substantial public support. The question is whether hydrogen makes economic sense for the freight services these vessels will provide.

GMI says its design can deliver lifetime costs 9–10% below conventional ships. Its argument combines fuel cells, batteries, an efficient hull and wind assistance. Those are useful engineering features, but most are not exclusive to hydrogen propulsion. A diesel or battery-electric ship can have a similarly efficient hull and sails. The fuel and energy systems still need to be compared on equivalent terms.

I modeled two hypothetical 3,000-tonne coastal bulk services, covering 80 and 55 nautical miles, using comparable hull performance and operating requirements. Over fifteen years, hydrogen propulsion came out 50–58% more expensive than conventional diesel, even after assuming approximately €13.1 million in public vessel support was received upfront. Battery-electric alternatives were €11.64–14.13 million cheaper than the subsidized hydrogen vessels. These are scenario results, not estimates of GMI’s actual operating contracts.

The company has not published the route and commercial data needed for a direct assessment, and the model’s vessel acquisition prices remain important uncertainties. The battery alternatives were not the cheapest option under every assumption. In the central cases they cost somewhat more than diesel over fifteen years. Their advantage was the much smaller gap to conventional operation compared with hydrogen. Battery-electric propulsion also requires adequate grid connections, charging equipment and berth time, which cannot be assumed available at every Norwegian port.

Hydrogen has a different set of requirements. Renewable electricity must be converted into hydrogen, compressed, stored, delivered to the vessel and converted back to electricity in fuel cells. Those additional processes introduce energy losses and capital costs that efficient hulls and sails cannot erase. They matter particularly for short coastal voyages where a practical charging arrangement may be possible.

Norway is using substantial public funding to support the hydrogen ships. Norsk Hydrogenforum reports Enova awards totaling roughly €42.9 million for the four vessels. Additional public support has been awarded to GreenH hydrogen production projects. Announced grants are not necessarily fully paid, and a subsidy changes the allocation of costs rather than eliminating the equipment and energy required.

There may be coastal services where voyage length, available berth time or grid limitations favour hydrogen over batteries. That needs to be established through engineering and commercial comparisons, rather than inferred from the existence of a funded shipbuilding program.

Before further public commitments to compressed-hydrogen coastal freight, Norway should require credible battery-electric bids using vessel, charging and energy prices appropriate to the expected entry-into-service dates.
