#5780. At $7,500, Will This 2003 Jeep Wrangler Sahara Get Its Just Dessert?

Introduced in the 1940s, the Willys Jeep has long been hailed as the "truck that won the war." Let's see whether any of that DNA remains in today's Nice Price or No Dice Wrangler and, if so, whether its price wins our admiration.

It's almost unheard of for an automobile model to switch from one end driving to the other, but that has happened on at least two occasions. The first time came in 1970 when Triumph released the Toledo, a model visually identical to the preceding FWD 1300, but featuring RWD under its twinsie bodywork. The Toledo went on to sire the legendary Dolomite Sprint, making that initially backward-seeming move a laudable decision. Another notable example of an existing model switching driving ends is the Polestar 2, which, with its 2024 refresh, changed its base single-motor layout from front- to rear-wheel-drive.

The 2024 Polestar 2 Long Range we looked at last Friday proved that point moot as the model offers dual motors driving both ends. It also had the model's biggest battery, a desirable driving assistance package, and, at $22,995, seemingly unfathomable depreciation. That latter affliction might be because Polestar sales are currently being banned in the U.S. due to the model's China origins, with owners possibly wanting out before the parts situation becomes dire. Regardless of threats of impending doom, our Polestar's condition and price had a number of you willing to take the chance—hypothetically, of course—earning the EV a respectable 66% 'Nice Price' win.

The name Sahara comes from Arabic, where it means "desert." Of course, that means we shouldn't call the world's largest non-polar desert the "Sahara Desert," since that is redundant. It's the same thing as calling Los Angeles' ancient fossil graveyard the "La Brea Tar Pits," since that is literally "The Tar Tar Pits."

Jeep chose the Sahara name for one of the myriad trim levels and special editions applied to the TJ Wrangler over its 10-year model run. The Sahara package included body-color fender extenders, full doors, cloth upholstery, and five-spoke alloy wheels.

This 2003 Jeep Wrangler Sahara is painted in Sienna Pearl matched to a gray hardtop and interior trim. Its running boards and outer bumper caps were likely once black but, due to the sun's daily attacks, have also faded to a similar gray hue. Other indicators of this Jeep's age include a cracked and dented right-front fender and rust bubbling through on both front wings. Fortunately, those are bolt-ons, and replacements are readily available from places like Amazon and eBay, making these aesthetic imperfections easy to address.

The rest of the Jeep appears to be in good condition, with the seller noting the frame and the rest of the bodywork are free of rust. That's a big deal, considering this TJ is offered in Pennsylvania, arguably the crusty buckle on the Rust Belt.

Another attractive aspect of this TJ is its removable hard top. Yes, removing or replacing the top is a job that'll take two (or three) people to complete, but it really makes this a four-season ride. The seller does warn, however, that while the A/C works fine, the heater is non-functional, so all passengers should be forewarned to bundle up in inclement weather.

Other notable info from the ad includes a new set of tires, a refreshed front axle driveshaft and U-joints, and a new battery and radiator. So far, this Jeep has done 144,370 miles and comes with a clean title and a current state safety inspection sticker.

It should be noted that the TJ edition of the Wrangler was the last to express any of its American Motors Corporation heritage. After this model, the legendary AMC straight six would be retired, exorcising the last vestiges of its former parent in favor of fully Daimler-Chrysler parts.

As such, it's good to see the AMC 4.0-six under this TJ's hood. Not much can go wrong with these cast-iron throwbacks, and they still make a reasonable 190 horsepower and 225 pound-feet of torque. Also in the plus column, this TJ mates that engine with a five-speed manual and part-time 4WD with Dana axles at both ends.

Things this Jeep might need? Well, there are those fenders and a bumper cap in the front that 'could' be repaired. Also, time should be set aside to bring the heater back up to snuff. Then there's the Phillies sticker on the rear door. That's gotta go, or at least be replaced with a new decal. The current one, faded from red to pink, looks a bit too limply phallic.

Okay, so this TJ is a bit of a mixed bag. It's far from perfect, but it's also perfectly usable as-is. Its issues are somewhat mitigated by its specs and the work already done (new tires, radiator, etc.). Could the Jeep's $7,500 asking price tip the balance? As we are all probably aware, Wranglers—except for the four-cylinder editions of the weird rectangular-headlight YJ—have a pretty big fanbase, making them a bit more dear than one might expect.

What do you think? Is this TJ Sahara a good deal at that price point? Or is that just too much to wrangle given the Jeep's inherent flaws?

#5779. Eli Lilly's 340B data policy draws new opposition from Missouri AG, Massachusetts hospitals

Eli Lilly's 340B data policy draws new opposition from Missouri AG, Massachusetts hospitals" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Eli Lilly’s policy requiring 340B hospitals to submit claims-level data in order to receive statutory drug discounts garnered a fresh wave of pushback this week from Missouri’s attorney general and a cadre of Massachusetts hospitals, joining others who have described the requirements as unlawful.

Lilly announced its controversial policy for 340B dispensations in January and first put it into effect for a subset of hospitals in June. It applies to all pharmacy and medical dispensations, including in-house pharmacy and contract pharmacy dispenses, in most states.

The company said doing so would allow it to spot instances when a drug purchase is improperly granted multiple discounts under overlapping programs. Hospitals have contended that the extra scrutiny is unnecessary and introduces substantial administrative burden.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway has come in on the side of the opposition. On Monday, she issued a cease-and-desist letter to Lilly, writing that the policy violates the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act, a consumer protection law. If the drugmaker doesn’t end its requirement for Missouri providers, the policy “may result in subsequent legal action,” including an injunction and monetary civil penalties, the letter reads.

“Big Pharma does not get to bully Missouri hospitals or hold prescription drug prices hostage,” Hanaway said in an accompanying release. “Eli Lilly is abusing its market power to impose higher prescription prices in Missouri. These tactics fall hardest on rural communities that depend on the 340B program to keep clinics open and ensure patients receive the care they need.”

Hanaway’s letter and release highlight Lily’s decision to end discounts for the University of Missouri Health Care in July. The system later agreed to provide the data as requested, but “now bears the heavy costs and burdens of complying with Lilly’s requirements,” the attorney general’s office wrote.

A day later, six Massachusetts hospitals hit Lilly with a new lawsuit to block the policy. Massachusetts General Hospital, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Salem Hospital, UMass Memorial Medical Center and UMass Memorial Health — Harrington Hospital filed the lawsuit.

Their complaint filed in federal court describes “corporate extortion” from “the largest pharmaceutical company in the world” that “deprives them of resources essential to serving their most vulnerable patients.”

The hospitals “rightfully refused to comply” with the policy and had their 340B discounts pulled, echoing the claimed injuries from others who have sued over the policy, such as Tampa General Hospital and Mary Hitchcock Memorial Hospital. Failing to “capitulate” would cost the plaintiff Massachusetts hospitals “tens of millions of dollars in annual losses” collectively.

However, the new complaint criticizes Lilly’s 340B ESP platform, “a unilaterally selected, private-equity-owned third-party platform,” whose use is required by Lilly as “a data dragnet that, so far, has been free from public scrutiny.”

The hospitals wrote that the practices violate Massachusetts’ consumer protection law and are unjustly enriching the company. They asked the court to enjoin Lilly from enforcing its policy and terms, and to require compensatory damages “including but not limited to the amounts plaintiffs have paid to defendant above the applicable 340B Ceiling Price, lost 340B savings and other consequential damages.”

Fierce Healthcare has reached out to Lilly for comment on the attorney general’s letter and the new lawsuit. Lilly has historically disputed hospitals’ portrayal of its policy’s burdens in prior litigation and asserted that the required data is already routinely collected by the organizations.

This week’s developments add to the substantial legal showdowns surrounding the controversial drug discount program, which has ballooned in scale over the last several years. Drugmakers critical of the program have sought to impose restrictions on contract pharmacies, prompting litigation in states where lawmakers have prohibited such restrictions.

Policymakers’ own appetite to curb the subsidy program, such as through a pilot rebate program, has also spurred its fair share of litigation.

The machine became a sled, slid through the run-off area and slammed into the barrier. It took a while for Bottas to get out of the cockpit, but he walked away. Race control was forced to throw a red flag to recover his car.

Back in fourth for the standing restart, Antonelli took advantage of Charles Leclerc locking up into Turn 1 to snag the final podium spot. He may have finished third behind Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, but the celebration under a blizzard of confetti might be the most memorable of the Italian's entire career. After the trophies were handed out and the champagne sprayed, Hamilton and Verstappen hoisted the new champion up onto their shoulders in front of the roaring crowd. It was the Hollywood freeze-frame ending to Antonelli's meteoric ascent to racing's highest summit.

It was a disastrous day on the other side of the garage. George Russell started 2nd, but had a power unit deployment issue on the opening run to Turn 1 and sank down the order. He then made contact with Isack Hadjar in Turn 6 and received a ten-second penalty for his trouble. Russell salvaged a sixth-place finish. While the British driver didn't hesitate to congratulate Antonelli after they climbed out of their cars, it was clear he was devastated to lose the championship to his teammate. Russell skipped the mandatory post-race media interviews. In Russell's absence, Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff heaped praise on Antonelli and the team's patience with the sophomore champion, saying:

"People said he shouldn't even be in F1, he should be at a smaller team, 10 races and no points, the tears in Spa, and then this. I'm just so proud for the team, all of them continued to trust him and he delivered."

The tumult at Scuderia Ferrari reached a new low. Ferrari seemed poised to take the victory with Lewis Hamilton taking his first pole since 2023. With how difficult it is to pass in Mexico City, the seven-time champion just needed to survive the start's lengthy run to Turn 1. His biggest threat turned out to be his own teammate. Leclerc slipstreamed from third to Hamilton, then tried to pass on the outside. The Monégasque driver took another shot at the lead heading into Turn 4.

Neither Ferrari driver kept their car on the track through Turn 4. While Hamilton re-entered the racing surface to make Turn 5, Leclerc cut the course across the grass to take the lead. Ferrari would ask the pair to swap positions to avoid a penalty, but this time was different. Max Verstappen had gotten past Hamilton. Ferrari and Leclerc opted to put their fates in the stewards' hands rather than yield the lead by choice. The decision: a five-second time penalty.

The penalty was enough for Verstappen to inherit the lead after pit stops, but not enough for Hamilton to take second. The decision's light-handedness was something Hamilton noted after the race, adding that he received a ten-second penalty for a similar infraction last year. He was far less calm during the red flag, telling his team over the radio, "We've got big problems. Big, big problems." After Hamilton returned to pit lane, he stormed off the back of the garage

As bad as things are at Ferrari, neither driver has been fired. Haas abruptly benched Esteban Ocon on Saturday. The American team had reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa serve as a substitute for the rest of the weekend. Relationships between Ocon and Haas were already strained as the French driver had already been axed from the team's 2027 lineup. The benching was allegedly the result of a heated argument on Friday between Ocon and team boss Ayao Komatsu that became physical, according to French newspaper L'Equipe. Ocon took to social media to deny the report that he resorted to violence.

Following the recent decision from Haas F1 Team confirming that I will not be participating in this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, I wish to formally address some media reports and speculation surrounding the situation.

Last night, a difference in viewpoints led to a...

— Esteban Ocon (@OconEsteban) October 31, 2026

It's unclear who will be in the empty Haas seat next weekend in Brazil. Hirakawa has a respectable debut outing, finishing 13th on the track. The 32-year-old Le Mans winner was promoted to tenth, scoring a point, after other drivers received post-race penalties. Unfortunately, Hirakawa is unavailable for Interlagos as he's racing for his third World Endurance Championship with Toyota in Monza. Komatsu implied that Ocon could return. Antonelli may have clinched the championship and made history, but this season's drama is far from over.

#5775. Oura, UC San Diego Health collaborate to study GLP-1 outcomes using continuous smart ring data

Oura, UC San Diego Health collaborate to study GLP-1 outcomes using continuous smart ring data" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Oura is pushing further into clinical healthcare research with its first clinical trial to study the link between smart ring data and obesity treatment outcomes.

The company is collaborating with UC San Diego Health on the clinical trial, called SMART-BMI. The multi-year study will investigate whether continuous data from the Oura Ring, including sleep, heart rate and activity, are associated with outcomes for patients receiving GLP-1 medications or bariatric surgery, the organizations said.

The Oura Ring data will capture changes between care visits, and researchers plan to examine associations with outcomes including weight loss, HbA1c and treatment persistence. The study is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07736729.

“Longitudinal and surgical management of obesity can unlock the power of continuous monitoring and precision medicine offered by wearables,” said Jeff Reeves, M.D., UC San Diego Health.

“UC San Diego Health is precisely where innovative technology and subject matter experts come together to advance human health,” said Alexander Khalessi, neurosurgeon and chief innovation officer at UC San Diego Health, in a statement. “We are proud of the thought leadership of Dr. Reeves and Oura’s engagement to take on these important clinical questions for our patients.”

The smart ring maker and health tracking company has ambitions to build an artificial intelligence-powered clinical health platform. Founded in Finland in 2013, Oura's smart rings continuously track more than 50 health metrics, including heart rate, sleep, daily movement and activity, stress, fertility windows and metabolic health. The company was gearing up to go public, filing an initial public offering in late September with plans to raise $2.2 billion in a U.S. IPO by offering 50 million shares priced at $40 to $44 per share.

In October, the company announced it was postponing its IPO due to "uncertainty in the IPO market." The company said it was delaying its public listing "despite strong demand."

The multi-year obesity outcomes study is part of a broader clinical push being coordinated through Oura's Office of Regulatory and Clinical Affairs (ORCA), which was built over the past year under Chief Medical Officer Ricky Bloomfield, M.D. ORCA combines scientific and medical evidence, regulatory and quality work, outcomes research and clinical informatics.

"Since I started at Oura, my focus has been on formalizing the clinical rigor behind the trust people already place in their ring,” Bloomfield said. "As we take on a bigger role in healthcare with new use cases, partnerships and levels of clinical evidence, that trust has to be earned at every step. We do that by ensuring the right measurement, the right validation, the right outcomes data at every layer. ORCA is how we hold ourselves to that standard, alongside the researchers and institutions we work with."

Oura Ring has been included in over 200 peer-reviewed publications spanning sleep, cardiovascular health, women’s health, metabolic health, mental health, pregnancy and other areas.

The company is pursuing other outcomes-focused studies to examine how continuous Oura data relates to health outcomes, healthcare utilization and cost of care. Oura is working with Maven Clinic on a study of fertility and pregnancy outcomes. The study will look at both Oura-only and Oura-plus-Maven experiences and is designed to enroll at least 5,000 participants. It's also working with the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine to investigate whether wearable data can identify changes associated with rehospitalization and recurrent acute kidney injury following hospitalization.

The company recently completed a large-scale blood pressure study through Oura Labs to explore how Oura data could inform future regulated features related to blood pressure.

Separately, researchers at hospital systems and academic medical centers have independently used Oura Ring in more than 150 studies. Researchers at institutions including NYU Langone, Mount Sinai, Cornell Tech, Weill Cornell and the University of Central Florida are using Oura data to study areas such as depression, heart failure and inflammatory arthritis.

Health systems are also beginning to bring Oura data into care delivery. Mount Sinai Doctors–Concierge Care’s Healthspan Membership is integrating Oura Ring 5 data to give physicians a continuous view of biometric trends between visits.

“The real opportunity is to understand what’s happening between visits, how a patient is sleeping, recovering, moving and responding to changes in their daily life,” said Fiorina Kyritsi, M.D., of Mount Sinai Doctors–Concierge Care. “By bringing those insights into the care relationship, we can have a much more informed conversation with our members.”

#5774. Which Automaker Has The Coolest Model Names?

Many car enthusiasts tend to view their car more as a family member than an appliance. Cars take us to some of the most important events in our lives, to some of the most memorable places in our lives, and hell, for a lot of us, they're the second place we ever see right after we're thrust into human existence and we leave the hospitals where we were born. To me, family members have names, not alphanumeric codes, so I've always preferred when automakers give their cars proper names.

Thankfully there have been scores of cool, memorable car names over the years, but we want to know which automaker you, dear Jalopnik reader, think has the coolest model names. There's no cutoff date for this one, mostly because I think a lot of the coolest model names have been discontinued or replaced with alphanumeric nonsense, so feel free to unearth some obscure carmaker that hasn't made a car in a century or something, as long as they had cool model names. Sound off in the comments section below!

In a rare change of pace, Lincoln went from using lame alphanumeric model names like MKZ and MKX to what I believe are the coolest model names in the industry. To clarify, the company started off with proper names for most of its models throughout the 20th century, but for some reason Lincoln decided to ditch those in the 2000s, which I lamented, even then as a child.

With current names like Corsair, Nautilus, Aviator, and Navigator, the modern lineup is stacked with heavy hitters, but Lincoln's classic names are really good, too. Of course there's also the classic Continental, and my beloved Zephyr. I don't know that I could honestly choose a favorite name from the brand — it would be a tie between Corsair, Nautilus, and Zephyr, which all evoke distinct pictures in my imagination.

Corsair makes me think of the Vought F4U Corsair warbird. Nautilus makes me think of the prehistoric undersea chambered mollusk that has barely evolved over the past couple million years, and Zephyr evokes images of Art Deco-era pie-in-the-sky inventions like early flying machines and trains. All of this imagery comes from the exciting and fascinating names given to Lincoln's cars, which is something that alphanumeric names just don't quite achieve in my brain. Okay, that's enough of my yapping, we're here for you! What automaker do you think has the coolest model names?

#5772. Kennedy's HHS relaxes enforcement on 6 popular wellness peptides

Kennedy's HHS relaxes enforcement on 6 popular wellness peptides" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides.

The move, which comes after the same peptides won favor at an FDA advisory committee meeting this summer, is being hailed by some in the industry as offering a more accountable alternative to the gray market many peptide-seekers currently use, while others have charged that it undermines institutional FDA pushback on the drugs, which have become increasingly popular among fitness influencer circles and the MAHA crowd.

Under Kennedy’s “enforcement discretion policy” issued Wednesday, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

The specific compounds included (PDF) in the list are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500, all of which were discussed in a meeting of the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) in July, with the panel ultimately voting to recommend including the treatments onto the 503A Bulk Drug Substances list.

Advisory committee votes are recommendations, not binding decisions, and the peptides still haven’t been added to the drug substances list in an official capacity.

Kennedy cited that meeting in his enforcement decision, alongside data on utilization of peptides, noting that HHS believes there is “significant interest in the use of these peptides in compounding given the lack of availability of approved products.”

The letter clarifies the agency may revisit the interim policy if it leads to new safety signals or product quality issues.

The new policy comes with several other caveats that compounders must satisfy too, including sourcing their bulk drug substance from an FDA-registered facility and ensuring that the ingredients are properly characterized and identified. The original manufacturer of the bulk drug substance must also be registered with the FDA, according to HHS’ document.

In another change from typical compounding practice, compounders will be required to report quality issues and serious adverse events associated with the newly unrestricted peptides that are associated with their use, whether the drug itself is considered related or not, HHS clarified.

Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. Traditionally, the compounding practice has focused on the mixing or altering of ingredients of a drug to create a custom medication for a patient.

The practice can also come into play in order to fill drug shortages, which led to the pop-up of a GLP-1 compounding cottage industry for obesity that branded drugmakers Novo and Eli Lilly have continued to grapple with, even after supply shortfalls of their licensed medicines were declared formally ended in the United States.

In a statement Wednesday, Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding (APC) CEO Scott Brunner said he welcomed the decision, noting that it isn’t a question of whether patients are already using these six peptides, but of “where they’re getting them.”

“Right now, far too many patients are obtaining peptides from illicit suppliers with little assurance about what's actually in the vial,” he said. “That's an existing public health threat, and one that isn't going away simply because compounding of the substances is prohibited.”

While noting that the policy now offers a “more accountable alternative” to that murky peptide supply chain, Brunner emphasized the importance of the limits the enforcement action puts in place as well, while also highlighting questions that remain, including when the policy actually takes effect, how API testing and analysis will be validated and how product utilization reporting will work.

“That last point is especially important,” Brunner said. “A credible federal policy with meaningful patient safety safeguards gives states a sound basis for their own oversight and helps discourage a patchwork of state rules and restrictions that could undermine the access HHS is trying to provide.”

Others, including consumer advocacy nonprofit Public Citizen, adopted a decidedly more antagonist tone toward the new enforcement policy. In a statement issued this week, the group noted the peptides included in the new list are “popular but unproven and unapproved,” flagging Kennedy’s own personal support of the compounds.

Questions around conflicts of interest among panelists on the PCAC panel were also raised this summer, with the FDA quickly slotting in eight temporary voting members ahead of the confab in a bid to appease some of the criticism.

With the move, Kennedy “has acted recklessly and unilaterally to put Americans in danger,” Robert Steinbrook, M.D., Public Citizen’s health research group director, said in a statement, contending that the HHS secretary ought to “support, not sabotage, needed FDA enforcement actions to protect consumers.”

#5771. NYU Langone brings OpenEvidence’s clinical AI into the EHR systemwide

NYU Langone brings OpenEvidence’s clinical AI into the EHR systemwide" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

OpenEvidence is expanding its footprint in New York City through a partnership with NYU Langone Health, adding another marquee institution to an existing concentration of partnerships across the city's academic medical centers.

OpenEvidence's AI-powered clinical evidence platform is embedded directly into NYU Langone's Epic electronic health record (EHR) workflows. NYU Langone has more than 12 million outpatient visits annually, 421,000 emergency department visits, seven inpatient locations and over 400 outpatient locations. The integration will span NYU Langone's hospitals, ambulatory network and the Family Health Centers and will also reach physicians who are training at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine and the NYU Grossman Long Island School of Medicine.

The system has more than 6,000 physicians and faculty, 2,000+ residents and fellows and 54,000 employees.

“At NYU Langone, we are committed to working with OpenEvidence to make the latest technology available to our clinicians in a safe and practical environment at scale,” said Nader Mherabi, executive vice president and vice dean, chief digital and information officer at NYU Langone Health said in a statement.

OpenEvidence developed an AI-powered medical search engine and a generative AI chatbot exclusively for doctors, which summarizes and simplifies evidence-based medical information. It has grown to become one of the most widely used medical AI and CDS tools in the industry. The company says its "patient-aware clinical intelligence" uses agentic clinical AI to integrate details of the patient record with the evidence from the medical literature.

NYU Langone clinicians will be able to ask complex clinical questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in peer-reviewed medical literature and read against the patient’s own clinical record, all without leaving their Epic workflow, according to OpenEvidence executives.

“NYU Langone cares for New Yorkers at a scale few institutions in the country can match, and it does so while setting the standard of care across specialties,” Daniel Nadler, founder and CEO of OpenEvidence, said in a statement. “New York has always been where American medicine goes to prove itself at scale. Putting OpenEvidence inside the chart at NYU Langone means the world's medical literature is now in the room for every one of the twelve million visits this system supports each year.”

OpenEvidence has already amassed a large following among individual clinicians, with the company saying roughly two-thirds of U.S. physicians use its platform. As of October, there were 1.2 million medical license-verified U.S. clinicians, including physicians and nurses, using OpenEvidence, Nadler told Fierce Healthcare. Verified U.S. clinicians consulted OpenEvidence 45 million times in October alone, he said.

AI has integrated deeply into specialized medicine as well. There are 300 million physical specialist visits, such as seeing a cardiologist or oncologist, in the U.S. per year. Nadler said OpenEvidence handles about one query from a medical specialist for every patient visit to a medical specialist in America.

Building on its massive adoption with clinicians, the company is now pushing deeper into health systems.

The agreement with NYU Langone builds on OpenEvidence's broader reach in New York. The company already has an enterprise rollout across NewYork-Presbyterian's 10 hospitals and nearly 350 care sites, a health-system-wide deployment at Mount Sinai, and a specialized precision oncology partnership with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. It also has partnerships with leading New York City medical schools around clinical training and research.

A recent large-scale study examined OpenEvidence’s rapid adoption and how clinicians are using AI in the clinic. Nearly 1 million U.S. clinicians submitted 271 million AI-enabled clinical queries through OpenEvidence's platform from January 2024 to June 2026, according to a paper published in JAMA. More than half of the users in the sample (556,200) were physicians, according to researchers from Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women’s Hospital. These physicians submitted an average of 37 queries per month of use. Early-career physicians and those in oncology, hematology, internal medicine and family medicine submitted a higher-than-average share of queries, according to the study.

The study found that most of the queries were related to clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management. Diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries.

“Two key takeaways are that an enormous number of physicians are using AI for clinical care and that they are often using it in areas where they don’t have specific expertise,” said corresponding author Anupam Jena, the Joseph P. Newhouse Professor of Health Care Policy in the Blavatnik Institute at HMS and HMS professor of medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital.

“Everyone appreciates the huge potential for AI to change how medicine is practiced, but right now, we have limited information on how many doctors are using it, what they are using it for, and how it’s impacting patients,” Jena said. The JAMA study tackles the first two of those questions, the researchers noted.

The study also found that monthly active OpenEvidence users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703,265 in June 2026. Queries per active user increased substantially, from 18 per month to 39.5, and month-to-month retention reached roughly 90% in 2026. By June, 92.5% of active users were returning users rather than brief adopters, according to the study.

#5770. Extra Genetic Testing in Young IVF Patients Cut Costs but Came With a Downside

— Lower cumulative live birth rates could be because more embryos are screened out, experts said

BALTIMORE -- Adding a broader genetic test to testing for single-gene disorders among younger patients undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) reduced costs -- but it also may lower cumulative live birth rates, a cost-effectiveness analysis suggested.

Among patients ages 36 and younger already planning to screen with pre-implantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M), adding on pre-implantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A) was modeled to result in a lower cost per initiated cycle ($38,518) compared with PGT-M alone ($40,002), reflecting a cost-effectiveness tradeoff, reported Vania Nwokolo, MD, of the University of Washington in Seattle.

However, patients who opted for both PGT-M and PGT-A also had lower cumulative live birth rates versus those who did PGT-M alone (35.3% vs 52.3%), Nwokolo noted at the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) annual meeting.

"What we found is that patients who are 36 and under who just do the PGT-M alone for a disorder or disease, they're more likely to have an actual live birth; however, the costs are higher," Nwokolo told MedPage Today.

She explained that those costs are likely higher because PGT-M alone could miss genetic abnormalities in the embryo that weren't tested for, which may result in a miscarriage. Both treating the miscarriage and doing another embryo transfer would add on costs.

"Whereas if we add a PGT-A on the front end, there's some cost in the beginning, but you're less likely to transfer an embryo that has that genetic abnormality," potentially avoiding miscarriages and additional embryo transfers, Nwokolo said.

"It may not lead to a higher cumulative birth rate, but the costs are cheaper," she added.

Patients undergoing IVF who want to prevent the transmission of single-gene disorders, such as Huntington's disease, often opt for PGT-M. Those who want to screen for chromosomal abnormalities more broadly would use PGT-A.

Both genetic tests involve a biopsy, so Nwokolo said that many PGT-M patients ask about adding on PGT-A to potentially decrease their risk of miscarriage.

The likelihood of extra or missing chromosomes increases with maternal age, so Nwokolo noted that women ages 38 and older are usually advised to do PGT-A. However, the benefit for good-prognosis women ages 36 and under remains uncertain.

Rachel Weinerman, MD, an ob/gyn and reproductive endocrinologist at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, told MedPage Today that there haven't been randomized trials showing that PGT-A improves cumulative or per-transfer live birth rates for younger patients, though past research has shown it's cost-effective in older patients.

Weinerman, who wasn't involved in the study, said she thinks the difference in cumulative live birth rates may be dependent on how many embryos were transferred.

"When you do PGT-A, you exclude embryos that were segmental aneuploid and sometimes high-level mosaic that you would transfer and may lead to live birth if you didn't do the testing," she explained.

For this analysis, Nwokolo and team created a decision tree to compare PGT-M alone and PGT-M plus PGT-A in women ages 36 and under. Embryo yield, including the number of blastocysts and the proportion of euploid and mosaic proportions, were derived from published data in women under age 37.

Primary outcomes were cumulative live birth rate, which is the probability of at least one live birth across all transfers; cost per initiated cycle, including IVF, genetic testing, embryo transfers, pregnancy care, and miscarriage management; and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER). The ICER for PGT-M alone was $8,737 per additional live birth.

Embryo outcomes were modeled per transfer. Euploid embryos were prioritized, followed by mosaic embryos, which contain both genetic chromosomal abnormalities and normal cells, if no euploid embryos were available.

Nwokolo said that mosaic embryos were a limitation, because there is debate in the field over whether to transfer low-level mosaics and it's hard to determine whether genetic abnormalities or normal cells dominate.

In a sensitivity analysis, PGT-M alone remained more expensive but more effective when mosaic transfer was allowed after euploid failure.

#5769. Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit

Millions of Americans take fish oil supplements in hopes of protecting their memory and keeping their brains healthy as they age. These products have become a major business, with Americans spending more than $1 billion each year on supplements containing omega-3 fatty acids. These essential nutrients help build and maintain the connections between brain cells that support memory, learning, and other cognitive functions.

But a new study suggests that getting more omega-3s into the brain through supplements may not provide the protection many people expect.

Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC found that even when high doses of omega-3s successfully reached the brain, they did not produce measurable improvements in memory, thinking abilities, or protection against brain shrinkage.

The findings, published in eBioMedicine, come from a two-year clinical trial involving older adults considered to be at increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. Despite taking omega-3 supplements daily, participants showed no significant cognitive advantage over those who received a placebo.

"We all wish there was a silver bullet for preventing Alzheimer's, but our findings showed that fish oil supplements do not appear to protect brain health," said Hussein Naji Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health and lead investigator of the study. "While omega-3s play an important role in forming brain cell connections needed for cognition, our results do not support fish oil supplements as a preventive measure against Alzheimer's."

A Two-Year Study Tests Fish Oil's Brain Benefits

To investigate whether omega-3 supplements could protect the aging brain, researchers enrolled 365 adults between the ages of 55 and 80. All participants rarely ate fish, a major dietary source of omega-3 fatty acids, and were considered at elevated risk for Alzheimer's disease.

Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4, a gene variant associated with a substantially higher risk of developing Alzheimer's later in life. Although having this variant does not mean someone will necessarily develop the disease, it is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's.

Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a daily fish oil supplement or a placebo, an inactive treatment used for comparison. The supplements provided 2,000 mg of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), an omega-3 fatty acid that is especially important for the brain.

DHA is a major component of brain cell membranes, helping maintain the structure and function of neurons. It also supports communication between nerve cells, making it an important nutrient for normal brain activity.

The study was double-blind, meaning neither participants nor researchers knew who was receiving the active supplement during the trial. This approach helps reduce bias and makes it easier to determine whether any observed benefits are actually caused by the treatment.

Omega-3 Levels Rose, but Memory Did Not Improve

Before evaluating whether the supplements improved brain health, researchers needed to answer a fundamental question: Were the omega-3 fatty acids actually reaching the brain?

To find out, they measured DHA concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord. Examining this fluid can provide information about substances entering and circulating within the central nervous system.

After six months, DHA levels in the cerebrospinal fluid had increased by an average of 17% among participants taking the supplements. This provided evidence that the omega-3 fatty acids were reaching their intended destination.

However, getting DHA into the central nervous system was only part of the goal. The more important question was whether those higher levels would translate into better brain health.

Researchers assessed participants' memory and other cognitive abilities at the beginning of the trial and again after two years. Despite the increase in DHA, those taking fish oil performed no better on the cognitive tests than participants receiving the placebo.

Brain imaging revealed similarly disappointing results.

The supplements did not prevent shrinkage of the hippocampus, a region deep within the brain that plays a central role in forming and organizing memories. The hippocampus is particularly vulnerable to changes associated with aging and Alzheimer's disease, making its size an important indicator researchers use when studying brain health.

Taken together, the results suggest that simply increasing DHA availability in the brain is not enough to produce measurable cognitive benefits in this group of older adults.

Why Fish Oil Supplements May Work Differently Than Food

The unexpected findings have raised a new question for researchers: If omega-3s can reach the brain, why don't higher levels necessarily improve its function?

Yassine and his colleagues are now investigating how the brain absorbs, processes, and uses these nutrients. Their earlier research suggests that omega-3s may be more beneficial when consumed as part of a broader dietary pattern rather than taken in isolation as a supplement.

One possibility involves the Mediterranean-style diet, which emphasizes foods such as fish, vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and olive oil. This eating pattern naturally supplies omega-3 fatty acids alongside other nutrients and has been associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

The researchers suspect that the combination of nutrients in a balanced diet, along with an individual's overall health, may influence how effectively omega-3s support the brain.

"We're focused on better understanding how the brain processes omega-3s and whether factors, such as poor health, dietary pattern, genetic risk and age, may change the brain's ability to effectively absorb and use omega-3s," said Yassine. "We are working to develop medications that may help the brain better utilize these nutrients to preserve cognitive function."

Understanding these differences could eventually help scientists identify why certain people might respond better to omega-3s than others and whether new treatments could improve the brain's ability to benefit from these essential fats.

Importantly, the findings do not mean omega-3 fatty acids are unnecessary or that eating fish offers no health benefits. Instead, they indicate that taking high-dose DHA supplements alone did not provide measurable protection against cognitive decline or hippocampal shrinkage in the population studied.

Healthy Habits Remain Key to Alzheimer's Prevention

Although the trial focused specifically on fish oil supplements, the researchers emphasize that protecting brain health requires a much broader approach.

Rather than relying on a single supplement, they recommend maintaining healthy habits throughout life, including regular physical activity, sufficient high-quality sleep, and a nutritious, balanced diet.

These behaviors support overall health and may help reduce factors associated with cognitive decline. Physical exercise, for example, promotes cardiovascular health and blood flow, while sleep plays an important role in memory formation and normal brain maintenance.

"Staying healthy throughout life remains the most powerful tool we have for reducing Alzheimer's risk, including regular exercise, quality sleep and a balanced diet," said Yassine. "Living a healthy lifestyle is the brain's equivalent of getting regular car maintenance and high-quality oil changes. The brain is more likely to lose greater function if health issues in other parts of the body go unaddressed, in the same way that car engines stop working if regular maintenance is skipped."

While these lifestyle factors were not directly tested in the trial, the researchers believe they offer a more promising foundation for long-term brain health than depending on fish oil supplements alone.

The results also highlight an important distinction: A nutrient can be essential for healthy brain function without providing additional protection when consumed in large doses as a supplement. Understanding why that happens may open new avenues for research into Alzheimer's prevention and the nutritional needs of the aging brain.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, grant numbers RF1AG076124, R01AG055770, R01AG067063, R01AG054434, R21AG056518, P30AG066530 and R01AG054434 and the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation, grant number GC-201711-2014197.

#5767. Christa Pike Says She's in Constant Pain, Blames Failed Execution on 'Incompetence'

— Tennessee governor has called for an investigation into the failed execution

Christa Pike said Friday she remains in constant pain, struggles to speak, and has been largely isolated in a prison hospital after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month.

In her first public statement since, Pike said she's "deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position."

"I continue to think about my victim's family," she said, "and the terrible pain and loss they have endured."

Pike and her boyfriend tortured and stabbed a 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, to death in 1995. Pike was 18 at the time, making her one of the youngest women sentenced to death. Slemmer's mother traveled from Florida to witness Pike's execution.

Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably didn't enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered. Unconscious, she was hospitalized on a ventilator for days, and at one point her lawyers said they didn't expect her to survive.

"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak," Pike said. "And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."

Pike said she had been prepared to die in peace, but instead woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed. She said she's "searching for meaning in what happened to me."

"I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next," Pike said in a statement dictated to her legal team from prison.

Pike remains sentenced to die, and her attorneys want Republican Gov. Bill Lee to change that to life in prison. However, Lee told reporters this week, "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts."

Pike's lethal injection was plagued by problems. Her attorneys had warned that her small veins and diagnosis of the blood-clotting disorder thrombocytosis could make IV access difficult.

In a court document, her attorney Randy Spivey said the execution team struggled to get working IV lines in Pike's arms and expressed concern that a vein might be "blowing." Pike remained awake for much of the lethal injection, saying her arm hurt and burned before falling unconscious. The execution began just before 7:30 p.m. and an ambulance arrived at the prison about an hour and 45 minutes later.

The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences.

In a 2025 deposition released with court documents this week, prison Warden Kenneth Nelson said the execution team doesn't practice inserting IV lines during training sessions, at the directive of the prison commissioner. Nelson said he did not know why the practice was discontinued or when the order was given.

Practicing insertion of IVs was part of Tennessee's prior execution protocol, but it is not included in the state's new protocol.

Dorinda Carter, a spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction, said she could not comment on the filing because of pending litigation.

Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, announced his resignation in the wake of Pike's failed execution. His final day is Oct. 31, Carter said.

#5766. Coffee calories have jumped nearly 40%. Sugar isn't the biggest culprit

Americans are getting more calories from their daily coffee, even though the amount they drink has barely changed. Researchers at the Gerald J. and Dorothy R. Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy at Tufts University have identified a surprising reason for the increase: non-dairy creamer, which has overtaken sugar and milk as the largest contributor to added calories in coffee.

The study, published online in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, examined dietary information from 30,000 American adults aged 20 and older. Between 2003 and 2018, average coffee consumption stayed relatively constant at approximately 13 ounces per day. However, the average number of calories consumed from coffee increased from 43 to 60 per day, a rise of nearly 40%. By 2018, the leading sources of added coffee calories were non-dairy creamer, sugar or syrup, and dairy milk.

"Coffee consumption has been associated with several health benefits. However, coffee is often accompanied by the addition of sugar and cream, which can contribute to an increased consumption of calories from added sugar and saturated fat," said Fang Fang Zhang, senior author of the study and Neely Family Professor at the Friedman School. "The more we know about what people are consuming, the better we can understand the link between nutrition and overall health."

How Researchers Tracked Changes in Coffee Habits

To investigate how Americans' coffee habits evolved, the research team examined eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), covering 2003 through 2018. The nationally representative dataset included 30,000 adults aged 20 and older, each of whom completed two 24-hour dietary recalls.

Researchers separated coffee beverages into two broad groups: non-combination beverages and those containing additional ingredients. They then classified the additions into several categories, including dairy milk, half-and-half, dairy cream, non-dairy milk, non-dairy creamer, sugar/syrup, sugar substitutes, and other ingredients such as alcohol and cocoa powder.

Some participants reported consuming pre-mixed coffee beverages/powder, making it necessary to estimate the amounts of individual ingredients they contained. To do this, the researchers used the USDA Food and Nutrition Database for Dietary Studies corresponding to each survey cycle, along with linked Standard Reference codes.

Non-Dairy Creamer Consumption More Than Doubled

The analysis showed that Americans' overall coffee intake, including coffee consumed without additions, remained largely unchanged between 2003 and 2018. What changed was the amount and type of ingredients being mixed into those beverages.

In 2018, dairy milk was the most commonly added ingredient by weight, averaging 21.4 grams per day. Non-dairy creamer followed at 8.1 grams per day, while sugar accounted for 4.4 grams per day. Consumption of dairy milk, sugar, and sugar substitutes showed no statistically significant changes over the study period.

Non-dairy additions, however, followed a very different pattern. Their average consumption rose from 3.65 grams per day in 2003 to 10.5 grams per day in 2018. Much of this growth came from non-dairy creamer, which increased from 3.37 to 8 grams per day. Non-dairy milk consumption also climbed sharply, rising from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

Other coffee additions increased slightly as well, with an average gain of 0.5 grams per day.

Why Non-Dairy Creamer Now Adds More Calories Than Sugar

Although dairy milk remained the most common coffee addition by weight, non-dairy creamer had become the leading source of added calories by 2018.

On average, non-dairy creamer contributed 18.5 calories per day, compared with 16 calories from sugar and 11 calories from dairy milk. In 2003, non-dairy creamer had contributed just 7.71 calories per day, illustrating how dramatically its role in Americans' coffee consumption had changed.

"We found that non-dairy creamer being added to coffee has now passed both sugar and dairy for its contribution to the total energy consumed from coffee. Non-dairy creamers can be high in saturated fat, which is calorie dense. This could explain the increased calories that non-dairy creamer is contributing," said Yongyi Pan, the study's lead author and a Ph.D. candidate at the Friedman School. "Even though it has been on the market since the 1950s, non-dairy creamer has increased in popularity in recent years as consumers seek plant-based or dairy alternatives."

Sleep, Work Hours, and Coffee Consumption

The researchers also investigated whether coffee consumption differed across groups of adults based on their daily routines and overall diet quality.

They found that people who slept fewer hours generally drank more coffee than those who slept longer. A similar pattern emerged among adults who worked longer hours, who tended to consume more coffee than those with shorter work schedules.

However, coffee consumption was comparable among people with higher and lower overall diet quality, suggesting that drinking more or less coffee was not strongly associated with how healthy their broader diets were.

The researchers acknowledged that the study relied on participants recalling what they had eaten and drunk, which can introduce measurement errors. Because food and beverage consumption can vary considerably from day to day, self-reported dietary information does not always perfectly reflect people's usual habits. The research team took steps to improve the reliability of its estimates.

Co-author Bingjie Zhou contributed to the research while pursuing a Ph.D. at the Friedman School.

Materials provided by Tufts University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5765. Labor Department finalizes PBM transparency rule

Labor Department finalizes PBM transparency rule" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has locked in a regulation that will require pharmacy benefit managers to disclose fees and compensation to self-funded employers.

The rule, finalized by the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration, aims to ensure that employers can see what drug manufacturers, pharmacies and other entities are paying their PBMs and any affiliated brokers and consultants.

The department said in an announcement that this data will support employers in negotiating contracts and pushing to lower drug costs for their workers and their dependents.

“This is a win for every American worker who has ever paid too much at the pharmacy counter,” said Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling in the announcement. “For years, PBMs have operated in the shadows, pocketing hidden fees while workers and employers were left in the dark."

Under the rule, PBMs must disclose several key sources of compensation, including manufacturer rebates, any compensation when the price for a drug paid by the plan exceeds reimbursement to the pharmacy, and any payments recouped from pharmacies for dispensed drugs.

The rule was first proposed in late January, and while it enjoys support with employer groups, pharmacy benefit managers have pushed back on the changes.

The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the leading lobbying organization for PBMs, in March called for the agency to rescind the proposed rule, as after it was unveiled, lawmakers passed industry reforms as part of a bipartisan health funding package.

Those congressional PBM reforms include multiple provisions around transparency, and PCMA argued that the DOL rule would create duplicative reporting and disclosure requirements for these companies to navigate.

In a statement Thursday, PCMA President David Marin said that the organization is "extremely concerned that it will lead to higher patient costs and less competition, the opposite of the Department’s stated intent."

"The Department has made modest efforts to harmonize the rule with the recently enacted federal law, but we are concerned it may have exceeded Congress’s intent and its own authority," Marin said. "Patients, employers and unions will have no new meaningful transparency from this action, but prescription drug benefits will now be more expensive."

"This could also lead to greater concentration in our industry as smaller PBMs face excessive reporting demands," Marin added.

DOL said in the announcement that the final rule "implements the bipartisan transparency reforms Congress enacted earlier this year." One of the key goals, the agency said, is to better support employers and plan sponsors in meeting their fiduciary duties under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA).

As they face additional pressure on their ERISA compliance, employers cheered the DOL rule and PBM reform more broadly. The ERISA Industry Committee (ERIC) said in a statement that the rule will offer "a clearer view of what their health plans actually pay."

"We applaud the administration for advancing much-needed transparency related to PBMs and affiliated entities," said James Gelfand, CEO of ERIC, in the release. "Large employers pay for their workers’ prescriptions, but many can’t see how much of that money their PBM and any affiliated entity keeps."

"This rule will fill a critical gap in the legislation Congress passed earlier this year, for the first time giving employers a real view into so-called 'spread pricing' arrangements and helping plan sponsors to improve the affordability of prescription drugs for working families," Gelfand said.

#5764. Does ChatGPT Measure Up to Doctors When It Comes to Questions About IVF?

— Physicians rated the chatbot's answers as very clear but lacking in other areas

BALTIMORE -- ChatGPT's answers to patient queries about assisted reproductive technology (ART) were generally accurate but less complete than professional society education materials, a comparative analysis showed.

On a scale of 1-5, with 5 being the best, physicians rated ChatGPT's responses to questions about the process and associated risks of in vitro fertilization (IVF) lower than the responses found in materials from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) in terms of accuracy (3.98 vs 5.00), completeness (3.40 vs 4.88), safety (2.92 vs 4.88), and quality (3.38 vs 5.00), reported Nicole Fischer, MD, MPH, a reproductive endocrinology and infertility fellow at the University of Pittsburgh.

However, ChatGPT's clarity was rated as comparable to that of ASRM documents (4.60 vs 4.63), Fischer noted at the ASRM annual meeting.

She and her team also assessed how many key concepts from ASRM's ReproductiveFacts.org were referenced in each response; ASRM materials achieved a mean checklist adherence of 100%, while ChatGPT averaged an adherence of 94.1%.

Alarmingly, half of the ChatGPT answers contained an unsupported claim, and 4.2% contained misinformation compared with none of the ASRM responses.

"The key point here is that fluent, confident wording can coexist with omissions, outdated information, and errors," Fischer said.

ChatGPT responses from prompts using conversational language were at an eighth grade reading level, while ChatGPT answers from generic prompts were closer to a 10th grade level and ASRM documents were roughly at a 12th grade level.

"This suggests that how a patient phrases a question can affect the readability or comprehensibility of the response that they get," Fischer noted.

ChatGPT was also asked what the chance of IVF success was for each age from 20 to 45. For most of these ages, ChatGPT's answers were in line with CDC and Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology (SART) data. It correctly showed a decline of birth rates with age, but it overestimated live birth rates at age 35 and underestimated rates at 37 and 40.

ChatGPT is trained on massive amounts of information to predict the most likely response. On technical or newer topics, there can be hallucinations, in which the large language model (LLM) produces a response that sounds correct but may include fabricated information or citations. This used to be more common, and the prevalence of hallucinations can vary by LLM and by version.

"The takeaway here is that topics where accuracy matters most is maybe where these tools are the weakest," Fischer concluded.

In explaining the rationale behind this analysis, Fischer said she and her team wondered, "when patients turn to a chatbot to understand things about IVF and ART, are they getting complete and safe answers?"

To answer this question, they used the free GPT-5.6 Luna. Their first aim was to compare the LLM's responses on common questions about the IVF process and risks to ASRM materials. Each prompt was run three times, resulting in 12 responses.

Four physicians reviewed these responses alongside two ASRM documents. The physicians rated each document on a scale of 1-5 on accuracy, completeness, clarity, safety, and quality. They also assessed checklist adherence, red flags, and grade-level readability on the Flesch-Kincaid scale.

The study's second aim was to compare the accuracy of ChatGPT's success estimates to CDC and SART data.

Fischer noted that the study had some limitations, including the small sample size and the use of only one version of a single LLM. Newer and specialized LLMs, including ChatGPT Health, are worth testing, she added.

Furthermore, some measures were subjective and descriptive, and there were no patient-level outcomes.

Fischer emphasized that patients are already using chatbots to make decisions and get information, and she encouraged clinicians to ask their patients about how they're using these tools, teach them how to prompt AI to cite sources, and point patients to trusted resources.

#5763. A revolutionary new microscope could reveal the hidden machinery of life

Almost a century ago, a breakthrough in microscopy gave scientists an entirely new way to examine the inside of cells. Known as phase contrast, the technique made previously faint or nearly invisible cellular structures much easier to distinguish. Its importance was recognized with a Nobel Prize in 1953.

Now, physicists at the University of California, Berkeley, have brought that same principle to electron microscopy, a technology capable of magnifying objects roughly 10,000 times more than conventional light microscopes.

The researchers have developed a device called a laser phase plate that could significantly improve cryoelectron microscopy (cryo-EM). This powerful imaging method has transformed the study of protein structures and helped speed up drug discovery over the past decade. Even so, it has a major limitation: Most human proteins are so small that obtaining clear images of them remains extremely difficult.

The new laser technology could help overcome that obstacle, potentially allowing scientists to image proteins as small as one-third the size of those that challenge current microscopes.

An even greater impact could come from improvements to cryoelectron tomography (cryo-ET). This newer approach combines images captured from multiple angles to construct three-dimensional views of proteins and other molecules. Unlike techniques that study isolated molecules in a solution, cryo-ET can reveal how proteins are arranged and interact within their natural cellular surroundings.

“Cryo-EM has become the new, fastest-growing method for resolving the structure of biological macromolecules, and cryo-ET is expected to show how these molecules work together in their natural, cellular context,” said Holger Müller, a UC Berkeley professor of physics and faculty scientist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory who led the development effort. “But because of signal-to-noise limitations, the majority of human and animal proteins are too small to be analyzed by these methods. The increase in signal-to-noise ratio provided by this laser phase plate is expected to overcome these important limitations.”

The breakthrough relies on what the researchers describe as the world's most intense focused continuous-wave laser. Rather than simply illuminating a specimen, the laser interacts directly with the microscope's electron beam, altering its phase to increase image contrast.

This adjustment makes it easier to distinguish small molecules, including hemoglobin, from their surroundings. It could also improve the visibility of structures inside cells, such as the nucleus and mitochondria.

“With cryo-ET, we're looking at small, very complicated cellular material that’s incredibly crowded inside the cell,” said Bridget Carragher, founding technical director of imaging at Biohub in Redwood City, California. “It’s like a forest of trees, and you’re trying to find one leaf on one tree in there. Cryo-ET needs a dramatic step forward in contrast, so we can start to see what's going on inside the cell. That's what the laser phase plate promises to give us.”

With financial support from Biohub, Müller acquired an advanced cryo-EM instrument and equipped it with the new laser phase plate. He named the resulting microscope Theia, after the ancient Greek Titaness associated with light and radiance.

Meanwhile, Carragher is directing the construction of a related microscope at Biohub's imaging facility in Redwood City. Her team's instrument uses two lasers rather than one, building on theoretical research conducted by Müller and his collaborators.

The two laser beams are arranged at right angles to one another and each operates at approximately half the power. This configuration helps prevent components from burning out while also reducing optical distortions that could interfere with image quality.

Both research teams are working with Thermo Fisher Scientific, the leading manufacturer of cryo-EM instruments.

“Theia is the Formula 1 microscope,” Müller said. “It has extra electron optics that give it better resolution than the standard cryo-EM, even without the laser. With the addition of the laser phase plate, we hope that it really becomes the world's best instrument overall.”

The Berkeley team's latest images and technical findings are presented in the journal Science. Details of Biohub's two-laser design are available in a recently posted preprint.

To understand why the new technology matters, it helps to look at a longstanding challenge in biological imaging.

Because plant and animal cells consist largely of water, they are relatively transparent when viewed under an ordinary light microscope. Although this transparency might seem beneficial, it creates a problem. Small cellular structures, including mitochondria and nuclei, scatter very little light and therefore appear only slightly darker than the surrounding material.

Scientists have traditionally addressed this problem by adding stains to create greater contrast. However, staining also kills the cells.

In 1930, Dutch physicist Frits Zernike realized that light passing through biological material changes in more ways than simply becoming brighter or dimmer. When light scatters inside a cell, it also experiences a tiny delay that changes its phase, or the timing of its wave peaks.

Although the human eye cannot directly detect this phase shift, Zernike discovered that it could be converted into a visible difference in brightness. By shifting the phase of the unscattered light by 90 degrees, he made subtle cellular features stand out more clearly against their background when the light reached the viewer's eye.

This innovation became the foundation of phase-contrast microscopy, earning Zernike the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics.

By the early 1940s, scientists had already recognized how useful phase contrast was for studying cells. They began exploring whether the same idea might improve electron microscopes, which use electrons instead of light to examine structures as small as individual proteins.

Unfortunately, early attempts encountered serious technical difficulties. Devices designed to alter the phase of electron beams often weakened the beam too much, introduced image instability, or reduced resolution.

A possible solution emerged in 2010, when Müller and Robert Glaeser, now a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of molecular and cell biology, proposed using an intense laser to produce the necessary phase shift. Their approach offered a way to improve contrast without sacrificing electron beam intensity.

Glaeser has played an important role in developing cryo-EM, which offers a potentially simpler way to determine molecular structures than traditional X-ray crystallography.

X-ray crystallography requires researchers to grow crystals of the molecules they want to study and obtain access to an intense X-ray source. Cryo-EM avoids the need to crystallize molecules, but it presents difficulties of its own.

One of the biggest problems is that an electron beam can heat and eventually damage the specimen being examined. This limits how much information can be collected and how detailed the resulting images can become. Covering specimens with metal can reduce damage and improve contrast, but it also makes the images less sharp.

During the 1960s, researchers began investigating whether freezing biological samples could protect them from radiation damage.

Glaeser demonstrated that cooling specimens helped preserve them during imaging. He also proposed using a less intense electron beam to examine thousands of frozen molecules at once, further limiting the damage.

Because the molecules would be positioned at different angles, computers could analyze and combine their images to reconstruct a highly detailed molecular structure.

These advances helped establish the foundations of modern cryo-EM, whose developers received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. During their acceptance remarks, the Nobel laureates acknowledged Glaeser's contributions.

The Nobel Committee praised the technology, explaining that cryo-EM “both simplifies and improves the imaging of biomolecules. This method has moved biochemistry into a new era.”

Turning the laser phase plate concept into working technology required years of engineering.

Following their 2010 proposal, Müller spent 15 years pursuing the idea, with part of the research supported by the National Institutes of Health.

The first major challenge was generating an extraordinarily intense laser beam concentrated into a tiny area. The researchers needed enough light intensity to change the phase of an electron beam by 90 degrees.

It took a decade to develop the necessary system.

Their solution was to confine a continuous laser beam inside a spherical chamber lined with mirrors. As the light repeatedly reflected through the cavity more than 10,000 times, its intensity increased dramatically while the beam became focused into an extremely small spot.

“It’s 75 kilowatts focused to a few microns,” Müller said. “That’s more powerful than what you use for welding. It's more power than a military laser. It builds up the brightest continuous laser focus ever.”

The team first demonstrated that the concept worked by installing a laser phase plate in one of Glaeser's older electron microscopes.

Additional funding from Biohub then made it possible to acquire a customized, state-of-the-art Thermo Fisher Krios cryo-EM microscope and modify it to accommodate the laser technology.

In their latest research, the scientists tested the upgraded microscope using six different samples that varied in size and preparation method. The laser consistently improved image resolution, with particularly important gains for specimens that are difficult to image using standard methods.

“For the most challenging cases — small particles, bad specimens — the laser produces a very considerable advantage,” Müller said.

To demonstrate the new microscope's capabilities, the researchers reconstructed images of two different proteins.

The first was aldolase, a protein found in muscle that modern cryo-EM systems can already image relatively easily. The second was hemoglobin, the protein responsible for carrying oxygen through the bloodstream.

Hemoglobin is much smaller and lies near the lower size limit of proteins that conventional cryo-EM instruments can reliably analyze.

Using the laser phase plate, the researchers improved the resolution of both protein structures. The improvement was especially pronounced for hemoglobin, highlighting the technology's potential to overcome the difficulties associated with smaller molecules.

“The bottom line is, if you have a large protein and a really good sample — a fresh one or one frozen without bubbles, for example — you may not need the phase plate to get a single, high-quality image. But for a small protein and a bad sample, laser-on is best,” Müller said. “This could fill an enormous gap in our knowledge of protein structures that can’t be crystallized or are too small for today’s cryo-EM. And it will be revolutionary for cryo-ET.”

Protein mass is typically expressed in daltons, a unit named after English chemist John Dalton. One dalton is defined as one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

Conventional cryo-EM struggles to image proteins smaller than approximately 70 kilodaltons. That limitation is particularly significant because proteins below this threshold account for about 90% of the human proteome, the complete collection of proteins produced by the human body.

With the laser phase plate, researchers can now image proteins as small as 50 kilodaltons, although doing so remains challenging. Such proteins are even smaller than hemoglobin.

Müller believes the technology could eventually allow scientists to study proteins as small as 17 kilodaltons (the size of the protein myoglobin).

Reaching that goal may require another improvement: using a tightly focused electron beam rather than the defocused beam currently needed to produce sufficient contrast without the laser phase plate.

According to Müller, the laser system should make it possible to obtain contrast directly from phase changes in a focused electron beam.

If successful, this adjustment could double the contrast and signal-to-noise ratio again, adding to the improvement already achieved with the laser phase plate.

Such progress could make it possible to study a far larger proportion of the body's proteins and provide unprecedented insight into how they interact within the complex environment of cells.

“This technology is a step function change for biology,” said Stephani Otte, Biohub’s Vice President of Imaging Science. “We are going to be able to see how molecular machines operate inside the living cell, in context, for the first time. What was once invisible will become visible — and that changes everything about how we understand disease.”

The Berkeley research team also includes Glaeser; postdoctoral fellows and co-first authors Petar Petrov and Jessie Zhang; staff scientist Jonathan Remis; postdoctoral fellow Hang Cheng; and current and former physics graduate students Jeremy Axelrod, Eric Cooper, Ian Hicklin, Shahar Sandhaus, and Cooper Schnurr.

At Biohub, Carragher and David Agard, the organization's founding scientific director of imaging, jointly lead the Dynamic Structural Cell Biology group. Both are co-corresponding authors of the Biohub preprint, alongside Biohub engineer Pavel Olshin.

Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
