#5762. Court rejects CMS' definition of 'medical frailty' under Medicaid work requirements

Court rejects CMS' definition of 'medical frailty' under Medicaid work requirements" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A Massachusetts judge has sided with a coalition of states in an ongoing lawsuit over the rollout of Medicaid work requirements, and rejected the Trump administration's definition of "medical frailty" for critical exemptions.

Judge Richard Stearns ruled Thursday that a regulation issued over the summer that aimed to offer guardrails to the implementation of the work requirements unlawfully limited the group of people who would qualify as "medically frail" and would thus be exempted.

In the rule, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said that the frailty exemption would apply when a "physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply with the community engagement requirement."

This runs afoul of existing law, as there are individuals in five frailty categories established by Congress who may not qualify for the exemption under CMS' definition, Stearns said.

"Because enforcement of an unlawful definition of 'medically frail' may lead to the disenrollment of otherwise eligible vulnerable individuals relying on Medicaid coverage for continuity of care, the States (and public) face potential for great hardship in the absence of an injunction," Stearns wrote. "The court accordingly will issue the permanent injunction requested by the States."

Stearns' ruling isn't a complete win for the state plaintiffs, as he allowed other challenged provisions to stand. Under the order, he determined that CMS should offer states a six-month stay of enforcement on frailty determinations given the short timeline ahead of the work requirements' rollout.

States are down to the wire in implementing the requirements, which were established as part of the massive H.R. 1 legislation in the summer of 2025. The eligibility determinations must be in place nationally on Jan. 1, and experts have warned that the added administrative burden is likely to lead millions to fall out of the Medicaid coverage rolls.

A federal judge has rejected a request from 26 states for a preliminary injunction in the Trump administration's rollout of work requirements in Medicaid.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services finalized implementation guidelines for states in June, with the eligibility requirements set to take effect on Jan. 1. States have until Aug. 31 to communicate with enrollees about the impacts of the changes.

In the lawsuit, the states argued that they do not have the resources necessary to meet the timelines that CMS established in June. They also pushed back on multiple provisions of the final rule, including regulators ultimate definition of medical frailty, which will have a significant impact on who qualifies for exemptions to the requirements.

In an order issued Wednesday, Massachusetts District Judge Richard Stearns wrote that the states did not prove that establishing the systems necessary to make the eligibility determinations would cause them irreparable harm, as CMS said it would reimburse them for 90% of the costs for setting up those mechanisms.

However, he said that the order does not reflect the court's opinion on the merits of the broader litigation, which challenge provisions of the rule under the Administrative Procedure Act. Making a determination on that, as it questions whether officials hewed closely to Congressional intent in regulating the rollout of the requirements, requires a more complete picture.

"These are determinations that, in the view of the court, should be made on a developed record of the kind that informs a court’s decision at the summary judgment stage of a case," wrote Stearns.

A coalition of 26 states is suing the Trump administration over its rollout of Medicaid work requirements.

In the lawsuit—jointly led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell, and New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport—the states seek to challenge provisions in the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services' recently-finalized rule establishing guardrails for the work requirements implementation.

A key pillar of that rule is the agency's definition of who would be considered "medically frail," and thus qualify for an exemption to the requirements. The states argue that the newly established definition will make it far harder for people who may need an exemption to obtain one.

In addition, under the rule, states are now asked to notify Medicaid enrollees of the incoming work requirements by Aug. 31, though the requirements will not be in place until Jan. 1. The suing states argue that this new window leaves them with insufficient time to reach out to members.

The lawsuit is asking the courts to block or strike down these parts of the rule, as they have already made strides toward implementing the work requirements based on previous CMS guidance and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which established the national mandate for the eligibility requirements.

If states fail to comply with the final rule, they face significant potential fines, the suing states said.

In a press release from Massachusetts Attorney General Campbell's office, the state notes that officials raised concerns with CMS about the impact of sudden changes to the timeline, which could lead to disruptions in implementation.

In addition, the states argue that the work requirements violate the Administrative Procedure Act, as there is "substantial" evidence that the administrative barriers can lead people who are eligible to lose coverage given the burden in keeping up with the requirements.

“The Trump Administration’s attempt to impose new, burdensome requirements on Medicaid recipients threatens access to healthcare for our most vulnerable residents and families,” said Campbell in a press release. “Congress made clear that people with serious medical conditions should not lose coverage. We are asking the court to block these unlawful provisions to protect Medicaid recipients and prevent needless strain on Massachusetts’ healthcare system.”

Beyond California, Massachusetts and New Jersey, other states signed on to the lawsuit include Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin.

#5761. As Measles Outbreak Hits Pennsylvania Amish Country, More Show Openness to Vaccines

— After a decline in trust, some minds are changing

EPHRATA, Pa. -- Amish and Mennonite shoppers in conservative dress mingled with shoppers from the wider public on a recent Friday at a vast outdoor market here, where vendors sold colorful pumpkins and mums, fry pies and squash, sports jerseys, and Barbie accessories.

Such interactions are common in Lancaster County in central Pennsylvania, home to the largest Amish population in the U.S. -- and the epicenter of the nation's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. While they avoid many types of civic engagement for religious reasons, the Amish -- like many other groups vulnerable to measles across the nation -- are not truly separate.

"We are all interconnected," said Diego Hijano, MD, MSc, of St. Jude Children's Research Hospital.

Robust vaccination rates once protected Americans much better. But rates among the general public are now falling, and rates have long been low among the Amish, creating the perfect conditions for the contagious virus -- officially considered "eliminated" from the U.S. since 2000 -- to spread here and beyond.

Pennsylvania has the most U.S. cases, with over 1,350 this year, more than a third in Lancaster County alone, according to state figures. That's a big undercount, community leaders say, since many people with measles never see a doctor.

The state has recorded three measles-associated deaths in Lancaster and two in other counties.

In Amish country, a Measles Surge Poses Questions About Vaccine Acceptance

The outbreak has especially hit the "Plain communities" of Amish and conservative Mennonites -- so named for their modest dress and limited use of technology. Vaccination rates, and attitudes about vaccines, range widely. But overall, they are less likely to be vaccinated than the general population, due more to culture and habit than doctrine.

Many are now showing a new openness to vaccines, while members of the general public are also taking extra precautions.

All of this has underscored the interconnectedness of Plain and wider "English" populations.

The Plain People avoid such areas of civic participation as holding public office. Still, they regularly shop and do business with their neighbors in this growing county of half a million people, where an urban core is ringed by suburban subdivisions abutting Amish farms.

"There's no way to imagine that this is going to be an isolated community," said Anne-Marie Derrico, MD, chief medical officer at the nonprofit Union Community Care. It has clinics in the city of Lancaster and outlying towns, along with a mobile unit operating a "Plain Healthy" outreach to the Amish and to Mennonites.

"We have Plain patients coming to the city, we have patients in the city who don't vaccinate, who are going to school, going to other programs with other children," Derrico said.

Pennsylvania's measles rates have declined from their September peak, but some doctors expect them to rise as winter brings more indoor gatherings.

While most cases are mild, measles can cause serious and even fatal complications, such as pneumonia and encephalitis.

Union has held small-scale vaccine clinics to reach Plain populations, resulting in about 450 measles shots. "That's hopefully made a significant impact," Derrico said.

Union's clinics are also offering vaccinations for infants earlier than normally scheduled, as health experts advise in areas experiencing measles outbreaks.

Lauren and Mason Spence brought their 10-month-old son, Bowen, to a clinic recently to get his first dose of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. The "English" family frequently goes to public places, including farmers markets.

"It's scary," Lauren Spence said. "It's spreading quick."

Attitudes toward vaccines in Plain communities have alternately warmed and cooled over time -- most recently cooling in reaction to strict COVID-19 public health measures, according to community leaders and scholars. The measles outbreak is prompting many to accept the shots while reinforcing vaccine skepticism in others.

One Amish farmer, Ephraim Zook, still opposes vaccines even after he and his wife nursed their young twins through the illness. "We just felt that measles is a natural thing," he said.

A Mennonite market vendor said his largely vaccinated community has had no infections.

One Plain farmer said he got vaccinated after his adult siblings began getting measles. With vegetables to harvest and tobacco leaves to pick, "I thought, if I get it, I'm going to be done," he said.

Most interviewed by the AP asked not to use their names, in keeping with Plain traditions of not calling attention to themselves.

Those who avoid vaccines usually aren't driven by ideology, community leaders and experts say.

"The overwhelming reason had nothing to do with being against vaccinations," said Allen Hoover, an Old Order Mennonite and former administrator of the Parochial Medical Center in the town of New Holland. "It was simply, 'Well, we never did before, and we came through all right.'"

Hoover said the most effective strategy for medical workers is to encourage vaccination -- not to push it aggressively.

It takes time for outside professionals to build trust in Plain communities, he said.

One cluster of Amish schools and individuals in New York is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to require their state to allow exemptions to school vaccine requirements on religious grounds, as Pennsylvania and most states do.

But the wider Amish leadership hasn't presented this as a religious issue, according to Steve Nolt, director of the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College in Lancaster County.

"There's nothing in Amish theology or historic documents that you can find that specifically addresses or is opposed to immunization," he said.

About 45,000 Amish and 6,000 Old Order Mennonites live in and around Lancaster County, according to the Young Center. Many rely on traditional remedies and visit doctors infrequently, Nolt said.

This year's outbreak follows ones in 2025 in Mennonite communities in Texas and elsewhere across North America.

Contagious Virus Is a Rising Threat to Everyone

Measles spreads easily when people who have it breathe, cough, or sneeze, or through contaminated surfaces.

"Measles is really the lion king of infectious diseases when it comes to transmission," said Michael Osterholm, PhD, MPH, who directs the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. "No one in the United States of America who is susceptible to the measles virus, either having not been vaccinated or not having previously had it, should feel safe from measles. No one."

The risk grows as vaccination rates decline.

According to the CDC, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-2026 received the required MMR shots. That's down from 95.2% in 2019-2020.

"Though Plain communities are an easy and recognizable target, declining childhood vaccination rates in our county are not limited to the Amish," wrote Berwood Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, in a recent commentary. "Kindergarten vaccination rates have declined in every central Pennsylvania county since 2020."

A 2022 survey by the center found the vast majority of Mennonite families reported having their children vaccinated, compared to about 3 in 10 Amish families.

Yost urged the public not to blame the Amish, or any group, for the outbreak. "Every one of us is susceptible to misinformation and confusing messages," he wrote.

Vaccine hesitancy that rose across populations during the pandemic still lingers.

That's eroded "herd immunity," which occurs when enough people in an area have immunity to measles that it no longer spreads easily. Although nothing short of 100% immunity guarantees the virus won't spread, an outbreak is considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate.

Pennsylvania's kindergarten MMR vaccination rate fell to 93.2% last year.

Lancaster County's rate is 88%, with rates lower in the county's religious and other private schools than in public schools, according to an AP review of state data.

Across the county and state, the percentage of students receiving religious or philosophical exemptions from at least one required vaccination has risen significantly.

Nolt said some anti-vaccine groups targeted the Amish with their messaging.

In 2021, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who helped lead the anti-vaccine movement for years, spoke at a Lancaster County fair, alleging the government was trying to force the Amish to vaccinate.

Now U.S. health secretary, Kennedy recently sparred with Pennsylvania's Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, over the extent of the outbreak. Further controversy ensued when the county coroner attributed the death of a measles-infected infant to a ruptured spleen, not the disease itself.

After a Decline in Trust, Some Minds Are Changing

Lancaster County Commissioner Alice Yoder said public officials should unite behind the message that the vaccine is safe and effective and should encourage people to get it.

That approach succeeded during Pennsylvania's last measles outbreak in 1991.

"There were lines of people in the Plain community that would come and get vaccinated," she said.

D. Holmes Morton, MD, who founded the Central Pennsylvania Clinic in Mifflin County -- which treats Plain patients with genetic diseases -- said the same is happening now.

"We are having more success at having vaccine days," he said.

Ultimately, this will keep everyone safer, said Hijano of St. Jude.

Getting the shot is "an act of love to your community," he said. "You will get protected yourself. But in truth, you are actually protecting everyone around you."

BCBSMA, Medzown team up to match members with clinical trials" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts is teaming up with precision medicine company Medzown to make it easier for members with complex conditions to participate in clinical trials.

In the partnership, Medzown's tech stack will identify the members that are most likely to benefit from a novel therapy for their condition, and then match them with potential clinical trials. The company will then deploy a team of scientists, clinical trial experts and care navigators to work alongside the patient and their care team through the process.

"The next frontier for precision medicine is making sure that the right patient can actually get access," Carter said.

Karl Laskowski, M.D., vice president for clinical programs and strategy at BCBSMA, said in an interview that complex diseases like cancer are often scary and difficult for patients to navigate, and clinical trials offer access to therapies or care they "wouldn’t have otherwise at their disposal."

"It is not always clear what to do, and there’s a lot coming at you," he said. "We want to show up as a trusted ally, making sure that we are filling a need there for people to get advice, taking advantage of whatever may be the most appropriate."

The insurer said that the partnership with Medzown builds on its existing work to manage complex diseases. For example, in June, BCBSMA entered a value-based care contract with Thyme Care, offering its services as an extension of the patient's current care team.

It's BCBSMA's first specialty-specific value-based care relationship, the insurer said.

Laskowski said that it's early days for the partnership with Medzown, but the team is gathering feedback on what's working and what's not to continue improving and building on this foundation.

Carter echoed the sentiment, saying that while there's likely "tremendous opportunity" to grow from here, the focus is on making sure the current program is functioning at the highest level for the members it serves.

She added that the Medzown team believes that a precision medicine data layer will be critical to healthcare more broadly as the treatment for complex disease becomes more and more personal.

"Treatment of cancer has totally changed for many cancer types," she said. "It has turned into a disease that can be managed on a long-term and chronic basis."

"We need to be able to integrate that ... so that these great and fabulous new esoteric therapies get into the continuum of care," Carter said.

#5759. Scientists discover a hidden immune weapon against deadly lung cancer

Scientists have identified a previously overlooked type of immune cell that can detect and destroy small cell lung cancer, the most aggressive form of lung cancer worldwide.

The discovery, reported in the journal Cancer Cell by researchers at WEHI, revealed that patients with greater numbers of these specialized immune cells tended to survive longer. The findings point to a previously unrecognized immune defense that could provide a new way to attack tumors that are notoriously difficult to treat.

The research team also demonstrated that medications already in use could enhance the ability of these immune cells to kill cancer. This approach could eventually improve existing treatments and increase the number of patients who benefit from immunotherapy.

Why Small Cell Lung Cancer Is So Difficult to Treat

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is among the deadliest cancers, with fewer than 7% of patients surviving for five years after diagnosis.

Immunotherapy has dramatically improved treatment for several types of cancer, but its success against SCLC has been much more limited. Only a small proportion of patients experience lasting benefits.

A major challenge is the cancer's ability to escape immune surveillance. SCLC tumors frequently avoid detection by the conventional immune cells that many immunotherapy treatments depend on, allowing the disease to persist despite the body's natural defenses.

The findings published in Cancer Cell suggest there may be another way for the immune system to recognize and attack these tumors. By identifying a previously overlooked immune pathway, researchers have uncovered a potential strategy for overcoming the cancer's ability to remain hidden.

Professor Kate Sutherland, the study's senior author and a laboratory head at WEHI, said the discovery could help address a longstanding challenge in lung cancer research: finding ways to make immunotherapy effective for more patients.

"For decades, we've known that small cell lung cancer is exceptionally good at hiding from the immune system," Prof Sutherland said.

"We've found an immune cell that appears to be able to see through that disguise.

"Strikingly, patients whose tumors contained more of these specialized immune cells often had better treatment outcomes.

"This is the strongest evidence yet that gamma delta T cells are present in small cell lung cancers and appear capable of fighting the disease.

"It suggests these cells may offer an alternative immune attack route for tumors that are able to evade conventional cancer-fighting immune cells, opening up new possibilities for treating a cancer that has seen few advances over the past decades."

Miniature Tumors Reveal a Powerful Immune Response

To investigate whether gamma delta T cells could directly attack lung cancer, the scientists developed miniature tumors in the laboratory using tissue samples donated by patients. The samples were obtained through the Victorian Cancer Biobank in partnership with the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

These miniature tumors, often called "mini tumors," provide one of the most realistic laboratory models of SCLC created so far, allowing researchers to study how cancer behaves and responds to potential treatments.

The team then introduced gamma delta T cells collected from the same patients' blood into the tumor models. The results showed that these immune cells were highly effective at identifying and destroying SCLC cells.

The scientists went a step further by testing whether two medications already approved for other uses could make this immune response even stronger. The drugs were tarlatamab (a cancer treatment approved for SCLC) and zoledronate (approved for osteoporosis and cancer-related bone disease).

Each medication contributed in a different way. Zoledronate increased the number of available gamma delta T cells and improved their ability to identify the lung cancer tumors. Tarlatamab helped bring the immune cells and cancer cells together, effectively directing the immune attack toward the tumors.

When used together, the drugs substantially increased the ability of gamma delta T cells to kill cancer cells in laboratory experiments. The findings suggest that combining existing treatments could provide a new strategy for strengthening the immune system's response to SCLC.

Could Existing Drugs Lead to New Lung Cancer Therapies?

Dr. Jin Ng, the study's first author, said the discovery could also support a treatment approach known as adoptive cell transfer. This involves collecting immune cells, multiplying them outside the body, and then delivering large numbers of those cells back into a patient to help fight cancer.

Because methods for expanding and reinfusing gamma delta T cells have already been developed, the researchers believe their findings could help accelerate the development of new treatments.

"For patients with lower gamma delta T cell levels, therapies such as zoledronate may offer a way to boost their cancer-fighting immune cells and responsiveness to treatments," Dr. Ng said.

"As therapies that expand and reinfuse gamma delta T cells already exist, our findings raise the exciting possibility of rapidly translating this discovery into new treatment strategies.

"This could open an entirely new avenue for personalized treatment approaches in small cell lung cancer and other solid cancers that are often missed by conventional immune cells."

Clues From Major Lung Cancer Immunotherapy Trials

The investigation began with an examination of data from two influential clinical trials, IMpower133 and CASPIAN. Both studies helped establish immunotherapy as a standard treatment option for patients with small cell lung cancer.

Researchers noticed evidence pointing toward an important role for gamma delta T cells and used sophisticated genomic and computational techniques to investigate further.

Analyses conducted by WEHI's genomics and bioinformatics teams revealed that patients with stronger gamma delta T cell signatures were among those who benefited most from immunotherapy.

Together with the laboratory findings, these results strengthen the evidence that gamma delta T cells play an important role in the immune response to SCLC and could become useful targets for future therapies.

The WEHI team is now working with scientists at the Doherty Institute to build on the discovery, with the goal of translating the findings into a new class of immunotherapy drugs for small cell lung cancer.

The research received support from Cancer Council Victoria, the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), The CASS Foundation, and The International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer.

#5756. Screened for Diabetes at 23 BMI, Denied GLP-1s Until 30 BMI

I am a South Asian physician -- Pakistani, to be specific. By the American Diabetes Association's (ADA) own rule, my doctor should begin screening me for diabetes once my body mass index (BMI) passes 23, because Asian Americans develop the disease at lower weights. And they did just that. Yet, when I asked about a GLP-1 receptor agonist, the answer was no. Eligibility for FDA-approved GLP-1s starts at a BMI of 30, or 27 with at least one weight-related condition. At my BMI of 26.5 but without diabetes, I meet neither threshold.

The ADA guideline that flags me for annual diabetes screening and the prior authorization form that denies me the drug are describing the same 26.5. Only one of them was written with an Asian body in mind.

Healthcare coverage for GLP-1s is shrinking. Medi-Cal dropped coverage for GLP-1s for weight-loss in January; MassHealth followed in July. When a benefit contracts, the patients whose eligibility was always marginal lose first. Meanwhile, in June, the ADA released Asian-specific waist and BMI thresholds for diagnosing obesity. The clinical definition moved in one direction while access has moved in the other.

A Closer Look at the Screening Guidelines

At the same BMI, people of Asian descent carry more visceral fat and less muscle than people of European descent, the body composition that drives insulin resistance. That fat is invisible to the scale, so BMI may read lower: the 2025 iCARDIO global obesity guidelines put an Asian person's BMI about two to three units under a white person's at the same level of body fat. This can manifest as chronic diseases.

Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease reach Asian adults at lower BMIs and, across every subgroup the American Heart Association has examined, at higher rates than white adults. The World Health Organization (WHO) saw this in 2004 and set lower action points for Asian populations, at BMIs of 23 and 27.5.

How large is the mismatch? In a study of nearly 1.5 million adults in England, researchers asked at what BMI each ethnic group reaches the diabetes risk that white adults reach at 30 BMI. For South Asians, the answer was 23.9. For Chinese adults, 26.9. A South Asian at 24 BMI carries the risk that earns a white patient the diagnosis of obesity, yet treatments that come with it are denied until 30.

The pivotal trials were designed around Western definitions of obesity, and the labels copied the trial entry criteria. A 2026 analysis of 352 GLP-1 trials found that of every inclusion criterion these studies used, BMI was the one that shut Asian patients out. A clinical trial inclusion cutoff of 30 resulted in 41.5% of non-Asian American adults being eligible, compared to 13.5% of Asian Americans and 7.2% of Koreans. Blood sugar, kidney function, and liver criteria admitted more than 93% of every group. Trials have under-enrolled non-white patients for 30 years, and each under-representative trial has become the reason the next label stays where it is.

More recent research invalidates that excuse. Published in 2025, STEP 11 tested semaglutide 2.4 mg in South Korea and Thailand using the local definition of obesity: a BMI of 25 or higher. Participants lost 16% of body weight compared to 3.1% on placebo. A post hoc analysis looked at 68 participants who started below a BMI of 30. Within that group, the 45 on semaglutide lost 17.6%, compared with 4.4% for the 23 on placebo. Under the American threshold, none of these 68 would qualify on BMI alone: most of them would need a second diagnosis before an insurer would cover the drug. In their conclusion, the authors highlighted the importance of population-specific approaches to inform reimbursement policies and public health strategy.

Meanwhile, across eight cardiovascular outcome trials, GLP-1 receptor agonists prevented a major cardiac event in 2.9 of every 100 Asian participants and 1.4 of every 100 white participants. The patients with the most to gain are the ones the threshold has kept waiting for access.

Current labels -- including the label for semaglutide (Wegovy) as revised in 2026, and the one for tirzepatide (Zepbound) -- now state the indication without a number: adults with obesity, or adults with overweight plus a weight-related condition. Yet, the 30 and the 27 survive in the trial descriptions and in payer prior authorization forms.

So, the question has shifted from arithmetic to definition. Which definition of obesity applies?

The ADA's 2026 Standards of Care tell clinicians to confirm excess adiposity with cutoffs appropriate to ethnicity, and name South Asian patients specifically. Britain's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence sets a higher starting line than any American insurer: a BMI of 35 with a comorbidity for tirzepatide; but they still tell prescribers to lower the threshold by 2.5 units for South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, and Black patients. A system that rations more tightly than ours built in the adjustment. Ours did not.

Medicine spent the last 5 years pulling race out of certain clinical calculators, and it was right to do so. The race coefficient in the old eGFR equation multiplied a Black patient's estimated kidney function by roughly 1.2 for no measured reason, which meant Black patients reached the thresholds for nephrology referral and transplant listing later than everyone else. The National Kidney Foundation and American Society of Nephrology retired it in 2021, and after transplant programs recalculated, more than 6,100 Black candidates had their waiting times backdated by a median of 1.7 years.

An ethnicity-adjusted BMI threshold runs the other way. This adjustment reflects a difference measured directly, in visceral fat and lean mass at a given BMI, since the WHO's 2004 review. Factoring race into BMI would widen access to care instead of narrowing it.

Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers should adopt the ethnicity-adjusted BMI bands their own clinical societies already publish, or accept an ethnicity-appropriate waist circumference as an alternate qualifier. Both documents exist. Both were written by the organizations these payers cite whenever it suits them.

The screening threshold was set low to find metabolic disease early in Asian patients. Yet, payers set the treatment threshold high. That decision lives in prior authorization criteria, and it contradicts the guidelines those same payers rely on. The fix needs no new law and no new trial. It needs someone at the payer level to read what is already on their desk.

#5755. Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles

Most primates have relatively large brains covered in distinctive folds and grooves. However, common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) are an unusual exception. These small monkeys have brains that are almost entirely smooth, with very little folding. Scientists at the German Primate Center (DPZ), the Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen, have now identified several cellular processes that help explain this difference.

Using miniature brain structures known as organoids, the researchers discovered that certain neural progenitor cells, which produce neurons, develop differently in marmosets than in humans. These differences involve the cells' structure, the speed at which they divide, and the timing of their development. Together, these changes reduce the number of neurons produced, contributing to the smaller size and smoother surface of the marmoset brain. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide new insights into primate brain evolution and could eventually improve our understanding of human brain development disorders.

Why Some Primate Brains Are Smooth Instead of Folded

Brain size and the extent of surface folding are important features that distinguish different primate species. The human brain, for example, has a highly folded surface resembling the ridges and grooves of a walnut. This arrangement greatly expands the brain's surface area, creating room for billions of neurons that support complex thinking and other advanced mental abilities.

Scientists believe that the common ancestor of modern primates already possessed a moderately sized brain with at least some folding. Yet not all primates living today retain these characteristics.

Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), small monkeys native to South America that are becoming increasingly important in biomedical research, have brains with almost no visible folds. Researchers at the German Primate Center set out to determine why their brains develop so differently from those of humans and other primates.

"We wanted to understand which changes at the cellular level cause the marmoset brain to grow less and form fewer folds," explains Lidiia Tynianskaia, one of the study's two first authors and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution at the DPZ. "At the beginning of development, the common marmoset brain exhibits the typical structure and composition of a large, folded primate brain. As development progresses, processes must therefore occur that effectively slow down the production of nerve cells."

Scientists Discover What Slows Brain Growth

To investigate these developmental differences, the team compared brain organoids grown from human and common marmoset cells. Their attention centered on neural progenitor cells, the cells responsible for generating neurons during brain development.

These progenitor cells play a major role in determining the eventual size and shape of the brain. The more neurons they produce, the greater the potential for the cerebral cortex to expand and develop folds.

The researchers found that the marmoset's smaller, smoother cerebral cortex is not the result of a single developmental change. Instead, several differences involving distinct types of progenitor cells work together to limit neuron production and brain folding.

"Our investigations have shown that certain progenitor cells in the common marmoset divide significantly more slowly than in humans," explains César Mateo Bastidas Betancourt, also a first author of the study and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group. "Other progenitor cells have a simpler structure than their human counterparts, with fewer processes, and are therefore less proliferative. Both of these factors ultimately result in fewer nerve cells, which contributes to a smaller size and less folding of the cerebral cortex in marmosets."

The scientists also identified important differences in when certain progenitor cell characteristics and behaviors emerge during development. Compared with humans, marmosets have a shorter overall period during which these cells can multiply rapidly.

Together, the slower rate of cell division, simpler cell structures, and shorter window for rapid growth help explain why the marmoset brain produces fewer neurons and develops far fewer folds.

Miniature Brains Reveal Important Developmental Clues

Much of the research relied on brain organoids, small, three-dimensional structures grown from cells that reproduce important features of early brain development. These miniature models allowed scientists to investigate developmental changes across multiple samples and compare the timing of key processes.

"The study combines the advantages of in vivo and in vitro methods," says Michael Heide, head of the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution. "Organoids are well-suited for obtaining statistically robust results because such sample sizes are not feasible in primates. We subsequently repeated some key experiments in fetal brain tissue to confirm the results from the organoids."

One particularly important finding involved the relationship between development in organoids and development in actual marmoset brains. The researchers determined that a marmoset brain organoid grown for 50 days closely matches the developmental stage of a natural marmoset brain at day 90.

Establishing this relationship was essential because brain organoids and actual brains do not necessarily develop at the same rate. By identifying corresponding developmental stages, the scientists could make meaningful comparisons and interpret their experimental findings more reliably.

What Smooth Monkey Brains Reveal About Human Brain Evolution

The findings help explain how relatively small differences in the behavior and developmental timing of brain-building cells can contribute to major differences in brain size and folding among primates.

They also offer a potential explanation for how the wide variety of primate brain shapes and sizes emerged over evolutionary time, including why some species developed relatively smooth brains while others possess much larger, heavily folded ones.

Beyond their evolutionary significance, these discoveries provide a foundation for investigating how the human brain develops and what happens when those processes are disrupted. A better understanding of the cellular mechanisms that control neuron production and brain growth could ultimately help researchers study developmental disorders affecting the human brain.

#5754. Community Health Systems logs $86M net loss in Q3, hopes for return of 'pent-up' electives in 2027

Community Health Systems logs $86M net loss in Q3, hopes for return of 'pent-up' electives in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A “challenging macro environment” serving up more uninsured patients and fewer commercial elective procedures dragged Community Health Systems below internal and analyst operating forecasts for the third quarter.

The 59-hospital system reported $2.76 billion in third-quarter net operating revenue, down about 10.7% year over year due to several divestments but up 3.8% on a same-store basis. Net loss was $86 million, -$0.63 per diluted share or -$0.48 after adjustment, compared to the prior year’s $1.27 per share net income.

The consensus estimates for revenue and earnings were $2.78 billion and -$0.22 per diluted share, per Zach’s Investment Research. The company’s shares were trading over 10% below the open late Thursday afternoon.

“While overall financial results fell below our internal forecast, due to the same factors that many peers are experiencing—namely elevated uninsured volumes and temporary softness in commercial elective procedures—we delivered sequential volume gains and solid cash flow performance,” CEO Kevin Hammons summarized Thursday morning on the company’s earnings call. “Importantly, our leading indicators clearly demonstrate that care is being deferred rather than lost to competitors.”

CHS has reduced its 2026 guidance ranges for net operating revenues, adjusted EBITDA and cash ranges.

Same-store admissions rose 2.2% while adjusted admissions increased 3.6% year over year. However, about half of the adjusted admissions growth was among uninsured patients, Chief Financial Officer Jason Johnson explained, and a 2% overall increase in same-store surgeries masked low numbers for commercial electives. These factors held same-store net revenue per adjusted admission to just 0.2% year-over-year growth.

Executives, in response to analyst questions, noted that the 2% increase is a clear improvement from recent quarters’ declines.

“We saw more cardiac procedures and more GI procedures this quarter,” Hammons explained. “The cardiac procedures, though, … are low margin because of the high cost of the devices. What we were short on were the elective orthopedic and elective general surgery-type procedures that are higher-margin business, and those are more elective type procedures. […] Again, kind of fits back into the story of we believe this is a patient decision around care, and being influenced by financial decisions.”

In the meantime, Hammons said the company is “proactively managing our cost structure,” yielding more than $100 million in projected annual savings so far “without compromising our clinical capacity or operational readiness for tomorrow” when those electives return.

Looking to the tea leaves in 2027, executives suggested there would be a “modest” headwind from Medicaid work requirements. While more than half of the company’s Medicaid volumes are in expansion states, “we think it’s likely that the very large majority will qualify for continued coverage under the various exemptions like age, caregiver status or medical frailty, but we really just don’t know exactly what the impact will be until the data starts coming in,” Johnson said during the call.

Exchange volume reductions due to coverage drop-offs could see “some potential future degradation” based on how open enrollment goes, he said, although “we think there will be a modest headwind there.” Provider tax cuts will also likely bring another “modest” hit, while medical specialty fees expected to grow “well above inflation” are “the big question mark on cost,” Johnson added.

On the other hand, executives counted payment rate updates, investments in outpatient and ambulatory locations, expense management and $25 million to $30 million in year-one funds from the Rural Health Transformation Program as positive factors for 2027 earnings.

Further, they suggested that this year’s “uncharacteristic” dearth in elective procedures could come to an end as cost-conscious patients—who are still captured in CHS’ care networks—eventually book their deferred care.

“There’s pent-up demand,” Hammons said. “Ultimately, we think that it comes back into the system because when you need a joint replacement, it’s not going to heal on its own.”

“Our initial expectations [were that when] we got into the back half of this year, we would see that seasonality growth. We did not see as much of that in the third quarter as we had previously expected,” he explained. “As you get to October, if people have not met their co-pay and deductible, it’s likely they could push that off until next year, get their procedures in the first half of the year and have a longer period of time to have other medical procedures done without having to pay a co-pay and deductible again. So we’ve adjusted our guidance accordingly to reflect our outlook on that.”

CHS is hardly alone in navigating surgery and payer mix challenges. Fellow for-profits HCA Healthcare, Universal Health Services and Tenet Healthcare each described varying levels of impact during earnings calls held this week. Each held off from detailing concrete estimates for the coming year, noting a need to monitor year-end trends and the exchanges’ open enrollment period, but acknowledged that Medicaid coverage will likely continue to be a sore spot.

#5753. Oxford scientists discover how viruses build themselves without a blueprint

Researchers at the University of Oxford have observed virus-like particles assembling themselves one molecule at a time, uncovering the surprisingly simple rules that allow complex biological structures to form with remarkable reliability. The findings, published in Nature, offer a detailed look at a process that scientists have struggled to observe directly for decades.

Understanding how viruses construct their protective protein shells, and how that construction might be interrupted, could lead to new antiviral drugs, improved vaccines, and other medical treatments. The discovery helps explain how individual proteins consistently organize themselves into the correct structures despite having thousands of possible ways to connect.

The researchers found that viral assembly resembles navigating a complicated maze, where only certain paths lead to lasting progress. At first, protein components form weak connections that can easily break apart if the arrangement is unsuccessful. This flexibility allows the molecules to keep trying different combinations until they form particular closed structures. Once multiple connections hold these structures together, they become far more stable.

These stable arrangements serve as molecular checkpoints, narrowing the enormous number of possible assembly routes into a much smaller set of successful pathways. One especially important milestone occurs when five larger protein building blocks connect to form a closed pentagonal ring. This is the first highly stable structure in the assembly process. Once it forms, each subsequent stable stage requires fewer additional building blocks, allowing the particle to grow more quickly.

Co-lead author Dr. Roi Asor (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) explained: "A virus has to solve an extraordinary construction problem. Its components somehow have to find the right arrangement among a huge number of possibilities, without a blueprint or machinery directing the process. We can now watch what happens molecule by molecule and see the physical rules that make it possible."

Watching Virus Particles Assemble Molecule by Molecule

Viruses store and protect their genetic material within organized protein shells known as capsids. Depending on the virus, these shells may consist of tens or even thousands of individual protein components. Remarkably, in many cases, the proteins can arrange themselves into the correct structure without any external machinery directing their assembly.

Although scientists have investigated viral self-assembly for decades, capturing the process as it unfolds has been a major challenge. Many of the intermediate structures exist only briefly and appear in very small quantities. As a result, traditional methods have generally allowed researchers to examine the starting materials and finished particles without clearly showing how one transforms into the other.

To overcome this limitation, the Oxford researchers studied an engineered virus-like particle composed of 60 protein units. They used mass photometry, a technique developed at Oxford that determines the mass of individual molecules by measuring the light they scatter. By combining this technology with a new approach for keeping individual molecules confined and continuously observable, the team could repeatedly measure the mass of a growing particle as additional proteins attached.

This approach allowed the scientists to follow the construction process as it happened, effectively tracking the addition of individual molecular building blocks over time.

Co-first author PhD student Dan Loewenthal (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) said: "This method lets us study the assembly process directly, we just take a video!"

Co-lead author Professor Philipp Kukura (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, Oxford University) said: "Until now, much of our understanding of how these structures assemble has had to be reconstructed from snapshots or theoretical models. Being able to both quantify the underlying interactions and follow one particle as it grows changes that. We can see the important intermediate structures appear and deduce a detailed model of the construction process."

The Surprising Trick That Makes Viral Assembly Work

The results help explain how a process involving an overwhelming number of possible molecular arrangements can consistently produce the correct structure. Rather than exploring every possible route, the proteins progress through a relatively small number of stable intermediate stages that guide assembly toward completion.

The findings also clarify why the earliest stage of construction, called nucleation, is particularly difficult and why growth becomes substantially faster after the first stable structure appears.

A key part of this efficiency comes from the ability of protein building blocks to make mistakes without permanently disrupting the process. Weak initial connections allow incorrect combinations to separate, giving the proteins another opportunity to find a better arrangement. When enough components eventually connect in the correct closed configuration, the resulting structure becomes stable enough to support further growth.

Dr. Asor added: "The weak interactions give the system room to make mistakes. Most encounters don't have to be successful: the components can separate and try again. But once enough of them come together in the right closed arrangement, the structure becomes stable, and assembly can move forward. That combination of trial and error followed by locking in successful structures is what makes the process so reliable."

New Possibilities for Antiviral Drugs and Vaccines

By identifying the molecular interactions that control viral assembly, scientists may eventually be able to develop treatments that interfere with the construction of viral protein shells. The same insights could also support efforts to engineer virus-like particles for vaccines and other therapeutic applications.

Co-author Dr. Jack Tan (MRC Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine and CAMS-Oxford Institute) noted: "The ability to understand these processes at the molecular level could have important applications in vaccine development and antivirals that disrupt viral assembly."

The implications may extend far beyond viruses. Self-assembly is essential throughout biology, helping create everything from the internal skeletons of cells to specialized molecular compartments and large protein complexes.

By making it possible to observe these intricate construction processes one molecule at a time, the Oxford team's approach offers researchers a powerful new way to investigate how complex biological structures emerge from relatively simple interactions.

TTHealthWatch is a weekly podcast from Texas Tech. In it, Elizabeth Tracey, director of electronic media for Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore, and Rick Lange, MD, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso, look at the top medical stories of the week.

0:35 Continuous glucose monitoring in type 2 diabetes patients not using insulin

2:35 Already shown to be beneficial in those using insulin

6:30 Pregnancy outcomes in women who donate kidneys

9:15 AI collaboration for managing epilepsy

Elizabeth: Targeting KRAS in different types of cancer.

Rick: Pregnancy outcomes in women that have donated a kidney.

Elizabeth: Utilization of AI and EEG in taking care of people with uncontrolled epilepsy.

Rick: And is there a role for continuous glucose monitoring in people with type 2 diabetes?

Elizabeth: That's what we're talking about this week on TTHealthWatch, your weekly look at the medical headlines from Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center in El Paso. I'm Elizabeth Tracey, a Baltimore-based medical journalist.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso.

Elizabeth: Rick, I'm going to kick the ball to you, to the New England Journal of Medicine, and take a look at this issue of continuous glucose monitoring in folks with type 2 diabetes who are not using insulin.

Rick: This particular study is for people that are just on oral medications. Or it could be an injectable, but they're not taking insulin. Because individuals with either type 1 or type 2 diabetes that are on insulin, glucose monitoring continuously has been proven to be helpful. Its role in the treatment of people with type 2 diabetes not on insulin required further study.

And that's what this study attempted to do. It's a 26-week trial in 22 primary care practices in the United States. Individuals were randomized to just routine care or to continuous glucose monitoring. There were 145 participants that received continuous glucose monitoring and 138 who just had routine care.

Those that had continuous glucose monitoring, their hemoglobin A1c decreased from 8.8 to 7.2. With routine care, 8.7 to 8.0. They looked at, OK, how often were you in the normal range? They were 21 absolute percentage points more likely to be in the normal range if they were receiving continuous glucose monitoring than if they didn't. Were they at an increased risk of developing hypoglycemia? And the answer is they were not.

Elizabeth: A very strong argument, of course, for the employment of this technique. And I would note that we are seeing devices that are way easier to use and integrations with watches and cell phones and the provision of that data back to the practice. And so, to me, this makes a lot of sense. What was the downside?

Rick: Really no downside at all. What they weren't able to ascertain is how did they get their hemoglobin A1c lower. Was it a change in medications? Or were people just more fastidious about either taking their medications or their diet? Or did they change their exercise? But downside? None. And as you mentioned, it's routinely available, and it's been already shown to be beneficial in people on insulin. I think we ought to be extending this to all of our patients that have type 2 diabetes, regardless of whether they're on insulin or not.

Elizabeth: And I would also note, of course, that people become really accustomed to monitoring their own numbers. And I'm wondering if, at some point -- and I'm not sure we've seen this demonstrated yet in any study -- if there's going to be fatigue after a while at always scrutinizing that data and then making choices based on it.

Rick: Yeah. I can't answer that for an extended period of time. The individuals in this 6-month study, the median use was 97% of the time. And 86% of the participants used continuous glucose monitoring at least 80% of the time, so they stuck with it at least during this 6-month period.

Elizabeth: This may argue for implantable monitors.

On to then Nature Medicine and something the [European Society for Medical Oncology] meeting just concluded, something much in the news, of course, was the use of vaccines for melanoma and this huge reduction, over 40% reduction in recurrence among the folks in whom that was used. This study is looking at lymph node-targeted KRAS-specific vaccines in pancreas cancer, another bad actor.

So what they did in this study was look at an agent that's called camupepimut. And this, of course, brings the question to my mind of how in the world do people create these names for these? I wish they'd reveal that, honestly, in these studies, because this is certainly a tongue twister. And this is an agent that drives mutated KRAS-specific T-cell responses.

They were looking at people who had pancreatic adenocarcinoma or pancreas cancer, and they randomized them 2:1 to receive this agent or standard-of-care observation. In their intervention arm, they had 96 people and they were looking at disease-free survival as their endpoint.

After 6 months, disappointingly, did not meet their disease-free survival endpoint in the folks who received it. However, they did see that there were some benefits that corresponded to the use of this agent. Those included this baseline circulating tumor DNA positivity. So, of course, we're looking for that in people who have cancer, increasingly looking for it as clinically informative, I would note. In this case, it was beneficial with regard to that. And they also were able to show that their KRAS-specific T-cell responses were robust. They were 9.17-fold over baseline. They look at this as efficacy and immunogenicity signals that will help them to advance this therapy in people who have pancreas cancer. And they're looking at a confirmatory phase III trial.

Rick: There was a robust response in some patients, but not all. But there seemed to be a dose-survivor relationship in that if the T-cell population did not increase ninefold, they didn't see an improvement in disease-free survival. But in those individuals in whom there did seem to be a response, it was because the T-cell population increased by at least 9-fold and some of them as much as 50-fold.

This Canadian study -- and by the way, a shout-out to our long-time listener, Tom Jackson, who's Canadian -- included female kidney donors aged 18-42 who had donated a kidney between July of 1992 and August of 2021. And they subsequently had pregnancy of at least 20 weeks gestation. And they matched them 4:1 with women who were matched on their delivery date, their age of delivery, their years of when they delivered. Four of those to every one kidney donor. How often were the women hospitalized with a diagnosis of gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, or eclampsia? Or they looked at 12 other maternal-fetal adverse outcomes.

In the 385 pregnancies in 252 women who had donated a kidney, the risk of being hospitalized for gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, or eclampsia was about 12% versus 8% in women who hadn't donated a kidney. It appeared that they were more likely to have a small-for-gestational-age child, about 14% versus 8%. And it also appears to be more common with the first pregnancy than it does with the second pregnancy. Counseling donor candidates about this, who may become pregnant, is really important.

The authors remind us that one-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures that are uncontrolled by medication. Frequently, of course, implantable devices are considered. They unfortunately are not able, these devices that we have currently, to share this information with patients in real time. And the idea is that this is a missed opportunity because it doesn't allow the devices to learn from clinical events and teach patients about how their behaviors may affect their health.

So they developed a device platform that converses with patients to help them manage their own epilepsy. They process this model -- biomarkers of sleep, medication, cognition, seizure probability -- and notifies patients of clinical events and trends, records their symptoms and responses, and uses their feedback to retrain the seizure detector. A very small number of folks in this study. Those who had the scalp EEG, 11. Intracranial monitors, two of them. And as I noted, they were all inpatients during this.

They actually were able to demonstrate that this model could potentially be helpful. They were able to train it so that it really radically reduced its false positives. If it alerts you that you're about to have a seizure, what's the intervention?

Bob Herman is the author of Health Care Inc., an award-winning weekly newsletter about the business of health and medicine.

Bob covers the money in health care, focusing on health insurance and hospitals. His stories delve into Medicare Advantage, opaque prescription drug benefits, and how much executives actually make. He is also the author of the Health Care Inc. newsletter. You can reach Bob on Signal at bobjherman.09.

The middlemen that oversee prescription drug spending for employers and workers will soon have to tell their clients all the different ways they get paid, a significant move that will unlock reams of highly protected data.

The Trump administration finalized a regulation Thursday that will force pharmacy benefit managers to disclose all the different fees and compensation they get from drugmakers, consulting firms, and other entities to the employers that hire them. The disclosures — which will be required starting on July 1, 2027 — will include drug rebates, spread pricing, and financial relationships with brokers and consultants that could create conflicts of interest.

Federal officials estimate the rule will apply to more than 70 PBMs and 130,000 employers, saving more than $800 million annually through lower drug costs.

#5749. Teladoc Health beats Q3 expectations as BetterHelp insurance growth accelerates

Teladoc Health beats Q3 expectations as BetterHelp insurance growth accelerates" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Teladoc Health raised its 2026 outlook after better-than-expected third-quarter results, as BetterHelp’s insurance pivot gained traction and Integrated Care profitability improved.

The virtual care company posted declining revenue but still beat Wall Street on both revenue and profit. Teladoc Health's Q3 beat drove shares up nearly 27% Thursday after the company reported Q3 earnings Wednesday after market close.

Teladoc Health faces near-term pressure as it transitions its virtual mental health business, BetterHelp, from a cash pay model to an in-network, insurance-covered model.

The company's consolidated revenue was $605.1 million, down 3.4% year-over-year but towards the high end of management's guidance range, as solid performance in the integrated care business and strong BetterHelp insurance growth was partially offset by ongoing headwinds in BetterHelp’s cash pay revenue, Chief Financial Officer Michael Grasher, who joined the company in August, told investors and analysts on the company's Q3 earnings call Wednesday. Teladoc's Q3 revenue exceeded the $588.4 million analyst consensus.

The company reported third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $79.4 million, up roughly 14% year-over-year and compared to the $67.7 million consensus target. Teladoc reported a net loss of $26.9 million, or a loss per share of 15 cents, versus Street expectations for a loss of 22 cents per share.

The company generated $79 million in free cash flow in the third quarter, and it ended the quarter with $850 million in cash and cash equivalents.

Teladoc Health raised its full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance. The company now expects 2026 revenue of $2.39 billion to $2.44 billion, raising the midpoint of its full-year 2026 revenue outlook by $13 million, “driven largely by the updated BetterHelp outlook,” Grasher said.

The company expects adjusted EBITDA of $277 million to $303 million, up $3 million at the midpoint versus the prior range.

Teladoc Health is focused on expanding access to its direct-to-consumer virtual mental health services, BetterHelp, through insurance coverage while also growing its integrated care enterprise business.

"As we consider the market more broadly as a company, we continue to see opportunities for virtual care to play an increasing role in addressing key challenges in healthcare," Teladoc Health CEO Chuck Divita said during the call.

As a scaled virtual care company, Teladoc's technology and services help address rising healthcare costs, expand access, improve chronic disease and mental health care and ease pressure on providers and the broader healthcare system, Divita said.

The BetterHelp segment brought in $207 million in revenue, down 13% year-over-year. BetterHelp commercial insurance revenue exceeded expectations, coming in at $32.1 million, up from $3.7 million a year ago and beating management's forecast of $25 million to $31 million. BetterHelp cash-pay revenue declined 25% to $174 million in Q3, as fewer users paid out of pocket. But cash pay performance for BetterHelp was "better than anticipated," Divita said. The company continues to reduce advertising spend for the BetterHelp business while also "adapting its advertising and marketing approach to reflect insurance priorities," he noted.

BetterHelp's pivot to an in-network insurance model is gaining momentum with 27,000 covered sessions per week in Q3, an annualized run rate above $140 million and more than 11,000 credentialed therapists, Divita told analysts and investors. That compares to the $110 million annualized run rate from weekly sessions referenced in Teladoc's second-quarter earnings call.

In Q3, 36% of acquired U.S. users came from insurance, up about 8 percentage points from the second quarter, according to executives. The company added more than 3,000 therapists to the network during the quarter.

"We believe expanding insurance access can help create a more durable position for BetterHelp over time," Divita said.

The company expects continued growth in 2027 as it expands provider capacity, improves therapist engagement and grows utilization of BetterHelp’s services, Grasher said.

Teladoc is targeting a $200 million annualized BetterHelp insurance run rate by the end of 2027.

“While there is more work ahead, this was a solid quarter driven by execution, and continued progress across our key strategic priorities,” Grasher said.

Teladoc Health continues to invest in its core business, integrated care, which brought in $399 million in Q3 revenue, up 2% year-over-year, and adjusted EBITDA of $74.9 million, up 13% year-over-year. Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 18.8%, and Grasher noted on the call that the Q3 margin expansion occurred despite the ongoing mix shift toward visit-based arrangements.

The virtual company is focused on moving health plan and employer clients away from fragmented point solutions to its broader Teladoc One model. Teladoc One, unveiled in July, is designed to offer a more coordinated, personalized approach for members, while tying payment to clinical and financial outcomes, executives said. As part of the model, Teladoc Health care teams deliver and coordinate care across virtual settings and in partnership with a member's local providers.

The company has moved forward with initial launch partners for Teladoc One, and the platform will be more broadly available in 2027, executives said.

"We are encouraged by the level of client engagement and member feedback on Teladoc One at this point, reinforcing our view that clients are looking for solutions that can deliver a more connected experience, address more care needs, and demonstrate greater accountability for outcomes and impact," Divita said.

Outside the U.S. market, Teladoc Health developed a "hybrid care" model that combines its technology with virtual clinical services delivered into physical healthcare settings. The company sees opportunities to build out that model with U.S. hospitals and health systems. To support that strategy, Teladoc Health acquired Teledigm Health, a company that provides virtual clinical services to U.S. hospitals and health systems. Teledigm partners with hospitals and clinics to deliver remote acute, outpatient and specialty care.

Financial details of the Teledigm Health deal were not disclosed.

"We believe the market dynamics supporting the adoption of our hybrid care models in other countries are also increasingly prevalent with hospitals and health systems in the U.S., including healthcare workforce and capacity challenges, financial pressures and the need to improve access for underserved and rural communities. As a result, we see an opportunity to leverage our experience in hybrid care within the U.S. to support future growth," Divita said during the call.

"This is a company that we've worked with for a long time that's used our technology and really commercialized the services part of the equation using our technology. The tracks have been laid in terms of using our technology and support and use cases to those health systems. We think bringing that expertise we have in non-U.S. markets, which is considerable and has been a nice source of growth for us, bringing that expertise combined with our technology and telehealth services together, we can really go after that market opportunity in 2027," he told investors and analysts during a Q&A on the earnings call.

Teladoc also continues to invest in product innovation to support its integrated care business. The company expanded its Solo enterprise platform with two AI tools designed to add clinical capabilities without forcing hospitals to adopt more standalone technology. The two new capabilities—dubbed SoloVitals and SoloScribe—bring contact-free vital sign measurement and ambient clinical documentation directly into clinical workflows.

Wall Street analysts saw positive signs of progress in the turnaround of Teladoc's BetterHelp business in the latest quarter.

Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote that Teladoc's third-quarter results provided a positive update on the company’s ability to convert strong insurance demand into revenue.

"We continue to view BetterHelp’s transition toward greater in-network coverage as the key driver of business stabilization, particularly as insurance growth increasingly offsets cash-pay declines and added capacity of credentialed therapists enables the company to capture strong underlying demand," Daniels wrote in an analyst note.

"We are also encouraged by the company’s continued 2026 product introductions and launches across virtual care, including implementing Teladoc One with early launch partners and expanding hybrid care and AI-enabled solutions set to support continued growth in the Integrated Care segment," Daniels wrote.

However, ongoing weakness in BetterHelp’s cash-pay business "is likely to weigh on overall segment performance and temper the pace of the company’s broader turnaround," Daniels noted.

Teladoc remains in a transitional phase, Daniels noted, "navigating slower growth and a challenging end-market, with increased emphasis on profitability, product enhancements and capital deployment into new growth avenues."

A federal judge on Thursday rejected the federal government’s new definition of “medical frailty” and ruled that states did not have adequate time or resources to overhaul their eligibility systems, injecting new uncertainty into the imminent rollout of Medicaid work requirements across the country.

Judge Richard D. Stearns of the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts ruled that federal regulations regarding who is considered too sick to work were overly restrictive, and said that the suit from over two dozen states successfully demonstrated that implementation of the Medicaid work requirements, as written, would cause “irreparable harm.”

“Because enforcement of an unlawful definition of ‘medically frail’ may lead to the disenrollment of otherwise eligible vulnerable individuals relying on Medicaid coverage for continuity of care, the States (and public) face potential for great hardship in the absence of an injunction,” Stearns wrote in his order.
