#5747. Glioblastoma breakthrough reveals how brain cancer cells become more aggressive

Glioblastoma is among the most lethal forms of brain cancer, and scientists have uncovered a surprising factor that may help its cells become more invasive. The fluid surrounding the outer edges of these tumors is much thicker than the fluid near their centers, forcing cancer cells to encounter increasing resistance as they move into healthy brain tissue. Rather than simply slowing their movement, however, this environment appears to help the cells adapt in ways that make invasion easier.

To investigate this unexpected behavior, researchers created an innovative microfluidic chip that recreates the physical conditions encountered by glioblastoma cells. They found that spending extended periods in thick fluid caused the cells to become smaller, more flexible, and better able to squeeze through narrow openings. The discovery suggests that fluid viscosity does more than obstruct cancer cells. It can actively influence their behavior and potentially make them more aggressive.

How Thick Fluid Influences Brain Cancer Invasion

Cancer research has traditionally concentrated on chemical signals and the stiffness of the tissues surrounding tumors. Far less attention has been given to the viscosity of the fluid through which cancer cells travel.

In glioblastoma, this difference is particularly striking. Fluid at the tumor's advancing edge is approximately eight times more viscous than fluid in its dead tissue at the center. As cancer cells move outward, they must push through an increasingly resistant environment.

Studying this process has been difficult because conventional closed microfluidic devices cannot accurately reproduce these conditions. Their enclosed channels can limit access to oxygen and nutrients, while friction against the walls introduces additional forces that influence cell behavior. These limitations also make it challenging to observe how cancer cells respond to prolonged exposure to viscous fluid.

Researchers therefore needed a way to isolate the effects of fluid viscosity from other mechanical influences and determine whether extended exposure produces lasting changes in glioblastoma cells.

A New Device Reveals How Cancer Cells Adapt

Scientists from Chongqing General Hospital and Chongqing University in China developed a specialized open microfluidic platform to address these challenges. Their findings were published in Microsystems & Nanoengineering.

The device consists of a two-layer open microfluidic membrane equipped with a removable cap and an array of tiny pillars. This arrangement allows researchers to control precisely when cancer cells begin migrating while observing how their nuclei change shape as they move through confined spaces.

Unlike traditional enclosed systems, the platform also supports continuous cell culture for up to one month. This makes it possible to examine how prolonged mechanical stress changes the movement and invasive behavior of glioblastoma cells.

The researchers tested two human glioblastoma cell lines, U-251 and LN-229. Both were grown for a month in a thick fluid designed to reproduce conditions at the tumor's invasive outer edge (7.1 cP).

When the cells were subsequently examined using the chip, those that had adapted to the viscous environment traveled faster and covered greater distances than untreated control cells. This result was especially surprising because thicker fluid would ordinarily be expected to impede movement.

Brain Cancer Cells Become Smaller and More Flexible

Microscopic observations revealed how the adapted cells overcame this resistance. After prolonged exposure to the viscous fluid, they had become smaller and easier to deform, allowing them to maneuver through the narrow gaps between the device's microscopic pillars.

As the cells squeezed through these restricted passages, their nuclei underwent visible deformation. Researchers also observed an accumulation of YAP, a protein involved in sensing mechanical forces, inside the nuclei. This is a recognized sign that cells have activated pathways involved in responding to physical stress.

Although both glioblastoma cell lines developed similar changes in shape and movement, their underlying molecular responses were unexpectedly different.

U-251 cells underwent a form of mesenchymal-like reprogramming, activating genes associated with cancer invasion, including CD44, FN1, and MMP9. LN-229 cells, by contrast, became more flexible and mobile without showing substantial lasting changes in gene expression.

Further analysis using Western blotting showed that protein changes remained detectable even after cells were transferred back into fluid with normal viscosity. This indicated that at least some of the adaptations were persistent rather than simply short-lived responses to their surroundings.

Scientists Discover a Strange Kind of Cellular Memory

One of the most unexpected findings was that exposure to thick fluid appeared to leave a lasting imprint on glioblastoma cells.

The researchers had anticipated that viscosity would primarily function as a physical obstacle. Instead, their experiments showed that prolonged exposure could alter how cells behaved even after the original mechanical conditions were removed.

This phenomenon points to a form of mechanical memory, in which cells retain changes produced by earlier physical stress.

The open design of the new chip was essential for identifying this effect. By separating resistance from the fluid itself from the confinement imposed by channel walls, the researchers could investigate viscosity without the additional mechanical interference that complicates conventional experiments.

Observing changes in nuclear shape and migration patterns after weeks of exposure provided evidence that glioblastoma cells can adapt to their mechanical environment in lasting ways.

The contrasting molecular responses of the two cell lines were particularly revealing. Although both appeared to undergo similar physical transformations, only one showed extensive changes in its gene activity. This suggests that glioblastoma cells may acquire comparable invasive characteristics through different underlying biological processes.

A Potential New Approach to Studying Brain Cancer Treatments

Beyond uncovering an overlooked influence on glioblastoma invasion, the researchers believe their device could provide a valuable tool for investigating potential cancer therapies.

The open microfluidic platform fits into standard multi-well plates, allowing it to be incorporated into existing laboratory procedures for cell culture and imaging. Its accessible design also enables researchers to stain cells directly and observe them over long periods without the clogging problems that can occur in closed systems.

These features could make it useful for testing drugs that interfere with the cellular pathways responsible for detecting and responding to mechanical forces.

For glioblastoma, the results raise the possibility that highly viscous environments may favor cancer cells that are better adapted to invasion. Treatments targeting YAP signaling or the remodeling of the cytoskeleton, the internal framework that helps cells maintain and change their shape, could therefore be investigated under conditions that more closely resemble those inside tumors.

The technology may also prove useful for studying other cancers in which fluid viscosity varies across different regions. By examining how tumor cells respond to these mechanical conditions, researchers could gain a better understanding of why some cancers are particularly invasive and potentially identify patients whose tumors depend on mechanical adaptation to spread.

Although further research is needed to determine how these laboratory findings translate to tumors in patients, the discovery highlights an important and previously underexplored aspect of cancer biology: the physical environment surrounding tumor cells may actively shape their ability to invade healthy tissue.

#5746. Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare

Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The debate over AI and inequality has largely focused on people—who will have access to the technology, who will benefit from it and who risks being left behind. But inside healthcare, another AI divide is already taking shape. This one is between the hospitals that have the money, talent and infrastructure to put AI to work and those that don't.

The numbers are striking. According to federal data on hospital AI adoption, 71% of U.S. hospitals used predictive AI integrated with their electronic health records in 2024. But adoption reached 96% among large hospitals compared with just 59% among small hospitals. Among hospitals belonging to multi-hospital systems, 86% used predictive AI. Among independent hospitals, it was only 37%.

That gap matters because AI is quickly becoming part of how hospitals survive, not simply an innovation project. The same federal data show some of the fastest-growing hospital AI applications are decidedly practical, including billing and scheduling. These are exactly the kinds of labor-intensive functions where financially stressed hospitals need to find efficiencies.

Yet those hospitals may be the least equipped to make the investment.

Hospitals remain extraordinarily dependent on people to operate. According to the American Hospital Association, workforce spending accounted for about 60% of hospital expenses in 2025, exceeding $1 trillion. Total hospital expenses grew 7.5% that year, more than twice the growth in hospital prices.

This creates a dangerous catch-22. The hospitals with the greatest need to use technology to redesign labor-intensive operations frequently have the least capacity to invest in doing so.

A large health system can afford an AI pilot that fails. It can hire an innovation team, absorb a lengthy implementation, build governance and compliance infrastructure, and try again if the economics don't work. A safety-net, community or independent hospital often has far less room for error. A multi-year software contract that might eventually produce savings still requires money today.

And buying the technology is only the beginning.

Successful AI deployment requires workflow redesign, change management, integration, measurement and governance. Even among hospitals already using predictive AI, the federal data show meaningful variation in how comprehensively models are evaluated for accuracy, bias and performance after implementation. Smaller, rural and independent hospitals also continue to lag their larger counterparts in adoption.

If we leave the market to work this out one hospital at a time, we should expect that divide to compound. Systems that successfully automate expensive workflows can reinvest those savings into their next technology investment. They build institutional knowledge. Their employees get better at implementation. They become more attractive partners to technology companies looking for sophisticated customers and proving grounds.

The hospitals that wait don't simply remain where they are. They lose ground. The answer cannot be telling every hospital to develop a better AI strategy. We need to change the ownership and financing model for healthcare AI.

Hospitals already know how to collaborate when acting collectively creates an advantage. Group purchasing organizations allow them to aggregate purchasing power rather than negotiate for every product independently. Clinical research networks allow institutions to pool patients, expertise and infrastructure to answer questions no single organization could address as effectively alone.

We should apply the same instinct to AI. Instead of requiring every health system to independently buy, implement and govern variations of the same technology, health systems should increasingly pool their purchasing power, operational expertise and capital to build common AI capabilities. And smaller, independent and safety-net organizations need a path into those collaborations rather than simply another vendor contract.

The venture community has a responsibility here as well. We need financing structures that acknowledge the economic reality of the organizations that really need to adopt technologies. That could mean performance-based models where payment is tied to verified savings rather than large upfront commitments. It could mean consortium models in which multiple health systems share implementation resources and governance.

And increasingly, it should mean giving health systems ownership in the companies and infrastructure they help create. Ownership matters because the economics of AI are changing quickly. As the technology itself becomes increasingly commoditized, enduring value will come from distribution, proprietary workflows, real-world implementation knowledge and access to the environments where healthcare actually happens. Health systems contribute enormously to each of those things. Under the traditional vendor model, however, they can provide the workflows, clinical expertise and proving ground and then pay someone else an annual fee for the resulting product.

That bargain deserves to be reconsidered. Collective ownership can help address the trust problem, too. AI adoption isn't only a technology decision. It requires decisions about validation, monitoring, clinical safety and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Federal researchers found that hospitals increasingly rely on multiple parties to evaluate AI, with 74% reporting more than one entity accountable for evaluation. Smaller hospitals should not each have to recreate that infrastructure from scratch.

Shared infrastructure could include common validation standards, clinical oversight, monitoring and implementation expertise. That would give more hospitals access not only to AI, but to the capabilities required to deploy it responsibly.

None of this means every hospital needs to own every AI company, or that traditional vendors disappear. It means we should stop assuming that the only scalable model for healthcare innovation is one technology company selling essentially the same capability to thousands of hospitals one contract at a time.

The AI divide between hospitals is already here. If adoption continues to depend primarily on the size of an organization's balance sheet, the institutions best positioned today will keep accumulating advantages while those with the least room for error fall further behind.

AI gives hospitals a real opportunity to break their dependence on increasingly expensive, labor-intensive ways of operating. But the organizations that need that opportunity most cannot be the last ones able to afford it. Preventing that outcome will require more than making AI cheaper. It will require giving more health systems the ability to build, govern and share in the technology's value, transforming them.

AI should become something hospitals build together, not another advantage reserved for those that could already afford to move first.

Amanda DeMano is SVP of venture creation at Abundant Venture Partners.

Editor's Note: Abundant Venture Partners is a strategic investor in the makers of certain AI technologies, including SpendRule and Playback Health.

#5745. STAT+: How a simple UTI turns into a $1,756 bill

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Bannow spoke with patients and reviewed their medical bills to report this story.

Tara covers the business of health care. Her stories focus on hospitals, doctors, and how their business practices affect patients — especially when private equity gets involved. She also writes about health insurance and ideas for improving our broken health system. You can reach Tara on Signal at tarabannow.70.

It was a simple urinary tract infection. A textbook urgent care visit.

Kristin Gills knew the drill. She peed in the cup, and the doctor confirmed her suspicion. He prescribed antibiotics. Before she left Methodist Legacy ER & Urgent Care in Allen, Texas, Gills paid her $211 bill and figured that was the end of it.

Then the real bill came, for another $1,756.

“I was like, ‘What in the world?’ I immediately tried calling them,” she said. When she couldn’t reach anyone, she sent three MyChart messages. Nothing.

So she took to the Internet, posting a negative Google review and writing about her experience in a local Facebook group for moms. Finally, a Methodist representative got back to her and offered a cash-pay discount that brought her balance down to $667. She’s still not paying.

“I’m going to fight it,” Gills said. “This will be the hill I die on.”

The facility Gills visited doubles as both an emergency room and an urgent care clinic. Intuitive Health, the private equity-backed company that runs the hybrid facility and nearly 50 others like it, says they’re great for patients because they prevent them from having to guess whether their conditions are emergencies. But patients told STAT they visited for what they thought were obvious urgent care issues — coughs, congestion, flu symptoms — and were shocked when they got bills for ER care instead, often totaling thousands of dollars.

#5744. Do We Diagnose Too Much Normal Distress?

— Psychiatrists must keep a patient's context front and center

A relationship ends, and she cannot sleep.

A parent dies, and his appetite disappears.

She loses her job and spends weeks feeling anxious and struggling to concentrate.

Some of these patients will arrive in our offices. They will tell you they are sad, anxious, exhausted, and unable to cope. They may even complete a PHQ-0 or a GAD-7 that shows they are depressed and anxious.

However, as a psychiatrist, I often pause and ask myself: is this person mentally ill or are they suffering?

Major depression, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder, psychotic illnesses, and other psychiatric conditions cause enormous suffering. Diagnosis can give patients language for experiences they have struggled to understand. Diagnosis can also allow treatment to be focused. And I diagnose and treat psychiatric illness every day. I have seen medication, psychotherapy, hospitalization, and other interventions change and save lives.

At the same time, we, as psychiatrists, must be mindful about what we ask diagnosis to do.

Psychiatry occupies an unusual place in medicine because many of the symptoms we assess also belong to ordinary human experience. Sadness is not exclusive to depression. Worry does not necessarily indicate an anxiety disorder. Insomnia can follow heartbreak. Poor concentration can accompany overwhelming stress. Appetite can disappear during grief. A person whose life has suddenly become frightening or unstable may feel frightened and unstable.

But I worry that healthcare increasingly relies on tools like questionnaires or brief telehealth assessments that make context difficult to capture. The tool should not be the entire assessment.

Consider a patient whose spouse recently died. They are sleeping poorly, crying frequently, eating less, struggling to concentrate, and experiencing anhedonia. Those symptoms overlap with major depression. But what do we label that experience?

There is no simple answer, and there should not be one. Grief does not protect someone from developing major depression, and bereavement can coexist with psychiatric illness. Conversely, the presence of depressive symptoms following a devastating loss does not automatically mean that grief has become a depressive disorder.

The distinction between the two requires clinical judgement. And we should not be diagnosing a patient without this careful judgment. Diagnosis does more than determine a billing code or treatment pathway -- it can change what our patients understand about what is happening to them.

"I am devastated because someone I love died" is a different narrative from, "I have a psychiatric disorder." While those statements can coexist, they are not interchangeable.

Medicine has trained us to identify pathology. We look for symptoms, name them, and decide what to do next. That often serves us well. But I wonder whether, at times, psychiatrists move too quickly from "This hurts" to "This needs to be fixed."

Sometimes what a patient needs most from a clinician is not a diagnosis or medication but someone willing to remain curious long enough to understand what happened. When every painful human experience is interpreted primarily through a medical lens, we risk communicating that emotional discomfort itself is evidence that something has gone wrong.

At the same time, context does not immunize someone against psychiatric illness. A recognizable precipitant does not make severe symptoms benign. The person whose marriage ended can develop major depression. The bereaved parent can become suicidal. The overwhelmed new mother can have a serious mood disorder. Saying "Of course you're sad" is not an adequate psychiatric assessment.

This is where clinical judgment comes in. We need to not only ask, what symptoms are present? But also: what happened? How long has this been happening? How much has functioning changed? Is the response evolving? Is the patient at risk? What was this person like before? And has something qualitatively shifted from understandable distress into psychiatric illness?

Those questions take longer than completing a screening tool; but they keep the human being behind the symptoms front and center.

Put simply, we should be able to hold two ideas simultaneously: psychiatric illness is real and deserves treatment, and not everything that hurts is an illness.

There is a space between pathologizing suffering and dismissing it, and this is the space where much of psychiatry actually happens. Sometimes the work is to diagnose, other times it is to treat, and many times it is to sit with someone long enough to understand why they hurt before deciding what to call it. Even with more tools emerging, psychiatrists must always keep this central to our practice.

Through that process, once the dust settled on the shift, Alignment found "a notable increase in aggressive provider appeal and disputes in our paid claims data" that also drove up costs, Kao said.

Kao said that the insurer has spent the last several months building out its payment integrity capabilities, as well as deploying additional resources to support clinical best practices to mitigate the variation in outcomes for members.

He said that these investments have driven improvements, particularly in September and into October, but the company is still taking a cautious approach to the end of the year.

"I want to emphasize that the guidance we have provided today is a guidance that we are confident in delivering."

Kao also addressed Alignment's performance in the latest round of star ratings scores. Based on federal data, 25% of its members are in plans with at least four stars in 2027, down from 100% in 2026. That four-star threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments in Medicare Advantage.

He said that six of the company's seven contracts were above four stars, but a 3.5 score on the remaining plan, a core HMO offering in California, dragged down its overall performance.

Kao said that the team is "focused on really getting to the root issues in Stars." Alignment has also sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services over the 2027 calculations.

#5742. Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain

Deep within the brainstem is a tiny group of nerve cells that plays an outsized role in how the brain functions. This region, called the locus coeruleus (LC), gets its name from the Latin words for "blue place." Although it contains only a small fraction of the brain's neurons, it produces norepinephrine (NE), a chemical messenger that helps regulate attention, learning, heart rate, and the body's reactions to stress and excitement.

Scientists have long assumed that the LC operates like a loudspeaker, sending essentially the same norepinephrine signal across the brain. However, a new study published in Nature challenges that understanding. Using brain imaging, recordings of neural activity, genetic techniques, and behavioral experiments in mice, researchers at the Allen Institute discovered that the LC communicates through several distinct pathways. Rather than broadcasting one general message, it delivers signals to specific destinations, with different groups of neurons responding to different experiences.

A Hidden Brain Network That Sends Precise Messages

By tracing the connections of LC neurons, researchers found that different groups of cells communicate with specific regions of the nervous system. These pathways determine where signals trigger the release of norepinephrine, creating a much more organized communication network than previously recognized.

Neurons in the upper (dorsal) portion of the LC primarily connect to the cerebral cortex and forebrain. Meanwhile, cells in the lower (ventral) portion send their signals mainly to the brainstem and spinal cord. This arrangement allows different parts of the LC to influence separate brain functions.

"The findings suggest the brain's norepinephrine system is far more like a targeted postal network than a foghorn," said Karel Svoboda, director of Neural Dynamics at the Allen Institute and study co-author.

Why the Discovery Could Matter for Brain Disorders

Understanding how this signaling network is organized could eventually change how certain neurological and mental health conditions are treated.

Norepinephrine plays a central role in regulating attention and mood, making it an important target for medications used to treat depression, anxiety, and ADHD. Neurons in the LC are also among the earliest brain cells to deteriorate in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the new findings could have implications for understanding and treating these conditions.

Current treatments that influence norepinephrine can affect multiple brain circuits at once, sometimes producing beneficial effects in one region while causing unwanted effects elsewhere. A clearer map of the LC's specialized pathways could help scientists develop therapies that act more selectively on the circuits involved in particular symptoms.

The research received support from the National Institutes of Health's Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies® Initiative, also known as The BRAIN Initiative®.

Scientists Identify Brain Cells Involved in Learning

The researchers also uncovered an important distinction between the functions of different LC neurons.

Cells in the dorsal LC that connect to the cortex were particularly active during learning. When mice performed decision-making tasks and adjusted their choices after an unfavorable result, these neurons increased their activity.

Neurons in the ventral LC behaved differently. Their activity rose shortly before mice ignored signals indicating that a reward might be available. This suggests that these cells help regulate whether animals respond to opportunities in their surroundings.

"What emerged was a clear map: neurons in the dorsal LC that send signals upward to the cortex are involved in learning, whereas neurons in the ventral region projecting downward to the brainstem and spinal cord govern whether animals engage with their environment at all," said Svoboda. "We also showed that these anatomical differences are mirrored by distinct gene expression patterns."

These findings indicate that the differences between the two groups extend beyond their locations and connections. They also have distinct patterns of gene activity that reflect their specialized roles.

Researchers Discover a Record-Breaking Neuron

The study involved an extensive examination of the mouse brain. Scientists used whole-brain imaging to study nearly 35,000 neurons, analyzed the genetic profiles of almost 400,000 cells, and reconstructed the complete structures of several exceptionally complex nerve cells.

During this work, they encountered another remarkable finding: LC neurons possess extraordinarily long axons. These projections carry signals from nerve cells to other cells, allowing information to travel across the nervous system.

The researchers found that LC axons measured approximately 35 centimeters long on average. One particularly extraordinary axon had a total reconstructed length of 70.32 centimeters, making it part of the longest single neuron ever measured in a mouse.

"This neuron, like many others that we studied, supplies NE to a very large volume of the cerebral cortex. For the brain, this is highly unusual. Most neurons are more specific in their targets," said Jeremiah Cohen, scientist at the Allen Institute and study co-author. "But this neuron doesn't release NE everywhere. It ignores the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord."

Despite its remarkable length and extensive reach, the neuron does not distribute norepinephrine throughout the entire brain. Instead, its connections remain selective, reinforcing the discovery that the LC operates through carefully organized signaling pathways.

A New Understanding of How the Brain Learns

The researchers also identified intriguing similarities between the norepinephrine system and the brain's dopamine signaling system.

Dopamine is another major chemical messenger that sends signals to the basal ganglia, a brain region involved in forming habits. Scientists suspect that dopamine and norepinephrine work together to support learning, potentially allowing the brain to acquire several complex and abstract concepts at the same time.

By revealing the intricate connections, specialized functions, and unusual physical structure of neurons in the locus coeruleus, the research provides a more detailed picture of how the animal brain communicates and learns.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice, they could eventually help scientists better understand human brain function and design treatments that target specific neural circuits rather than affecting entire signaling systems.

Materials provided by Allen Institute. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5741. Opinion: How Congress can fix expert advisory committees

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By C. Joseph Ross Daval and Aaron S. Kesselheim

Daval is a research specialist at the Program On Regulation, Therapeutics, And Law (PORTAL) at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School and a former lawyer in the FDA’s Office of the Chief Counsel. Kesselheim is a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, director of PORTAL, and a former member of the FDA’s Peripheral and Central Nervous System Advisory Committee.

In September, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fired the two vice chairs of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. This move was both unsurprising and troubling. The task force is a critical advisory body to HHS, reviewing scientific evidence to provide recommendations on whether private health insurers should be required to cover services like cancer screenings at no cost to patients. Congress created the task force as part of the Affordable Care Act and require by law that it be staffed by people with “appropriate expertise,” and “to the extent practicable, not subject to political pressure.”

These firings are the latest chapter in a vast project of eliminating, ignoring, and replacing scientific advisory committees. In 2025, the Trump administration terminated 151 advisory committees at scientific government agencies, including 75 in HHS. It has altered or ignored those that are left. In 2025, Kennedy fired the entire Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which provides public recommendations on vaccines. His replacements are, to varying degrees, sympathetic to his unscientific views, and a majority lack substantial expertise in vaccines and immunology.

At the Food and Drug Administration, agency leadership has largely ignored the standing advisory committees that have historically weighed in on new drug approvals. The FDA convened a record low number of advisory committees in 2025. Instead, it hosted a handful of pseudo-scientific look-alike meetings called “expert panels.” Panelists were handpicked and invited for a single meeting to share their own data, analysis, and conclusions, unmoored from any semblance of collaborative consensus and, too often, scientific rigor.

Expert advisory committees matter for two reasons. The first is obvious: Agency policymakers need high-quality, independent advice to improve the quality, credibility, and legitimacy of agency decision-making. Agencies can’t possibly have the internal expertise to handle every question. This is especially true after staffing cuts to agencies like the EPA, FDA, and CDC.

The other reason is accountability: When a legitimate expert advisory committee makes a recommendation about what an agency should do, it leaves a public record that enables us to hold our government accountable if it declines to follow that advice.

Over the past few decades, courts, Congress, and the public have come to rely on these public recommendations — in congressional oversight, judicial review, and science journalism — to better understand the choices expert agencies make.

This is what happened when the FDA approved the Alzheimer’s drug aducanumab in 2021 despite the near-unanimous vote of the advisory committee (which included one of us) against approval. The committee noted conflicting evidence on the drug’s efficacy and clear safety risks, including brain bleeds, in large numbers of patients.

The negative vote anchored the debate that followed. Critics pointed to it as evidence that the FDA had made a terrible mistake, and payors and hospital systems used it to justify not paying the outlandish price set by the manufacturer. Patients largely avoided drug, with the whole episode culminating in investigations by the media and Congress that demonstrated improper pressure by the manufacturer on the FDA leading to the approval decision.

Advisory committees don’t just provide recommendations to agency policymakers. They enable us to literally hold the agency to account for its decision — to explain why it thinks its advisers were wrong. With no advisory committee to create a record, policymakers can more easily evade hard questions about unscientific or politically motivated decisions.

The dismissals at the USPSTF follow a Supreme Court decision in 2025 stating that the secretary of HHS can remove members at will. The court reasoned that the secretary has the power to appoint them, and “no statute restricts [their] removal.”

But Congress can, and should, change this. It has an array of tools at its disposal. Depending on the circumstance, it could enact for-cause statutory removal protections, staggered terms, formal expertise and qualification requirements, and enforceable conflict of interest rules. It could require that advisers be chosen more transparently and according to stricter criteria. It could even vest the power to choose advisers in another body entirely, akin to how independent redistricting commissions draw state electoral boundaries.

These reforms would likely survive constitutional scrutiny because advisers do not actually make policy. Their advice is nonbinding. The Supreme Court’s recent decision striking down statutory removal protections for agency heads depended on the idea that the agency head was exercising executive authority that must ultimately be accountable to the president. But independent expert scientific advisers do not exercise authority; they merely speak authoritatively. And when they speak, they are heard by those of us — courts, Congress, the press, and through them, the public — to whom public policy must ultimately be accountable.

This evisceration of scientific advice is untenable. If Congress is committed to the idea that evidence, science, and expertise should guide public policy, then it needs to act by insulating expert advice from arbitrary political control.

C. Joseph Ross Daval is a research specialist at the Program On Regulation, Therapeutics, And Law (PORTAL) at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School and a former lawyer in the FDA’s Office of the Chief Counsel. Aaron S. Kesselheim is a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, director of PORTAL, and a former member of the FDA’s Peripheral and Central Nervous System Advisory Committee.

Sutter Health calls off flagship hospital build in SF's East Bay, citing regulatory issues" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Sutter Health scrapped plans to build a flagship campus on property it owns in Emeryville, California, and instead is shifting its focus to outpatient care in the area, according to a Sept. 30 statement.

The health system announced those plans in early 2025 (see that story below), with a medical center of up to 200 beds as the centerpiece of a $1 billion investment into San Francisco's East Bay. It attributed its decision to "the lack of a clear and predictable regulatory path" related to California environmental and land use law.

"Over two years, we pursued relief under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA," the statement reads. "Those efforts did not secure the certainty needed to advance the hospital project, leaving it vulnerable to litigation that could delay construction and new hospital services for years."

Accompanying plans surrounding outpatient services "including primary and specialty care, diagnostic services and outpatient surgery" are now the priority for that community, though Sutter said it's still keeping an eye out for another potential location for a future hospital.

"Separating these projects keeps healthcare investment moving and allows us to advance additional outpatient services that can bring care to patients sooner. No alternative location has been selected, and we are assessing several options that can support comprehensive hospital, emergency and specialty care and the infrastructure needed for the future."

Sutter said that services will not be affected at Alta Bates, another hospital in the area it was planning to relieve with the new build, and that it plans to keep supporting that campus until another hospital can be finished. It added that hospitals across California have and continue to face "legal and regulatory challenges [tied to] significant seismic deadlines, while efforts to modernize or replace facilities can be exposed to lengthy regulatory reviews and litigation. A different location alone will not resolve these challenges."

Sutter Health will invest $1 billion to expand its services across Northern California's East Bay region, including a new flagship campus in Emeryville.

The health system announced Wednesday that the campus will feature a new medical center with up to 200 beds as well as a regional destination for ambulatory care. The plans also leave room for future expansion, according to the announcement.

The ambulatory services complex at the 12-acre campus will feature a wide array of specialties and will offer imaging and laboratory services. It expects to welcome its first patients as early as 2028, Sutter said.

The 335,000-square-foot medical center will include labor and delivery, surgical services, intensive care, emergency care and neonatal intensive care. The facility will be designed with the potential to add additional patient rooms in the future.

Sutter is targeting a 2032-33 opening date for the medical center, according to the announcement.

“Our Emeryville campus project represents one of the most significant investments we’re making across our system over the next decade and is part of our broader vision to meet the community’s growing demand for expanded access to our services across the East Bay footprint,” said Warner Thomas, president and CEO of Sutter Health, in the press release.

Sutter said it will put a focus on recruiting both primary care physicians and specialty care doctors, breaking down patient barriers to appointments and referrals and investing in initiatives to bolster the healthcare workforce. It expects to have 190 primary and specialty care clinicians staffing the new campus.

Beyond building the new campus, Sutter said it plans to grow the behavioral health services offered at its Herrick campus in Berkeley. The health system's Alta Bates campus will continue to operate as an acute care facility until the new medical center opens in Emeryville and then will be overhauled to provide ambulatory surgery services, urgent care and potentially skilled nursing services.

The health system is also renovating a medical office building in Berkley to serve as a primary care facility that will also offer OB-GYN care, according to the announcement.

Additional renovations are in the works as well, Sutter said.

“Too many people face challenges in accessing the care they need," Thomas said. "At Sutter, we’re committed to breaking down those barriers—expanding care facilities, enhancing imaging capabilities, improving online appointment scheduling and collaborating with the Sutter East Bay Medical Group and our community physician partners to attract more primary and specialty care physicians.

"These efforts will allow us to care for more patients while also investing in programs and partnerships that build the healthcare workforce of the future—ensuring more people get the right care when and where they need it," he said.

#5738. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5737. Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s

People with Parkinson's disease who are more physically active may experience slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement, according to a new study published October 7, 2026, in Neurology, the official medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology.

The findings suggest that staying active could offer two important advantages for people living with Parkinson's. However, researchers emphasize that the study identified a connection between physical activity and slower symptom progression. It does not establish that exercise directly causes the disease to progress more slowly.

"Parkinson's disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen leading to disability and a loss of independence," said study author Dong-Woo Ryu, MD, PhD, of the University of Cincinnati in Ohio. "Previous research has shown associations between physical activity and movement symptoms. Our study found physical activity may have dual benefits, with associations with slower declines in movement and cognition."

Tracking Exercise and Parkinson's Symptoms Over Seven Years

The research involved 294 adults with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease. Participants were 66 years old on average, and researchers monitored their health for up to seven years.

To understand their activity habits, participants completed questionnaires estimating how many hours each week they spent being physically active. The questions covered activities performed at work, around the home, and during hobbies or recreation.

Researchers classified activities by their intensity. Moderate activities included brisk walking, doubles tennis, leisurely swimming, and household tasks such as cleaning windows, vacuuming, or mowing the lawn. More demanding activities included running, cycling at higher speeds, participating in team sports, playing singles tennis, shoveling, and carrying heavy objects.

The team examined physical activity in three ways. First, they calculated the total time participants spent doing moderate or vigorous activities. Second, they estimated overall activity volume by combining duration with intensity, giving greater weight to strenuous exercise. Third, they separately measured the amount of time spent doing vigorous activities.

Based on total weekly activity time, participants were placed into three categories. Those in the least active group reported up to four hours per week, the moderately active group reported four to eight hours, and the most active group reported more than eight hours.

Each year, participants also completed assessments designed to track changes in thinking and memory, along with tests evaluating the severity of their Parkinson's symptoms.

More Activity Linked to Slower Memory Decline

One of the most striking differences emerged in cognitive performance. Researchers used a 30-point test of thinking and memory, with lower scores reflecting poorer cognitive function.

Among participants in the least active group, scores fell by an estimated average of 0.478 points each year. The moderately active group experienced a much smaller annual decline of 0.090 points.

For the most active participants, the estimated average yearly decrease was only 0.007 points, indicating that their cognitive scores remained nearly unchanged over time.

The researchers also examined changes in Parkinson's movement symptoms using an assessment scored from zero to 132. Higher numbers represented more severe symptoms, and participants began the study with an average score of 23.

In the least active group, symptom scores increased by an estimated 0.143 points annually, indicating a slight worsening. By contrast, scores decreased by 0.225 points per year in the moderately active group and by 0.783 points in the most active group.

Even after accounting for participants' age, sex, and how long they had been living with Parkinson's, the researchers found that the most active group experienced slower cognitive decline and less worsening of movement symptoms than the least active group.

The connection was not limited to one measure of exercise. Higher total activity time, greater overall activity volume, and more time spent exercising vigorously were each associated with slower deterioration in both thinking abilities and movement symptoms.

Why Consistent Physical Activity May Matter

The results suggest that remaining physically active over time could be especially important for people with Parkinson's disease. Researchers noted that even relatively small differences in the rate of decline might become more significant when they accumulate over several years.

"The possible benefits of physical activity for people with Parkinson's disease may depend on how long they stay active and whether they continue exercising over time," said Ryu. "While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time. Since participants generally had good thinking and memory skills at the start of the study, our results should be interpreted with caution and further studies are needed."

The researchers also identified an important limitation. Physical activity levels were based on participants' own reports rather than direct measurements, meaning some estimates may have been inaccurate.

Although the findings strengthen the evidence connecting physical activity with better long-term outcomes in Parkinson's disease, additional research will be needed to determine whether exercise itself can slow the progression of symptoms.

Funding for the study came from a grant provided by the Gardner Family Foundation and the Precision Medicine in Neurodegenerative Diseases Fund.

#5735. Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds

Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Oct. 26 to 30.

Doximity launched DoseCheck, a new safety feature within Doximity Ask designed to catch unsafe or incorrect medication dosing recommendations generated by artificial intelligence.

Doximity Ask is the company's clinical decision support tool.

Rather than relying on an LLM to double-check another LLM, DoseCheck adds a deterministic, rule-based verification layer, checking AI-generated dosing claims against structured information including FDA labeling and professional guidelines, the company said. By checking against FDA labeling and professional guidelines, DoseCheck increases accuracy to more than 99%, the company claims.

Doximity tested nine widely used AI models with over 8,000 dosing questions based on real physician queries. At least 2.3% of dosing claims made by these models were wrong, and 43.8% of detected errors were serious or potentially lethal.

According to the analysis, common sources of errors include dosing newer drugs, failing to account for patient-specific factors such as kidney function, age, weight and medical history, and mistakes involving units, decimal points or drugs with similar names.

"AI is probabilistic. Drug dosing can’t be," said Louis-Antoine Mullie, M.D., chief AI researcher at Doximity. "DoseCheck doesn’t ask a language model to grade its own homework. It checks dosing claims against a structured, authoritative database, so physicians get the same verified dosing answer every time."

DoseCheck is free and has been rolled out to all Doximity Ask users across mobile and desktop.

Health and wellness platform Hims & Hers plans to launch a peptides specialty after the federal government signaled it will allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture six peptides temporarily.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services will not take action against licensed pharmacists who dispense certain unapproved peptides, according to a new policy published this week in the Federal Register.

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides, Fierce Pharma reported. Under Kennedy’s "enforcement discretion policy" issued Wednesday, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

The specific compounds included (PDF) in the list are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500, all of which were discussed in a meeting of the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) in July, with the panel ultimately voting to recommend including the treatments onto the 503A Bulk Drug Substances list.

Through its new Peptides+ specialty, Hims & Hers plans to offer access to Sermorelin, Glutathione, B12, NAD+, and L-carnitine, with BPC-157 and TB-500 to follow when allowable. "If a customer is eligible, a personalized treatment plan will be prescribed and delivered by independent providers, treatments supplied by licensed pharmacies, with ongoing clinical support our customers can trust," CEO Andrew Dudum wrote in a blog post.

"We’re focused on entering this specialty the right way, not the fastest. Most of what we know about these compounds is still early—with limited published studies, we draw primarily from clinical experience from the last decade. We’ve consistently acknowledged that while these compounds hold promise, there is still information we do not yet know. Provider-supervised use is how we plan to build on this foundation and make sure that access and innovation can move at the same pace," Dudum said.

The tech giant launched Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate, a new program designed to teach healthcare professionals responsible, practical ways to use AI in their day-to-day work. Clinicians at Google developed the virtual course, and the program is accredited for up to five American Medical Association (AMA) continuing education credits.

The NYU Grossman School of Medicine, the University of Alabama at Birmingham and Touro University are offering the program to their faculty, residents and medical students. Leading nursing institutions, including Purdue University School of Nursing, are offering the certificate as part of their healthcare professional training, according to Google.

"As I’ve traveled around the world this year, I’ve heard loud and clear from healthcare professionals how much need there is for a thoughtful but practical educational resource on AI, made specifically for healthcare," Michael Howell, M.D., Google’s chief health officer, wrote in a blog post.

Large language models recommend more up-front testing, referrals and treatment than the physicians who actually saw the patients and at more than three times the cost, according to a study published in NEJM AI.

Researchers from the Technion, Stanford University and collaborating institutions tested 20 general-purpose and four specialized medical AI systems on records from 200 real outpatient and emergency visits. Each received the clinical presentation without the physician’s assessment and plan. The team priced the recommended tests and referrals in both the AI and physicians’ plans using the same 2026 Medicare rates.

Across the 20 general-purpose systems, AI-suggested care cost a mean of $314 per visit, compared with $97 for care recommended by attending physicians. Suggested care was more costly in 180 of 200 cases. The average cost of care per AI system ranged from $209 to $599.

Diagnostic testing rose from $71 per visit in the physicians’ plans to $176 across the systems, about $105 more per visit. The referral rates for the physician’s plans were 0.15 per visit compared to 0.87 for the LLM’s plans, which, at the corresponding Medicare rates, is $111 more per visit, according to the study.

"The four specialized medical systems showed comparable excess (2.7× to 3.5×), so medical fine-tuning did not curb—and may reinforce—cost escalation," the study authors wrote.

The researchers used MTSamples, a publicly available collection of 4,999 real de-identified medical transcription sample reports contributed by practicing clinicians as reference material for medical transcriptionists. The notes are documentation from real patient visits, but they are a convenience sample assembled for transcription training rather than a representative draw from U.S. ambulatory practice, the study authors wrote.

"Under a single standard prompt, every AI system we evaluated, general purpose and medically specialized alike, suggested more diagnostic tests, medications and specialist referrals than the treating physician on the same cases," the study authors wrote.

LLMs appear optimized to be comprehensive and avoid missing diagnoses, and may show an analogous tendency toward exhaustive workup, the study authors noted.

The researchers argued that much of the excess can be reduced through better prompting, suggesting cost inflation is partly a deployment and design problem rather than an unavoidable feature of AI.

Researchers reevaluated 19 models using different instructions. A simple cost-aware prompt telling models to recommend only clinically necessary, cost-effective items reduced average recommended costs from 3.2 times physician costs to 2.5 times.

A stronger "parsimonious-but-safe" prompt told models to focus on the three most likely diagnoses, explicitly rule out dangerous "cannot-miss" conditions, and recommend only tests whose results would change management. That cut costs to just 1.4 times physician costs. But diagnostic agreement with physicians fell in 17 of the 19 systems, illustrating why cost reductions need to be evaluated alongside other changes in the recommendations, the study authors noted.

"Getting the diagnosis right matters, but so does the path you take to get there," said Prof. Dvir Aran of the Technion, the study’s corresponding author, in a statement. "Accuracy and safety have dominated how clinical AI is trained and evaluated. Efficiency needs the same attention: whether each test or referral is likely to help the patient."

Digital health company Eko Health launched a new stethoscope, the CORE 300, that integrates traditional and digital listening modes directly into a single chestpiece.

The AI-enabled stethoscope, which received FDA clearance, is also in line with premium traditional stethoscopes, making the digital technology more accessible to a broader group of healthcare professionals, the company said.

With a twist of the chestpiece, clinicians can switch between familiar traditional listening and Eko’s advanced digital listening technology, with up to 35x amplification, active noise cancellation and real-time heart rate displayed directly on the device. When connected to the Eko App and Eko's FDA-cleared AI for structural murmur detection, CORE 300 can also bring AI disease detection into the physical exam.

"Millions of healthcare professionals around the world use a stethoscope to examine patients every day," said Connor Landgraf, co-founder and CEO of Eko Health, in a statement. "Our goal is to bring the most ubiquitous clinical exam into the precise digital era. Once the physical exam becomes digital, we combine better listening with objective measurements and AI-powered clinical decision support right at the point of care."Clinical technologies are evolving quickly, but adoption depends on making new capabilities fit naturally into the way clinicians already practice, said Steven R. Steinhubl, M.D., chief medical officer of Eko Health and a board-certified cardiologist.

"CORE 300 bridges that gap. It preserves the traditional experience of auscultation while putting enhanced digital listening, objective measurements, and access to clinical decision support a twist of the chestpiece away. That combination can help make a smarter, more connected physical exam a routine part of care rather than the exception," Steinhubl said.

With Eko's digital stethoscope, clinicians can record, visualize and save heart, lung and body sounds and interpret the data with Eko’s FDA-cleared AI and software. According to the company, the device could expand screening capabilities in primary care offices, busy clinics and rural healthcare settings.

Eko Health launched its first Eko CORE digital stethoscope attachment in 2025, and to date, has delivered more than 750,000 digital stethoscopes and AI-enabled devices worldwide.

Healthcare engagement and payment solutions provider RevSpring debuted a conversational intelligent virtual agent that helps patients manage payment plans over the phone.

Let’s Talk expands on RevSpring’s voice platform and is integrated with its payment portal. It gives patients the ability to make payments, create payment plans, ask questions and respond to outbound voice reminders.

Initial results of the tool show a 36% increase in patient payment rates and a 27% decrease in transfer to live agents, the company says. Moreover, average call durations decreased 25% with Let’s Talk.

“Healthcare organizations are looking for ways to automate more patient interactions and improve financial outcomes without losing sight of the need for patient empathy,” said Scott MacKenzie, RevSpring CEO, in a statement. “Adding payment plans to Let’s Talk expands what patients can accomplish through conversational self-service, helping more callers resolve their needs without transferring to a representative. We’re building on years of proven payment automation to help providers improve efficiency and scale self-service across the patient financial experience.”

Enterprise healthcare operations software provider symplr launched Monday an integrated workforce management solution combining AI-driven scheduling and timekeeping.

The tool—dubbed symplr Time and Scheduling—combines symplr’s predictive nurse and staffing scheduling tool with its timekeeping solution. Nurse managers can identify and address staffing gaps "hundreds of days in advance," ultimately reducing time spent on staffing and timecard tasks by approximately 50%, executives say.

"Nurse leaders shouldn’t have to spend hours building schedules and scrambling to fill open shifts when they could be supporting their teams and patients," said Ali Morin, symplr chief nursing informatics officer, in a statement. "Nurses want more flexibility and predictability, while health systems need the right people in the right place at the right time. We designed symplr Time and Scheduling to deliver both, giving nurses and nurse leaders more time for patient care and less time managing the work around it."

Additional AI capabilities are expected to roll out in 2027, the company says.

Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute launched an AI task force Monday in a bid to evaluate the technologies and streamline adoption in a "safe and deliberate manner."

The task force is dubbed the Cancer Institute Office of Technology and Digital Strategy. It is led by Paul Thambi, M.D., and Louis Williams, M.D. AI is currently being used by the institute to personalize radiation doses, reduce note-taking time and streamline patient referral processes, according to the Oct. 27 announcement.

Williams said in a statement that it’s "crucial to have a system to continuously re-evaluate the effectiveness of each tool," adding that outputs of models should be analyzed on "an ongoing basis."

"There can be drift in a model that may influence its accuracy over time or there may be bias in the model that isn’t apparent upfront," Williams said. "That’s why it’s necessary to have a unified strategy that includes training models to identify mistakes before a model goes into production as well as longitudinal risk assessment to ensure safety."

#5733. Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial

A new approach to treating post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has received FDA clearance, offering a personalized alternative for people who have not found sufficient relief through existing treatments. Developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology, the technology uses brain activity measurements to guide targeted magnetic stimulation.

Early clinical trial findings have been encouraging. According to Wave Neuroscience, patients experienced a 52% reduction in PTSD symptoms, while 68% achieved remission. The full findings are still being prepared for public release, but researchers believe the technology could significantly expand treatment options for millions of people.

The need for more effective PTSD care is substantial. In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day, and about 7% of veterans receive a PTSD diagnosis annually.

PTSD can develop after traumatic experiences such as military combat, serious accidents, natural disasters, or violence. An estimated 6% of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans.

Why Current PTSD Treatments Are Not Enough

Since PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980, treatment has largely centered on psychotherapy and medications known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), including sertraline and fluoxetine.

Although these approaches can help, many patients continue to experience symptoms despite receiving treatment.

A 2020 review of PTSD medications found that patients reported improvements ranging from 6.8 to 10.1 points on symptom assessments. However, remission rates reached only 10.9% at most.

Wave Neuroscience reported substantially stronger preliminary outcomes in its clinical trial. Erik Won, DO, the company's chief medical officer, described the results as a major advance over previously reported medication outcomes.

“In comparison to that study, our FDA trial reported a 52% reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” Won said. “And more importantly, we saw 68% remission in our clinical trial. So, it’s really a quantum change, an inflection point in what we can offer to patients. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.”

These findings are promising, although the results come from different studies and should not be interpreted as a direct comparison of treatment effectiveness.

The newly cleared system uses Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), a technology that combines measurements of brain activity with targeted magnetic stimulation.

First, an electroencephalogram (EEG) records the brain's electrical signals. This information helps guide a personalized treatment plan using transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS.

During TMS, a coil positioned against the scalp delivers magnetic pulses that stimulate brain activity. The technique has already been used for other psychiatric conditions, including treatment-resistant depression.

What distinguishes MeRT is its use of an AI-assisted algorithm to customize stimulation protocols based on each patient's brain activity rather than relying on a standardized approach.

“Transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, was previously FDA cleared for treatment-resistant depression,” Won said. “By adding an augmented AI derived multivariate algorithm, we were able to personalize protocols that received FDA clearance for post-traumatic stress disorder, which should open up market access to about 13 million people who may be struggling with PTSD.”

Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a physician-scientist at Texas A&M Health with extensive experience in precision medicine, helped guide the research.

His work focuses on adapting medical care to the characteristics of individual patients instead of assuming that everyone will respond to the same treatment.

“Most clinical interventions for the treatment of PTSD do not work very well,” Ramos said. “So, this is a huge area where identifying interventions that could hopefully add quality of life to the people impacted by this disorder would be tremendously impactful.”

Wave Neuroscience CEO Fred Walke said Ramos was a natural fit for the project because of his expertise in personalized medicine.

Conventional TMS generally follows treatment protocols that are less individualized. MeRT builds on the same underlying technology but adjusts treatment according to the patient's specific brain activity.

Ramos emphasized that even small biological differences between people can have major implications for medical care. Humans are approximately 99.9% genetically alike, yet the remaining 0.1% contributes to differences that can influence how individuals respond to treatment.

By accounting for these differences and tailoring stimulation to each person's brain, researchers observed substantial reductions in PTSD symptom severity.

Ramos illustrated the distinction with an analogy involving a leaking roof.

He likened conventional TMS to covering a leak with a tarp to manage its effects. MeRT, in contrast, aims to provide a more targeted solution, comparable to identifying and replacing the damaged shingles responsible for the problem.

The broader goal is to move beyond treating patients with standardized protocols and toward interventions guided by measurable biological information.

From Breakthrough Designation to FDA Clearance

The regulatory process reached an important milestone in 2024, when MeRT received an FDA Breakthrough Device designation.

Dr. Rick Silva, executive director of clinical trials at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology, explained that the designation helps promising technologies move through regulatory review more efficiently.

It does not eliminate scientific or medical requirements. Instead, it can streamline communication and reduce administrative delays while preserving the standards needed for FDA clearance.

Silva said the progress was particularly meaningful because the project began during the COVID-19 pandemic and advanced through the regulatory process unusually quickly.

According to Silva, medical device development and clinical evaluation can often take around 10 years before clearance is obtained. This project completed the relevant process in just over two years.

He credited the experience and dedication of the Wave Neuroscience team with helping make that accelerated progress possible.

“I’ve been involved in probably close to 1,000 projects in academic medical centers over the years at varying degrees of depth and detail,” Silva said. “Patients are why I do what I do. It’s hard, and the failure rate is high, and it’s a lot of work. But when you get to a point where something is going to benefit patients, it’s very professionally gratifying and personally gratifying in many ways as well.”

Dr. Israel Liberzon, distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, served as the study's lead psychiatrist and PTSD specialist.

He believes the clearance represents an important expansion of the available treatments for PTSD.

According to Liberzon, MeRT will become the only FDA-cleared nonmedication treatment specifically for PTSD once it reaches patients.

“Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” Liberzon said. “It doesn’t mean that only two of them are used, but both are SSRIs. This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.”

In the clinical trial, participants received five treatment sessions each week over a period of five to six weeks.

Researchers reported that the improvements appeared to persist after the treatment sessions ended, suggesting the benefits may extend beyond the active therapy period.

For patients who struggle with medication side effects or find psychotherapy difficult to complete, a treatment based on personalized brain stimulation could provide another option.

“People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.”

Won also believes the technology could eventually be adapted to other psychiatric conditions, including depression and anxiety.

Could Personalized Brain Therapy Transform Mental Healthcare?

Dr. Leslie S. Prichep, chief scientific officer at Wave Neuroscience, sees the FDA clearance as an important step toward treatment decisions guided by objective measurements of brain function.

“The FDA clearance of the MeRT System reflects decades of scientific research using electrophysiological biomarkers in identifying abnormal brain activity profiles and guiding personalized intervention strategies,” Prichep said. “We believe this represents an important advancement toward a more objective, data-informed model of mental healthcare.”

Walke believes that giving patients clearer information about their brain activity could also help change public attitudes toward mental illness.

He compared the idea to treating a broken bone with a cast. By making mental health conditions easier to understand through measurable physical information, the company hopes to reduce stigma and help patients better understand their experiences.

“One of the goals of the company is to create a platform for mental healthcare that uses objective imagery to help patients understand why they’re experiencing life the way that they are,” Walke said. “That insight, compounded with proven technologies, promises incredibly high efficacy when personalized.”

An important next step will be ensuring that patients can actually obtain the treatment. Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working with other stakeholders to expand availability and make the therapy more affordable through insurance coverage.

“Our hope is that this research and technology can be a catalyst for more widespread development and innovation of more effective, personalized and precision-guided treatments,” Won said. “This is proof positive that population-scale personalized medicine is not just an aspirational goal but is an achievable reality today.”

The project combines years of work across medicine, neuroscience, clinical research, and technology, all directed toward improving the lives of people affected by PTSD.

For Ramos, the opportunity to help veterans carries particular significance because of Texas A&M's longstanding involvement in military and veteran initiatives.

“Texas A&M has a very rich history of military and veteran priorities,” Ramos said. “It’s a no-brainer that Texas A&M faculty would be interested in and supportive of an initiative that hopefully would bring positive solutions to a big problem. And anything we could do to help alleviate that problem is going to go a long way towards making a difference in the individual’s life as well as the people who are close to them. I feel very fortunate that we at Texas A&M were meaningfully involved in this project.”

Mario covers technology in health care, including FDA regulation of artificial intelligence; how Medicare pays for health tech; the use of AI in clinical care; mental health chatbots; and consumer wearables. He’s also the co-author of the free, twice weekly STAT Health Tech newsletter. You can reach Mario on Signal at mariojoze.13.

Health officials hoping to boost adoption of artificial intelligence in health care have been moving behind the scenes to address brewing conflict between states and the federal government over the technology.

The Trump administration has sought to alleviate regulatory burden on companies developing health AI and created new ways to pay for the technology. But there remains a key problem: The federal government and states have overlapping jurisdiction over AI that performs clinical work, like writing prescriptions.

States regulate the practice of medicine and issue licenses to doctors and other clinicians. If AI performs these tasks without human supervision, that would likely push those products into the jurisdiction of the Food and Drug Administration, which regulates medical devices.
