#5731. Why Oscar Health is putting a focus on personalization for ACA exchange plans

Why Oscar Health is putting a focus on personalization for ACA exchange plans" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Another open enrollment period is set to begin on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges, and the team at Oscar Health is focusing on the unique ways it can innovate in the turbulent market.

Oscar is growing the number of counties in its geographic footprint by 24% in 2027, offering plans across 713 counties in 21 states. It is also investing in new specialized plans, such as its RetireEase offering, and in expanding coverage options designed for individuals with certain conditions.

Janet Liang, president of Oscar Insurance, told Fierce Healthcare that it's critical for plans to learn as much as they can about the individual consumer, so that they can shape benefits that effectively meet the needs of the people who are coming to the marketplaces for coverage.

"We are completely dialed in to the individual consumer," she said. "We know the people who are in the ACA, and it's a broad, broad range of people. It's not one size fits all, and what we do is we spend the time to understand who comes into the ACA and what are the services and needs that individuals have."

That includes putting a focus on collecting plenty of feedback from existing members, and what they're searching for as existing enrollees, as well as collecting data on broader consumer behaviors on the exchanges.

The RetireEase plan, for example, was born from this thinking, Liang said. The offering, which is launching in five states next year, aims to support members in the transition to Medicare coverage, targeted to people aged 55 to 64.

Benefits include set prices for key services in this age range, from preventive care to physical therapy to cardiology. Members that enroll in RetireEase can also access specific supports designed for the handoff to Medicare, for caregivers and transportation if needed.

Liang said this population tends to have unique concerns about affordability as employers shift their approaches in a way that is leading more people to retire early, leaving them on a fixed income. It's also an age range where people begin to develop challenging chronic conditions that will need to be managed in the future.

The team took that feedback and those particular needs it heart when building out RetireEase, Liang said.

Oscar's suite of specialized offerings includes some of its most popular plans, she said. In addition to the new launch, Oscar is expanding the reach of its existing specialized plans. HelloMeno, its plan designed for women navigating menopause, will grow to 15 states by 2027, for example.

Liang said that these plans have higher Net Promoter Scores than its traditional plans, and they also tend to have higher retention rates than the broader offerings.

"Based on the retention rate and the high NPS scores, we know that we're meeting an unmet need," she said.

And the Oscar team is already planning for the future around these specialized plans, and has determined where to go next for 2028. Expanding this slate is a central part of Oscar's broader strategy around the ACA, which also includes enhancements to bronze, silver and gold plans as well as a focus on individual coverage health reimbursement arrangements, or ICHRA.

ICHRA plans have rebranded as Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense, or CHOICE. But in these models, an employer offers workers a stipend to purchase an exchange plan, rather than offering coverage directly.

Liang said Oscar believes this is an area that will continue to grow. She said that they're seeing higher numbers of employers requesting quotes for potential CHOICE arrangements, and Oscar has doubled its membership between 2025 and 2026.

She added that Oscar expects to triple its CHOICE market share by 2029.

"So there's an obvious interest by employers to reduce their costs," Liang said. "And we also look at markets where there's just a lot of interest by both small employers, regional employers, to just start off. What you see is new employers and new companies that are forming will go straight to CHOICE instead of starting on the traditional insurance path."

#5730. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5729. Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist

A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision

Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."

The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare

To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."

The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough

The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.

Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."

As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

#5728. GLP-1 Drugs May Help Combat Antipsychotic Weight Gain in Schizophrenia

— Meta-analysis ranks weight loss from drugs for antipsychotic-treated patients

Antipsychotics have been a mainstay treatment for schizophrenia spectrum disorders for decades, but their metabolic side effects carry a significant treatment burden.

Life expectancy for individuals with serious mental illness, including schizophrenia, is roughly 10 to 25 years shorter than the general population, primarily due to weight gain and subsequent metabolic disease.

"Appropriate weight management in people with psychotic disorders is an important unmet need," said Jose Rubio, MD, of the Psychosis Center of Excellence at Northwell Zucker Hillside Hospital in Glen Oaks, New York. "Overweight is not an unavoidable price to pay for treating acute psychosis or preventing relapses."

Before weight-loss drugs like GLP-1 receptor agonists became available, many clinicians and patients viewed metabolic side effects as the inevitable price to pay for treating acute psychosis and preventing relapses, Rubio told MedPage Today.

These side effects also contribute to medication nonadherence, low self-esteem, decreased quality of life, and worse cognitive functioning, leading to significantly greater healthcare costs, noted Sri Mahavir Agarwal, MBBS, MD, PhD, of the University of Toronto Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, and colleagues in a systematic review and meta-analysis in JAMA Psychiatry.

"Thus, addressing the metabolic disturbances associated with antipsychotic use is necessary to improve the overall health and quality of life of individuals being treated with these medications," they emphasized.

To find effective ways to tackle this burden, Agarwal's research team performed a network meta-analysis of 95 trials, identifying the treatments associated with the greatest weight loss in antipsychotic-treated patients with schizophrenia.

"This was the largest systematic review and meta-analysis of pharmacological interventions for reducing body weight in individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders treated with antipsychotics," Agarwal told MedPage Today.

The study examined 39 individual pharmacological interventions across 5,898 trial participants. Based on moderate-certainty evidence, the following drugs were associated with the largest, statistically significant mean reductions in body weight compared with placebo:

Among these, semaglutide and metformin were observed to achieve a clinically meaningful weight loss of at least 5% of body weight. Beneficial effects on other metabolic outcomes, such as lipid and glucose levels, were also noted.

Other therapies, including ramelteon, nizatidine, and aripiprazole (Abilify), also demonstrated weight-reducing effects but were supported by very low-certainty evidence.

The findings build on prior network meta-analyses that have assessed pharmacological interventions to treat antipsychotic-associated weight gain.

"Metformin consistently had the most evidence for its effectiveness in this population, followed by moderate evidence for other interventions, such as topiramate, nizatidine, and sibutramine," Agarwal and team noted.

Prior reviews had included older GLP-1 agents, but the "field of neuroendocrinology has rapidly shifted in recent years, including introduction of newer GLP-1 receptor agonists like semaglutide, which are revolutionizing management of obesity and related comorbidities," they wrote.

Of note, the group's analysis did not include even newer therapies like tirzepatide (Zepbound). However, the authors emphasized that "there is potential for patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders to benefit from ... emerging treatments across research and clinical contexts."

As expected, GLP-1 agents were associated with slightly higher rates of mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal (GI) side effects -- such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and dyspepsia -- though discontinuation rates were not significantly higher compared with placebo.

Beyond well-established GI side effects to be cognizant of when starting GLP-1 drugs, Rubio noted that this drug class has been linked with fatigue, stomach paralysis, and inflammation of the pancreas.

"Pre-existing conditions need to be weighed in when making a decision about using these drugs, but for many people the risks are worth it given how much weight can be lost, the long-term consequences of overweight, and the relatively low risk of these complications, particularly the most severe," he said.

Despite robust data supporting the efficacy of these therapies, access remains a major hurdle. Rubio pointed out that overcoming this barrier requires a fundamental paradigm shift.

"Now patients, families, and prescribers must change how they think about overweight in schizophrenia. They may need to 'denormalize' the association between psychotic disorders and overweight," he said. "As a field, we must emphasize that overweight is an avoidable driver of medical morbidity and premature mortality."

Insurance coverage restrictions continue to block patient access, emphasized Rubio. "We still see many patients for whom these drugs are not covered by their insurance," he said. "Regulations that assume explicitly that overweight is an avoidable driver of morbidity and premature mortality -- and therefore a quality target -- would facilitate more widespread coverage."

"We do not have paradigm changes every day in our field but certainly this is one of them, which is exciting," Rubio stated. "We must work to make sure that patients with psychosis, who may at times be in vulnerable positions, also benefit from this existing resource."

#5727. Opinion: What a mother’s 1834 letter about measles tells us about MAHA

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Downs is the author of “Medicine by the People: How Ordinary People Changed American Healthcare.”

On Sept. 23, I sat in a small glass reading room at Yale’s medical library, turning the rag-paper pages of the Medical Dissenter, a London journal from the 1830s. At the bottom of one page, under the headline, “Report from Mrs. Butt to Mr. Hudson,” I met Jane Butt. Her letter was dated Sept. 23, 1834. I was reading it 192 years later to the day.

Jane lived in the village of Broughton and explained that measles had spread through the children around her earlier that year. She described how one of her own children had caught it. She then reported 36 other cases in her community. Some, she noted, developed severe inflammation of the lungs, one of the complications that can make measles deadly. She believed a cold east wind aggravated their symptoms. Nevertheless, she reported, all of them recovered.

Jane attributed the recoveries to Morison’s pills. James Morison was a merchant with no medical training who believed that a purgative could expel “impure blood” from the body and restore its natural balance. She administered the pills to the sick — sometimes twice a day — and gave as many as six at once to a toddler not yet 2 years old. She also gave the pills to women and, later, to their newborns, she wrote.

Morison’s followers called themselves Hygeists and attacked physicians as a monopoly that bled and poisoned its patients, which was not inaccurate in the 1830s. Much of medicine before the advent of germ theory and bacteriology provided incorrect diagnoses and problematic treatments.

When Jane wrote her letter, women could not train as physicians and were being displaced as midwives by the growing professional authority of doctors. She lacked medical credentials or the authority that came with them, but the Hygeist movement gave her a platform and a space to speak. She said that because “so much [was] said and done to prejudice the public mind against Mr. Morison’s most invaluable medicine,” she was left with no choice.

The journal that printed Jane’s letter sold the cure she praised. The office of the Medical Dissenter on the Strand was one of Morison’s official London depots for the pills in 1837. The same periodical mocked Edward Jenner, who had effectively used cowpox as a vaccination for smallpox, and ridiculed “vaccinic mania.”

After reading Jane’s story, I pulled out my iPhone and took photos of it, which I turned into a PDF. As a historian of medicine, I have seen cases of measles often in historical sources from the Civil War to life among the poor in tenement houses, but when I read those cases measles had long been the province of the past.

As I read Jane’s letter measles was back and raging in my home state of Pennsylvania, where six measles-associated deaths have been reported and federal health officials have disputed how many of them to count. In 2026, the United States has already recorded more than 4,500 measles cases, the largest number since 1991. Last school year, a record 4.2% of kindergartners were exempted from at least one required vaccine, and coverage for the measles vaccine fell to 92.4%, below the level needed to keep outbreaks from spreading. In some communities, the percentages of children who are vaccinated are far lower.

The current explosion of measles in the present had changed how I see the past. I didn’t preserve Jane’s story to indict her or to provide an antecedent to the unfounded arguments against vaccination, which have directly harmed innocent children. I documented her story instead because I had just finished a book on the ways ordinary people changed health care in the United States, and yet their stories have often been neglected, marginalized, or perceived to interfere with the real work of physicians. I wrote the book to show that medical knowledge is not an unalloyed concept created by professionals, but that ordinary people have continually provided evidence, offered interpretations, or even, in the case of Jane, simply counted the number of people who were sick in their communities.

Today, health populism takes shape in the Make America Healthy Again movement, which is rooted in part in grievances over how medical authority has dismissed patients, especially women. According to Politico, MAHA is “made up largely of women who followed Robert F. Kennedy Jr. into the MAGA fold.” Many of these women are moms. MAHA has, in turn, capitalized on the chauvinism of medical authority that began nearly 200 years ago that dismissed women as caregivers and often neglected their insights, their concerns, and their fears about epidemics.

The very act of counting, which might seem obvious or like a natural response to an epidemic, was part of a broader movement that eventually provided a framework for public health. Long before epidemiology developed as a discipline, patients and practitioners observed contagion — that disease seemed to spread from person to person, through households and across villages and nations. Before there was an official public health authority to count, people counted. Counting was also a move toward empiricism. It offered a bird’s-eye view of an epidemic and could provide local physicians or municipal authorities with some sense of the extent of an outbreak.

Counting mattered more than it might seem. Jane lived between two ways of explaining illness. In 1832, when a cholera pandemic reached New York City, clergy called for a national day of fasting and prayer. President Andrew Jackson refused to proclaim one, citing the separation of church and state, so states and churches held their own. Meanwhile, the city published daily counts of the sick and the dead. As the historian Charles Rosenberg showed in “The Cholera Years,” Americans read the epidemic as a judgment on sin even as they tracked it case by case. Jane blamed the wind and thanked God for her family’s recoveries, and she counted, reflecting the beginning of the shift from supernatural explanations to an empirical rationale. Documenting which children grew sickest and following an illness from house to house was a method aimed at articulating an explainable pattern. That method was not dissimilar to what physicians, ship surgeons, and military officials did in the first half of the 19th century when an epidemic erupted.

Jane’s method of dosing pills suffered from one problem: She did not observe what happened if a child did not receive the pills. Most children who caught measles in 1834 survived it, with or without pills. Thirty-seven recoveries indicated to her that the pills worked. They could not tell her what the pills did, or whether children like that toddler recovered despite them. Around the same time, the Paris physician Pierre Louis was also counting patients, and his numbers challenged bloodletting, one of medicine’s most trusted treatments, as a treatment for pneumonia. Louis asked what happened to comparable patients treated differently.

The vaccine does what Jane believed her pills did, and it was tested in ways her pills never were. Parents who refuse it are making Jane’s mistake in reverse.  She credited a cure that did nothing. They discount a protection that works, because measles has become a stranger.

Jane wrote her letter two years after the Provincial Medical and Surgical Association, a precursor to the British Medical Association, was founded in 1832 and more than a decade before the American Medical Association was founded in 1847 — a period in which men on both sides of the Atlantic were defining themselves as the institutional medical authority.

Ordinary people have been actively involved in the conversation since the beginning, but the medical populism of MAHA is making it appear as a new, novel, and even groundbreaking rebellion. Jane’s document reveals that ordinary people’s ideas have often been part of medicine, but medical authority has grown in ways that make them appear as dissenting.

Jane could not be heard in traditional medical circles. Sexism landed her in a fringe periodical, and her endorsement of the quackery of purgatives gave her a headline.

If men had not systematically excluded women from medicine and had recognized that ordinary people’s ideas, insights, and concerns are part of it, Jane might not have reached for purgative pills, and women today might not be reaching for pyrotechnic platforms to be heard.

I have been trained not to write in the conditional tense but instead to explain what happened and how it all went down. I wasn’t looking for her. I found her by accident, but I am drawn to ordinary people’s stories. That’s why I found Jane’s letter so appealing. Before I contextualized it and realized it was part of a radical publication, I was amazed to see the name of a woman in a headline in boldface in a rare book.

Although Jane does not appear in my book, she embodies its thesis — even though her method was wrong. In fact, much of medical practice was wrong or ineffective before the late 19th century, and plenty remained so afterward. There were many ordinary people, like Jane, who witnessed outbreaks and illness in their communities and reported what they saw.

When I closed the volume containing Jane’s letter and walked out of the secure room, through the Victorian reading room, through the rotunda, and past the portraits of physicians whose names circle its walls, Jane’s name was not there, nor were those of any other women from 200 years ago.

It does not have to continue to be that way. Ordinary people’s voices matter and they often begin not in the throes of a national polemic or screamed through a speaker at a MAHA rally but begin, like Jane, with an observation of a child’s health.

Jim Downs is the author of “Medicine by the People: How Ordinary People Changed American Healthcare” (W. W. Norton, October 2026). He is the Gilder Lehrman–NEH professor of history at Gettysburg College and a visiting faculty fellow at Brown University’s Center for the Study of Race and Ethnicity in America. He is a 2025–26 Guggenheim fellow.

#5726. Fierce Healthcare Policy Brief: HHS launches breast cancer screening initiative; RHTP funds flow to 6 states

Fierce Healthcare Policy Brief: HHS launches breast cancer screening initiative; RHTP funds flow to 6 states" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest across Washington, D.C. with this weekly brief. Read below for news from Oct. 26 to Oct. 30.

HHS’ Office on Women’s Health (OWH) announced Tuesday a coordinated initiative with the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) and DenseBreast-info.org (DBI) to improve breast cancer screening and early detection efforts nationwide.

The OWH–AHRQ Breast Cancer Screening and Diagnostic Follow-up Initiative will analyze national screening and follow-up patterns, with more than 40 health systems poised to expand evidence-based practices and address delays in care.

“Women deserve clear information about breast cancer screening options beyond mammography, particularly if they have dense breasts or other risk factors,” said Tammy Huizenga, AHRQ senior advisor for nutrition and women’s health, in a statement. “Understanding their individual risk and available options helps women and their healthcare providers make informed decisions that support earlier detection.”

OWH and DBI will also collaborate through a memorandum of understanding to expand access to evidence-based educational resources aimed at supporting informed discussions between women and providers, promote understanding of screenings and diagnostic follow-up options, and improve breast density awareness.

HHS' health information technology arm finalized a rule that streamlines the health IT certification program, projecting to save billions in compliance costs.

The rule, called Health Data, Technology and Interoperability: ONC Deregulatory Actions to Unleash Prosperity (HTI-5), is projected to save more than $1.5 billion in regulatory costs, according to the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC). Full story.

The Trump administration awarded $233 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to improve healthcare access across California. This investment will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care locally through regional care networks, telehealth, workforce development and upgraded healthcare technology. California has committed its full fiscal year 2026 funding to improve healthcare in rural communities across the state.

The state plans to use the investment to expand rural primary, maternal, specialty and behavioral healthcare; grow the healthcare workforce; expand telehealth and regional care networks; modernize technology and infrastructure; and support new care delivery and payment models, according to a CMS announcement. Regional care networks and telehealth will connect patients with providers and help coordinate care, while partnerships with midwives, doulas and community health workers will support maternal and primary care. Investments will also support education and training pathways to grow the rural healthcare workforce, improve technology and modernize infrastructure.

It is the full amount of funding the state will receive for fiscal year 2026.

CMS doled out $193.7M in RHTP funding to 45 organizations across Florida to expand healthcare access in rural communities, with a particular focus on bringing care closer to patients.

Florida will use the substantial investment to build out telehealth, remote monitoring, mobile and community-based services; increase access to preventive and specialty care; strengthen rural providers and the healthcare workforce; and support new care delivery and payment models.

The state's approach uses telemedicine, remote patient monitoring, pharmacy-based services, diagnostic kiosks and community paramedicine to give patients more ways to access needed care. Partnerships are a defining feature of Florida’s approach, with more than 500 partnerships across the 45 awardees bringing hospitals, clinics, local governments and community organizations together to support statewide rural healthcare transformation, according to CMS in an Oct. 23 announcement.

Florida will receive $209,938,195 in total RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

CMS awarded $186 million in funding to improve healthcare access across rural Idaho. This investment will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care locally through modern technology, new care models, an expanded healthcare workforce and improvements to healthcare facilities, the agency announced.

The investment supports five initiatives designed to strengthen healthcare delivery and modernize rural Idaho’s healthcare system. Funding for telehealth, cybersecurity and electronic health record modernization will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care better locally. Investments in community health workers and emergency medical services professionals will help bring services into homes and communities, while training, recruitment and retention efforts will grow Idaho’s rural healthcare workforce. The funding will also support programs addressing chronic disease, behavioral health, maternal and child health as well as improvements to rural healthcare facilities and equipment.

It is the full amount of funding the state will receive for fiscal year 2026.

The Trump administration locked in a regulation that will require pharmacy benefit managers to disclose fees and compensation to self-funded employers.

The rule, finalized by the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration, aims to ensure that employers can see what drug manufacturers, pharmacies and other entities are paying their PBMs and any affiliated brokers and consultants.

The department said in an announcement that this data will support employers in negotiating contracts and pushing to lower drug costs for their workers and their dependents. Full story

CMS awarded $87 million in RHTP funding to 129 rural healthcare providers through Rural Texas Strong to strengthen healthcare across rural communities. The investment will help improve health outcomes for rural Texans, build a strong healthcare workforce and modernize facilities and equipment across rural Texas, according to an agency announcement.

The funding will help rural providers prevent and manage chronic conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic respiratory disease; recruit and retain physicians, emergency medical personnel and other healthcare professionals; replace aging medical equipment; and improve existing facilities. Together, these investments will help rural providers maintain essential services and bring quality healthcare closer to home for rural Texans.

Key initiatives the overall RHTP funding will focus on include:

Texas is slated to receive $281,319,361 in total RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

A Massachusetts judge has sided with a coalition of states in an ongoing lawsuit over the rollout of Medicaid work requirements, and rejected the Trump administration's definition of "medical frailty" for critical exemptions.

Judge Richard Stearns ruled Thursday that a regulation issued over the summer that aimed to offer guardrails to the implementation of the work requirements unlawfully limited the group of people who would qualify as "medically frail" and would thus be exempted.

In the rule, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said that the frailty exemption would apply when a "physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply with the community engagement requirement."

This runs afoul of existing law, as there are individuals in five frailty categories established by Congress who may not qualify for the exemption under CMS' definition, Stearns said. Full story

Missouri will receive nearly $40 million in RHTP funding to modernize rural healthcare services and expand access to care across the state. The investment will support 26 rural healthcare providers as they renovate, reconfigure, equip or repurpose existing facilities and expand maternal health, behavioral health, diagnostic, outpatient and chronic disease management services across Missouri, according to an announcement.

The funding will support new labor, delivery and private triage rooms; expanded behavioral health services for older adults and people with substance use disorders; and upgraded diagnostic equipment, including MRI, mammography and ultrasound services. The funding will also expand primary care and increase the capacity of rural health clinics, helping rural providers update existing facilities and capabilities to better match the healthcare needs of the communities they serve, CMS said.

In total, Mississippi will receive $216,276,818 during fiscal year 2026.

The Trump Administration announced more than $19 million in RHTP funding through 11 awards to strengthen and modernize healthcare delivery throughout rural West Virginia. The state plans to invest in virtual and specialty care, mobile health services and chronic disease management, growing the rural healthcare workforce and modernizing technology and health data systems.

The investment will support new tools and services across the state, including mobile health units and drone delivery for time-critical medical supplies; remote eye care and patient monitoring technology; nursing education and apprenticeship programs; and secure systems that allow healthcare providers to better share information. Investments will also support mental health and substance use disorder recovery services and tools that reduce administrative burden for healthcare professionals, CMS announced.

West Virginia will receive a total of $199,476,099 in RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

#5725. The persisting paradox of men’s health

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Buongiorno! As you put the final touches on your Halloween costumes, here is a spooky story for you: Imagine going to urgent care for something as trivial as a UTI, and getting a bill for $1,756, on top of $211 you already paid at the clinic! Keep reading to learn more.

Intuitive Health, a private equity-backed company that runs about 50 hybrid ER-urgent care clinics, was launched on the idea that it could offer an alternative to costly hospital visits, providing under the same roof a clinic for uncomplicated issues and an ER in case of necessity.

But for many patients, the opposite has happened: They came in with simple, urgent care-appropriate conditions but were billed for ER services — think close to $2,000 for an UTI or $7,000 ($2,100 after insurance) for congestion and cough. Company officials say every patient should be asked to sign a form before the “upgrade,” but Tara Bannow found in her investigation this was far from standard practice.

A federal judge in Massachusetts has rejected the federal government’s definition of “medical frailty,” ruling that states didn’t have enough time to assess eligibility status. The decision overturns an interim CMS rule that substantially limited the pool of people eligible for exemptions to the work requirements, in particular by requiring that medically frail people demonstrate that their condition prevents them from working. The rule also didn’t list conditions that would automatically be exempt from work requirements.

The lawsuit was brought on by states claiming that CMS didn’t have the authority to narrow the definition of medically frail, and that the rule would create red tape for beneficiaries having to demonstrate their status, as well as an additional burden for state workers. Thursday’s ruling complicates the already tangled web of work requirements, and might lead to a delay in their rollout past the beginning of 2027, when they were slated to go into effect. More here.

At a rally for Zach Lahn, the farmer-turned-unlikely Republican candidate for Iowa governor, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. called Lahn’s opposition to Big Agriculture, a key tenet of his platform, a “spiritual battle.”

“We have to figure out a way to grow food without poisoning our kids, without giving ourselves cancer, without destroying the soils that enrich us and enrich our microbiome that connect our brain and all of our organs. And make us healthy, robust and vibrant people,” Kennedy told the crowd.

Chelsea Cirruzzo, who reported on the rally, also takes a broader look at RFK Jr.’s big talking points, with the midterms around the corner: fighting fraud, doubling down on “medical freedom” in the form of vaccine choice, and pushing MAHA, even as the political future of the movement looks shaky. (Also don’t forget to check out our 2026 midterms roundup for the most important political news.)

People who are diagnosed with colorectal cancer earlier in life, especially younger than 35, often have a grimmer prognosis than people who develop the disease older. Researchers have been trying to understand why. A new “atlas” of 189 colorectal cancer tumors from patients in their 20s to their 90s could help explain the differences in the disease, while controlling for variables that may have confounded previous studies.

“It is devastating to care for young patients diagnosed with often advanced stages of colorectal cancer. These are people in the prime of their life,” Kimmie Ng, the colorectal cancer researcher who authored the database study, told Angus Chen. “That’s what motivates us to do the work, find out what might be causing this, and what unique features we could target so that we can better treat these patients. It’s something that keeps me up at night, and one of the biggest questions facing our scientific community today.”

Ng, who serves as the director of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, discussed in a Q&A what kinds of insights the database might offer, and what her team is learning about the increasing rate of colorectal cancer in young patients.

A new series in The Lancet argues for the need to investigate a paradox of men’s health: why men experience worse health outcomes than women, even though they hold undeniable privilege. In their approach, the series authors move away from looking at men’s health as an issue of sex, broadening the frame to focus on gender. “Men’s health is defined and shaped by the culturally defined roles, responsibilities, attributes, and entitlements associated with being (or being seen as) a man, as well as power relations between and among women and men,” they write in the introduction.

A first paper proposes a framework that analyzes men’s health through an intersectional lens, focusing on structural determinants of health. A second looks at the available data about men’s life expectancy and burden of disability, trying — with limitations due to the lack of an intersectional perspective in many of the studies so far — to tease out risk factors and causes. The third paper proposes a political strategy that advances men’s health as a contributing factor to the shared public good.

Discussion of men’s health is wont to raise the question of whether it is detracting from women’s. The authors defend their choice. “A gendered approach to health is not a zero-sum game; it can serve to enhance wellbeing for all,” they write.

This week, STAT Executive Editor Rick Berke travelled to Washington, D.C., to accept in memory of Helen Branswell the Kovler Prize for Trust in Life Science Journalism at the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health dinner. It was an elegant event at Union Station, with 350 luminaries from science and health, including current and former NIH directors.

The highlight of the evening was a video that Helen recorded in late summer to accept the award. She talked about her work and a career she so deeply loved. As readers of this newsletter know, Helen has been a frequent contributor to Morning Rounds over the last 11 years, tirelessly sharing her insights on infectious disease news. (In fact, Helen’s first writings on Covid-19 appeared here.)

Heartbroken as we all are by her loss, I hope you’ll watch and come away inspired but one of the truly greats.

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

#5724. Dental implants can hijack your immune system, scientists discover

For tens of millions of people, dental implants have provided a way to replace missing teeth with a full set of fixed, functional teeth rather than removable dentures. However, an estimated 10% to 20% of implant patients eventually develop peri-implantitis, a serious infection that damages the surrounding jawbone.

Antibiotics frequently fail to control this condition, and scientists have struggled to understand why. Now, researchers believe they have uncovered the mechanism responsible.

A new study published in PNAS Nexus by scientists at the Rutgers School of Dental Medicine reveals that bacteria can gradually corrode dental implants, releasing microscopic titanium particles into nearby tissues. These particles interfere with the immune cells responsible for fighting infection, trapping them in a state of excessive inflammation that progressively destroys jawbone.

The researchers examined human tissue samples, studied human immune cells in the laboratory, and conducted experiments using genetically engineered mice. Their investigation identified a calcium channel in macrophages, the immune cells that engulf bacteria, that becomes activated by titanium particles. When this channel was disabled in mice, the disease was prevented.

This discovery provides the first credible drug target for a condition that affects as many as one in five dental implant recipients and costs healthcare systems worldwide more than $1 billion annually.

"For the first time, we show why all the antibiotic treatments that work around teeth do not work around implants," said Georgios Kotsakis, senior author of the study and assistant dean for clinical research at Rutgers School of Dental Medicine. "Now that we know the cause, we can start developing therapeutics."

Why Dental Implant Infections Resist Antibiotics

One of the biggest mysteries surrounding peri-implantitis has been its similarity to periodontitis, the gum disease that develops around natural teeth. Both conditions begin with the same types of bacteria found in the mouth, yet they respond very differently to treatment.

For natural teeth, antibiotics combined with routine professional cleaning can resolve the infection. Around dental implants, however, the same medications are successful in fewer than half of cases. Even when treatment is attempted, the underlying jawbone may continue to deteriorate.

For the past two decades, scientists have largely concentrated on the bacteria responsible for these infections. Researchers in Kotsakis' laboratory decided to investigate another possible contributor: the implant material itself.

Their work showed that bacteria accumulating on implant surfaces create acidic biofilms that slowly damage the titanium. Over time, this corrosion can release billions of microscopic metal particles, each smaller than a red blood cell.

Titanium particles can also be dislodged during routine dental cleaning. This is particularly concerning when instruments designed for natural teeth are used on implants, because they can scrape and damage the metal surface.

How Titanium Particles Hijack the Immune System

Once released into the gums, the tiny titanium fragments attract a bacterial toxin known as lipopolysaccharide, which coats their surfaces. This combination creates a deceptive target for the immune system, making the particles resemble unusually large bacteria that cannot be broken down.

Macrophages, the white blood cells responsible for engulfing and destroying harmful microorganisms, attempt to consume these particles. But because the cells cannot digest titanium, they become stuck in a prolonged state of excessive inflammation.

As a result, the macrophages produce large quantities of inflammatory signaling molecules, including interleukin-1 beta. This protein is also associated with inflammatory processes involved in rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease.

The resulting immune response gradually breaks down the bone supporting the dental implant. At the same time, the macrophages become less effective at fighting the bacteria that triggered the infection in the first place.

Laboratory experiments revealed just how severely their defenses were disrupted. Macrophages exposed to titanium particles engulfed fewer than half as many bacteria as immune cells that had not encountered the particles.

"These particles are little magnets that attract the bacterial toxin, and they hijack the immune system, preventing it from clearing bacteria," said Kotsakis. "You have a perfect storm that defies antibiotics."

Scientists Identify a Potential New Treatment Target

After uncovering how titanium particles disrupt immune defenses, the researchers investigated the molecular pathway responsible for the damaging reaction.

They traced the process to TRPC1, a calcium channel (a specialized, pore-forming protein structure within cell membranes) found in macrophages. This channel plays a central role in the inflammatory response triggered by titanium particles and bacterial toxins.

To test its importance, the team used genetically engineered mice that lacked TRPC1. When these animals were exposed to the same combination of titanium particles and bacteria, their immune systems responded much more effectively.

The mice developed dramatically smaller abscesses, produced fewer inflammatory signaling molecules, and regained the ability to clear bacteria. Disabling the channel prevented the destructive disease process observed when TRPC1 was present.

The results point toward a potentially new approach to treating peri-implantitis by targeting the immune system response rather than relying exclusively on antibiotics.

With funding from the National Institutes of Health, Kotsakis and his colleagues are now evaluating potential drugs that act on the same molecular pathway in human cells.

Why Proper Dental Implant Cleaning Matters

Although the research opens the door to future therapies, it also reinforces an important preventive measure for people who already have dental implants.

Regular professional cleaning remains the strongest known protection against peri-implantitis. However, the instruments and techniques used during those appointments can make a significant difference.

Until approximately a decade ago, many dentists routinely cleaned implants with the same metal scalers used to remove deposits from natural teeth. Research by the Rutgers team and other scientists has since demonstrated that these tools can damage and corrode titanium surfaces, potentially releasing additional particles and accelerating the disease.

Today, nonabrasive cleaning methods have become standard practice, helping protect implant surfaces while reducing the risk of complications.

By revealing how corroded titanium can interfere with immune defenses, the findings offer a new explanation for why some dental implant infections are so difficult to treat and identify a promising direction for developing more effective therapies.

#5723. Who’s responsible when clinical AI goes wrong? AMA weighs in

Who’s responsible when clinical AI goes wrong? AMA weighs in" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Building on its recent guidance for organizations’ use and governance of clinical AI, the American Medical Association on Thursday gave a deeper breakdown of how it believes different parties should be responsible for decisions, actions and failures involving the technology.

The latest framework from AMA’s Center for Digital Health and AI addresses liability issues the group said are currently unanswered by existing liability frameworks. Those structures, it said, could leave physicians facing "liability for risks they cannot reasonably prevent, while patients may struggle to seek remedies when AI causes harm."

Other key issues with the status quo liability frameworks, AMA said, are ambiguity around when product liability applies to AI; how contract terms and disclaimers from developers can distance responsibility from risk control; and whether deploying healthcare organizations hold various responsibilities specific to AI, such as local testing or outcomes monitoring.

AMA said the clinical AI liability framework it’s advancing "recognizes that multiple parties may bear liability for the use of AI when something goes wrong," and then aligns that accountability based on a party’s ability to prevent harm. Responsibility is spread out in areas where control is shared, but it does not become interchangeable, and no party’s obligations disappear because another party also bears some,” AMA wrote in a brief outlining its thinking.

As for the physicians AMA represents, the liability framework calls for doctors to "be responsible for the clinical judgment they can meaningfully exercise, based on the system’s intended use, known limitations and the information available at the point of care."

The group also said that oversight from a physician "cannot substitute for adequate evidence, appropriate system design or the conditions necessary to make clinical review meaningful." Physicians should also retain the authority to decline an unproven AI system, or those "whose clinical validation, usefulness or place in the standard of care remains uncertain," without penalty from their organization, AMA said.

"Patients must have meaningful avenues for recourse when clinical AI causes harm, and physicians must be able to use these technologies with confidence that responsibility reflects what they can reasonably know and control," AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., president of the AMA, said in a release on the liability framework. "As AI assumes more clinical functions, developers, healthcare organizations and physicians each have important responsibilities. We need clear expectations that protect patients, support sound clinical judgment, and ensure accountability remains with those best positioned to prevent harm."

The liability framework breaks down in detail one aspect of a broader clinical AI governance framework unveiled by AMA and its Center earlier this month. Those principles and focus areas will guide how AMA works with providers and stakeholders as it tackles issues like licensure and regulation for the fast-moving technology.

"We cannot afford to wait for these questions to be answered through trial and error in patient care," AMA CEO John Whyte, M.D., told Fierce Healthcare of the efforts earlier this month. "The AMA's new framework sets out our ambitious agenda to address these questions. … It will guide our work with physicians, patients, technology developers and policymakers to ensure clinical authority is earned through evidence, how oversight must evolve with risk, and how accountability is maintained."

AstraZeneca has launched a three-year cost-cutting program that aims to slice off $1.5 billion a year, with the savings reinvested in R&D, Pharmaphorum writes. There’s no word yet on the job implications from the initiative, which the company estimates will carry a one-time charge of around $2 billion and is expected to be completed by the end of 2029. The drug maker is already facing headwinds from the loss of patent protection for some products, including diabetes blockbuster Farxiga, with a string of other big brands due to lose exclusivity between now and the mid-2030’s, including three cancer drugs.

Indian regulators ordered Sun Pharmaceutical to stop manufacturing, selling and distributing ophthalmic products made at its Assam facility after finding failure in ​its quality management system, Reuters reported. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organization and the office of Drugs Controller Assam ordered the shutdown on ‌Aug. 20 after a joint federal-state inspection identified lapses in the system meant to ensure product quality and safety, following Sun Pharma’s move in July to voluntarily recall about 11 eye-care brands. Sun Pharma had previously said the site was expected to become one of its largest manufacturing ⁠hubs for sterile products in a business identified as a key global growth driver.

#5721. Starting Antipsychotics for Schizophrenia Tied to Blood Sugar Spikes

— Weight and glucose should be assessed at baseline and 12 weeks after initiation, researcher says

When patients with schizophrenia begin second-generation antipsychotic therapy, clinicians typically monitor the scale for early signs of metabolic harm.

However, findings from a recent electronic health record study of adults with severe mental illness (SMI) suggested that blood glucose can surge rapidly within the first 90 days of treatment through both weight-dependent and weight-independent pathways.

Published in the Lancet Psychiatry, the study from Juan Carlos Bazo-Alvarez, PhD, of University College London, and colleagues tracked within-person trajectories of HbA1c and body weight before and after initiating antipsychotics. "The first 3 months after starting an antipsychotic appear to be a particularly important metabolic window," Bazo-Alvarez told MedPage Today.

"Clinicians should not wait for substantial weight gain before checking glycemic measures, because HbA1c and weight do not always change in parallel," he said. "Early monitoring of both outcomes may help identify risk sooner and support timely intervention."

Using England's Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum database (2000-2023), the researchers evaluated 96,849 adults ages 18 to 59 (mean age 37.2) with SMI -- including schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and bipolar disorder -- who initiated oral second-generation antipsychotics.

Median baseline weight across the cohort was 167.6 lb and HbA1c was 35 mmol/mol (5.4%). Prior to treatment, participants' HbA1c rose by 0.01 mmol/mol weekly, while weight rose by 0.04 lb weekly.

In the 90 days post-initiation, the weekly rate of HbA1c increase jumped roughly 14 times to 0.12 mmol/mol, producing an excess increase of 1.42 mmol/mol compared with what would be expected had the pre-treatment trend continued. Beyond day 90, the rate of increase returned to baseline levels (0.01 mmol/mol per week), though the early increase was not reversed.

Weight followed a similar surge. Patients gained an average of 0.46 lb weekly during the first 90 days (an excess gain of 5.22 lb) before slowing to 0.07 lb weekly from day 91 onwards.

Notably, testing was skewed. While 76.6% of patients had a recorded weight during follow-up, only 24.9% had an HbA1c measurement.

Early weight and glycemic changes were not the same across individual medications at day 90:

"The pronounced increases in both weight and HbA1c with olanzapine were consistent with its well-established metabolic liability," Bazo-Alvarez noted. However, the team was surprised by how quickly the HbA1c trajectory climbed.

"We were also struck by the fact that weight and HbA1c did not always move together; for example, quetiapine was associated with substantial weight gain but relatively little HbA1c change," he said. "This reinforces the message that weight alone does not fully capture early glycemic risk."

Disparities were also evident across subgroups. Women experienced steeper initial surges than men (excess 90-day HbA1c of 1.68 vs 1.18 mmol/mol; excess weight of 5.73 lb vs 5.18 lb), peaking in women starting olanzapine (excess 9.17 lb; excess HbA1c of 3.27 mmol/mol).

Additionally, baseline prediabetes substantially amplified long-term risk, as 13.7% of these patients were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes during follow-up (estimated 2-year cumulative incidence 19.0%) compared with 3.0% of normoglycemic patients.

Commentators Call for Earlier Prophylaxis

In an accompanying commentary, Caroline Hynes-Ryan, MSc, of St. John of God University Hospital in Dublin, and colleagues noted that rapid HbA1c shifts often go unnoticed compared with visible weight gain.

"As weight gain is rapid, visible by the individual and their clinician, and associated with distress, it often receives the most attention as a modifiable or preventable risk factor in this population," they wrote. "However, other cardiometabolic risk factors, such as dysglycemia and dyslipidemia, can be present but asymptomatic and are only identified on routine screening as recommended by international guidelines."

Because current guidelines generally reserve preventive metformin for higher-risk agents -- such as olanzapine or clozapine -- or for patients who have already experienced substantial weight gain, Hynes-Ryan's group suggested the findings support considering metformin (unless contraindicated) for all patients with SMI starting a second-generation antipsychotic.

The findings support assessing both weight and HbA1c at baseline and at 12 weeks after initiation, rather than relying on weight change as a proxy for metabolic risk, Bazo-Alvarez stressed.

"Patients starting antipsychotics with greater metabolic liability, particularly olanzapine, as well as women and those with prediabetes or other cardiometabolic risk factors, may benefit from closer follow-up and earlier preventive support," he said. "Monitoring should also continue beyond the first 3 months in line with clinical guidance."

However, he cautioned against using the observational findings to avoid specific therapies altogether. "These findings should not be interpreted as meaning that one antipsychotic is always preferable to another," Bazo-Alvarez stated.

"Treatment choice has to balance psychiatric effectiveness, previous response, patient preference, and adverse-effect profiles," he pointed out.

"Our study was observational, so it was not designed to make formal causal comparisons between individual drugs. The practical implication is therefore less about prescribing a specific antipsychotic and more about recognizing that metabolic effects can emerge early and vary between patients," he said.
