#5701. Opinion: The economics of the U.S. health care system are broken

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Markovich is president and CEO of Ascendiun, the nonprofit parent company of Blue Shield of California, Blue Shield Promise Health Plan, Altais, and Stellarus.

On my recent travels, I met a healthy, active man in his early 60s who runs a small business.  This year, his family’s monthly premium reached nearly $5,000 — more than a quarter of his pre‑tax income. He made the difficult choice to keep coverage only for his wife and two children, hoping to stay healthy until he is eligible for Medicare.

No family should have to make that choice, but this story is not unusual. More than 27 million Americans lacked health insurance in 2024, and millions more have coverage they cannot afford to use because their deductibles are so high. The average employer‑sponsored family premium is nearly $27,000 a year.

So why not just have the federal government pay more? Increasing federal subsidies is helpful in the short term, but it is not a sustainable long-term solution. In August, the federal debt exceeded $40 trillion. This sum is larger than the entire American economy and is nearly enough to purchase every single-family home in the country. Meanwhile, nearly 70% of federal, non-interest spending is on health care and income support like Social Security. Therefore, the only way to make health care affordable for everyone is to get costs under control.

The core problem is that the economics of the U.S. health care system are broken: There is no mechanism to keep total spending within any reasonable bounds. Every other major industry faces market checks when prices rise, from groceries to the family car. Health care does not.

One clear way to break this cycle is to put American health care on a budget, one that applies to all participants in the system. Everyone must be tasked with holding health care cost inflation at or below the rate of inflation, and must be held responsible for meeting the same target.

One way to do this is to create a national office of health care affordability responsible for ensuring that health care costs become sustainable. This new body would require reporting and analysis of how prices are set to drive greater transparency in health care costs. It would set thresholds for year-to-year cost increases, holding health care cost hikes at or below the rate of inflation.

When targets are not met, the office would work with the organization on corrective actions and, as a final step, could levy progressive financial penalties on organizations that did not fall within these thresholds. Finally, the office would establish mechanisms to ensure these savings resulted in lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs for families, employers, and taxpayers.

California is showing what this could look like. Its Office of Health Care Affordability sets enforceable cost‑growth targets for the whole sector and for individual organizations, with fines beginning in 2028 and a goal of holding growth near 3%, in line with wages. This is not the first time a state has tried such an idea. Eight states have set cost-growth targets over the past decade. But California is the first state to combine transparency of cost increases with financial enforcement that holds entities accountable to a target.

California’s approach was supported by a coalition of unlikely allies, including health plans like mine, labor unions like the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), large businesses including the Purchasers Business Group on Health (PBGH), and consumer groups led by Health Access California. Today, California’s Office of Health Care Affordability continues to seek feedback on its work from an advisory committee and workgroups comprised of stakeholders to ensure it has the benefit of a breadth of experience and expertise, including California consumers, insurers, labor unions, hospitals, and physician organizations.

As my colleagues and I at Blue Shield of California have said publicly, we support this approach because it is rooted not in the costs of one industry segment, but in a complete transformation of the entire health care system in the state. For example, a big part of OHCA’s work is focused on encouraging value-based payment models and ensuring investments in primary care.

But even with that support, California’s approach is drawing fire. The state’s hospital association has gone to court to block the targets, arguing they don’t reflect the real cost pressures providers face. Those concerns deserve a serious answer. But they also reinforce the need for a federal version of this model since these issues are national forces.

Without enforceable cost targets, every breakthrough, from GLP‑1s to gene therapies to artificial intelligence, risks becoming another layer of cost rather than a source of savings. Because the entire system is rewarded by doing more, investments in prevention are financially irrational. Without accountability, payment reform stays incremental. And without cost certainty, policymakers cannot responsibly expand access to coverage.

Health care has put Americans and America in a massive financial bind, and no one is coming to bail us out. The only way fix this is to make our wasteful health care system a lot more efficient and effective, which is only going to happen when we demand that the health care industry do what most American families have to do every year: manage to a budget.

Paul Markovich is president and CEO of Ascendiun, the nonprofit parent company of Blue Shield of California, Blue Shield Promise Health Plan, Altais, and Stellarus.

#5700. Opinion: Cancer patients are often pressured to end a pregnancy early. They shouldn’t be

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Cardonick is a maternal fetal medicine physician and founder of the Cancer and Pregnancy Registry.

Early in my career as a maternal fetal medicine specialist, I met two pregnant women who had ovarian cancer. One of them was expecting twins. They were introduced to be each other’s support network during and after the pregnancy, often meeting for coffee with their newborns and comparing wigs after hair loss from the chemotherapy they received.

The mother of twins is still alive today. The other didn’t survive beyond her child’s second birthday. When I spoke with the one who is still alive, she was distraught that her new friend died of her disease. “Why did she die and I am still alive?” she asked.

I didn’t know how to answer her out loud, but in my head, I thought: “Your doctor went to the library and researched managing ovarian cancer during pregnancy, and her doctor didn’t.”

The woman who lived was treated as if she were not pregnant. Without delay, she underwent a CT scan and workup of her ovarian cyst, and even received chemotherapy while pregnant. Her twins are now 28 years old, and all are thriving.

For the woman who died, treatment was electively delayed until her third trimester.

I do not know if removing her mass or giving chemotherapy earlier in pregnancy would have made a difference in her case, but I can’t help wondering.

Patients diagnosed with cancer are often advised to terminate their pregnancies without discussing the very real option of treating cancer during pregnancy. Other women diagnosed in their second or early third trimesters, after the fetal organs have developed, are advised to have an elective preterm birth.

But much of the time, chemotherapy can be safely administered during pregnancy and the infant delivered at term.

Compounding the problem, cancer is diagnosed significantly later in pregnant women. This is partly due to common symptoms between certain types of cancer and pregnancy, but also because physicians (and patients) are reluctant to perform imaging during pregnancy, which delays biopsies and management.

Why are doctors not offering cancer treatment to their pregnant patients? Is it fear of litigation, as obstetrics is one of the most litigated of all medical specialties? Lack of medical investigation? Or just paternalistic advice?

I recall a patient diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma in pregnancy. When I discussed starting chemotherapy in the second trimester, another physician told me: “She already had two kids. She should terminate.”

People often assume that ending a pregnancy, whether through termination or early delivery, improves the mother’s outcome. But that is not the case. When compared with non-pregnant women with the same cancer, pregnant women have similar survival rates. No study has shown an improvement in a woman’s survival if she terminates her pregnancy compared to if she continues.

When I observed during my fellowship that oncologists and obstetricians very infrequently faced a pregnant woman with cancer, I realized the medical community needed a way to pool all of the scattered cases into a central database to track these pregnancies and follow the outcomes for women and their babies. Six hundred and fifty cases later, I am still asking the same questions I asked when I encountered that very first pregnant cancer patient:

Understandably, giving chemotherapy to a woman during pregnancy sounds dangerous, but the longitudinal research closely examining children exposed to chemotherapy backs up this approach. Children exposed to chemotherapy perform as well on standardized tests for development as unexposed children. This has been repeated at ages 18 months to 3 years, 6 years, 9 years, and 12-15 years of age. We did find that children exposed to chemotherapy are three times more likely to need eyeglasses.

And guess which children didn’t do as well? The ones electively delivered preterm to avoid maternal cancer treatment.

No options in such cases are without risk: an elective preterm birth to avoid cancer treatment, delaying cancer treatment until after delivery, or starting chemotherapy during pregnancy so the fetus can develop longer in utero and reach term. As any treatment in medicine, it is a balance between risks and benefits.

I understand many physicians are afraid to do something wrong when it comes to a pregnant woman. But denying cancer therapy by withholding or underdosing chemotherapy doesn’t serve her well, either. You can do everything to protect the fetus during the remainder of the pregnancy and forget that if their mother dies too young, due to delayed diagnosis or treatment, the child will still be affected. What is best for the mother/baby unit as a whole is a healthy mother.

I’ve worked with the Society of Maternal Fetal Medicine and the American Society of Clinical Oncology to publish guidelines to help other physicians handle this medical dilemma.

These guidelines address avoiding delays in pregnant women and discuss the safety to perform MRIs without contrast and CT scans with contrast. They also discuss performing necessary surgeries at any gestational age in pregnancy when this would be the clinical solution if the patient were not pregnant.

And they lay out how to give chemotherapy during the second and third trimesters and time treatment for safe delivery for mother and child.

I am honored to have participated in the development of these guidelines to increase the chances that when cancer and pregnancy collide, saving both lives will be considered.

Elyce Cardonick is a maternal fetal medicine physician and founder of the Cancer and Pregnancy Registry. She has spent nearly three decades caring for women diagnosed with cancer during pregnancy and advocating for mothers and their babies.

#5699. Popular cannabis sleep gummies may have a hidden dark side

Cannabinol (CBN) has become a popular ingredient in sleep supplements, often promoted as a natural, gentle way to relax and get a better night's rest. However, new research from the University of Connecticut suggests that this widely available cannabis compound may have risks that consumers should know about.

Scientists found that repeated exposure to CBN caused mice to develop signs of physical dependence. The findings, published in the November issue of the journal Drug and Alcohol Dependence, raise questions about the safety of using CBN regularly, particularly over long periods.

"CBN is everywhere right now. Gummies, tinctures, capsules, and it's marketed as a safe, herbal sleep supplement," says Steven Kinsey, professor in UConn's Elisabeth DeLuca School of Nursing. "Our findings suggest consumers should be aware repeated use may carry risks."

Popular Sleep Aid Shows Effects Similar to THC

CBN is a naturally occurring compound in cannabis, along with THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) and CBD (cannabidiol). Although CBN is generally considered less psychoactive than THC, the researchers discovered that it affects some of the same biological systems and can produce several key signs associated with drug dependence.

In the experiments, mice received CBN twice a day for three consecutive days. As treatment continued, the animals became less responsive to the compound, indicating that they had developed tolerance. When CBN was withdrawn, the mice also displayed physical symptoms resembling withdrawal, including head twitching and paw fluttering. These movements are comparable to the shaking that people can experience during drug withdrawal.

Another experiment revealed a surprising connection between CBN and THC. Mice previously trained to recognize and respond to THC's psychoactive effects reacted similarly when given CBN. This suggests that the two compounds produce overlapping subjective effects, at least in mice.

Together, the results indicate that CBN, despite its reputation as a milder cannabis compound, interacts with some of the same receptor systems that contribute to THC dependence.

Scientists Raise Concerns About CBN Sleep Supplements

The findings are particularly relevant because CBN products have become increasingly common, even though scientists still have limited information about their long-term effects.

The lead author of the study, Olivia Vanegas '26 Ph.D., notes "The marketing of minor cannabinoids is pretty wild right now. There are so many therapeutic claims about these drugs, but we really don't know much about their potential risks, especially with repeated use."

CBN is now widely promoted as a sleep aid, yet important questions remain unanswered. Researchers do not fully understand how CBN affects sleep quality or whether taking it repeatedly at doses commonly found in supplements could lead to addiction in humans.

There is also a historical reason for caution. Over the past century, several medications initially promoted as helpful sleep treatments were eventually found to carry serious risks of dependence and habit formation.

Potential Benefits Come With Unanswered Safety Questions

The researchers also identified potentially useful properties of CBN. The compound demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects, including at lower doses that did not produce psychoactive effects.

However, the experiments revealed another possible concern. During a simulated bacterial challenge, CBN reduced the body's ability to defend itself. This weakening of immune protection could make it easier for an infection to develop, similar to how bacteria can enter through a cut on the foot and cause illness.

These findings suggest that CBN may have medical applications, but scientists need a clearer understanding of its benefits, potential side effects, and appropriate doses before determining how it can be used safely.

Importantly, the experiments were conducted in mice, so the findings do not establish that CBN causes dependence or withdrawal in people. Additional studies are needed to understand how the compound affects humans, especially when taken frequently, at higher doses, or over extended periods.

"CBN may still have therapeutic value," he says. "But until we know more about dosing and long-term effects, the message for consumers is simple: buyer beware."

#5696. Inflation Ticks Up as Housing Headwinds Continue to Brew

Despite the Federal Reserve’s decision not to raise rates yesterday, the latest data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) still showed a 0.5% month-to-month increase in inflation as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, 0.2% higher than the increase in August.

The PCE index has enjoyed a reputation as the Fed’s favored indicator of inflation, and is released monthly by the BEA along with a bevy of related indices and measures. One of those related indices is the “core” PCE price index, which, by excluding food and energy from the data, aims to provide a less volatile long-term indicator of inflation.

The core PCE price index increased 0.3%, also up from 0.2% in August. Even so, both month-to-month price indices fell in line with expectations based on previous months.

The year-to-year PCE price index, which is now 3.6% higher than last September, may reveal greater cause for concern. The core year-to-year PCE price index sits not far behind at 3.1%.

Navy Federal Chief Economist Heather Long said on social media that 3.6% is the highest PCE Inflation has been since May. According to Long, “inflation is back near a 3-year high,” probably “largely due to war in Iran.”

The report comes as home sales continue to hover at historic lows, with existing-home sales on track to come in below 4 million this year (compared to longer-term averages of over 5 million going back to the Great Recession). Mortgage rates are back above 7% as the Iran war and other geopolitical instability have put pressure on prices and rattled the economy.

Long, however, hesitated to make it all about Iran. She identified three trends—a “(b)ig rise in goods prices,” “service sector inflation” and “sideways” housing inflation as indicative of rising core inflation in general.

“Bottom line: America’s inflation problem is bigger than the war in Iran,” Long wrote.

A pending inflation problem could signal another rate hike in December. Chris Osmond, chief investment officer for Fifth Third Wealth Advisors, told Yahoo Finance that yesterday’s hold is likely only a pause in a tightening cycle.

As for other statistics from the report, consumer spending as measured by the PCE recorded a 0.5% or $113.1 billion increase.

The BEA reported that this increase was split between a $35.1 billion uptick in spending on goods and a $78.1 billion uptick of spending on services this month. Of the goods and services counted in the data, gasoline and energy goods experienced the most dramatic increase in spending at $45.7 billion, while motor vehicles and parts clocked in the most dramatic decrease at $14.0 billion.

Current-dollar disposable personal income (DPI), or personal income minus personal current taxes, rounded out the highlighted personal income measures at a 0.2% or $52.7 billion increase. Its inflation-adjusted counterpart, real DPI, clocked in at a -0.3% decrease.

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

#5694. Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication

Missing doses of blood pressure medication could significantly reduce its ability to protect against heart attacks, strokes, and other serious cardiovascular problems, according to findings presented at ESC Congress 2026.

An estimated 1.4 billion adults worldwide between the ages of 30 and 79 have high blood pressure (hypertension), a major contributor to illness and death. Although medications that lower blood pressure are proven to reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications, approximately half of patients do not take their prescriptions as directed.

"We have evidence that poor adherence to antihypertensive medication is associated with worse outcomes," explained presenter, Miss Qianqian Yang from the University of Oxford, UK. "However, previous data has come from observational studies and could be confounded by other factors. We undertook an analysis of randomized trial data to assess the true impact of adherence on the benefits of antihypertensive treatment."

Major Study Examines the Impact of Missed Blood Pressure Medication

To better understand how consistently taking medication affects its benefits, researchers analyzed individual patient data from 91,339 participants across nine clinical trials. Each trial compared a blood pressure treatment (intervention group) with an alternative approach (comparator group: either placebo or a less-intensive regimen).

The researchers divided participants into two categories based on how closely they followed their prescribed treatment. Those who took at least 80% of their assigned medication were considered to have higher adherence, while those who took less than 80% were placed in the lower adherence group.

Even with the regular monitoring and structured conditions of clinical trials, patients became less consistent about taking their medication as time passed.

"A decline in adherence over time was apparent, even in the structured setting of trials," noted Miss Yang. Overall, 88% of participants met the higher adherence threshold during the first year, but that figure had dropped to just 79% by the fifth year.

Skipping Blood Pressure Pills Reduces Treatment Benefits

The difference in medication adherence was reflected in how much patients' blood pressure improved.

Among participants with higher adherence, systolic blood pressure, the top number in a blood pressure reading, was 5.2 mmHg lower in the intervention group than in the comparator group. For those with lower adherence, the difference was considerably smaller at just 3.0 mmHg.

Researchers then examined whether these differences translated into protection against major cardiovascular problems. The outcomes included strokes, heart attacks (myocardial infarction), ischemic heart disease, and heart failure that resulted in hospitalization or death.

The findings revealed a striking contrast. Among patients who consistently followed their treatment plans, the intervention group experienced an 11% lower incidence of major cardiovascular events compared with the comparator group. However, among patients with lower adherence, there was no statistically significant reduction in these events.

"Notably, our results reinforce the saying that 'drugs don't work in patients who don't take them.' Patients with lower adherence derived little or no cardiovascular benefit, whereas those with higher adherence had greater reductions in blood pressure and prevention of cardiovascular events," said Miss Yang.

Helping Patients Get Lifesaving Heart Protection

The researchers believe that helping people take their medication consistently should become a greater priority in the treatment of high blood pressure. They recommend more routine assessments of medication adherence, along with better patient education and practical strategies to make treatment easier to follow.

Possible approaches include simplifying medication schedules, combining multiple treatments into a single pill, and prescribing longer-acting drugs that can help limit the consequences of an occasional missed dose.

Professor Felix Mahfoud, Chair of the ESC Communication Committee, emphasized that missed medication has received too little attention as a contributor to poorly controlled blood pressure.

"For years, we have neglected non-adherence to medication as a cause for uncontrolled hypertension. Assessment of adherence should become a routine part of hypertension care so patients do not miss out on life-saving benefits. As healthcare providers, we are here to have open, non-judgmental conversations with our patients about any barriers they may have to taking medication, to help improve adherence."

The procedure, popularly called mitochondrial replacement techniques or “three-parent IVF,” is illegal in the United States, but it is accessible via a sprawling for-profit tourism industry, connecting women in the U.S. and Europe to clinics abroad.

#5692. Real Estate CEO and His Daughter Are Shot in Violent Home Invasion at Toronto Mansion

A Canadian real estate CEO and his daughter are fighting for their lives after three armed suspects forced their way into the family’s Toronto home in a violent early-morning invasion.

The Mac Group CEO David Morton, his wife, Doriana Zohil-Morton, and their adult daughters, Cristina and Maggie, were injured as they tried to fight off the masked intruders who were armed with guns and a hammer, Toronto Police Service Inspector Kristy Smith said during a press conference, according to CP24.

Morton and one of his daughters suffered gunshot wounds and are in life-threatening condition, while the mother and their other daughter sustained injuries that are not considered life-threatening, the National Post reported.

Police responded to the attack at the home in the city’s affluent Bridle Path neighborhood around 3:44 a.m. local time on Thursday.

“There was a violent interaction,” Smith said, according to the Toronto Sun. “There was a demand made for valuables from within the home–whether or not they escaped with anything is uncertain.”

The three suspects fled the scene in an SUV, police said. The home is located on Hyde Park Circle, near Bayview and Lawrence avenues. Authorities have not released descriptions of the suspects.

“This is a very active and ongoing investigation,” Smith said during the press conference. “While we don’t have any detailed suspect information at this time, I can assure you that we are doing our best to provide information to you with regard to the potential three suspects that we are aware of at this time.”

Police have not determined whether the family was targeted, according to the National Post.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow condemned the attack, saying she was “deeply troubled” by the violence.

“My thoughts are with the family and their loved ones, who are going through something no family should ever have to face,” Chow wrote in a post on X. “I am praying for their full recovery.”

#5691. A STAT reporter on covering MRT as an experimental fertility treatment

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Amanda Erickson is a news editor at STAT.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Good morning! We’ve got something a little different for you today – an amazing new story from Megan Molteni, and also a peek at the story behind the story.

And speaking of peeks — I’d recommend this new episode of Commons Healthcare, which examines STAT’s investigative prowess and features interviews with Executive Editor Rick Berke and the late, inimitable Helen Branswell.

Heidy Willis was struggling to get pregnant. And after several rounds of failed IVF, she was willing to try anything.

So Willis flew to Albania for a process known as mitochondrial replacement therapy, or MRT. Willis’ genetic material was inserted into another woman’s egg cells. The idea is that the donor’s healthy mitochondria power the embryo into a healthy fetus and, eventually, a baby.

MRT is not legal in the U.S. But medical tourism agencies charge thousands of dollars to connect women to clinics around the world. Many of these companies target women over 40, even though there’s scant evidence the procedure can help unwind age-related infertility.

“You’re paying for the privilege of being a guinea pig,” a John Hopkins bioethicist told STAT’s Megan Molteni.

Megan has spent the last eight months doggedly investigating the companies connecting women to MRT treatments, talking to dozens of patients, employees and researchers. Some of her findings are, quite frankly, shocking. There’s a coda to Willis’s story, for example, that made me gasp out loud.

Set aside some time today or this week to dive into the story. And below, Megan took the time to answer some of my questions about this remarkable piece of journalism.

How did the idea for this story come about?

Back in 2019, I’d reported on the results of a small pilot study of MRT for infertility and since then have continued to cover developments.

In February of this year, I was contacted by a couple in the U.K. who wanted to tell me about an experience they had with a reproductive tourism company called IFG that was marketing MRT as a sort of miracle treatment for age-related infertility. The woman in this couple was a doctor in her 40s and she’d been taken in by the hope that was being offered for her to have a genetically related child of her own, despite there being scant evidence that it improves the odds of pregnancy for older women.

Ultimately, she didn’t go through with MRT because of some bad experiences she had leading up to it. But she was in touch with a number of other women who were actively in the process and she helped me get connected to them to hear more about their stories.

What was the biggest reporting challenge?

Reproductive tourism is the business of breaking procreation into distinct components that can be routed around regulations and assembled at the end to result in a baby. It is, by design, a complex chain of events often facilitated by multiple companies across multiple jurisdictions to circumvent local laws and so is a pretty opaque process.

With MRT, you’re adding even more layers of scientific and legal maneuvering to make it possible. So getting inside required actually going to the places that patients were going, including a clinic in Albania, where the laws are more amenable to technologies like MRT.

What was the most surprising thing you learned?

One of the things that was most surprising was that we were able to get our hands on this long-awaited data from a clinic in Ukraine that had been at one time the most prolific provider of MRT, before the full-scale Russian invasion of 2022.

I had been aware of them for years, thanks to reporting by NPR and this Netflix documentary.

Scientists I know in this space have been awaiting this publication of data, but with the war breaking out, things had gone rather silent. I reached out to their former embryologist, Pavlo Mazur, to ask him what he thought about these commercial clinics offering MRT for age-related infertility, not really expecting to hear back.

Instead, that started months of conversations. He had data he wanted in the world but hadn’t been able to publish, for some reasons that make a lot of sense, and for some others that have to do with biases against science coming out of countries like Ukraine without a long history of evidence-based medicine and well-regulated biomedical research. Their results are the strongest refutation of the idea that MRT can be a silver bullet remedy for age-related infertility.

No matter what happens tomorrow, health care policy could be in for a shakeup. That’s the message from more than two dozen policymakers, lobbyists, and experts STAT’s Daniel Payne spoke with.

Of course, control of Congress will shape what happens next. But some of Daniel’s sources said the anger with the health care status quo runs deep. One health policy consultant said they’re telling insurance leaders that they predict “significant” changes to the fundamentals of American health care, and that they should “be afraid.”

If you prefer your election predictions via video, check out our new “STATus Report”. And if you haven’t yet checked out our midterms page, do it today! Who knows what it will hold after tomorrow!

Did Daniel’s story about the stakes of tomorrow’s election get your heart racing? It turns out, you’re not alone.

As STAT’s Liz Cooney reports, “studies have found a significantly higher chance of arrhythmias in the weeks just before and after elections, and an increased rate of hospitalizations for heart attacks right after voting day.”

The issue is stress. A deluge of news can raise your adrenaline and amp up your sympathetic nervous system, which can in turn alter the heart’s electrical activity. This makes abnormal rhythms more likely in someone already prone to them. Interested to learn about what researchers found when they looked at heart health around the 2020 and 2016 elections? Read more.

Years ago, maternal fetal medicine doctor Elyce Cardonick met two pregnant women, both suffering from ovarian cancer. The women became friends, meeting up with their newborns and comparing wigs after hair loss.

One of those mothers is thriving, alongside her 28-year-old twins. The other didn’t live to see her child turn three.

Why did one die and the other survive? Read this new First Opinion for answers.

Amanda Erickson is a news editor at STAT.

#5690. Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think

Even alcohol consumption that many Americans would describe as moderate may carry significant health risks, including a greater likelihood of premature death, disability, cancer, and heart disease. That is the conclusion of a new study published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, a journal published at Rutgers University.

The research, known as the Alcohol Intake and Health Study, was originally commissioned by the U.S. federal government to help shape updated national dietary recommendations. Researchers estimated that people who consume an average of 14 alcoholic drinks per week face a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of dying from alcohol-related causes. By comparison, consuming up to seven drinks weekly was linked to only small increases in risk for most health conditions.

"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," says lead study author Kevin Shield, Ph.D., an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."

How Scientists Measured the Health Risks of Alcohol

To better understand the long-term consequences of drinking, Shield and his colleagues in the United States and Canada investigated how alcohol consumption over a lifetime contributes to disease and premature death among Americans.

Medical experts first examined more than 7,200 scientific publications covering illnesses and injuries associated with alcohol. Using this evidence, they estimated the risks for individual health conditions and combined those findings with large national health data sets. Statistical models then allowed the team to calculate how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious health problems or dying prematurely.

The findings provide specific estimates that are missing from the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines. The updated recommendations simply encourage Americans to "limit alcoholic beverages" without identifying a particular consumption threshold. Earlier versions advised men to drink no more than two alcoholic beverages per day and women no more than one.

"While the new U.S. Dietary Guidelines contain a useful 'less-is-best' message, they provide no quantitative framework. Our study was designed to do just that across the drinking spectrum," says study co-author Timothy Naimi, M.D., M.P.H., director of the University of Victoria's Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research and an adjunct professor at Boston University.

"It turns out that two drinks per day, which might be considered 'moderate' from a social standpoint, is associated with a substantially elevated risk of a premature death caused by alcohol," explains Naimi.

Moderate Drinking Offers No Significant Overall Health Benefits

The researchers looked beyond the risk of premature death to examine alcohol's connection to a wide range of immediate and long-term health problems. These included cancers (e.g., esophageal, oral, and breast), cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and injuries.

One of the study's most important findings challenges the longstanding belief that consuming small amounts of alcohol can improve health, particularly heart health.

"We did not observe a significant protective effect of alcohol on health at any level of consumption," says Shield. "At low levels, alcohol may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. But when you look across the full range of health outcomes, including cancer and other chronic diseases, those potential benefits are outweighed by the risks even at 7 drinks per week."

In other words, while some studies have suggested that light drinking may benefit certain aspects of cardiovascular health, those possible advantages do not translate into an overall health benefit once alcohol's links to cancer and other diseases are taken into account.

Although the analysis drew on extensive scientific evidence, the researchers emphasize that its estimates describe risks across populations rather than predicting precisely what will happen to any particular person.

Shield says the statistical calculations relied on "the best possible data." However, he cautions that individual circumstances can substantially influence the results.

"However, we can't assume that means one person's individual health risk is the same as what is reported here -- that depends on other factors like lifestyle, genetics, drinking patterns, and other choices that differ person to person."

To estimate alcohol's overall impact, the researchers calculated risks for health conditions already known to be caused by alcohol and combined them into a broader assessment. However, scientists are continuing to investigate additional possible consequences of drinking, including emerging evidence connecting alcohol consumption to pancreatic cancer.

"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," says Shield.

What the Findings Mean for U.S. Drinking Guidelines

The results suggest that alcohol-related health risks become more pronounced when consumption exceeds one drink per day, regardless of whether the person is male or female. This provides a more specific reference point for people trying to understand how their drinking habits might affect their long-term health.

Rather than suggesting that any particular amount is completely safe, the findings show how risks increase with greater consumption and why drinking less generally reduces exposure to alcohol-related harm.

"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking," says Shield.

The study has also raised questions about how scientific evidence was incorporated into federal dietary recommendations.

In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former Associate Administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, offers his perspective on the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the development of national guidance.

"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

Materials provided by Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5689. Lady Gaga’s Former New York City Penthouse in the Iconic Hit Factory Building Is Available for $7 Million

A New York City penthouse that once served as the home of Lady Gaga has officially hit the market, asking $6.995 million.

The pop star’s former duplex residence is a 3,700-square-foot condominium at the top of an iconic Hell’s Kitchen building called The Hit Factory.

From 1993 to 2005, the location was the headquarters of the legendary recording studios, where artists including Michael Jackson, Mariah Carey, Bruce Springsteen, and U2 recorded some of their most popular albums.

According to Robb Report, the seven-story building became a 27-unit condominium after recording operations shut down, and the residences sold out in 2011.

In addition to the impressive slate of A-listers who have passed through the hallways of the building to make music, there are also a handful of notable residents who have shared the same address as the “Abracadabra” singer.

Retired basketball player Carmelo Anthony, comedian Tracy Morgan, and former NBA coach Amar’e Soudemire have all lived there at some point, too.

The home has not been on the market since 2018, when it last made an appearance asking $6.495 million, according to records. Previously, it had been offered as a rental, with a monthly rent of $24,500.

The dwelling has three bedrooms with an opportunity to turn a flexible space into a fourth. There are also three full bathrooms and a powder room the listing describes as “glamorous.”

The home makes a fantastic first impression with a double-height foyer that leads way to a great room with soaring ceilings. A smart gel fireplace is a bold statement in the otherwise bright and airy room, which is naturally well-lit thanks to the 9-foot double-paned windows.

There’s plenty of space to entertain here, with room for more than one lounge area and formal dining.

A “brand-new chef’s kitchen” defined by dazzling white marble countertops is tucked away behind sliding glass doors. With a Sub-Zero refrigerator, six-burner vented Viking range, Bosch dishwasher, and a wine fridge, it’s well equipped for a homeowner who loves to cook—even though there are plenty of celebrated restaurants just steps away, thanks to the prime location.

The first level also has two sizable bedroom suites, each boasting bespoke wardrobe spaces and full en suite bathrooms. A home office, in-unit laundry, and storage rooms thoughtfully designed with useful built-in solutions are here, as well.

Upstairs, a sprawling primary suite has enough room for both a cozy king size bed and dedicated seating areas. A skylight and complete wall of windows keeps the room flooded with sunshine.

The primary bathroom is a spa-inspired retreat, designed with marble, a walk-in glass shower, and a large soaking tub.

Perhaps the most exciting physical feature of the abode is the private 1,100-square-foot terrace with views of the skyline and Hudson River.

Additionally, the residence’s footprint is expanded by a deeded garage parking space and a cellar storage room—two underrated features in a Manhattan home.

The building also offers additional amenities, including concierge services, a full-time doorman, and a gym. Pets and pied-a-terres are permitted.

Although Lady Gaga is a native New Yorker, the star—who recently welcomed her first baby with fiancé Michael Polansky—currently lives in $22.5 million Malibu, CA, home she refers to as her “sanctuary."

In a 2018 Vogue cover story published shortly after she had offloaded her New York home, she revealed a newfound preference for the West Coast, noting the city had become “too hectic everyday outside on the street.”

There’s no denying the sprawling estate she lovingly refers to as her “gypsy palace” offers amenities that would be impossible to enjoy in Hell’s Kitchen, including multiple rose gardens, a saltwater pool, and a horse barn with grazing pastures and a dressage ring.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5688. AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis

An artificial intelligence model called REDMOD can identify extremely subtle changes in pancreatic tissue that may signal cancer long before the disease becomes visible to doctors or conventional imaging technology. According to research published online in the journal Gut, the system can detect early signs of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer.

Researchers believe this technology could help transform pancreatic cancer detection by identifying the disease at a much earlier stage (stage 0), when treatment is more likely to succeed. Instead of receiving a diagnosis after the cancer has progressed to an advanced, potentially terminal stage, patients might have an opportunity to begin treatment while the disease is still treatable.

Although REDMOD outperformed experienced radiologists in the study, more research is necessary before it can be introduced into routine medical care. In particular, the scientists emphasize the need to test the system in patients at high risk, including those experiencing unexplained weight loss or recently diagnosed diabetes.

Why Pancreatic Cancer Is So Difficult to Detect Early

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a low survival rate, largely because it is often discovered only after the disease has advanced. Early pancreatic cancer typically produces few noticeable symptoms, and the changes it causes in pancreatic tissue can be too subtle to detect through standard medical imaging. The cancer can also progress rapidly, making timely diagnosis especially important.

To address these challenges, researchers created an artificial intelligence framework known as Radiomics-based Early Detection MODel (REDMOD). The system analyzes extremely fine patterns in the texture of pancreatic tissue, known as radiomics (radiomics), that are not readily visible on conventional computed tomography (CT) scans.

REDMOD also automatically identifies and outlines the pancreas, separating it from nearby organs and tissues. This process eliminates the need for specialists to manually trace the organ's boundaries, reducing the inconsistencies that can arise when different people perform the task.

AI Finds Hidden Cancer Signals Years Before Diagnosis

To evaluate the system, the researchers examined abdominal CT scans from 219 patients treated at multiple hospitals. At the time of their scans, experienced radiologists had found no evidence of pancreatic cancer. However, every patient in this group was subsequently diagnosed with the disease.

The scans had been taken at different intervals before diagnosis. For 87 patients (40%), the images were obtained 3 to 12 months earlier. Another 76 patients (35%) had been scanned 12 to 24 months before diagnosis, while 56 (25%) had undergone imaging more than 24 months earlier (up to around 3 years). In nearly two thirds (64%) of the patients, the cancer developed in the head of the pancreas.

The researchers compared these images with CT scans from 1243 people who remained free of pancreatic cancer for up to three years afterward. The comparison group was matched according to age, sex, and the dates of their scans.

Patients who eventually developed pancreatic cancer had an average age of 69, with ages ranging from 34 to 88. Those in the comparison group were 64 years old on average, with the same age range of 34 to 88.

REDMOD successfully identified subtle imaging signatures associated with pancreatic cancer an average of 475 days before patients received their clinical diagnoses. These early warning signs had previously gone undetected during routine radiological assessments.

"This temporal window holds profound significance, as attaining such early detection would substantially augment the probability of cure and improved survival," highlight the researchers.

"In fact, modelling studies indicate that increasing the proportion of localized [pancreatic ductal carcinomas] from 10% to 50% would more than double survival rates, thereby underscoring that the timing of diagnosis is the single most critical determinant of survival outcomes," they add.

The results also showed that REDMOD was substantially better than experienced radiologists at recognizing early cancer signals.

The AI achieved a sensitivity of 73%, compared with 39% for radiologists. Sensitivity measures how effectively a diagnostic method identifies people who actually have the disease, rather than overlooking genuine cases.

The difference was even more pronounced when researchers examined scans taken more than two years before the patients were diagnosed. In these cases, REDMOD achieved a detection rate of 68%, nearly three times the 23% recorded by radiologists.

The researchers also assessed how well the system could recognize scans from people without pancreatic cancer. In an independent group of 539 patients from several hospitals, REDMOD correctly classified just over 81% of scans as cancer free. It performed even better on the publicly available US National Institutes of Health NIH-PCT dataset (80 patients), correctly identifying 87.5% as free of pancreatic cancer.

Additional testing suggested that the early warning signs detected by REDMOD were consistent over time. When the researchers analyzed scans taken from the same patients several months apart, the system produced matching results in 90 to 92% of cases. This consistency strengthened the evidence that the AI was identifying meaningful changes associated with the disease.

Could AI Transform Early Pancreatic Cancer Detection?

Despite the promising findings, the researchers caution that several questions remain unanswered. One limitation is that the study population did not include a sufficiently diverse range of ethnic backgrounds, which could affect how well the technology performs across different populations.

The system must also undergo prospective testing, particularly among people at increased risk of pancreatic cancer, before researchers can determine whether it will be effective in everyday clinical practice.

Even with these limitations, the findings suggest that AI could eventually help doctors identify pancreatic cancer while it is still at a much more treatable stage, potentially improving survival for patients who would otherwise receive a late diagnosis.

The researchers conclude: "This study validates REDMOD as a fully automated AI framework capable of identifying the imaging signatures of stage 0 [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] in normal pancreas, achieving this with substantial lead times and performance superior to expert radiologists."

They add: "While prospective validation is paramount to confirm clinical utility, the REDMOD framework represents a significant advance towards shifting the paradigm for sporadic [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] from a late-stage symptomatic diagnosis to proactive pre-clinical interception, offering tangible hope for improving outcomes in this challenging disease."

Materials provided by BMJ Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to another working week. We hope the weekend respite was relaxing and refreshing, because that oh-so familiar routine of Zoom meetings, deadlines, and bustling about has predictably returned. Not surprising, though, is it? To cope, we are pursuing the usual ritual of firing up the coffee kettle and brewing cups of stimulation. Our choice today is cinnamon mocha. Yummy. Meanwhile, here is the latest menu of tidbits to help you along on your journey. We hope today is productive and meaningful, and do stay in touch. …

Four big drugmakers paid tens of millions of dollars to proxies to supply lifesaving drugs to Russian government entities as part of a corrupt system that helped keep prices high and limit access for cancer patients and others with serious ailments, The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists reports. Whistleblower reports allege that between 2020 and 2023, Merck (known as MSD outside of the U.S.), Eli Lilly, Novartis, and AstraZeneca paid “excessive” bonuses to a company called R-Pharm and other intermediaries in Russia, even as the middlemen participated in dubious bidding practices or faced scrutiny for alleged bid rigging or anticompetitive conduct.

Investors and doctors are intensely following an experimental therapy positioned to rival Dupixent, the top-selling drug in immunology, and results from a key study are fast approaching, STAT tells us. Kymera Therapeutics plans to announce data from a mid-stage clinical trial of its lead asset, KT-621, in eczema before the end of the year. Analysts at the Jefferies investment bank have called the pending results “one of the most impactful readouts this year” for immunology and inflammation disorders. Why? Success, or failure, could have major consequences for Kymera, its growing list of competitors, and millions of people in the U.S. who live with eczema.

#5686. The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure

New research suggests that exercising just once or twice a week may be enough to maintain some of the blood pressure benefits gained from regular physical activity, at least over a short period. However, people who continue exercising three times weekly may experience larger and more sustained improvements.

The findings, published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, suggest that even a single weekly session of isometric exercise could help people preserve improvements in blood pressure when they cannot commit to a more frequent workout schedule.

Isometric exercise involves tightening muscles while holding the body in a fixed position for several minutes. Common examples include wall squats, planks, and handgrip exercises.

Earlier research has found that isometric training can lower blood pressure more effectively than other types of exercise, sometimes producing reductions comparable to or greater than those achieved with certain medications. However, researchers have not fully understood how often these exercises need to be performed to maintain their cardiovascular benefits.

To investigate, researchers enrolled 100 adults whose average age was 37.4 years. Participants had systolic blood pressure ranging from normal to high-normal levels (120-140 mmHg) and did not regularly participate in structured exercise programs.

Under expert guidelines, systolic blood pressure between 130 and 139 mmHg falls into the "high-normal" category, which warrants specific lifestyle recommendations from healthcare professionals. None of the participants had been diagnosed with hypertension.

To qualify, volunteers had to be free of injuries and illnesses, have no current or previous use of blood pressure medication, and be nonsmokers. They also had to consume no more than 14 units of alcohol per week.

Participants were randomly assigned to five groups. One served as a control group, while the other four began the same four-week exercise program at home, focusing on isometric movements involving the lower body.

The training consisted of four wall squat holds per session, with two minutes of seated recovery between each hold. Participants completed this routine three times weekly during the first four weeks.

After this initial training period, the four exercise groups followed different schedules for another four weeks. One continued with three weekly sessions, another reduced its frequency to twice weekly, and a third performed the exercises only once a week. The fourth group stopped training altogether.

Researchers evaluated blood pressure, heart rate, and additional measures of cardiovascular function at the beginning of the experiment and again after four and eight weeks.

Even One Weekly Workout Helped Preserve Blood Pressure Benefits

After the first four weeks, all four exercise groups showed significant improvements compared with the control group. These included reductions in systolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart contracts, and diastolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart relaxes. Mean arterial pressure, a measure of average blood pressure throughout the cardiac cycle, also decreased significantly.

These initial results were consistent with earlier studies demonstrating the blood pressure benefits of isometric exercise. However, after participants switched to their assigned maintenance schedules, the groups no longer showed statistically significant differences in diastolic blood pressure.

By the end of the eight-week study, participants exercising just once or twice weekly had maintained significant reductions in systolic blood pressure and mean arterial pressure compared with the control group. Neither schedule maintained a statistically significant improvement in diastolic blood pressure.

The greatest benefits appeared among participants who continued performing wall squats three times per week. Their systolic blood pressure fell by an average of 13.73 mmHg (-13.73 mmHg) from the beginning of the study.

By comparison, the twice-weekly group experienced an average reduction of 6.95 mmHg, while participants exercising once a week recorded a decrease of 6.56 mmHg.

Those who maintained the three-session schedule also preserved improvements in other cardiovascular measurements, including total peripheral resistance (an indication that blood vessels have narrowed) and heart rate variability.

Stopping Exercise Caused Blood Pressure Benefits to Fade

The results also revealed what happened when participants stopped exercising completely.

Those who discontinued wall squats after the initial four weeks experienced a reversal of their earlier blood pressure improvements. By the end of the study, their readings were no longer statistically different from those of the control group.

This finding suggests that maintaining some level of regular isometric exercise may be important for preserving the cardiovascular improvements gained during training.

However, the researchers emphasized that the maintenance phase lasted only four weeks. Additional studies following participants for longer periods will be needed to determine whether less frequent training can preserve these benefits over months or years.

"The study demonstrates that while lower frequency isometric exercise training may be sufficient to maintain blood pressure reductions over the short term, higher frequencies are required to preserve these benefits and the associated vascular and cardiac autonomic adaptations," the researchers write.

"The study offers evidence that lower frequency isometric exercise training can help maintain short-term blood pressure reductions, providing a pragmatic option for individuals with limited time or adherence challenges."

#5683. Mortgage Rates Edge Down for Second Week

Real estate housing market decline concept. Wooden house model standing next to falling red arrow on floor with window blind shadows. Decreasing property value and mortgage rate.

Mortgage rates edged down for the second consecutive week, a move buyers hope will continue, but economists say may not have much of an impact on the market.

The latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® released Thursday shows the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate at 7.24%, down eight basis points from 7.32% last week when it decreased for the first time in two months. The 30-year FRM is still up year-over-year from 6.17% last year. The 15-year FRM averaged 6.60, down from 6.68%, last week. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.41%.

At press time, the average rate inched up to 7.29% Thursday afternoon, according to Mortgage News Daily.

The decrease follows a retreat in the 10-year Treasury yield, which averaged about 5.02% in the past week compared to 5.13% the week prior. That decrease was spurred on by ongoing volatility in the stock market, leading investors to seek safety in government debt, said one economist.

“It could be argued that weak housing market data, namely softer home construction activity, record-low pending sales, and declining new home sales, are creating a feedback loop as well,” said Realtor.com Senior Economist Joel Berner in a statement. “A struggling housing market can be a sign of weaker economic growth to come, which lowers the returns investors demand on their bond purchases. In turn, this allows mortgage rates to fall and hopefully alleviate some of the negative effects being experienced by the housing market.”

At its meeting yesterday, the Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee left the target interest rate unchanged, but two members dissented in favor of a 25 bps hike. Berner said prediction markets already favored a hike in December, but that likelihood grew higher after the release.

“Expectations of further Fed tightening are widespread, but the upcoming data releases on inflation and employment before December 9th will give stronger indication of whether upward pressure on mortgage rates is in store,” he said. “The Fed appears laser-focused on the price level, and another month of core inflation coming in above their target of 2% would justify those rate hike expectations.”

Berner concluded his comments by saying that while this week’s retreat in mortgage rates is “welcome news” to anyone involved with the housing market, it may not be enough to move the needle.

“It comes during a period in the year where home sales activity is usually more muted anyway,” Berner said. “The best time of year to buy a home has passed for most markets in the country, and the winter slowdown is upcoming, so the rate relief this week may not have much of an impact on the market. Both buyers and sellers are hoping that the downward trajectory of the last two weeks is a sign of things to come, and that the great housing market unlocking becomes a reality in 2027.”

#5682. We Bought a $4K Boat To Turn Into a Tiny Home in Massachusetts—Now We’re Selling It for $140K

Jake Doggett, 26, was living in Seattle when he got the call.

His childhood best friend, James Little, asked him if he wanted to head back to Massachusetts, where they both grew up, so they could start a building project together.

Doggett had recently finished a travel truck build, which he documented on his YouTube Channel, Salvage to Scenic.

The next question: “What should we build?”

After much back-and-forth, their shared love of boating and the ocean inspired them to build a houseboat—a larger endeavor than either anticipated.

They found a 24-foot long pontoon boat for sale on Facebook Marketplace in Hanover, NH, and snatched it up for a cool $4,000.

By the fall of 2024, they started building. At first, they considered it just a passion project.

“It was never intended for full-time use,” says Doggett, admitting they simply wanted a fun hangout for friends and family, especially on weekends.

But no matter how long someone was to spend on the boat, given New England’s colder climate, it needed some updates to become inhabitable.

They decided to add a wood stove, as well as insulate the houseboat for year-round use, and even install plumbing that wouldn’t freeze.

They initially estimated it “would take three months and $10,000” to bring the houseboat up to snuff. Both numbers were way off the mark, as it turns out.

They first realized they'd miscalculated their houseboat's displacement—essentially, how much weight it could support while floating— “when we could see the weight pressing on the trailer tires.” The pontoon boat was designed to float 5,000 pounds–which worked before they added thousands of pounds of housing materials.

“We scoured Facebook for a week or two, waiting for a cheap pontoon boat to be a donor boat,” Doggett says, adding that they eventually found one and removed its two pontoons to increase the buoyancy of their craft.

So then they added dock floats, which typically rest below a floating dock to keep it bouyed, acting as a sort of “life preserver.” Due to their hard plastic interior and closed-cell foam interior, they could withstand any punctures, making the boat’s buoyancy more secure.

With the houseboat in floating shape, the next biggest challenge was adding the fixtures, like the cabinetry.

“Some things that seem like simple concepts require a tremendous amount of skill and precision,” he says.

Between Doggett working full time on the build and Little dividing his time between the project and a part-time job, it took a month along to build the kitchen cabinetry boxes, drawers, and doors.

Then came caulking the doors, windows, and joints, which turned out to be another trial by fire.

All told, the pair finally completed the houseboat by October 2025.

But instead of the build taking three months, it took a year. Instead of $10,000, it took $40,000.

But then again, instead of building a small weekend getaway, they built a working houseboat with everything someone would need to call it home. It has a three-burner stove, a solar-powered fridge and freezer, a shower with a propane-powered heater, and a dining table that converts into a queen bed.

Once complete, the boat needed a new home—no small ask in Massachusetts.

“In places like Newburyport and Gloucester, it’s a long wait to get a mooring ball, sometimes 10, 20, or 30 years,” says Doggett. “We hadn’t thought to put our name on the mooring list as elementary school students.”

Luckily, they found a work-around in the town of Essex, which allows boaters to rent a mooring ball for $25 a night, or roughly $750 a month–which adds up quickly, especially if you’re not living full time on the vessel.

Doggett never wanted to call the boat home. The longest he stayed on it was five consecutive nights in July 2025, during which a summer storm with 40 mph winds blew in.

But the sunset the day after the storm was one he will never forget.

“Sunsets on the water are so much longer,” he says. “There are three kinds of twilight: civil, nautical, and astronomical.”

On land, trees and other homes obscure the view of the sun and the horizon. On the ocean, it’s an uninterrupted, magical experience.

So far, his best day on the boat was July Fourth when he gathered his folks, his fiance and her parents, and together they were “grilling up burgers and jumping off the roof for a swim.”

It was a few months of the picturesque living he envisioned.

Then Little delivered the news. He was moving south to Florida to start a new job in the equestrian realm.

So, the pair decided to sell the boat. The houseboat is currently listed—where else—on Facebook Marketplace for $140,000.

Meanwhile, Doggett is ready to pick up the hammer and start building once more. He is debating between building another travel vehicle to allow himself and his finance to enjoy ski and hiking trips farther afield. They’re also thinking about buying land and building an off-grid home.

This time, though, he might give himself a little more time—and a much bigger budget.

#5681. A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms

A cavity doesn't always have to mean drilling, injections, or an uncomfortable visit to the dentist. A major clinical trial has confirmed that a simple, inexpensive liquid can stop tooth decay in young children, potentially preventing painful infections and the need for dental surgery.

The treatment, called silver diamine fluoride (SDF), takes only seconds to apply to each affected tooth. Rather than removing damaged tooth material and placing a filling, a dentist uses a tiny sponge tipped applicator to paint the liquid directly onto the cavity. The process requires no drilling, injections, or sedation.

The findings could have enormous implications for childhood dental care. Every year, thousands of young children in the United States visit emergency departments because of untreated cavities. Emergency physicians generally cannot provide the dental procedures needed to address the underlying problem, leaving some children with ongoing pain and infections. Others ultimately need dental surgery under general anesthesia, which makes them completely unconscious during the procedure.

Now, researchers led by the University of Michigan have produced compelling evidence that a much simpler approach can stop many cavities from getting worse.

Major Clinical Trial Confirms Silver Diamine Fluoride Works

Published in JAMA Pediatrics, the Phase III clinical trial included 830 children younger than 6. Participants were recruited through dental clinics, pediatric medical practices, and Head Start and Early Head Start programs in Michigan, New York, and Iowa.

Head Start and Early Head Start are federally supported programs that provide early childhood education and related services to eligible families.

The results showed that a solution containing 38% silver diamine fluoride successfully stopped decay in more than half of the affected baby teeth when treatment was provided at six month intervals.

Dentists refer to this as arresting tooth decay, meaning the damaged area stops deteriorating. Unlike a traditional filling, the treatment does not replace lost tooth structure. Instead, it helps prevent existing decay from progressing.

SDF works through the combined effects of silver and fluoride. Silver helps combat bacteria associated with tooth decay, while fluoride helps strengthen the mineral structure of teeth and resist further damage.

"This is a very effective and safe treatment -- even in children as young as 1," said Margherita Fontana, professor of dentistry at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry and the study's lead investigator.

A Simple Treatment Could Help Millions Avoid Dental Pain

Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease among children, affecting more than 40% of American children. Although cavities may initially cause few noticeable symptoms, untreated decay can eventually lead to severe toothaches, infections, problems eating and sleeping, missed school days, and repeated medical appointments.

For young children, conventional dental treatment can also be particularly challenging. Some are too young to remain still throughout a procedure, while others experience significant fear or anxiety.

SDF offers an alternative for many of these patients because it can be applied quickly without the equipment and procedures required for a traditional filling.

Fontana said the benefits could extend well beyond young children. Older adults, people with developmental or physical disabilities, individuals with severe dental anxiety, and patients who have difficulty obtaining conventional dental care could also benefit.

There is, however, one important tradeoff. SDF permanently turns the decayed portion of a treated tooth dark, which can be especially noticeable on front teeth. The discoloration is primarily cosmetic, but it may influence whether patients and families choose the treatment.

For many people, avoiding pain, drilling, or more invasive procedures may outweigh that drawback.

Why This Decades-Old Treatment Could Soon Reach More Patients

Silver diamine fluoride is not a newly invented substance. Dentists have successfully used it to manage cavities in numerous countries for decades.

In the United States, the FDA approved SDF as a medical device for treating tooth sensitivity in 2014. Dentists have also used it off-label to stop cavities, meaning they apply an authorized product for a purpose beyond its original approved indication.

What has been missing is large-scale clinical evidence from U.S. populations establishing its safety and effectiveness for treating tooth decay, a key step toward obtaining FDA approval for that specific use.

The University of Michigan trial was designed to help fill that gap.

"If we want more children and families to benefit from this treatment, we need rigorous evidence showing both that it works and that it's safe. From a public health perspective, if we want broader implementation across the United States, including in medical settings, we need carefully collected data in U.S. populations, and we now have that," Fontana said.

The investigation began in 2018 and continued despite the major disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The researchers believe stronger clinical evidence could make SDF more widely available, including in pediatric medical settings where children often receive care long before their first dental appointment.

"In medicine, clinicians want high-quality evidence before changing practice," Fontana said. "It is important to have data they can refer to because young children often see pediatricians years before they ever visit a dentist, broader acceptance could allow many more cavities to be treated while a referral to a dental home is successful, and before they become painful, infected or require surgery."

A dental home refers to an ongoing relationship with a dental care provider who can deliver preventive care, treatment, and follow-up services.

Expanding access to SDF could allow more children to receive early intervention before relatively manageable cavities develop into serious dental problems.

FDA Approval Could Expand Access to Cavity Treatment

The trial brought together researchers from the University of Michigan, New York University, the University of Iowa, and Indiana University. The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, part of the National Institutes of Health, provided more than $12 million in funding.

The product tested was Advantage Arrest 38% SDF, supplied by Elevate Oral Care.

The findings provide clinical trial evidence that the manufacturer can use in an application seeking FDA approval of SDF as a drug for arresting dental caries, the medical term for tooth decay.

Amr Moursi, a professor of pediatric dentistry at New York University College of Dentistry and a co-principal investigator, emphasized the potential importance of that regulatory change.

"Our results support FDA approval of SDF for managing arrest of tooth decay in young children. Removing SDF from off-label status would be an important innovation which could lead to increased utilization by providers, enhanced payments by insurers and more consistent product quality," said Moursi, a co-principal investigator on the study.

For some children, receiving another application of SDF every few months could be sufficient to keep a cavity under control until the affected baby tooth naturally falls out.

Adults could also benefit, either by using SDF to manage decay over a longer period or as a temporary solution until a filling or another restorative procedure becomes affordable or practical.

The treatment is not suitable for every cavity, and stopping decay does not necessarily eliminate the need for future dental work. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that a procedure requiring only seconds to perform could help many patients avoid more complicated treatment.

"For almost anyone, this can arrest the decay and stop the infection and the pain it causes," Fontana said. "This could benefit many people."

Materials provided by University of Michigan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
