#5680. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5679. The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut

Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between the bacteria living in the human gut and the speed at which the body ages. Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa found that certain gut microbes are associated with slower biological aging, while others are linked to faster aging.

The study, published in Scientific Reports, found that differences in gut bacterial communities accounted for approximately 15% of the variation in participants' biological aging rates. The results suggest that the gut microbiome, the vast community of microorganisms living in the digestive system, may provide valuable clues about aging at the molecular level.

"This study advances our understanding of the relationship between the gut microbiome and biological aging," said senior author Alika K. Maunakea of the UH Mānoa John A. Burns School of Medicine. "We found that microbial patterns in the gut were significantly associated with molecular measures of aging, even independent of chronological age. These findings open important new directions for understanding how modifiable biological systems influence long-term health trajectories and longevity."

Scientists Identify Gut Bacteria Linked to Faster and Slower Aging

To investigate the relationship between gut bacteria and aging, researchers examined stool and blood samples collected from 123 adults across a wide range of ages. They identified the bacteria present in each participant's gut and compared those findings with blood-based molecular markers used to estimate the body's rate of aging.

These biological measurements differ from chronological age, which simply reflects how many years someone has been alive. Instead, they are designed to assess how quickly aging-related changes are occurring within the body.

The researchers found a notable association between the composition of the gut microbiome and DunedinPACE, an advanced biomarker that measures the pace of biological aging.

Some bacterial species stood out for their particularly strong relationships with aging. Bifidobacterium adolescentis was among the microbes most strongly associated with slower biological aging. In contrast, Succinivibrio dextrinosolvens showed one of the strongest associations with faster aging.

These differences suggest that particular patterns of gut bacteria may offer important information about how rapidly the body is aging.

How Diet, Lifestyle, and Environment May Influence Gut Health

Lead author Braden P. Kunihiro said the discovery adds to growing evidence that the gut microbiome could play an important role in precision health research, which aims to better understand individual differences in health and disease.

Unlike chronological age, the composition of the gut microbiome can change in response to everyday influences, including diet, lifestyle, and environmental conditions. This makes it a particularly interesting area of investigation for scientists studying healthy aging.

"The gut microbiome is highly responsive to lifestyle, diet, environment and other everyday exposures," Kunihiro said. "Our findings suggest that the microbiome may reflect important aspects of biological resilience and aging in ways that could eventually help inform future wellness and healthy aging strategies."

The research also included Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander participants, groups that have historically received limited representation in studies of aging and gut microorganisms.

Co-author Ruben Juarez explained that including these populations could help scientists investigate how social circumstances and environmental conditions leave lasting biological effects over the course of a person's life.

"The microbiome exists at the intersection of behavior, environment and human biology," Juarez said. "Studies like this help illuminate potential pathways through which lived experiences and social factors influence long-term health outcomes."

Could Changing Gut Bacteria Influence How We Age?

Although the findings reveal a meaningful relationship between gut bacteria and biological aging, researchers stress that the study does not establish cause and effect. In other words, finding certain microbes in people who age more slowly does not necessarily mean those bacteria are responsible for slowing the aging process.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether deliberately changing the gut microbiome can influence biological aging or improve long-term health.

Still, the findings offer a promising starting point for exploring how the microorganisms living inside us relate to the aging process and whether they could eventually help guide more personalized approaches to healthy aging.

"This is an important early step toward understanding the gut microbiome's relationship with healthy aging," Maunakea said. "Future research will help clarify the mechanisms involved and whether these microbial signatures may eventually contribute to precision approaches for promoting long-term health and wellness."

#5678. Real Estate Influencer ‘Flipping NJ’ Pleads Guilty to Multi-Million-Dollar Investment Fraud Scheme

A popular real estate influencer has pleaded guilty to defrauding investors of millions of dollars of their hard-earned cash in a ‘ponzi-like’ scheme that also involved money laundering for drug traffickers and the bribing of a New Jersey politician.

Cesar Humberto Pina, 48, also known as “Flipping NJ,” of Franklin Lakes, New Jersey, pleaded guilty on Oct. 22 to wire fraud, money laundering conspiracy, bribery of an agent of a program receiving federal funds, and travel act bribery, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Jersey.

The scheme dates back to at least 2017 when Pina began accepting investments from individuals, promising to use their money to purchase, renovate and sell specific properties in New Jersey and other states, federal prosecutors said.

He developed a large following after hosting several real estate investment seminars throughout the country, often appearing alongside a celebrity disc jockey and radio personality. Although that DJ is not named in court filings, Pina was a close associate of The Breakfast Club co-host DJ Envy, who denies knowledge of Pina's crimes and has not been charged with any wrongdoing.

To attract investors, Pina often promised returns of 30% or higher within just four to five months, according to court documents. But prosecutors say the investment opportunities were not what they appeared to be.

Rather than using the money for the promised real estate projects, Pina misappropriated investor funds, using money from new investors to repay earlier ones in a Ponzi-like scheme.

Pina spent the funds of his investors on luxury clothing, travel, cars, and even beauty products for himself and others, federal prosecutors said.

In total, Pina fraudulently obtained and then misappropriated millions of dollars through his scheme.

“Cesar Pina admitted to misappropriating millions of dollars meant for real estate investments, laundering cash for narcotics traffickers, and bribing a politician in furtherance of real estate projects,” U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer said.

“It is hard to imagine a more varied spate of criminal activity, which robbed investors of their life savings, helped facilitate drug trafficking, and undermined confidence in our elected officials.”

Pina conspired to launder proceeds from the sale of controlled substances on behalf of individuals he knew were involved in narcotics trafficking and other criminal activity.

He also bribed a Paterson official to advance his real estate development projects, including “Old School 5,” which had applications pending before the city's Zoning Board of Adjustment.

According to prosecutors, Pina gave the official cash and other bribes in exchange for official action, assistance and influence, including help securing approval for the project's applications.

“Pina lured in victims and exploited their trust by using his online influencer persona,”  FBI Newark Special Agent in Charge Stefanie Roddy said. “Not only did he steal millions of dollars from investors, but he also laundered money for drug traffickers and bribed a politician along the way.”

The wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy charges each carry a maximum of 20 years in prison. The federal bribery charge carries a maximum of 10 years, and the travel act bribery charge carries a maximum of five years.

Each charge also carries with it the potential for significant financial penalties, which could vary from offense to offense and could even exceed the amount of money Pina made from his illegal activities.

Pina is scheduled to be sentenced on March 10, 2027.

#5677. Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver

Low testosterone can contribute to several health problems, and an unhealthy diet may make some of those risks even worse. One major concern is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a condition that affects approximately 40% of adult men worldwide and has become a significant global health issue.

Fatty liver, the earliest stage of MASLD, occurs when excess fat builds up in the liver. Several factors are associated with the condition, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, low testosterone levels, and excessive fructose consumption from sugary drinks and processed foods. However, scientists have not fully understood how these factors interact or whether their combined effects are more harmful than each one individually.

How Low Testosterone and Fructose Affect the Liver

To investigate this connection, a research team from the Graduate School of Agriculture, led by graduate student Hiroki Takahashi and Associate Professor Naoki Harada, examined how reduced testosterone and high fructose intake influence liver health.

The researchers used eight-week-old male mice and divided them into six experimental groups. Some underwent castration to lower testosterone levels, while others received a sham operation. The groups included Sham/Control, Sham/Fructose, Sham/Fructose + Antibiotics, Castration/Control, Castration/Fructose, and Castration/Fructose + Antibiotics.

To determine how these conditions affected the animals, the team analyzed liver cells and tissues, blood plasma, organic acids from the cecum, and samples of gut bacteria.

The results revealed that mice with reduced testosterone levels developed heavier livers when they consumed fructose. However, this increase in liver weight was smaller in mice that also received antibiotics.

When examined separately, low testosterone and fructose intake produced only modest changes in liver triglyceride levels. When combined, however, the two factors had a much stronger effect, significantly increasing fat accumulation and worsening fatty liver.

The researchers also identified changes in the composition of gut bacteria, altered liver gene activity, and elevated levels of pyruvate in the cecum among mice exposed to both reduced testosterone and fructose.

These findings suggested that the gut microbiome could play an important role in explaining why the combination was particularly harmful.

Further experiments helped the researchers identify a possible biological explanation for the increased liver fat.

"Upon examining this mechanism, we found that changes in the gut microbiota led to increased levels of pyruvate within the intestine. Furthermore, experiments using mouse-derived primary hepatocytes revealed that pyruvate acts synergistically with fructose to promote neutral lipid accumulation in hepatocytes," explained Takahashi.

In other words, changes in gut bacteria appeared to increase intestinal pyruvate, a compound involved in energy metabolism. Laboratory experiments with liver cells isolated from mice showed that pyruvate and fructose worked together to increase fat storage in those cells.

The discovery suggests that interactions among testosterone levels, dietary fructose, and gut bacteria may help explain how fatty liver develops and worsens.

Potential New Ways to Prevent Fatty Liver Disease

Understanding this relationship could eventually help researchers identify new approaches to preventing or treating fatty liver disease. In particular, targeting the processes through which pyruvate contributes to fat accumulation may offer promising possibilities.

"Going forward, we hope to clarify the mechanism by which pyruvate promotes triglyceride accumulation to pioneer the development of therapeutic drugs and establishment of preventive methods through dietary interventions," added Professor Harada.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and isolated mouse liver cells, they provide new insight into how hormonal changes and diet may interact to influence liver health.

The study was published in American Journal of Physiology-Endocrinology and Metabolism.

#5675. Classic Horror-Movie Towns Where Homes Aren’t Frightfully Expensive

On the silver screen, these rural hamlets and quiet woodlands served as the unsettling backdrops for cursed witches, possessed children, and machete-wielding psychos.

In real life, however, horror cinema’s most notorious filming locations tell a far more welcoming story—one anchored by tight-knit communities, preserved landscapes, and surprisingly accessible home prices.

Just in time for Halloween, this is what it actually costs to plant roots in the real-world towns behind classics such as "The Blair Witch Project," "Friday the 13th," and "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre."

In these towns made famous by classic horror movies, the local scenery is breathtaking, the neighbors are friendly, and the housing markets are anything but a nightmare.

Median home price: $539,974 (Frederick County)

Picture this, three students hike into the mountains behind Burkittsville, MD, to shoot a documentary about a local myth called the Blair Witch, and they're never seen again except in the terrifying footage they leave behind. That was the premise of the 1999 sleeper hit "The Blair Witch Project," which put tiny Burkittsville on the radar of horror fans everywhere.

For full-time residents of the area, however, Burkittsville is simply a quiet farming town with a strong community and colorful history.

Established in 1824, it's listed on the National Register of Historic Places for its ties to a major battle during the Civil War. And now, it's known for being the location of one of the highest-grossing independent films of all time ($248.6 million).

"The residents find it curious and are somewhat entertained by the 'Blair Witch' notoriety. But if you grew up in Burkittsville or lived there for generations, you do not view the town as the movie presents it," says Gary Gestson, a Certified Historic Maryland Properties Specialist (CHMP) and agent with Long & Foster Real Estate Inc.

"Few properties change hands in Burkittsville," says Gestson, who currently has one of only three active listings in Burkittsville, which aptly went live just days before Halloween. "It has history and charm, and families living here tend to stay."

Median home price: $220,000 (Monona County)

If you've ever done a Maize Maze, you know there is nothing scarier than a deserted cornfield after dark. Unless that cornfield is also filled with possessed children trying to murder you.

The 1984 movie adaptation of Stephen King's terrifying "Children of the Corn," starring a pre-"Terminator" Linda Hamilton, was shot mostly in and around Northwestern Iowa—including Sioux City, Hornick, Sergeant Bluff, and Whiting, IA.

"They wanted to film it in a small town that they could literally shut down, and they found Whiting," Leslie Beneda tells Realtor.com®. Beneda was a child extra in the movie when she was in sixth grade and attending the elementary school there.

"Every morning, we would go to school dressed as 'Children of the Corn,' and each grade would line up outside the school, and they would pick who they wanted and bus us to wherever they were filming that day."

Pretty much anyone living there who was interested in being in the movie got their shot, and they even invited the whole town of Whiting to a big pre-release screening at the Orpheum Theater in Sioux City.

"You grow up in a small town in Iowa and not a whole lot exciting happens, and it was a really cool experience," says Beneda.

Today, the town embraces its horror film past, but Beneda says most days it's just a cute small town in Iowa. And homes in these areas are still spacious and affordable—but yes, probably located near a corn field.

Lest the children be the only ones scaring moviegoers, horror author King made sure to include some creepy cats in his book "Pet Semetary."

Filmed in Bangor, ME, which was coincidentally the author's primary residence for almost 40 years, the movie serves up a heap of horror, and thanks to King, the town attracts a lot of fans.

"Living in Bangor means living alongside a piece of pop-culture history, and locals truly embrace our spooky claim to fame," says Peter McPhail, broker and owner of United Country Lifestyle Properties of Maine. "Between taking photos by Stephen King’s wrought-iron spider gates, walking the historic Mount Hope Cemetery where 'Pet Semetary' was filmed, and touring our stunning Victorian and Greek Revival homes, the horror connection adds a fun, legendary charm to an otherwise warm, tight-knit Maine community."

Homes in the area are also on the more affordable side in this current climate, and many sport gorgeous Victorian details. If you can handle the fear factor (and winter), it's a market with lots of opportunity.

In 1974, the slasher film "Texas Chainsaw Massacre" hit theaters and changed the landscape of the horror genre. This classic helped birth several scary movie tropes, including the masked villain and assorted tools as murder weapons.

It also introduced people to Central Texas as a movie location, with many of its key scenes filmed in and around Austin, including a cemetery in Leander, a farmhouse now in Kingsland, and a gas station in Bastrop.

It turns out that Bastrop is also a potentially nice place to live in real life (fictitious cannibals aside).

Located about 30 miles east of Austin, this charming historic town is home to the Lost Pines Forest, which sounds scary, but is actually filled with unique loblolly pine trees that are thought to have originated during the Ice Age.

Birding and outdoor activities are as popular as antiquing. And homes are still available under $400,000, making this a horror town with historic charm and a rich cinematic terrain.

If you like your horror flicks with a side of camp, then you’ve probably seen "Friday the 13th." The original 1980 movie that introduced viewers to Jason, that infamous hockey-masked butcher, was filmed mostly at Camp NoBeBoSco in Hardwick Township, NJ, a still-active Boy Scouts camp founded in 1927.

Though it was called Camp Crystal Lake in the film and tours are available only when real-life camp isn't in session, the natural beauty of the surrounding Kittatinny Mountains (minus the machete-wielding menace) is another big draw for people to the area today. In fact, 75% of Hardwick falls within some form of land preservation, including 95 acres of a butterfly habitat and limestone forest within the Hardwick Limestone Greenway.

As such, pop-culture pride aside, residents of the area are treated to a rustic and relaxing rural environment on a day-to-day basis, while still being close enough to New York City when they need a culture fix (it's about 65 miles away). Though there is good available inventory at the moment and housing prices are in the more accessible category, with all it's got going for it, one thing you probably won't see slashed in Hardwick Township, NJ, is future home values.

Kimberly Dawn Neumann is a journalist based in New York City and the author of hundreds of articles on home-related topics for major publications, including Forbes, Real Simple, and Realtor.com. For more information, visit www.KDNeumann.com or IG @dancerscribe.

Actress Brooklyn Decker and retired tennis star Andy Roddick are sharing the vibrant interiors of their Charlotte, NC home with the world—after the extensive home renovation project was “nine years in the making.”

The 7,000-square-foot home was built in 1964, and was in rough shape when the couple—who married in 2009—came across it.

However, Roddick, 44, convinced her to take a chance on the property, which had previously only been owned by one family and needed considerable work.

“Our home was brought back to life by countless talented artisans and craftspeople in North Carolina," Decker tells Realtor.com®. "It's a home rooted in history, but brought alive by family and community. It really feels like a love letter to our state."

Decker’s affinity for interior design has taken a more serious turn in the past few years. Though she previously considered herself a “design hobbyist,” the former Sports Illustrated cover model would eventually find herself consulting on design projects for friends before developing a professional team of her own.

“A friend called in the middle of Covid, back when we wondered if TV production would ever resume, and asked if I could put my design eyes on a new golf concept he was starting,” Decker shared in a June 2026 Instagram caption.

Decker would go on to design seven Intown Golf Club properties with her friend, picking up a creative process she is “so proud of” and a lot of knowledge about “fire codes, ADA, and commercial grade everything” along the way.

The home is filled with whimsical details that reward those who take the time to notice them, such as a mahogany fireplace with wooden mice scurrying across the mantle—a detail Decker confirmed in an Instagram comment was inspired by British furniture designer Robert Thompson.

Carefully-curated vintage finds have been given the perfect home, with Etsy-sourced rugs, bold chandeliers, and a nearly century-old coffee table among some of the most interesting.

#5672. Want a More Affordable Home? Don’t Overlook Condos.

When you picture buying your first home, chances are you’re imagining a traditional single-family house with its own yard, maybe a garage, and little extra room to grow. But with affordability still tight, getting everything on that list right away may come with a higher price tag than you’re comfortable with right now.

So, if you’re running the numbers and buying a house like that feels like a stretch, there may be another way in. A condo.

Because in a lot of markets, condos come with a significantly lower price tag. And that could make them a smart way to get your foot in the door.

“Condos are the most commonly affordable home type in virtually every metro. At the starter level, the savings can be pretty significant. Nationally, starter condos average $197,468 — that’s about 6% less than the typical starter home.”

And depending on where you live, the difference can be much bigger.

Zillow identified metro areas where typical starter condos are priced significantly below the estimated home price a median-income household could afford. Here are the top 10 according to that research (see chart below).

In Houston, the gap is at its widest. There, a typical starter condo was valued at about $85,600 – 72% below the price considered affordable based on the area’s median household income.

Of course, every market is different. But the bigger point is this: if you’ve only been searching for traditional single-family houses, you may be overlooking some of the more affordable options on the market.

And even if your city didn’t make this list, that’s okay. The trend holds true in many places across the country. Here’s why.

Part of the reason condos can cost less is pretty straightforward. They’re typically smaller. And less square footage can mean a lower purchase price.

So, if you can make do with a bit less space or you’re coming from a smaller apartment now, this can be a great way in. Plus, on the upside, you won’t have to buy a ton of furniture to fill out a bigger house. You can get a potentially lower price up front and spend less once you move in because you’ll need less new stuff to fill that empty space.

And more buyers are making that trade off on space to offset the current affordability challenges. Ali Wolf, Chief Economist for New Home Source, explains:

“In addition to favoring smaller floor plans, more consumers are showing a willingness to live in an attached home. This shift is not driven by a preference for shared walls, but by a pursuit of value.”

That’s really the heart of it. Looking at condos isn’t necessarily about wanting less. It’s about finding another way to make your move happen with the budget you have.

If you’ve been struggling to find a house you like at a price you can comfortably afford, talk to your agent about adding condos to your search.

You may find something in a neighborhood you thought was outside your budget. You could get access to amenities you wouldn’t otherwise have. And you may be able to become a homeowner sooner rather than waiting for the numbers on a single-family house to work.

While there are trade-offs like shared walls, less outdoor space, and an HOA fee to factor into your monthly budget, maybe that’s worth it if you finally get your own set of keys.

Plus, a lot of the times, a condo community comes with great amenities like pools, gyms, and the condo association handles at least some of the maintenance. Which is closer to what you’re used to from your apartment – it could make the transition to homeowner not just more affordable, but that much easier too.

The first home you buy doesn't have to be a single-family house. If affordability has been holding you back, talk to a local agent about expanding your search and see whether a condo could fit the price point you're looking for.

#5671. EXCLUSIVE: Influencer Rachel Martino Reveals How To Bring Color Into Your Home—Even if You’re Renting

Influencer and interior design expert Rachel Martino has lifted the lid on her ultimate home tips for adding color to your home—even in the most unassuming places.

In her New York City rental, the home guru has found a way to give a hallway washer and dryer their own colorful moment—and conceal the appliances when they're not in use.

Speaking with Realtor.com® about her partnership with Tide, which reveals that Tide Orange is officially a Pantone-recognized color, Martino shared how she approaches decorating a rental, why wallpaper has become one of her favorite tools, and how spending more time at home changed her relationship with her surroundings.

The colorful interiors she embraces today weren't always part of her decorating style. Although Martino had long experimented with bold fashion, her earlier living spaces were considerably more restrained.

That began to change during the COVID-19 pandemic, when being at home prompted her to reconsider whether her interiors actually reflected her personality.

“I realized I really want a space that actually reflects who I am and my personality,” she said. “And my personality is very bold and bright and colorful.”

Instead of continuing to gravitate toward neutral rooms, she started experimenting with the colors and patterns she already loved wearing.

Today, that approach extends to some of the most practical corners of her home, including the hallway where her stacked washer and dryer are located.

Without a separate laundry room to decorate, she used wallpaper and a custom sliding mirror to make the area feel intentional.

The mirror moves aside to provide access to the appliances and slides back into place to conceal them.

The setup allows her to incorporate a necessary household function into her home while still giving the surrounding space a decorative identity.

Martino's enthusiasm for wallpaper also carries into her closet, which she described as her favorite room in the home.

“It has a bright pink wallpaper that has large-scale florals,” she said. “And then I have a library ladder that goes in like a U shape around the room.”

Her living room offers another example of using a practical feature to introduce color: painted shelving.

For Martino, shelves can bring personality and visual interest into a room while also providing storage. And their color can change again if a homeowner or renter wants a different look.

That willingness to experiment underpins her broader decorating advice. A small room, she explained, can offer an opportunity to try something more adventurous without needing to rethink the entire home.

“The fun thing about a laundry room is that you really can play,” she said.

Martino pointed to laundry rooms and bathrooms, particularly powder rooms, as places where people can explore color and pattern.

Because those rooms are often enclosed, their design doesn't necessarily have to match every other space in the home.

“It's like a little jewel box within a home,” she explained.

Wallpaper is one way to create that effect, with both traditional and renter-friendly options allowing people to personalize a room.

Martino also encouraged people to give DIY projects a chance, even when the prospect seems a little intimidating.

For those who aren't ready to commit to an entire patterned wall or a room filled with one bold shade, she suggested starting smaller.

A colorful pillow, a lamp, or even a coffee-table book can introduce a brighter accent without requiring a major transformation.

Her own color preferences include reds, pinks, and oranges. Through her Tide collaboration, she is bringing that approach to a contest offering winners a laundry-space redesign incorporating Tide Orange, which she discussed in connection with the brand's Pantone partnership.

The shade could appear throughout a room or in smaller decorative touches, depending on the space.

That flexibility reflects Martino's emphasis on choosing a design that speaks to the person who lives there.

Still, her personal preference is clear: She gravitates toward warm, colorful rooms with plenty of personality. The popularity of white, gray, and beige interiors hasn't persuaded her to set aside her own taste.

“It's so easy to kind of go with the flow and just do what's trending or what's popular and stick with easy white things or gray and beige,” she said.

For Martino, introducing a bolder shade is also a way to take a more active role in shaping a home.

“But when you take that power back into your hands and you use a bold color, it can really affect your mood and the joy that you feel in your home.”

The Betsy Ross house: A home woven into the American story

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a fascinating glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding, Redfin writes.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

1892 Bishop’s Palace: A Remarkable Gilded Age Home

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children, Redfin writes. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Every detail of the “Broadway beauty” was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

#5669. Confused by Home Price Headlines? Here’s Why.

Whether you own a house already or you’re looking to buy one, you probably care about home prices. But it’s not always easy to figure out what’s really happening right now, especially if you look at the headlines.

One says home prices are falling. The next says they’re still climbing.

So, which one’s right? It comes down to where you live.

Part of the confusion out there may be based on what’s happening to asking prices and how the media is talking about it. They’re calling attention to how asking prices are falling, but don’t give the full context or say that seasonality is at play. So here it is.

Right now, there are more homes on the market than at any other time since November 2019. And with mortgage rates rising since the spring, those homes are taking a little longer to sell. One way to help a home sell quickly in that environment is to have a lower asking price.

According to HousingWire Data, the median asking price is down from $449k in early August to $435k just 2 months later (see graph below):

That’s a dip of about 3%, and a lot of it is normal for this time of year.

Asking prices cool off every fall once the busy summer season wraps up. With fewer buyers this time of year, sellers price a bit more competitively. Today’s rates play a role too, since sellers are pricing to match what buyers can afford right now. And that’s a good thing. Smart pricing helps homes sell.

Just keep in mind, that’s a national list price. It doesn’t show what homes near you are actually selling for. So before you react to a headline, ask a local agent what’s really happening in your area.

“While national headlines might suggest a buyer’s market is taking hold, the reality on the ground depends heavily on where and what you’re trying to buy. Local trends can diverge sharply from national averages, especially when you factor in price range, property type, and post-pandemic market dynamics.”

The latest numbers from S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index show how true that is. Over the past year, sales prices in Chicago rose almost 7%. In Seattle, they dipped about 1.6%. That’s a gap of nearly 9 percentage points between two major cities (see graph below):

That gap changes your game plan. Selling in New York, where prices are up almost 6%? You may not need to cut your price. Buying in Denver or Las Vegas? You may have more room to negotiate.

Just in case you’re seeing those slight declines in some markets and worried it means a bigger crash is coming, here’s what you need to remember. Even in the major metros where prices are down, the declines are 2% or less. That’s a long way from a crash like 2008. And if you look back at the graph above, there are more cities in the green than in the red.

And over time, home values have a strong track record. The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) says national prices have grown year-over-year every quarter since 2012. Go back further, and a $100k home bought in 1991 would be worth about $436k today, even with the 2008 crash factored in (see graph below):

So, this short-term dip probably won’t stick around. The small declines we’re seeing now are in markets that overheated during the pandemic. As a whole, the market is headed back to normal – and normal means prices should rise over time.

National headlines can’t tell you what your home is worth or how much room you have to negotiate. Local data can. If you’re thinking about buying or selling, connect with a local real estate agent to look at how prices are moving in your area, so you can set your price or make your offer with confidence.

#5668. The Hidden Housing Cost Pushing Millions of Homeowners Over Budget

A new roof can be just as essential to homeownership as a monthly mortgage payment. Yet only one of those expenses is factored in when determining whether an owner is housing cost-burdened.

Now, preliminary findings from Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies (JCHS), presented on Friday, suggest that the omission has been hiding a much larger affordability problem in plain sight.

Under conventional measures, 22.7 million homeowners, or 26%, spent more than 30% of their incomes on housing in 2023—the threshold for being considered cost-burdened.

But when researchers included spending on routine maintenance and major replacement projects, that figure jumped to 28.4 million—nearly 1 in 3 homeowners.

"It would be a surprise to many that nearly every measure of cost burdens that you see out in the wild, including those that we most often published, do not account for these expenditures," says Alexander Hermann, a senior research associate at JCHS and co-author of the analysis.

For some homeowners, even that expanded measure may underestimate the financial strain.

Much of the housing affordability debate has focused on home prices and recurring expenses such as property taxes and insurance—and for good reason.

Between 2019 and 2025, homeowners' property tax expenses rose 31%, while average monthly homeowners insurance premiums jumped 72%, according to ICE Mortgage Technology data cited by Harvard.

But spending on home maintenance has also surged, with considerably less attention.

Between 2019 and 2023, homeowners' collective spending on routine maintenance climbed 61%, from $65 billion to $105 billion, according to Harvard's Improving America's Housing 2025 report. Even after adjusting for inflation, spending increased 35%.

And in the American Housing Survey data underlying the new analysis, maintenance and replacement spending grew faster than other housing expenses, including taxes and insurance, Hermann says.

So why has it been missing from affordability calculations?

Part of the problem is the data itself. Most major housing surveys don't ask homeowners what they spend on repairs. And unlike mortgages or property taxes, maintenance costs are irregular. A homeowner might spend thousands replacing a roof one year and nothing the next, making it difficult to translate into a consistent measure of affordability.

Then there's an even larger complication: What homeowners spend doesn’t necessarily reflect what their properties need.

Unlike a mortgage or tax bill, a major repair can be postponed when money is tight. That means a homeowner might report little or no spending even as their house deteriorates.

"These expenses can be deferrable to a point, but you can't put them off indefinitely," Hermann explains.

To capture costs that actual spending might conceal, the researchers developed a second estimate based on what homeowners could be expected to spend on upkeep, using property characteristics and spending patterns among middle-income households.

Under that approach, 30.8 million homeowners, or 35.5%, would be considered cost-burdened—roughly 8 million more than conventional estimates suggest.

As the U.S. housing stock gets older, understanding the nuance between what owners are spending and what their homes actually need is poised to become more important than ever.

The median owner-occupied home was 42 years old in 2023, compared with just 27 years old three decades earlier, according to JCHS.

And that age is already catching up. More than 22% of owner-occupied homes built before 1960 had a structural deficiency in 2023—more than twice the rate for homes built since 2000.

But the households facing the greatest upkeep needs are often those least equipped to pay for them.

"Lower-income homeowners, for example, are more likely to live in homes that require greater upkeep in the first place, and these households are at the same time least likely to have the resources they need to address those repair needs,” Hermann explains.

That disparity is already evident in what homeowners spend.

Among owners of homes built before 1960, households in the highest income quintile spent an average of $12,700 on improvements and repairs in 2023, compared with just $3,400 among those in the lowest quintile.

Of course, that difference doesn't necessarily mean lower-income homes need less work. Instead, it may mean their owners simply cannot afford to do it.

And that distinction helps explain why Harvard's estimates of expected upkeep spending reveal a much wider affordability gap than conventional measures suggest.

Three-quarters of homeowners earning less than $30,000 annually already exceeded the traditional housing-cost threshold. When researchers accounted for modeled upkeep spending, that share reached a staggering 93%.

For those earning $30,000 to $45,000, the rate climbed from 43% to 64%.

Older homeowners also face a particularly difficult version of this affordability squeeze.

Among homeowners aged 65 and older, 32% were cost-burdened under conventional measures, compared with 45% when modeled upkeep costs were included.

Part of that can be attributed to the fact that retirement often brings lower incomes, even as aging homes require more expensive repairs. And while some homeowners can draw on savings or investments, others face a choice between preserving cash today and maintaining the value of their largest asset.

There’s already data that the trade-off can eventually work its way into the sale price of these homes.

An 80-year-old homeowner realizes an annualized return that's roughly half a percentage point lower than a 45-year-old homeowner, equivalent to a sale price that's more than 5% lower over the average 11-year holding period, according to research from the National Bureau of Economic Research.

Differences in renovations and property upkeep explained about a quarter of that age-related gap, while selling practices, including off-market transactions and sales to investors, also contributed.

The dilemma is gaining attention in Washington.

Earlier this month, a bipartisan group of lawmakers urged the Department of Housing and Urban Development to implement a new home-repair program, warning that some seniors cannot afford the updates needed to sell their homes without accepting steep discounts.

The Whole-Home Repairs pilot was authorized under the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, enacted in July, but federal funding has not yet been appropriated and the program has not been implemented.

Rachel Drew, director of Harvard's Remodeling Futures Program, argues that assistance should prioritize households with the greatest repair needs, ideally through grants rather than loans or tax benefits requiring upfront spending.

For homeowners who cannot afford to preserve their properties, repair assistance could protect both their housing and the wealth they have built.

As Hermann puts it, "All repair programs are affordability programs."

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5667. Home Price Growth Picks Up, But Inflation Still Wins in August

U.S. home prices continued to lose ground to inflation in August, even as nominal price growth accelerated slightly, according to the latest S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index.

The National Index posted a 2.1% annual gain in August, up from 1.9% in July. Consumer prices, meanwhile, increased 3.4% year over year, meaning inflation outpaced home price growth by roughly 1.3 percentage points. It marked the 15th consecutive month that U.S. home values declined in real terms.

The 10-City Composite recorded a 3.6% annual increase, up from 3.4% the previous month, while the 20-City Composite increased 2.7%, compared with 2.5% in July.

“U.S. home prices declined in real terms for the 15th consecutive month in August 2026, though the gap narrowed as nominal home price growth strengthened,” says Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices.

Regional differences remained pronounced. Chicago led the 20 markets for the sixth consecutive month, posting a 6.7% year-over-year gain, followed by New York at 6.2% and Cleveland at 4.3%.

At the opposite end, Seattle recorded the largest annual decline for the third consecutive month, falling 2%. Las Vegas prices declined 1.3%, while Denver prices fell 0.8%. The gap between Chicago and Seattle approached 9 percentage points, highlighting the continued geographic divergence in home-price performance.

On a month-over-month basis, prices softened before seasonal adjustment. The U.S. National Index declined 0.2%, while both the 10-City and 20-City composites fell 0.4%.

After seasonal adjustment, however, each index increased. The National Index rose 0.3%, the 10-City Composite increased 0.4%, and the 20-City Composite gained 0.3%.

“The divergence suggests that the typical post-summer slowdown is obscuring some underlying strength in home prices,” Kaufman says.

Despite that strength, affordability remains a significant hurdle for prospective buyers. Kaufman pointed to 3.4% inflation, Brent crude near $100 per barrel, and mortgage rates in the mid-to-high 6% range as factors keeping household costs elevated alongside persistently high home prices.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5666. To Sell or Rent? How To Choose the Best Path for Your House.

Selling your house is a big step, and you want it to go smoothly. And with houses taking a little longer to sell these days, renting it out might start to sound like a nice backup plan.

But the reality is, while renting can work well for some people, it’s also a big commitment. So before you decide, it helps to see the whole picture first.

Lately, some sellers are choosing to hang on to their houses and rent them out instead. According to Parcl, around 9% of homes for rent right now were previously up for sale.

Some homeowners put their houses on the market expecting a faster process than they got or a certain price buyers didn’t respond to. And when things didn’t go exactly as planned, they decided to rent instead. As Kara Ng, Senior Economist at Zillow, explains:

“Bargaining power is tilting toward buyers and homes are taking longer to sell, making renting out a property one way to buy time rather than compete aggressively on price.”

But here’s the important distinction. Just because some sellers are choosing to rent doesn’t mean selling isn’t working. In many cases, the difference comes down to how well a house is priced, prepared, and marketed for today’s buyers.

Parcl data shows where these “accidental landlords” – owners who planned to sell but decided to rent instead – are most common (see graph below):

They make up around 17% of homes for rent in places like Sherman and Houston, TX, but less than 4% in markets like Des Moines, IA and Bloomington, IN.

That’s a pretty big difference. And it shows why you have to know what’s happening in your neighborhood. Your market, your asking price, and your strategy all play a role in how your sale goes.

A local agent can show you how houses like yours are selling, what strategies work best, and help you weigh your options – not to push you to sell, but so you at least have the full picture based on today’s market. And part of making an informed decision is understanding what renting your house would actually take.

While renting might sound like easy passive income on paper, in practice, it’s a hands-on job with rules to follow. As Invest West Management puts it:

“Even if you never intended to become a landlord, the law still sees you as one — and you must meet all legal obligations that come with that role. This often includes registering the tenancy, providing tenants with certain disclosures, and ensuring the property meets safety standards.”

You’d also be the one chasing missed rent payments, fixing damage between tenants, and covering unexpected repairs. Not to mention fielding weekend calls about leaky dishwashers or broken AC units.

There are expenses beyond regular maintenance and repairs, too. According to Bankrate, these are a few of the biggest:

Insurance premiums (landlord insurance typically costs about 25% more than a standard homeowners policy)

Management fees (if you hire a property manager, they usually charge around 10% of the rent)

Gaps between tenants, when you pay the mortgage without rental income

If you want to be a landlord and you’re prepared for the responsibility, renting may be a great fit. But if you’d really rather sell, don’t let today’s market convince you that you can’t.

A great agent can make it happen. The key is having an open conversation up front with your agent about pricing and how to market your house. Nailing those details from day 1 helps your house make a great first impression, so renting doesn’t have to be your fallback.

Renting can be a good fit for the right person with the right house, but it isn’t the only option. A smart sales strategy can help your house stand out to buyers from day one.So, if you’re on the fence, a local real estate agent can help you compare what selling and renting would each look like for you.

#5665. What Rising Bond Yields Mean for Housing

The latest move in the bond market may look like a story for Wall Street, but its consequences extend directly to the housing industry. Long-term Treasury yields have risen sharply as investors demand greater compensation to hold government debt, reinforcing the possibility that elevated borrowing costs could remain part of the economic landscape.

Several forces are pushing yields higher. Inflation remains persistent while the economy continues to show resilience, raising questions about how quickly price pressures will normalize. At the same time, investors are paying closer attention to federal deficits and the growing supply of Treasury debt.

Artificial intelligence is adding another dimension. Massive investment in data centers and related infrastructure could support economic growth while also keeping inflationary pressures firmer than they otherwise would be. That expectation can feed into higher long-term bond yields.

For housing, the most immediate concern is mortgage rates.

Higher Treasury yields generally put upward pressure on mortgage rates, creating another obstacle for prospective buyers already struggling with affordability. There is some relief from the mortgage spread, or the difference between the 10-year Treasury yield and the 30-year fixed mortgage rate. That spread, which historically averages about 1.7 percentage points, widened beyond 3 percentage points during the pandemic but has since narrowed to roughly 2.3 points. If the spread were still above 3 percentage points, mortgage rates would be closer to 8.3% rather than 7.6%.

For businesses, elevated rates translate into higher borrowing costs and interest expenses at a time when operating costs are already challenging. Consumer confidence could become even more sensitive as households react to negative economic headlines.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

Ali Wolf is the chief economist for Zonda and NewHomeSource. As head of the economics department, Wolf manages and analyzes the content, runs special research projects, strategizes with the nation’s largest home builders, and presents nationwide covering topics across the housing market and wider economy.

#5664. ‘In Over Their Heads’: Red Flags Before the Sudden Collapse of ‘Perpetual Cruise’ That Left Residents Stranded

Kit Cassingham credits her yoga practice and her experience as a life coach with keeping her sane these days.

And Cassingham has a lot of reasons to feel crazy: Earlier this week, she and her husband Randy were told to permanently disembark from the Villa Vie Residences Odyssey cruise ship they’d been living on for the last two years.

The Cassinghams, along with around 200 or so fellow passengers, were told that the Villa Vie Odyssey had run out money and could no longer afford fuel, so passengers would need to collect their belongings and find another place to live.

Their odyssey with the Odyssey started more than two years ago, when Cassingham and her husband decided to sell the dream home they had built in Colorado.

“Randy realized he was allergic to Colorado,” Cassingham told Realtor.com. “He was allergic to four-legged animals, mold, dust, grasses, weeds, pinyon and juniper trees. And we lived in a pinyon-juniper forest. His allergies got worse and worse, and even his allergists couldn't stay on top of it.”

So, the couple decided a never-ending cruise was the one place where Randy might be safe from the scourge of grass and tree allergies.

The Cassinghams initially put a deposit down with Victoria Cruises before realizing that the company didn’t actually own a ship (and still doesn’t, though it continues to sell cabins).

By then, they had already sold their home and taken off on a pre-cruise road trip to say farewell to friends. So they then began looking for other options.

Enter Villa Vie Residence’s Odyssey, where passengers were promised the opportunity to cruise for the rest of their lives, if they wanted.

The Cassinghams purchased a cabin with a balcony on the Odyssey’s 7th floor deck, for $369,000. Monthly charges, which covered housekeeping, laundry, fuel, and three meals a day, were $8,000, though the couple purchased stock in the company, which gave them “founder” status and knocked their monthly fees down to $6,000.

From the start, things were a bit rocky. The Odyssey was supposed to leave in May 2024, but mechanical problems kept the ship docked in Belfast until October 2024.

That's when she says she began noticing that the Villa Vie’s owners were in over their heads.

“We were we're gonna go up to Amazon, and it turns out our boat was too big,” she says. “And they just weren't paying attention to some details.”

Cassingham believes delays leaving Belfast put the company on the backfoot.

“Because we were in Belfast so long, they spent a lot more money on the problems. Every time they would fix one thing, two other problems would come up. So they went into deep debt in Belfast.”

And then when the Iran War broke out in February and the Strait of Hormuz closed, “our fuel bills doubled and then tripled. Yeah. And so if you already are spending more than you're making, having it double and triple was insane. They did ask several times for us to pay fuel charges.”

Through it all, Cassingham says, “the mood on the ship stayed strong because we were all doing what we loved and wanted to do.”

The ship got to the Philippines days after a deadly typhoon hit the country, and the passengers held a fundraiser and contributed to care packages for victims.

“We're doing this kind of community stuff, and have no problem raising money for that. We just got tired of raising money for stuff we thought we were already paying for.”

Things took a turn, though, when the ship hit Thailand, and Petterson told passengers that he wouldn’t leave the country until he had secured an investor.

“Next thing we know, he's pulling up the stakes, and off we go to Cambodia where there's no Starlink, the cell service is bad, and the fuel is expensive.”

According to Villa Vie’s estimates, per-cabin fuel expenses rose from $1,800 to between $6,000 and $8,000 per month, putting “its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure.”

“Since the conflict [in Iran] began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company’s statement continued. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.”

In an interview with Business Insider on Wednesday, Villa Vie Residences founder Mikael Petterson called himself “the villain in the story.”

“Nobody that’s tried residential cruising has succeeded, and we have gone further than anyone else,” he said. “I think we would have been absolutely fine and we would have seen this through, if there was no Iran war.”

In retrospect, Cassingham says there were a raft of red flags.

“I personally had red flags because when we would talk to Mikael, he could never look into the camera. His eyes were always shifting back and forth and mysterious—off into space.”

“Another red flag for me was the revolving door on their employees. Other red flags were invoices... Our monthly invoices were never correct. We always triple checked them if we could get them. Because they were using, it turns out, a spreadsheet to manage the company. Now I'm no bookkeeper, but I know a spreadsheet's not what you use to manage a large business.”

Cassingham says she and her husband have no plans to come back to the U.S. at this point, especially since Randy is in the middle of treatment for prostate cancer. They want to see what happens with the ship, and Randy has further cancer tests in Thailand in December.

A group of passengers has formed an LLC and is looking into how they can possibly get the ship back into operating order. But for now, Cassingham thinks things won’t be resolved for at least another 60 to 90 days.

Still, Cassingham seems sanguine about her current predicament. The yoga and meditation helps, as does her work as a transformation life coach.

“When the pioneers headed West from the East Coast, they didn't know what was ahead of them,” she says. “You make it or you don't.”Realtor.com has reached out to Villa Vie Residences for comment.

#5663. Turning Trash Into Treasure: The Ups and Downs of a Miami Home Flipper’s 12-Year Career

For real estate investors and home flippers, one thing is key for remaining successful in a turbulent market: patience.

At least, that’s what South Florida investor, house flipper, and licensed real estate agent Branden Rivero thinks.

Rivero founded his company, Prop Hunters, in 2014. The Miami-Dade-based company has completed hundreds of flips, in addition to building and selling single-family homes.

“I started out just wholesaling, getting affordable properties and assigning the contracts until I was able to build some capital,” Rivero tells Realtor.com®. “I started flipping just one or two houses, and now we usually do about seven to 10 at a time.”

Prop Hunters flipped 25 homes last year, according to Rivero, but they’ve completed between 30 and 40 homes some years. This year’s gross profit is around $200,000 so far, accounting for both flips and new homes.

In his 12 years in business, Rivero has learned to go with the flow of the sometimes volatile Florida real estate market. Looking ahead 90 days to six months is a vital part of being prepared for anything.

“Everything is based on the market. Sometimes you can go full throttle when things are good,” says Rivero. “Then, once you see more turbulent times coming, you become more cautious, you underwrite a little more aggressive—you kind of have to play it by ear.”

Although Miami’s current market feels slow to some, Rivero is optimistic, saying that the real estate market is simply returning to the pre-pandemic norms.

“People are just used to the COVID rush, but I feel like it’s normal, just how it was in 2017, 2018, and 2019. Homes are taking a month, month and a half to sell,” he notes. “Between 2020 and 2024, a house wouldn’t last a week on the market. So, compared to that, it’s a big difference, but I just feel like it’s back to normal.”

In 2018, the median number of days on the market was 63, according to the Realtor.com March 2018 Monthly Housing Trends Report. As of the week ending Oct. 24, 2026, the median days on the market nationally was 64.

Miami comes in slightly slower, at a median of 83 days on the market as of October 2026. That number has decreased from both last month and last year, pushing the number toward the national norm.

These numbers are vastly different from the post-pandemic boom, when, in 2021, the typical home spent just 32 days on the market nationally.

A Realtor.com international report from June 2018 places Miami’s median listing price at $395,000, in line with October 2026’s national median listing price of $414,000. Again, Miami itself comes in a bit higher in 2026 numbers, with the median listing price sitting at $620,000.

One major difference between 2018 and 2026: mortgage rates. In 2018, the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 4.7%. This week, the average 30-year mortgage rate is 7.2%.

While many aspects of the market are settling closer to pre-pandemic levels, mortgage rates are responsible for a major shift in affordability.

This is why Rivero has spent so much time getting to know the market and practicing patience.

He notes that, for new single-family homes, the permitting process is very slow. However, not many Miami developers are building single-family homes, so the wait is worth the payoff.

“In Miami, everything that’s getting built is townhouses and condos. So when you put a good product out there, a single-family home in a great neighborhood with great schools, it’s going to move,” Rivero says. “Patience is the key thing. I’d rather do one or two deals a year than jump into five, 10 bad ones.”

With over a decade under his belt, Rivero gets to focus on what he considers the most fulfilling aspect of working in real estate: seeing a home transform and become the perfect place for a family.

“To turn what most people see as trash into somewhat of a treasure, someone’s American dream where they’re going to raise their kids, is very satisfying,” says Rivero.

#5662. Why More Buyers Are Turning To Adjustable-Rate Mortgages Today

When mortgage rates climb, buying a home can start to feel like trying to hit a moving target. Every jump in rates makes monthly payments bigger, and that pushes a lot of buyers to look for another way in.

More and more of them are finding it in the adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM.

Here’s how an ARM differs from a more traditional mortgage. With a regular fixed-rate mortgage, your rate stays the same for your whole loan. But with an ARM, your rate is locked for the first few years, then it can move up or down based on market conditions.

Some people don’t like that level of uncertainty – and that’s okay. But others are drawn to this option specifically because there’s usually a lower rate to start when you opt for an ARM. And in an affordability-strapped market, that’s going to gain popularity.

Bankrate recently found that, in September, rates for ARM products were over a full percentage point lower than a regular fixed-rate loan. Depending on the ARM product, that can make a difference of $150-300 in the monthly payment on a median-priced home.

And for some buyers, that’s enough to turn “not right now” into “let’s do this.” You can see it in the numbers. Data from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) shows that, in October, roughly 1 in 10 people applying for a mortgage chose an ARM (see graph below):

If you think you may want to consider this yourself, here’s what you need to know about how it works.

An ARM is like a phone or cable plan that has an introductory deal for new customers. You start out at a lower price, and then it adjusts after a specified amount of time. A popular loan is the 5/1 ARM.

The “5” means your introductory rate is locked for the first five years, and the “1” means that the rate can change every year after that. The rate change is called the “reset.” And here’s the really important part.

When your rate resets, your mortgage payment could go up or down. The good news is that most ARMs have caps, which are limits on how much your rate can rise each year and over the life of the loan. But either way, you have to be ready.

To see if this type of loan may be right for you, here are some things to think about and discuss with your loan officer:

Before you decide, ask your lender to work up the numbers and walk you through the different potential scenarios you could run into with an ARM. That way, you go in with your eyes open.

And, if you do go with an adjustable-rate mortgage, just know that you’ll have choices when the reset time arrives. You could:

Do nothing and keep your loan in place if the new payment still fits your budget.

Refinance into a fixed-rate loan with a payment that never changes.

Refinance into another ARM with a new lower rate locked for a specified timeframe.

Talk to the loan servicer about assistance or modification.

Remember, a refinance is a brand-new loan that you’ll have to qualify for – even if it’s on a home you already own. So, keep tabs on your credit and debt levels and ask your loan officer how major financial moves like job changes and major purchases will affect your mortgage readiness. It’s important to keep your credit and finances in “mortgage shape.”

One more quick note. ARMs got a bad name after the financial crisis of 2008. Back then, there were some risky loans with small starting payments that later shot way up. Others let people borrow without proving how much money they earned.

But now, there are new laws to protect both borrowers and lenders. The biggest change is the Ability-to-Repay Rule, which says that before a lender makes a home loan, it has to check real paperwork (like pay stubs, W-2 forms, and tax returns) to make sure you can afford it. The lender also has to look at what your payment could be after the reset, not just the low starting payment.

So, you don’t have to worry that today’s ARMs are the same as the ones we saw back during the crash.

Today's market has more options than many people realize. Finding the right one could be as simple as getting more information about tools like ARMs. A trusted lender can run the numbers with you, walk you through the what-ifs, and help you explore the possibilities.Is an ARM a good option for you? Talk to a loan officer to find out.

#5661. New-Home Front Porches Show Spooktacular Style This Halloween

Two trends are converging at an opportune time for new-build homeowners: the revival of front porches in home design and the hottest Halloween decorating trends that are centered, quite literally, on the front porch.

In new-home design, front porches are making a comeback alongside the growth of walkable neighborhoods and homeowners’ desire for community connection. Also, homes and yards are getting smaller, so homeowners are relying more heavily on outdoor spaces, like the front porch, to extend living space without increasing square footage.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), porches rank as the most popular outdoor feature on new homes.

Meanwhile, Halloween is big business, and homeowners are getting serious about decorating. Over a third of consumers say Halloween is their favorite holiday, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual Halloween consumer shopping survey. They report that consumer spending on Halloween is expected to reach $13.5 billion in 2026.

Halloween decor used to be somewhat limited to front door wreaths, a jack-o’-lantern or two, or for more ambitious homeowners who had the space, lawn decorations and even some special effects. But the availability, square footage, and design of today’s front porch are offering new opportunities for homeowners who are Halloween fans too.

Sheltered from the elements, the front porch has enough space for decorative vignettes, wide front steps that encourage traffic flow, room to gather with neighbors and trick-or-treaters, and electrical outlets that make lighting and special effects easy.

Want to style your porch, but don’t have time to scour your local pumpkin patch, or are unsure of how to curate the bespoke pumpkin-inspired designs that are everywhere on social media?

Style support is available, very possibly in your neighborhood. The growing popularity of front porch decor has given rise to a niche industry: pumpkin concierges, a reportedly in-demand service in several regions of the country.

For a fee, pumpkin concierges work with local farmers to source pumpkins, then arrange elaborate, coordinated displays with seasonal greenery and other decorative accents, and some companies even return to remove everything at the end of the season.

The growing popularity of these services underscores how much attention homeowners are paying to their front porches, particularly during the holidays, and how intricate some of the seasonal designs are becoming, not only for the pros, but for DIY homeowners too.

Want to conjure Halloween magic on your front porch this holiday? Here are the spooky and stylish trends to watch.

Today’s front porches are intended to be additional living space, so homeowners are embracing many of the same design elements outside that they are inside, including layering materials and colors cohesively.

Rather than relying on a traditional orange-and-black color scheme, homeowners are using harvest-inspired curated palettes with sage, marigolds, and creams, or plums, deeper greens, and muted oranges for Halloween style.

Instead of one-off pieces of Halloween decor, Halloween front porches are being layered with textiles and accents that complement the existing porch furniture, like themed doormats, patterned pillows and throws, and seasonal candles.

Although Witchcore, a micro-aesthetic inspired by witchcraft, folklore, mysticism, and nature, isn’t specific to Halloween, several elements of this look are perfect for the holiday and for your front porch.

Assemble decor using twisted branches, wildflowers, and leaves, along with weathered and slightly spooky accents, like vintage books, lanterns, and apothecary bottles, that may or may not contain magic potions. Broomsticks, black cats, ravens, and cauldrons are nice Witchcore-inspired touches too.

Moody, atmospheric haunted gardens are taking over front porches this Halloween, drawing on Gothic and Victorian influences for a hauntingly romantic look.

Think oversized planters with dark, spiky foliage, weathered urns, brass, dried flowers, and twisty, “creeping” vines. Cluster pumpkins of various sizes, and strategically place cobwebs for a hauntingly romantic look. Consider uplighting to create shadows, or weave twinkle lights through the porch, for an ethereal feel.

Design in general is leaning more heavily into the experiential, and Halloween, for its spine-tingling fun and jump scares, aligns perfectly with decor curated to assemble an emotional response, fun or fright, depending on your spooky goals.

​Consider your front porch a mini-stage for a theatrical, immersive trick-or-treat experience, with a defined, enclosed space for a backdrop, as well as easy access to electrical outlets for special effects.

Popular are fog machines, flickering lights, motion-activated skeletons, creepy soundtracks, and animatronic figures that spring to life as trick-or-treaters approach, if they dare. Make use of architectural elements, like porch columns, to enhance the decor, with wrapped cobwebs or tattered materials.

This article was originally published on NewHomeSource.com.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.
