#5629. Earnings Roundup: Higher Rates Test Green Brick, Meritage, and Dream Finders

The challenging housing environment remained front and center as Green Brick Partners, Meritage Homes, and Dream Finders Homes reported third-quarter results.

Rising mortgage rates and affordability constraints continued to pressure consumer sentiment and margins. Green Brick Partners grew orders and deliveries despite the difficult backdrop, while Meritage Homes prioritized margins over a higher sales pace. Dream Finders Homes achieved record third-quarter closings while absorbing costs associated with its acquisition of Beazer Homes.

“Despite continued affordability pressures, broader economic uncertainty, and an increasing rate environment, demand across our markets remained resilient as buyers responded to our incentive strategy and attractive product offerings, particularly within Trophy Signature Homes. We continue to respond to deteriorating market conditions to maintain sales pace.”— Jim Brickman, co-CEO and co-founder, Green Brick Partners

“In the third quarter of 2026, we navigated an increasingly challenging home buying environment marked by rising mortgage interest rates and persistent geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty. Constrained affordability weighed on consumer sentiment, which was reflected in our 15% year-over-year decline in third quarter orders despite achieving an average absorption pace of 3.0 net sales per month per store.”— Steven J. Hilton, executive chairman, Meritage Homes

“Buyers faced a challenging summer, as rising mortgage rates further strained affordability and weighed on consumer confidence. I’m proud of how our team navigated these market conditions. We closed 1,967 homes in the quarter, a third-quarter record, and 6,127 homes year-to-date, also a record, while net sales increased 6% compared with the prior year.”— Patrick Zalupski, founder, co-chairman and CEO, Dream Finders Homes

Since quarter-end, Dream Finders Homes completed its approximately $2.2 billion acquisition of Beazer Homes. Zalupski said the company expects additional nonrecurring transaction and integration costs during the fourth quarter as it works toward $100 million in targeted cost savings from the combination. The company reiterated its full-year 2026 guidance of approximately 9,250 home closings.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5628. Inside a Marvel Showrunner’s $2.4 Million Topanga Compound Featuring a 1970s Geodesic Dome and Private Oak Grove

A tree-lined retreat nestled beneath a “canopy of magnificent mature oaks,” featuring illuminated pathways, has recently hit the market in Topanga, CA, for $2.4 million.

Built in 1935, the “thoughtfully cared for” 1,547-square-foot sanctuary boasts stone pathways, footbridges, and a seasonal creek. It is located in the Post Office Tract near Topanga State Park.

“What makes this property so special is its setting within a private oak grove,” says listing agent Nina Kurtz of Compass. “It genuinely feels like having your own private park.”

That private-park feel extends across the compound, which includes a two-bedroom primary residence and additional living space.

According to public records, the four-bedroom property is currently owned by Hollywood writer and producer Andrew Guest, co-creator, showrunner, and executive producer of Marvel’s "Wonder Man." Guest purchased the property for $2.75 million in 2022.

Expansive windows were designed to frame the lushly landscaped lot and bring the outdoors into the living spaces.

“Properties like this rarely come along,” Kurtz notes. “The opportunity to have an entire compound nestled beneath these majestic oaks, yet still so close to Los Angeles, is pretty magical.”

A light-filled interior in the two-bedroom primary residence boasts exposed beams, vaulted ceilings, hardwood floors, casement windows, and French doors.

The sun-soaked kitchen has direct access to the outdoor living area. A primary bedroom is surrounded by tree-lined scenery.

Also found on the nearly 1-acre private property are a one-bedroom cottage, a barn, and a 1970s geodesic dome, which was transformed into a contemporary art gallery in 2024.

The dome structure has geometric-style windows, an additional kitchen, and expansive space that could be used as additional guest accommodations. An enormous wraparound deck was designed for soaking in the peaceful views.

“You’re right next to Topanga State Park, with incredible access to hiking trails, sweeping ocean views, and spectacular sunsets,” Kurtz adds.

“Yet once you’re on the property, you feel completely tucked away from the outside world, as though you’ve entered a little universe of your own. And when the sun goes down and the twinkle lights come on beneath the oak canopy, the entire place transforms. It almost feels like a portal to another world.”

Kellie Speed is a contributor to Realtor.com. As a writer and editor, she has worked for a variety of online and print publications, including Inked magazine, Jetset, Westchester magazine, JustLuxe, The Boston Globe, and U.S. Veterans Magazine. A Massachusetts native, Kellie attended Northeastern University for journalism, was previously the Boston editor for Haute Living, and contributed to Avalon Publishing's Moon Metro Boston guidebook. Kellie writes celebrity profiles and covers restaurants, travel, and lifestyle.

#5627. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5625. Housing Week Ahead: Monthly Trends Data, Mortgage Rates, and Jobs Report

With all eyes on Election Day, this marks a relatively light week for new Realtor.com economics research reports and housing market indicators.

On Wednesday, I'll be issuing our October monthly housing trends report, taking a look at whether elevated mortgage rates caused buyers or sellers to pull back more, as well as what happened to inventory, asking prices, and contract signings.

The September snapshot showed a housing market softening under the weight of rising mortgage rates. Median list prices fell, while inventory and price cuts rose. I expect more of the same from the October data, after mortgage rates hit their highest levels since 2023.

On Thursday, senior economist Joel Berner will issue our Realtor.com weekly listing data update. As well, senior economist Hannah Jones will have commentary on Freddie Mac's latest mortgage rate reading on Thursday.

It’s too early to call the direction of rates this week. But I’ll be watching the bond market, especially the 10-year Treasury yield, for any reaction to the midterms, new developments in the Middle East, and any Fed signals about a December hike.

Rates matter locally, too. For buyers in Phoenix; Tucson, AZ; Raleigh, NC; Charlotte, NC; and Louisville, KY, Nov. 1–7 is your best time to buy. If rates ease for a third week in a row, buyers there and elsewhere could have more purchasing power than a month ago, more homes to choose from than a year ago, and fewer buyers to compete with. That’s a winning combination heading into the slow season.

One final indicator: I’ll be up bright and early on Friday morning to track the latest labor market data, which covers October unemployment and job growth.

September's jobs report was disappointing but not a disaster, adding just 29,000 jobs while unemployment rose to 4.2%. We expect the low-hire, low-fire labor market to continue, which keeps the Federal Reserve focused on inflation ahead of its December meeting.

Jake Krimmel is a senior economist at Realtor.com.

#5624. Great Spaces: A Private Modern Compound in Paradise Valley

For buyers looking for high-end Arizona luxury living, 6232 E Bret Hills Drive combines mid-century modern design, resort-caliber wellness and private compound living on a 1.1-acre estate in Paradise Valley. Built by Nick Hammond of Diamond West Construction, this newly constructed 8,487-square-foot, single-level contemporary residence was engineered as a self-contained sanctuary. Framed by mountain views and the open desert sky, this Great Space brings residence, retreat and entertainment together across an open-concept footprint.

The $15.75 million estate pairs vast indoor-outdoor living areas with dedicated lifestyle spaces. Inside, six bedrooms and eight bathrooms are anchored by expansive glass walls, a bonus game room and a state-of-the-art wellness center. Outside, a private pool and spa are complemented by a detached guest house and an attached casita, giving family and visitors total independence. For the car enthusiast, a five-car climate-controlled garage features a dedicated show garage and private lounge. Representing the wave of high-end new construction entering the market this fall buying season, this home is move-in ready for buyers seeking modern design without compromise.

RISMedia spoke with listing agent Jill Brenenstuhl of RETSY and the founder of PV Luxury Real Estate Group to explore the architectural vision behind the estate, its custom amenities and how this Great Space reflects shifting buyer demands in the Paradise Valley market.

Paige Brown: What makes this a Great Space? Jill Brenenstuhl: This property is a Great Space because of the attention to detail and natural artistry throughout. Thoughtfully curated architecture, natural materials, rich textures and distinctive finishes create a sense of artistry without ever feeling cold or overly formal. Each window offers a curated view, whether it’s the beautifully highlighted Joshua Tree in the foyer or the artful way the mountain is framed from the primary bedroom. There are thoughtful vignettes throughout the home that make this space feel as much organic art museum as home, but with the warmth available from both spheres.

PB: Designed and built by Nick Hammond of Diamond West Construction, this contemporary estate blends mid-century modern architecture with clean, single-level living. How does this home’s scale and structure capture the signature modern desert aesthetic that buyers are looking for? JB: This home represents a warmer, more contemporary take on the traditional modern architecture many have become accustomed to seeing. Subtle yet elegant earth tones have been blended throughout to bring the warmth of the desert into the space. By bringing the texture of the exterior stone into the interior, it seamlessly integrates the indoor-outdoor livability of the home while adding interest. The scale and structure of the property is what today’s modern luxury buyer is looking for, where the main entertaining spaces are more expansive and open, but the private spaces are more cozy and intimate. Every space feels curated, inviting and deeply personal. This is a home designed to be admired, but even more importantly, lived in.

PB: As luxury living shifts from basic home gyms to holistic wellness spaces, what specific design elements and amenities were built into this estate’s custom wellness center to create an elevated, resort-level retreat at home? JB: In this modern market, a savvy luxury buyer expects so much more than just a basic home gym. Buyers of this caliber value not having to leave home to experience resort-style amenities. The crown jewel of our wellness center is the spacious sauna, which was created by hand by a local artisan as opposed to a prefabricated sauna like many new homes at this level incorporate. The wellness center also has an integrated sound system and a state-of-the-art cold plunge to assist with muscle recovery and general well-being. Complete with a private shower, this one-of-a-kind wellness center is the ultimate in home recovery.

Paige Brown is the managing editor, blog/social media for RISMedia.
